# Tears of a Father

**by Michael Banks**

## Dedication

*For Theresa Banks,*

*my beloved wife, whose beautiful soul shone brightly through twenty-one years of fighting breast cancer with faith, courage, and grace. She went home to be with the Lord on March 9, 2020.*

*Until I see you again.*

> *Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies... Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all. Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.* — Proverbs 31:10, 29–30

> *Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father.* — Jesus, Matthew 13:43

A novel in nine acts. Opens on the morning of the Rapture, then goes back two years to the dinner table on the night the call began.

## Prologue: The Trumpet

> *And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.* — Genesis 5:24

**Word study: *walked* — הָלַךְ** Hebrew *halak* (Strong's H1980). To walk, to go, to keep going. Here it is in a form that means to walk about continually, as a way of life. Enoch did not take one walk with God. He lived walking with Him, day after day, until God took him home.

Long before the flood, a man named Enoch walked out past his fields with God and never walked back. His son searched until dark. The sandal prints ran down the path and ended, the last one pressed deep, the dirt beyond it smooth. He *was not found, because God had translated him: for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.* (Hebrews 11:5)

\* \* \*

The sound came first.

Everyone in Washington heard it. Ezra Patterson, a widowed carpenter and the father of two, slept through all of it.

He would hear it described a thousand times in the weeks that followed, by people whose hands still shook when they told it.

It began with light: one white flash, lightning with no storm behind it, that threw every window in the city into noon for the length of a heartbeat. Then the sound came down.

It was thunder and trumpet together, a single colossal crack that fell out of the sky from every direction at once and hit the city like a wall, a sonic boom with a horn's voice inside it. Glass burst in its frames up and down every street. Storefronts came down in sheets. Windshields went white. The kitchen window over Ezra's sink split from corner to corner. Car alarms screamed by the thousand, and the shards were still falling when the sound came back across the rooftops a second time, and a third.

Behind it came the wind. It had no direction. It came down the avenues and up the alleys at the same time, tore the last leaves off the trees in one breath, flipped trash cans, peeled tin off a church roof on Rhode Island Avenue and sailed it over three houses. On the Potomac the water stood up in the channel, gray and white, and ran backward against the tide, and the river roared under the bridges like something alive.

Grown men dropped to their knees on the sidewalk. Some of them did not get up. A bus driver on Georgia Avenue pulled to the curb and slumped over the wheel, and two of his passengers went down with him, and their hearts had simply stopped. People who heard it said the same thing afterward, in every language on earth: it was the most terrible sound they had ever heard, and it sounded like it was calling someone.

Ezra slept. He had fallen asleep with a drink in him, the way his father used to, and the dead sleep of it held through all of it.

He was on the couch, still in yesterday's work jeans, one boot on. The television was murmuring to itself. He had been dreaming the red dream again: the red room, the red moon, the whole sky the color of blood. What woke him in the end was the silence that followed, and he came up out of the dream with his shirt stuck to his back. It smelled of the bar: stale beer, chicken wings and onion rings. Under that, faint, a perfume that wasn't Angela's. He lay there hating the man who had worn that shirt. In the half second between sleeping and waking he thought, *It's the dream again. The red room.*

But the room wasn't red. It was dark.

Beyond the front window the sky was black, the streetlights burning along the rooftops, with no trace of morning in it anywhere. Only the dream, then. Relief ran through him, warm and brief.

Then he heard what was under the quiet. Car alarms, dozens of them, all over Brookland, thin and far off and endless. A siren that climbed and did not come down. Cold air was moving across the floor from the kitchen, where it had no business coming from. The furnace was silent. The television had gone to a soft gray hiss.

He sat up. His late father's watch said 3:17. It had stopped at 3:17 more than thirty years ago.

"Jalen?"

Nothing.

He took the stairs two at a time. His eighteen-year-old son's door was open, and that was the first wrong thing; Jalen slept with the door shut and a towel pushed along the bottom so his father wouldn't hear him playing recordings at two in the morning. He had come home from his dorm downtown earlier that week for the Thanksgiving holiday. The bed was unmade, the sheet still holding the long shape of him. The cello leaned against the wall by the window, its bow laid across the seat of the chair, rosin dust pale on the strings. It was the cello he had played every night in the studio they had built together, back before Angela got sick. On the pillow, Jalen's phone was ringing with an alarm that no one was there to silence.

"Jalen. This isn't funny."

He crossed the hall to the room of his six-year-old daughter, Mia. Her nightlight was still on, throwing paper stars across the ceiling. Her nightgown, the yellow one with the moons, lay in the bed in the shape of a small sleeping girl, the blanket still tucked neatly around nothing. On the pillow lay her birthday book, *The Kingdom of Little Things: Captain Crumb and the Tangled Web*, open face down where Jalen had stopped reading.

He touched it. It was warm. And the small hope he had been holding, that it had only been the dream, went out of him all at once.

He called her name, then called it louder, his voice cracking. He checked the closet, under the bed, the bathroom, the attic stairs, the garage. He ran out into the backyard barefoot on one side and booted on the other, and stood on the cold grass shouting his children's names into a sky still black.

Across the fence, Mrs. Okafor, his next-door neighbor of fourteen years, was screaming too. Not words. Just one long sound.

When she saw him, she grabbed the top of the fence with both hands. "You heard it," she said. "Tell me you heard it. Ezra. The horn."

"What horn?"

She stared at him. Then she began to cry, and she could not stop.

At the corner, a car had drifted into a lamppost and stopped, its engine still running, its driver's door hanging open. No one was inside. A coffee cup sat in the holder, still steaming.

Then he heard the plane.

It came in low from the south, too low and too fast, its engines making a sound engines should never make. He watched it drop below the treetops toward the river. He felt the impact through the soles of his feet a full second before he heard it.

His hands were shaking so badly he dropped the phone twice. He called his mother. It rang and rang. He called Mia's school, though it was hours before anyone would be there, and got a recording. He called nine-one-one and got a busy signal, which he had not known nine-one-one could give.

Then his thumb found her name.

Kambria. Angela's best friend. The scientist with the notebooks. The woman who had stood on his porch a week ago, crying, begging him to open a book he had shoved in the hall closet. The woman he had told to get off his property.

It rang four times. Then her voice, warm and steady, recorded only days ago:

*"Hi, you've reached Kambria. If you're hearing this and I don't call you back, it already happened. Don't be afraid. It's not too late. Read Joel 2:32. Call on the name of the Lord."*

He hung up. He could still see her face on his porch, wet with tears, as he shut the door on her.

He went back into the kitchen, glass grinding under his one boot. The refrigerator hummed. On its door, under a magnet shaped like a cello, was Mia's last drawing.

Crayon. Their house, with its crooked porch light. Above it, a night sky colored black from edge to edge, and in the middle of all that black, a moon. Huge. Round. Colored red, scrubbed in so hard the paper had pilled.

A blood moon.

She had drawn it a week ago and stuck it there herself, standing on a chair. He had walked past it every day since without once looking.

Ezra Patterson slid down the refrigerator to the kitchen floor and sobbed. Then he screamed it at the ceiling, at the roof, at whatever was above the roof.

"Where are they? Where are my kids? You took her. Now You took them. What do You want from me? Answer me! Answer me!"

He did not know yet that God was listening.

The answer had been sitting in his hall closet for a year, in his dead wife's handwriting.

It had started long before that, at a dinner table.

## Act 1 — Two Lives

## Chapter 1: The Dinner Table

> *By faith Noah, being warned of God of things not seen as yet, moved with fear, prepared an ark to the saving of his house.* — Hebrews 11:7

**Word study: *warned of God* — χρηματίζω** Greek *chrēmatizō* (Strong's G5537). To give a divine answer, to be instructed by God. The word was used for an official reply from a king or a court. Noah's warning was not a hunch or a feeling. It was a word from the throne.

On summer evenings the neighbors brought their wine out to the hill to watch the old man work. Gopher-wood beams as long as a street. Pitch boiling in pots. His sons hauling timber while the town's young men called up to them, laughing. "When's the rain coming, Noah?" Nobody on that hill had ever seen the kind of rain he was building for. Noah wiped his forehead, picked up his hammer, and went back to work. A hundred and twenty years is a long time to be laughed at. (Genesis 6:3, 14–22)

\* \* \*


*Long before the trumpet.*

Ezra Patterson grew up in Cedar Hollow, Maryland, twenty minutes past the District line, where the county road gives up and turns to gravel.

There was no stoplight. There was a general store with one gas pump that quit in 1986 and was never fixed. The movie theater was forty minutes north, and they never went. Eggs came from the coop behind the house on Old Ferry Road. If you wanted a toy, you built it: a go-cart from a lawnmower engine and a pallet, a raft from oil drums, a tree fort with a trapdoor and a rope. They didn't have much money. By the time Ezra was ten he could frame a doorway plumb with a bob he made himself from a creek stone and a length of twine.

Calvin Patterson threw switches at the rail yard in Hollis Junction six days a week. On the seventh he wore a gray suit to Pilgrim Rest and stood at the deacons' table with one hand on the offering plate. He shook every hand in the vestibule. He knew the names of everybody's grandchildren. When it rained he carried old Mrs. Tolliver's casserole dish out to her car, and the church women told his mother, Loretta, she was a blessed woman.

At home he took the suit off and hung it on the back of the bedroom door, and the house went quiet. Supper was at six, and nobody talked. When his boots hit the hall floor, the television went off. After Loretta went to bed, the bottle came down from the cabinet over the refrigerator, and some nights it never went back up. Nobody at Pilgrim Rest ever saw the hole in the hallway wall, because Loretta hung a calendar over it.

Ezra learned two things in that house. He learned that God was a voice a man used in public. And he learned to sit very still, so the voice wouldn't find him.

His mother kept going to Pilgrim Rest after his father was gone. Ezra stopped the day he was old enough to drive himself somewhere else.

At eighteen he caught a ride into the city with a framing crew and didn't go back. He was good. He was fast and careful and didn't talk much, and foremen liked all three. Elijah Brooks, from the next house down Old Ferry Road, the loudest boy in Cedar Hollow, followed him in a year later and couldn't hang a door straight if you held the level for him. Ezra got him hired anyway. They had been friends since the worst night of Ezra's life, when he was eight years old.

\* \* \*

He met Michelle at twenty-three, on a job in Silver Spring where she was the one telling the contractors they were behind. She came from a town like his, with one gas pump and a church at the crossroads. She didn't talk much either. She worked the way he did: early, quiet, and all the way to the end. The first time she laughed at something he said, he went home and lay awake half the night.

They married at twenty-five in her mother's backyard. Jalen came the next spring, eight pounds with a full head of hair and long fingers that wrapped around Ezra's thumb and would not let go.

Then the firm made her a project manager, and then a regional one. She was good, she wanted more of it, and he was proud of her. She was in Richmond three nights a week, then four. She called at bedtime, then texted, then forgot. They stopped arguing, because arguing took two people in the same room. By the summer Jalen turned three, they were two quiet people who were very good at their jobs, handing a little boy back and forth at the door.

It was Elijah who dragged them both to the house party in Brookland, that last summer, the summer of 2011. A narrow clapboard house full of people and music. A cooler of ice in the bathtub. Michelle had driven up from Richmond that afternoon and spent the party in the kitchen on her phone. Ezra stood by the back door with a cup he wasn't drinking.

That was where he first saw Angela.

She had come with two girlfriends and she was standing in the middle of the living room talking with her hands. She had a pencil skirt and a cardigan, and she held herself like a woman who had not slouched at a dinner table since grade school, and still every man in that room knew exactly where she was. She caught him looking. She looked back. She didn't blink first, and neither did he.

He couldn't go to her. He had a ring on.

So he listened instead. He stood by the back door and listened to her talk to a man about why third graders are the best age to teach. *Because they still believe you, and they're finally old enough to argue.* She was a teacher. She had a master's degree she was still paying off. She talked about a boy in her class who couldn't read yet, and she talked about him the way other people talked about someone they loved. She laughed with her whole face. The smile started on one side and took its time getting to the other.

He drove home with Michelle, who answered work email the whole way and didn't speak to him in the truck. He did not see the woman in the cardigan again. He told himself he had not been looking for her.

By August, Michelle was gone. The firm offered her Atlanta, and she took it. She left a note on the kitchen counter, and she did not take Jalen. *He needs one of us who's home,* the note said. *That was always going to be you.*

\* \* \*

The Montgomery County Fair, in Gaithersburg, the third week of August. Ninety-four degrees. Ezra brought Jalen, who was three, because the boy had stopped asking where Mommy was and started asking nothing at all, and Ezra wanted one day that would take both their minds off it and bring the boy a little happiness.

They rode the carousel four times. They looked at a pig the size of a car. Jalen fell asleep on his shoulder in the poultry barn, and Ezra stood in the dusty aisle between the cages, holding his sleeping son, and thought, *This is it. This is the whole rest of my life. I'll never leave his side.*

When he came out of the barn, she was standing in line at the fried-dough truck.

Same smile. Sundress this time, and a straw hat, and two girlfriends on either side of her, both of them talking at once. She saw him. She saw the sleeping boy. She looked at his left hand, and he watched her see that the ring was gone, and he watched her decide not to ask.

"You were at the party in Brookland," she said. "By the back door. You didn't say one word all night."

"I was listening."

"To what?"

"You. Talking about the boy who couldn't read."

She held his eyes and said nothing. Then she turned back to the window and said, "One more," and when the paper plate came, she put it in his free hand. A slab of fried dough the size of a hubcap, hot, slick, buried under powdered sugar.

"No," he said. "Let me." He fished out his wallet one-handed. Jalen woke up, saw the plate, and went for it with both fists, and sugar went down the front of Ezra's shirt and all over the boy's face. Angela laughed with her whole face.

\* \* \*

She was from Erie, Pennsylvania, up on the lake, where the snow comes in sideways off the water from November to April and nobody thinks anything of it. Her father, Joe, was a retired Navy captain who had commanded a destroyer out of Norfolk and still made his bed every morning with hospital corners. Her mother, Pat, ran the church kitchen and every bake sale within twenty miles. They had raised two children, Angela and her older brother, on schedule, on Scripture, and on the strict understanding that you finished what you started, you said what you meant, and you were home by ten.

They drove down the first Thanksgiving. Joe walked through Ezra's one-bedroom apartment the way he had once walked a ship at inspection, ran his thumbnail along the seam of a bookshelf Ezra had built, and said nothing. Pat brought a plate of chocolate cupcakes with sprinkles and stuck one candle in the middle of them, though it was nobody's birthday. "We do one candle in our house," she said. "One candle, one wish, and you share the rest." She made Jalen blow it out. She made him do it twice.

That night, in the parking lot, Joe stood by his car with his keys in his hand and looked at Ezra for a long, plain moment.

"She prays for you," he said. "You know that."

Ezra found no answer to that, so he gave none. Joe nodded once, as if that told him something, and got in the car.

\* \* \*

They married in June, in Angela's church, a small brick church in Northeast with a basement fellowship hall. Jalen, four, carried the rings on a pillow and dropped it twice. Pat cried through the vows. Joe walked his daughter down the aisle with his jaw set, and when he put her hand in Ezra's, he held on a second longer than he had to.

Ezra's father had been in the ground at Arlington for twenty-one years. Ezra looked out at the pews anyway, once, and hated himself for looking.

That fall a gutted brick house came up on Twelfth Street in Brookland: no windows, no wiring, a roof you could see the sky through, and behind it a long, deep lot gone wild with sumac and broken glass. Nobody wanted it. Ezra sold his truck and his good table saw to make the down payment and rode the bus to job sites for a year.

Jesus had a parable for it: *Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto treasure hid in a field; the which when a man hath found, he hideth, and for joy thereof goeth and selleth all that he hath, and buyeth that field.* (Matthew 13:44)

He rebuilt it with his own hands. Every joist, every stair tread, every door. Angela painted. Jalen hammered nails into a scrap of two-by-four in the backyard, crooked, all day, perfectly happy.

One Saturday that first spring, Ezra was in the back lot with a shovel, digging footings for an addition, down in red clay to his knees, filthy and soaked through. Angela came out with two glasses of iced tea and sat on the back step and watched him.

He stopped and leaned on the shovel.

"You know you could have done better," he said. He kept his eyes off her. "Teacher. Master's degree. Joe's daughter. You could have had a lawyer. Somebody who didn't come with all this."

Angela set down the tea and walked out into the mud in her good sneakers and stood in front of him.

"Ezra," she said. "Look where you're standing." He looked down: clay, roots, a broken bottle, a rusted hinge. "That's what a field looks like before you find what's in it. You have to dig through the dirt to get to the treasure." She wiped a streak of clay off his jaw with her thumb. "I'm not going anywhere. Keep digging."

\* \* \*

Those were the good years.

The house came together a room at a time. Jalen grew long and quiet and found a cello at a church rummage sale when he was nine and would not put it down. Ezra poured a slab at the end of the yard and framed him a studio, and the boy played out there every night with the windows open. Angela taught third grade four blocks away. Walt Simmons, across the street, read his newspaper on the porch every morning and never once waved first.

In the summer of 2020 Mia was born, small and loud and furious, with a full head of curls. Pat came down for two weeks and cooked for an army. Joe held his granddaughter on the back step for an hour and didn't say a word. When he handed her back to Ezra, his eyes were wet, and he pretended they weren't.

Saturdays they went to the park on Bunker Hill Road. Ezra pushed Mia on the swings until his arms ached. Angela read on a blanket. Jalen practiced scales under a tree, and strangers stopped to listen. Every August they went back to the fair for one fried dough and split it, and she always took the half with more sugar.

At supper Angela bowed her head over the food and rested her left hand open on the cloth beside his plate. Jalen took her other one. Ezra kept his on his fork. She never said a word about it, and she never stopped leaving it there.

\* \* \*

Angela had always believed. But in the spring Jalen turned ten, something in her went deeper. She started a Thursday-night women's study in the basement fellowship hall of the church where they were married. Fourteen women the first week. She came home from it talking faster than he had heard her talk since college. She bought spiral notebooks in four colors and a Strong's Concordance so thick it needed both hands. She read at the dinner table after Jalen was in bed, a pen in her teeth, drawing boxes around lines.

On the third Thursday, a young biochemist named Kambria came in late, in a lab coat, and sat in the back.

She had known her Bible since she was a girl. She could quote it. But she had never been taught how to *study* it, how to take a single word down to its root, how to keep a notebook so that ten years of reading added up to something. Angela showed her. Kambria went at it like a child let loose in a library. She came back the next week with three pages of questions. The week after, six. By the third spring, when the study had shrunk to the two of them and moved into Angela's kitchen, Kambria was there every Thursday at a quarter to seven, and Angela had a sister she had never had to share a bathroom with.

Jesus had said it plainly: *Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven.* (Matthew 18:3)

Ezra came home on Thursdays to two women at his kitchen table with their heads together over the Hebrew, and something in him went cold and hard.

He couldn't have said why. He started taking more jobs. He started stopping at Rooney's with Elijah on the way home, then staying. He started complaining: about money, about the roof, about the noise from the studio, about pierogies three nights a week. He stopped noticing the clean shirts in his drawer and the plate kept warm in the oven. When Angela turned to him in bed, more and more often he was already asleep, or pretending.

She never stopped praying for him. That was the worst of it. Sometimes he came down for water at two in the morning and found her at the kitchen table with her eyes closed and her lips moving and his name in it.

When she prayed out loud, he heard Pilgrim Rest. That was the thing he could never explain to her. It was not her voice. It was the words. The *Lord, we just* and the *in Jesus' name*, the holy words his father had shouted from the deacons' table on Sunday morning and then carried home in a bottle on Friday night. Every time she bowed her head, Ezra was six years old again in the front pew at Pilgrim Rest, sitting very still, so the voice wouldn't find him.

On Mia's third birthday, Joe and Pat drove down. Pat brought the cupcakes, chocolate, with sprinkles, one candle. The family stood around the kitchen table, and before Mia could blow, Angela touched Ezra's arm.

"Would you bless it?" she said quietly. "Just this once. For her."

The kitchen went still. Joe was watching him. Pat was studying the cupcakes. Mia had her eyes on the candle, which was burning down.

Ezra heard the deacons' table. He heard the bottle. He heard *you're just like him.*

"You do it," he said. "You're the one who's good at it."

He said it harder than he meant to. Angela's face didn't change, but something behind it closed. She bowed her head and said the blessing herself.

Mia blew out the candle.

Joe found Ezra on the back step afterward, in the dark, and stood beside him with his hands in his pockets.

"I had three hundred sailors under me," Joe said. "I know what it looks like when a man's angry at somebody who isn't in the room." He waited. Ezra said nothing. Joe nodded once, as he had that first Thanksgiving in the parking lot, and went inside.

\* \* \*

*Two years before the trumpet.*

Across the city from the Pattersons' house, in a government building with no windows, Angela's closest friend spent her days at a lab bench. Her name was Kambria Whitfield.

The morning the newspaper announced that someone had found Noah's ark, Kambria read the headline in the lab's break room and laughed out loud. Then she read the second paragraph, and she stopped laughing. She cut the page out with the lab's good scissors and carried it in her coat pocket the rest of the day.

Such days were what her work was made of. She was a biochemist with the Centers for Disease Control, and when people got sick and nobody knew why, the samples came to her bench, and she traced the germ back to where it started: the farm, the plant, the water main, the one bad shipment out of ten thousand good ones. That week it was two children in a hospital in Ohio and a bagged-lettuce plant in California, tied together by nothing but a fingerprint of bacterial DNA.

One thing did not fit. A single isolate from Ohio carried a stretch of thirty-odd bases in a region where nothing was supposed to be written at all, a patch of sequence that matched nothing in any database she could reach. It was too orderly to be damage and too short to be anything a germ would keep for itself. The confirmation run had come back from Verity Health Labs in Rockville, the private bench the agency used for its overflow, stamped clean. She logged the patch as probable contamination, because that was the honest category for a thing she could not explain. Then she exported the run to her cloud drive and sent it to Francesca Moretti, who had worked two benches down from her for years before she moved up to New York, and asked for a second opinion.

At a quarter to seven she turned onto Twelfth Street in Brookland, in Northeast Washington, still in her gray slacks and flat shoes, her agency badge flipped backward on its lanyard. Thursday evenings in that neighborhood had a sound of their own. Somewhere on Otis Street a speaker sat on a porch rail, sending a Christian hip-hop song out over the rooftops, and from Rhode Island Avenue the bell at Mount Zion began to ring the hour. Kambria caught her head nodding before she had decided to let it. The old porch-front houses, brick below and painted wood above, stood shoulder to shoulder behind small, fierce gardens, and two doors down from the Pattersons' house Mr. Odell sat in his lawn chair, as he had every warm evening since before Kambria knew the street. He lifted two fingers from the armrest as she parked. She lifted two back.

Angela Patterson's house was the brick one with the crooked porch light and the front step that Ezra had been promising to rebuild for six summers. Nobody knocked there. Kambria went in through the side door, into a kitchen that was all steam and noise: Swedish meatballs simmering in cream gravy on the back burner, loaded potato pierogies browning in butter in the skillet, a small pot of lingonberry jam warming beside them. In the middle of it stood Angela, the closest thing Kambria had to a sister, a dish towel over one shoulder and a wooden spoon in her hand, conducting.

"You look like you haven't eaten since Monday," Angela said, without turning around. "Sit. You will not read the Word on an empty stomach in my house."

"I ate."

"A granola bar in a parking lot is not eating."

At the table, Angela's four-year-old daughter, Mia, knelt on a chair with her hair in two puffs tied up in yellow ribbons, working a purple crayon across a coloring page with the focus of a lab tech plating cultures. "Miss Kambria! I know my verse!"

"Let's hear it."

"Jesus wept." She said it proudly, and at a great volume.

"It's the shortest one in the whole Bible," Angela said, "and she has decided that is the one she's keeping."

The screen door slapped, and Jalen came in from the backyard: sixteen years old, lanky legs, unkempt hair, and glasses, with headphones around his neck and calluses on the fingertips of his left hand from hours with the cello. He kissed his mother on the cheek, stole a pierogi straight out of the skillet, and dodged the spoon.

"Hey, Miss Kam."

"Hey, maestro."

"Is Dad home?" He asked it of the skillet instead of his mother.

"He's finishing a job in Takoma," Angela said. "He said he would try."

"Cool," Jalen said. He carried a plate piled high back out to the little studio at the end of the yard, and the screen door had barely finished its second slap when the cello began to play.

They ate standing at the counter, as Thursdays always went, and Kambria noticed that Angela, who had fixed three plates, only moved the food around on her own. She noticed, too, that Angela's left hand drifted to her side and away again, twice. Kambria filed it where she filed everything. Then Angela asked about the lab, and Kambria told her about the lettuce, and the moment passed.

Kambria had been at Angela's table every Thursday since the study shrank to two.

Now the plates were rinsed and stacked, Mia had been carried up to bed with a cup of water and three promises, and the two women sat across from each other as they had every Thursday night for years: two cups of coffee going cold, two worn King James Bibles, and a dozen spiral notebooks spread out between them.

Each notebook had a color. Blue for Israel. Red, the one she had labeled *Of the Nations*. Green for money. Gold, the thinnest one, for the church.

Kambria dated everything, in small square letters, each one standing apart from the next. Angela kept her own habit. On every page she drew a box around one line, in whatever pen was nearest, the line she would look for first if she lost all the rest.

"Why that one?" Kambria had asked her once, years ago, tapping a box with her pen.

"Because if the house burned down and I got one line back," Angela said, "I want it to be that one."

Between the two Bibles sat Angela's Strong's Concordance, two thousand pages thick, its spine split and mended with packing tape. Every Thursday started the same way. One verse. One word in it. Then down to the root, in the Hebrew or the Greek, until they knew what that word had meant to the people who first heard it.

Tonight the word was *watch*. Angela had her finger on it in Matthew 24, and Kambria was running down the columns in the back of the concordance, past thousands of numbers, to the Greek.

"Here. Eleven twenty-seven." Kambria sounded it out. "*Grēgoreuō. γρηγορεύω.* To keep awake. To be vigilant." She read the next line twice. "It comes from a word that means to rouse up. To wake somebody who's asleep."

Angela sat back. "So it doesn't mean look out the window."

"No. It means don't fall asleep."

Angela wrote it in pen in the margin of her Bible, small and neat, beside the verse: *1127. Stay awake.* Then she glanced through the doorway at the couch in the living room, where her husband fell asleep in front of the television most nights, and said nothing.

"What did you bring?" Angela said.

Kambria pulled a newspaper clipping from the back of the red notebook and smoothed it out with her palm. Four wars on three continents, all of them flaring in the same month. She had clipped one like it on Monday, and another the week before that.

She read it aloud to Angela. Then she laid her pen across the open notebook and sat back, silent. Every week she would find something in the newspaper, and then she would find it in the Bible, and the two would line up so closely that it frightened her. Wars and rumours of wars. Nation against nation, kingdom against kingdom. She had been reading those words her whole life. She had never expected to watch them come up off the page and onto the front of the paper.

"Angie," she said, barely above a whisper. "It's all in here. All of it. Just like He said it would be." She pressed her fingertips against her closed eyes. "Some nights it's more than I can hold."

Angela flipped through her Bible and found Jesus' answer in Matthew 24 quickly. "'For nation shall rise against nation, and kingdom against kingdom: and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places.'" She tapped the next line with one finger. "'All these are the beginning of sorrows.'"

"The beginning," Kambria said. "That's what keeps me up. It's not the end yet, but it's definitely intensifying." She slid the clipping into the red notebook and dated it in the corner. "It's like He's turning the pages faster, Angie. Ten years ago I'd find one of these articles a month. Now I see it every day."

Kambria took the ark clipping from her coat pocket. "And one more." She laid it on the table. It was from that morning's paper. It showed a long, boat-shaped hill on a mountainside in eastern Turkey, snow above it. The headline said NOAH'S ARK FOUND, and under it, in smaller type, *Scientists confirm structure in Ararat region is man-made.*

Angela read it twice. Then she turned back to His words in Matthew 24 and ran her finger down the page. "'But as the days of Noe were, so shall also the coming of the Son of man be.'" She looked up. "They were eating and drinking, and marrying, right up to the day Noah went into the ark. And they knew not until the flood came and took them all away." She set her hand on the photograph. "He's showing them the boat, Kam. Right before."

Kambria dated the clipping and slid it into the red notebook with the others.

On the windowsill over the sink, Angela's little radio went on talking under the clink of the coffee cups. Kambria half-listened to the announcer: a recall of bagged romaine lettuce in fourteen states, E. coli, two children in the hospital in Ohio. Then a report on the drought in the West, the land gone brown from Nevada to Texas, and Lake Mead lower than it had been since the dam was built. She wrote both of them down in the margin of the red notebook, small, under the date. She was studious, and she remembered to write it down, the way any thorough scientist would. *Famines, and pestilences.* Then she looked through the doorway at the empty couch, the dent in the cushion where a tired man slept through the news most nights, and the word they had just learned came back to her. *Stay awake.*

The back door banged open.

Ezra trudged in with muddy work boots, a dusty tool belt, and drywall dust in his hair. He was a big man, broad in the shoulders, with hands rough as unplaned oak.

He kicked off his boots, glanced past the table where the ladies studied, and started toward the fridge. "Well," he said. "I can see the doomsday club is in session."

"Hi, honey." Angela tipped her face up, and he kissed her forehead, and for one second the teasing went out of his eyes. It always did with her.

Then he looked at Kambria. "Let me guess. World's ending Tuesday."

"Nobody knows the day or the hour," Kambria said, without looking up at him.

"Then why do y'all keep writing this stuff down?"

"Because He told us to watch," Angela said. "So His coming won't catch us by surprise." She never argued with him about it. She just kept inviting him, even though she had stopped expecting him to say yes.

Ezra opened the refrigerator, took out a beer, and let the door swing shut harder than it needed to. From the studio came the long, low groan of a cello: a single note, held until it trembled, then sliding up into what sounded almost like grief.

Through the window over the sink he could see it: the little studio across the grass, its windows glowing amber in the dark. He had poured the slab for it himself five summers ago and framed every wall, with Angela holding the level and an eleven-year-old Jalen at his elbow, handing him nails and asking a hundred questions about construction. He had taught his son to frame a wall, hang a door, and finish the trim on the studio that summer, and they had grown close doing it. When it was finished, they flipped the breaker together and stood in the doorway, grinning while every light came on at once.

Ezra looked at the glowing windows for one second. Then he looked away.

"He's still at that thing?"

"That thing," Angela said, "got him a scholarship audition."

Lionel Hart had been Jalen's teacher since the boy was nine years old. He had played viola with the Capital Philharmonic for thirty-one years, and there was no string instrument he couldn't teach. The first time he heard Jalen sawing away at that rummage-sale cello in the church basement, he walked over, fixed Jalen's bow hold without a word, and told Angela he would teach him for nothing. He had been to every recital since. Ezra had been to two. When Mr. Hart retired from the orchestra, he began coaching the student orchestra at Coolidge High three afternoons a week, unpaid, and Jalen had sat in its cello section ever since.

"Scholarship for what? Sitting in a chair?" He twisted the cap off the bottle. "Boy's sixteen. When I was sixteen I was framing houses."

"When you were sixteen," Angela said, "you didn't have a father who came to anything."

The kitchen went still. Even the cello seemed to pause.

Ezra stood there with the bottle halfway to his mouth. His father's watch, the stopped one, gleamed on his wrist. Kambria had never once seen him without it, and never seen it tell the right time.

"I'm going to shower," he said, and left.

Angela closed her eyes. Neither spoke. They had prayed for this man together for years, and some nights there was nothing left to say but his name.

"Mommy."

Mia stood in the doorway in her pajamas, four years old and solemn, clutching a sheet of paper to her chest. She had been sent to bed an hour ago.

"Baby, what are you doing up?"

"I made a picture for Miss Kambria." She padded across the linoleum and laid it on top of the red notebook, then stepped back and watched their faces, proud of what she had made.

It was a house. Their house; Kambria recognized the crooked porch light. But the sky above it was not blue. Mia had colored it red from edge to edge, pressing so hard the crayon had gone waxy and dark, and in the middle of all that red she had drawn a small yellow circle, with light pouring out of it.

"That's beautiful, sweet pea," Kambria said. "Why is the sky red?"

Mia considered this seriously. "That's what the sky does when Jesus is almost here."

Angela's pen stopped moving.

"Who told you that, baby?"

"Nobody." Mia shrugged, already bored with the question. She pointed to a small rectangle in the front window of the house, with a brown shape inside it. "That's Daddy on the couch. He doesn't see it because he's sleeping."

Kambria looked at Angela. Angela looked at the drawing. Upstairs, the shower came on.

"Bed," Angela said finally, too brightly, and scooped her daughter up.

When she came back down, she sat across from Kambria again and pulled her Bible toward her, and they went on. Angela found her place in Matthew 24, where Jesus tells His disciples to watch, and began to read aloud in her clear, even teacher's voice.

"'*Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come. But know this, that if the goodman of the house had known in what watch the thief would come, he would have watched…*'" (Matthew 24:42–43)

She stopped.

Not at the end of the verse. In the middle of it. Her finger stayed on the page, and she did not look up.

Then she looked up, and reached across the table, across the red notebook and the blue one and Mia's waxy red drawing, and took both of Kambria's hands in hers.

Angela reached for people's hands all the time. She held them to pray, to comfort, to welcome; it was the most natural thing in the world to her. Yet in all their years of Thursday nights, Kambria had never seen her reach out like this, for herself, to be held. Her hands were cold now, and trembling.

She had seen it in other women, at other times, and she knew what it meant.

"Angie," she whispered. "What is it?"

Angela started to speak and stopped. Tears ran down to her chin, and still Angela didn't let go to wipe them away.

"I found a lump," she said. "Three weeks ago. Right here." She drew Kambria's fingers to her side, just below her left arm, and let it rest there. "I had the mammogram Monday. They called me back today. The radiologist..." She stopped and pressed her lips together. "He thinks it's cancer, Kam. They want to do a biopsy Thursday."

Out in the studio, even the cello had stopped. Kambria didn't know when. Nothing moved in the house.

"Does Ezra know?"

Angela shook her head. "Not yet. I can't. Not until I know for sure." A small, broken laugh escaped her. "You know what he'll say. He'll look at me and say, 'Where's your God now?'"

Kambria came around the table. She knelt beside Angela's chair, and Angela bent forward into her arms, and the two women held each other in the warm yellow kitchen with the notebooks of the end of the world spread out around them. Kambria felt her friend's shoulders shaking and heard a sound she had never heard Angela make in all their years: a low, wordless weeping.

"I'm scared," Angela whispered into her shoulder. "I'm not scared to die. I'm scared to leave them. Mia's four. Jalen's sixteen and he barely talks to his father. And Ezra..." Her voice cracked. "I'm scared to leave him like this. Who's going to pray for him?"

"I will," Kambria said. "Every day. As long as it takes."

They stayed like that while the clock above the stove ticked on.

At last Angela sat back and wiped her face with the heels of her hands and laughed through it, a real laugh this time. "Look at us. Two old prophecy ladies crying all over Matthew." Her eyes went to the Bible, still open where she'd stopped, and fresh tears came, but she was smiling now. "Whatever it is, He already knows. He knew before I did. He knew before the foundation of the world."

They prayed then, holding hands across the notebooks, as on every Thursday. This time Kambria's voice shook.

"Father, it's Kambria. And Angela. You know why we're here. You knew before she did. Hold her, Lord. Whatever is in her body, be bigger than it. And hold Ezra. He's going to need You more than either of us."

"Amen," Angela whispered.

\* \* \*

The next afternoon, between two sequencing runs, Kambria's phone buzzed in the pocket of her lab coat.

*Biopsy is Thursday at 2. Still haven't told Ezra. Pray for me.*

She read it in the lab stairwell, between the third and fourth floors, where no one could see her face. Then she took out the small gold notebook, the one for the church, and opened it to a clean page. She didn't write a headline or a verse. She wrote a name. Then, underneath, she wrote the date.

That same night, across the city, Angela Patterson sat alone at her dinner table after everyone was asleep and opened a brand-new notebook, a plain black one, never used.

On the cover she wrote two words, studied them until the ink had dried, and closed the cover.

*For Ezra.*

## Chapter 2: Last Call

> *For as in the days that were before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day that Noe entered into the ark.* — Jesus, Matthew 24:38

**Word study: *eating* — τρώγω** Greek *trōgō* (Strong's G5176). To gnaw, to crunch, to munch. It is the plain, unthinking eating of an ordinary day, not a feast. Jesus did not describe the world before the flood at the height of its wickedness. He described it chewing its dinner, too busy to look up.

There was a wedding in the town that week. The bride wore copper at her wrists, and the groom's father roasted three lambs, and the music carried all the way up the hill to where the great boat sat finished in the field. Someone joked that the old man should come down and dance. Someone else said he'd spent seven days now loading the thing, the animals going up the ramp two by two, and wasn't that the strangest thing. They laughed and filled their cups. Above the music, if anyone had been listening, they might have heard the first low roll of thunder. (Genesis 7:1–10)

\* \* \*

Rooney's sat on the corner of Twelfth Street in Brookland, six blocks from the Patterson house, one of the oldest bars in the neighborhood: a brick box with a green awning, a jukebox nobody had updated since 2009, and a back room where the same six men had been playing the same game of pool, as far as Ezra could tell, for most of his adult life.

Lately, Thursdays had become Ezra's night. Angela had her Bible study and he had Rooney's, and that was the arrangement, and it worked because neither of them asked too many questions about the other's.

Tonight she'd said she had a thing after school. A teacher thing. He hadn't asked. Lately there were a lot of things he hadn't asked, and somewhere underneath the beer and the jokes, he knew it.

"There he is!" Elijah, Ezra's oldest friend, called out, spreading his arms from the corner stool like a preacher welcoming a sinner home. "The prodigal carpenter. Sit down, sit down, your seat's been cold too long."

Elijah Brooks, Eli to everyone who knew him, could make a whole bar laugh, then sit in his truck in the lot for an hour before he drove home. They had been friends since they were boys, and they'd been drinking together on Thursdays ever since: through Ezra's wedding, through Elijah's to Marsha, the older girl he had chased for two years until she let herself be caught, and through the divorce, when Marsha packed her car and left him over the drinking, and he swore it was the best thing that ever happened to him, and through the long year when Elijah lived in his car and told everybody he was "between addresses."

"How's my goddaughter?" Elijah asked.

"Drawing red skies. Angela says she told the prophecy club Jesus is coming."

Elijah wheezed. "Your house is a cult, man. I keep telling you. You got the church ladies in the kitchen and the little prophet in the bedroom and Jalen out back in that studio playing funeral music on a giant violin."

"Cello."

"I know what it is, I'm just saying it's big." He signaled the bartender with two fingers. "Sal, my friend here is in mourning. He lives with saints."

Ezra laughed, and the week's tightness went out of his shoulders. The first beer went down cold and easy. The second went down easier. The jukebox played a song with horns.

At the end of the bar, Trent Walker was holding court with two guys from the drywall crew. Trent was Ezra's apprentice, or had been for six years, which in Ezra's opinion was about five years longer than he needed to be. He was quick, he was good, and he knew it, and he walked onto a job already sure of the cuts, waiting on everyone else to catch up.

He'd also grown up in a church, a big one out in Prince George's County, and every so often it slipped out of him, whether he meant it to or not.

"Boss man!" Trent called down the bar, raising his glass with a smirk. "'Let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die.' First Corinthians, fifteen and thirty-two."

"You know what that verse is actually saying?" Ezra called back, irritated. "Paul's mocking people who say that."

Trent grinned. "I know exactly what it's saying. I'm just choosing the fun half." He winked and turned back to his drywall guys, and Ezra shook his head, and it bothered him, because his father used to twist scripture the same way, picking out the half that suited him.

"Kid's gonna own the whole company someday," Elijah said.

"Kid's gonna own somebody's company," Ezra agreed. "Hopefully not mine."

\* \* \*

Around nine the door opened and let in a gust of October and a knot of young women in sweaters, laughing at some joke before they were even through the door. A birthday, it turned out. One of them wore a plastic tiara.

One of them, a red-haired woman with her hair pinned up in a loose knot, caught Ezra's eye in the long mirror behind the bar and held it longer than strangers do. Then she smiled and turned back to her friends.

"Careful," Elijah murmured into his glass.

"I'm married."

"I know you're married. I'm saying careful."

At the far table, Kyle Bennett looked up from the paper he was grading and forgot to look back down.

Kyle was twenty-six and a graduate student at Catholic University, studying French literature, which Ezra had stopped trying to understand. He came to Rooney's on Thursdays because it was cheap and quiet in the corner, and because, he'd once admitted to Ezra after a few too many, his mother used to bring him here for fries when he was a boy. She'd been gone three years. He still had her last voicemail saved on his phone, and on her birthday he played it in his car with the engine off.

Right now he was staring at a dark-haired woman in a green sweater who was trying, and failing, to light a birthday candle in a basket of onion rings.

"Oh, no," Elijah said happily. "Oh, look at this. Look at our boy."

"Leave him alone."

"I'm not gonna bother him. I'm gonna help him." Elijah was already off the stool. He ambled to Kyle's table, murmured a word, and pressed a lighter into his hand. Kyle went red to the ears. Elijah clapped him on the back hard enough to move him two steps toward the birthday table, and then a third, and then Kyle was there, holding out the lighter.

"Pardon me. I'm told it's bad luck to leave a birthday unlit. Worse luck to let it burn the onion rings."

The woman in the green sweater laughed. "Sarah. Second grade, Rhode Island Avenue. And you?"

"Kyle. French literature, which is an expensive way of saying I read sad books in a nice accent."

"Say something in French."

"*Je ne sais pas ce que je fais ici.*" He flushed. "It means I'm not sure what I'm doing here, but I'd like to keep doing it."

Within twenty minutes Kyle had learned that she kept a jar of quarters on her kitchen counter labeled SOMEDAY ITALY, and she had learned that he spoke French and had offered to teach her, and they were leaning toward each other over the onion rings.

Elijah came back to his stool and slapped the bar. "That," he announced, "is a wedding. Mark my words. I'm gonna be in that wedding."

"You've known them twenty minutes."

"And I'm never wrong about love." Elijah drained his glass. "Only about my own."

He laughed when he said it. He always laughed when he said things like that.

Down at the far end of the bar, a man in a gray overcoat had been nursing the same club soda since before Ezra came in. He did not watch the birthday table. He watched the door, and then, once, Ezra himself in the long mirror, long enough to be sure. When Ezra turned on his stool, the seat was empty, and a hundred-dollar bill lay folded under the glass for a four-dollar drink. Sal held it up to the light and shrugged. "Nobody tips like that on a Thursday." Ezra forgot about it before his next beer.

\* \* \*

By eleven, the birthday party had gone, and Kyle with it, walking Sarah to her car. Trent had left with the drywall crew. Sal was wiping down the taps. Elijah was on his fifth "just one more."

"You know what my ex said when she left?" Elijah said, to no one in particular, to the mirror behind the bar. "She said, 'Elijah, you're the funniest man I ever met, and I've never once heard you say a true thing.'" He turned his glass on the wood. "I told her that was the truest thing anybody ever said to me. She didn't laugh."

Ezra didn't laugh either.

"You ever think about it?" Elijah said. "All that stuff Angela's always reading? The end of the world and all that?"

"No."

"Me neither." Elijah picked at the label on his bottle. "I mean, if it was true, though. If it was true, wouldn't we know? Wouldn't there be, like, a sign?"

"My daughter drew one," Ezra said, and they both laughed, too loud, in the empty bar.

On the television over the register, the late news was on, and Sal, the bartender, reached up and turned the sound on, which he never did. A map of Iran filled the screen, with red arrows moving across it, and then missiles streaking over a city at night. "The war in Iran," the anchor called it, as if everybody already knew which one. Then oil derricks in a green Venezuelan valley, with American flags over the gates. The administration had taken control of the country's oil fields, the anchor said, and the largest private stake in the new operation belonged to the fund of a billionaire whose name Ezra didn't catch. There was a picture of the signing: a silver-haired man smiling for the cameras, and a step behind him, half out of the frame, a thin, dark-haired man holding the pen. *Alexander Vale, chief of staff,* the caption said. Then a man at a podium at the International Collective, and the crawl at the bottom of the screen said something about a vote on a new Organization for World Peace.

"Fourth war this year," Sal said, to nobody. "Fourth one."

Elijah raised his glass to the screen. "And yet the beer is still cold. God bless America."

A couple of men down the bar laughed. Ezra didn't. He watched the screen until the picture changed, and then he studied his beer, and he told himself he was tired.

\* \* \*

The kitchen light was on when he got home.

He noticed that from the street and felt guilty, as he always did when Angela waited up. He eased in through the back door. He'd had four beers and told her it would be two, and he had driven home on them anyway, his hands steady at ten and two. They had been steering a truck, one way or another, since he was a boy on a stack of phone books, and not one of them had ever asked whether he should.

Faintly, from the studio, came the cello, the same slow, sorrowful melody Jalen had been working at for weeks, the one Ezra had long since stopped hearing. But tonight it went somewhere new. It climbed three notes higher than it ever had before, held there, trembling, and then fell back.

She was sitting at the dinner table in her robe. No notebooks tonight. No Bibles. Just Angela, a cup of tea she hadn't touched, and a small white bandage on the inside of her left arm, just below the elbow, where they'd taken blood.

And a plain black notebook in front of her, closed, with her hand resting on its cover.

"Hey," he said. "You're up late. How was your teacher thing?"

She looked up at him, and he knew. What, he couldn't yet say, but he set his keys down very carefully.

"Sit down, honey," Angela said. "I was going to wait for the results. I can't. I need to tell you something. And I need you to let me finish."

He sat down across from her. His hand moved an inch toward hers across the table, then stopped. It always stopped. Outside, a car passed, its headlights crawling across the ceiling and down the wall.

He looked at the black notebook under her hand.

She slid it off the table and into her lap, out of sight, before she began. But not before he saw the cover. Two words, in her round, careful handwriting, in the blue ink she used for grading papers.

*For Ezra.*

He did not ask what was in it. She did not tell him.

## Chapter 3: The Sixth Floor

> *The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart; and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.* — Psalm 34:18

**Word study: *contrite* — דַּכָּא** Hebrew *dakka'* (Strong's H1793). Crushed, broken to pieces, ground into powder. Its root is used for crushing something into dust. God is near to the one who has been crushed so fine there is nothing left of him to hold together.

When Job's three friends heard of all the evil that had come upon him, they came from their own places to mourn with him. They did not know him at first; he was sitting in the ashes, scraping his sores with a broken piece of pottery. So they tore their robes and threw dust upon their heads, and sat down with him on the ground seven days and seven nights. And none spoke a word unto him, for they saw that his grief was very great. (Job 2:8, 11–13)

\* \* \*

The word, when it came, was a long one. Invasive ductal carcinoma. Stage three. Two lymph nodes.

Dr. Sandoval folded her hands on the desk.

"Invasive ductal carcinoma," Angela said slowly. "Would you spell that for me? I want to write it down." Kambria watched her print each letter in the black notebook in her neat, round handwriting. Angela wanted to know the name of what she was fighting.

"Chemotherapy every other Tuesday for months," the doctor said. "Then surgery, then radiation." The oncologist said the word *aggressive* four times, once about the cancer and three times about the treatment. She said *hopeful* once.

In the car afterward, Angela sat with the notebook closed on her lap and watched the October trees go by.

"Months," she said. "That's the whole school year." Then, after a while: "I'm going to need a really good substitute."

Kambria heard the tremble in those words and kept driving.

\* \* \*

The infusion center was on the sixth floor of the hospital whose lab sent the Centers for Disease Control its samples, where Kambria knew half the staff by name. It sat at the end of a long hallway that smelled of hand sanitizer and burnt coffee: a wide, bright room ringed with recliners, each one with its own IV pole and its own small window onto the city. On Tuesdays it filled with the same quiet company: a retired bus driver named Mr. Harold who did crossword puzzles in pen; a young mother named Rosa who knitted hats for her twins; a teenage boy with headphones who never spoke.

Kambria took every other Tuesday off from the lab, out of leave she had been saving for years. Nobody asked her to. Nobody had to.

The Tuesday volunteer on the sixth floor was named Celeste Moore.

She had started on the sixth floor that September as a volunteer in the hospital's Patient Companions program, Tuesday mornings only, and by October the whole floor was half in love with her. When anyone asked what she did the rest of the week, she said she worked in public health, mostly paperwork, and changed the subject. She remembered every patient's birthday, and their children's names, and which of the techs took their coffee with oat milk. She had red hair that she pinned up for her visits and let down the minute they ended, and she knew exactly what it did to a room. She laughed at their jokes and touched their arms and called the older patients "sweetheart," and all the while her eyes kept count. At her throat she wore a small gold pendant shaped like a tree: ten tiny circles joined by lines, climbing from the roots to the crown. On her left wrist she wore a thin red string, knotted three times. When one of the residents asked her about it, she told him it was Rahab's scarlet cord, from the Book of Joshua: the outsider who was brought inside when the walls came down. "We're all inside now," she said, and smiled. She had two hundred thousand followers online, where she posted photographs of herself in the morning light at her front window, in a robe slipping off one shoulder or a top cut low, because the more she showed, the more they answered. She posted soft-spoken videos about self-love and letting go of guilt, filmed in front of a framed drawing of the same tree. The Tree of Life, she called it. *Nobody has to die for you,* she told her followers. *You climb. Your joy is holy. God wants you to have it. All of it.*

Kambria had been prepared not to like her. A biochemistry degree and years of tracing outbreaks through hospitals had left her suspicious of anyone who smiled that much at seven in the morning.

But Celeste was good at it. Kambria watched her warm Angela's blanket in the cart dryer before she tucked it around her knees, and remember which tea Angela could keep down, and bring a second blanket without being asked. Kambria could not find anything wrong with her, and she tried. The trouble was that every kindness arrived a moment too well timed, like a result that comes back too clean.

By the third session, the two women had brought the Thursday-night study to the sixth floor. Angela would settle into her recliner with a warm blanket over her knees and the bag of red medicine dripping into the port below her collarbone, and Kambria would pull up a plastic chair and open the notebooks on the rolling tray table between them. They read Psalms mostly, now. The prophecies could wait.

"'Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,'" Angela read one morning, "'I will fear no evil.'" She paused and looked around the room at the IV poles standing all around them. "Well. Here's the valley."

Mr. Harold looked up from his crossword. "Keep going," he said gruffly. "I like that one."

At the next session, Loretta came.

Ezra's mother stood at the glass doors at half past nine in her church coat, small and straight-backed, with a foil-covered pan held level in both hands like something that might spill. Before the doors had finished closing behind her, the smell reached the recliners: warm flour and butter, a smell that had no business on a floor that ran on hand sanitizer and burnt coffee. Heads turned. Rosa lowered her knitting. Even the teenage boy slid his headphones down around his neck.

"I know you can't eat much, baby," Loretta told Angela, folding back the foil. "But you can smell them. And you can try one."

They were dinner rolls, golden on top and shining with butter, packed shoulder to shoulder in the pan. Loretta had baked them every Sunday of Ezra's life from a recipe she had never written down and never given away, not to the church mothers who had begged her for it for forty years, and not even to Angela, who had asked more than once. *Some things you keep,* she always said, and smiled, and changed the subject. Angela pulled one apart, and it came away in soft, flaky layers with the steam still rising from the middle, buttery and smooth on her tongue. It was the first thing in two days that had not turned her stomach.

"Mama Loretta," she said, and for a moment that was all she could say.

Loretta did not stay by that chair. She went around the room with the pan, chair to chair, the way she had gone down the pews with the offering plate for fifty years. Mr. Harold took two and set down his pen to eat them. "Lord have mercy," he said, with his mouth full, and then, to no one, "My mother used to make these." Rosa wrapped one in a napkin for her twins. The teenage boy ate three without a word and then said, very quietly, "Thank you, ma'am," and it was the first thing anyone on that floor had heard him say. The nurses came by in twos on their way past the desk and left with their hands full.

Celeste took one, with a warm smile and a murmur of thanks. Kambria noticed afterward that she had held it the whole morning and never taken a bite.

So Angela kept reading. At the next session Rosa asked if they could hear the psalm again. At the one after that, the boy with the headphones took them off.

One Tuesday that fall, Kambria brought a question instead of a psalm.

She had been up since four o'clock reading Genesis 5, the long list of fathers and sons, and every name on it ended the same way. *And he died. And he died. And he died.* Hundreds of years, and then a funeral. Except for one man in the middle of the list.

"'And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.'" She turned her Bible around on the tray table so Angela could see it. "Everybody else in this chapter dies, Angie. Everybody. Except him."

Angela read it with the blanket pulled up to her chest. The red medicine went on dripping. "Hebrews tells you why," she said. She always knew where everything was. "Chapter eleven."

Kambria found it. "'By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death... for before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.'" She looked up. "He walked with God, and he pleased Him, and God just took him. He never saw death."

"Keep going," Angela said. "Jude."

Jude was one page long, tucked in right before Revelation, and Kambria had read it maybe twice in her life. Near the bottom she found him again. "'*And Enoch also, the seventh from Adam, prophesied of these, saying, Behold, the Lord cometh with ten thousands of his saints, To execute judgment upon all…*'" (Jude 14–15) She read it again to herself. Then she flipped back to Genesis 5 and ran her finger down every line of it.

She sat back. "He saw it," she said. "Before the flood. Before Noah ever picked up a hammer, Enoch saw the Lord coming back with His saints."

"And then God took him," Angela said. "Before the flood ever came." She smiled, tired. "Noah went through the water, Kam. Enoch never saw a drop of it."

Kambria wrote it in the margin of her notebook, in ink, in her precise hand: *Enoch. Taken before. Hebrews 11:5. Jude 14–15.* That was all the Bible said about him, and it was enough. She dated the entry in the corner and numbered the page, as she numbered every page. Angela's pages had no numbers. "The Lord keeps count," she said, when Kambria offered her the pen, and she went on turning her own pages by the corners.

Later that afternoon, before she closed the notebook, she turned back one more time to the man in Genesis 5 who walked with God and was not, and she looked across the tray table at Angela, asleep in the recliner with the line in her chest. She did not write down what she prayed. She said it under her breath, so low it hardly moved the air.

"Father, if You are going to take her, take her the way You took Enoch. Walking. Not through the water. Please."

\* \* \*

On the second Tuesday in November, Celeste came by Angela's recliner on her lunch break with a thermos of golden turmeric tea and a little book wrapped in tissue paper. It was a paperback of daily affirmations, with the gold tree on the cover.

"It's what got me through my divorce," she said, unfolding the tissue. "You don't need anybody to save you, Angela. You just need to believe in your own light."

Angela laid her hand over Celeste's. "Honey, that is the sweetest thing," she said. "But I already have Somebody who saved me." She folded the book back into its tissue paper and closed Celeste's fingers around it, and she held on to Celeste's hand a little longer. "Everything I need was finished on a cross. You keep this. But I'm going to pray for you. Is that all right?"

Celeste laughed, surprised, and tucked the little book into the pocket of her cardigan. "Of course it is."

Celeste perched on the arm of the empty recliner and looked at the open Bible on the tray table with real tenderness. "Oh, I love that you have your practice," she said. "I think it's all the same light, really. All paths up the same mountain. Whatever brings you peace."

Kambria felt the words before she said them. "Jesus said, '*I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.*'" (John 14:6)

Celeste turned and gave her a smile of such untroubled sweetness that Kambria felt, absurdly, that she had been unkind.

"That's beautiful," Celeste said. "Well, that's your path." Then, lightly: "Angela says you work in a lab. What do you actually test, if you don't mind my asking?"

"Outbreaks," Kambria said. "Mostly lettuce."

Celeste's eyes went to the government badge clipped to her coat. She read the name on it, then the department under the name, and only then looked up.

Celeste laughed and asked nothing more. It was only afterward that Kambria noticed she herself had answered exactly the question and not one word past it.

On her way out, she paused at the double glass doors and glanced down the hall toward the waiting room. "Is that him?" she murmured to Kambria. "The husband? In the work jacket?"

Kambria hesitated, then nodded.

"He looks so alone," Celeste said, and let the doors swing shut behind her.

That night, in the parking garage, Kambria opened her laptop on the passenger seat and looked again at the thirty bases from Ohio, and found she had no wish to mention them to anyone, including her own supervisor. She kept hearing it, too: *Is that him?* As if Celeste had been expecting someone.

\* \* \*

Angela's hair began to fall out in November.

She found the first handful on her pillow on a Sunday morning and sat up in bed with it cupped in her palm until the room grew light. Then she walked into the kitchen, handed Ezra the clippers from the bathroom drawer, and said, "Get it over with."

He stood behind her chair holding them. Kambria, who had come over with groceries, watched from the doorway as his hands shook. Then he steadied them.

Mia came in to them. She climbed into her mother's lap, studied her face seriously, and announced, "Mommy's going to look like a baby bird." And Angela laughed, and Ezra laughed, a hoarse, startled bark, and the clippers buzzed to life.

When it was done, Jalen came in from the studio, took one look at his mother, took the clippers out of his father's hand, and shaved his own head right there at the kitchen sink without a word.

Ezra stared at his son. Kambria thought he might say something. Then he turned and went out the back door, and through the window she watched him walk to the end of the yard and stand in front of the little studio he had built, with his palm against its wall, until his arm grew tired.

\* \* \*

Ezra drove Angela to every session.

He took the whole day off every other Tuesday. He had not missed a day of work in nineteen years. He carried her bag, signed her in, kissed her forehead at the double glass doors, and then he went back out to the waiting room and sat there for five hours. He never went in. He told himself it was because they only allowed one visitor, and Kambria was already there.

The truth was that he had tried, once, on the first Tuesday. He had made it as far as the doorway, seen his wife in the recliner with the line running into her chest, felt his legs nearly give out, and walked back out before she saw his face.

So he sat in the gray vinyl chairs in his work jacket, scrolling through his phone without seeing it, while the television bolted above the vending machines played the news with the sound off. The captions trailed a few seconds behind the pictures and misspelled half the names. He read them because it was easier than thinking. An earthquake in Turkey, the second in a month. A salmonella outbreak traced to a farm in Iowa, and a hundred million eggs pulled off the shelves. A woman across the room shook her head at the screen. "Lord, what is this world coming to," she said, and the room let it pass.

Everyone asked about Angela. His foreman asked. His mother called every night and asked. Pastor Grant from Angela's church left voicemails every Sunday, and Ezra deleted them without listening. *How's Angela? How's she holding up? Tell her we're praying.* Nobody asked how he was. He would have hated it if they had.

On the last Tuesday in November, a woman in a navy cardigan with a volunteer badge clipped to it sat down two chairs away from him with a coffee in each hand.

"You're the carpenter," she said.

He looked up. Red hair pinned up in a loose knot, with a few strands falling around her face. A face he'd seen somewhere.

"Rooney's," she said. "Back in October. My friend's birthday. You were at the bar with the funny one." She smiled. "I'm Celeste. I volunteer on Angela's floor." She held out one of the coffees. "I didn't know how you take it, so I guessed black. You look like a black-coffee guy."

He was. He took it.

She didn't ask about Angela. She looked him in the eye. No one had done that in weeks. She said, "How are *you* doing?"

He opened his mouth to say *fine*. What came out was, "I don't know."

She nodded. "That's allowed."

That was all. She quoted no scripture and said nothing of God's plan. Angela's church friends treated him like a project, and Kambria treated him like a lost cause. Celeste did neither. She stayed ten minutes, talked about nothing, laughed at his one bad joke, and returned to the floor.

It wasn't until she was gone that he realized he had told her about his father. He never told anyone about his father.

Two weeks later, she came again. And at the session after that.

On the third visit, she told him she had looked up his name. "Ezra means help," she said. "Did you know that? You were named to be a help. But who helps you?" Ezra snorted. But she only smiled and laid two fingers on his wrist, right over his father's stopped watch, and left them there longer than she needed to.

"Everything that breaks is waiting to be repaired," she said. "That's the whole secret. Nobody has to die for you. You climb. You just have to let yourself want something again."

He didn't believe in any of it. He'd grown up under a man who quoted the Bible at the deacons' table every Sunday and drank it all away every Friday night, and some old reflex in him recoiled from the talk of light and the little gold tree at her throat. But sitting there in the gray vinyl chair, with her fingers resting on his wrist, he did not move his arm.

What he could not shake was the question. *Who helps you?* He had asked it of himself once, in a cold back stairwell at Coretta Elementary, with his knees pulled up, and worked out the answer alone. No one. He had gone on giving the same answer for thirty years, and it had cost him a great deal, and he had yet to hear it spoken aloud.

He started noticing, without meaning to, when the elevator doors opened.

He told himself it was nothing. A kind woman being kind. That was all.

\* \* \*

On the first Saturday in December, the infusion center held its holiday open house, and Jalen brought his cello. Mr. Hart, the retired violist who had taught him since he was nine, came with him and brought his viola, and played a quiet harmony underneath him.

Jalen was sixteen, thin as a bow stick, and painfully shy, and he set up in the corner by the window without looking at anyone. The nurses had hung paper snowflakes from the ceiling. Mr. Harold wore a reindeer sweater. Angela, in her soft purple scarf, was partway through her chemotherapy. Purple had always been her favorite color.

Jalen drew the bow across the strings, and every conversation in the room stopped mid-word.

He played "Amazing Grace." He played it unhurried, exactly as it was written, and the deep, warm voice of the cello filled the bright room and seemed to fill the hallway beyond it, because nurses began drifting to the doorway one by one and stopping there. Rosa put down her knitting. Mr. Harold took off his reading glasses and pressed his thumb and finger against his eyes.

And from her chair, thin and bright in a borrowed sweater, Angela began to sing.

*Amazing grace, how sweet the sound, that saved a wretch like me...*

Her voice was thin from the chemo. It cracked on the high notes. She sang anyway. By the third verse, half the room was singing with her, and Kambria couldn't sing at all.

When the song was over, nobody clapped. It was not a song to clap after. Jalen sat with his bow resting on his knee, and then, almost to himself, he began to play another piece.

Kambria had never heard it before. It began low, on the cello's deepest string, slow and grieving. It climbed a little, searching, then fell back. Climbed again, a few notes higher this time, held there, trembling.

Then it stopped. Not ended; stopped. In the middle of a phrase, unfinished.

"What was that?" Angela asked, hushed.

Jalen flushed to the tips of his ears. "Nothing. Something I'm working on."

"It's beautiful. What's it called?"

"It's got a name. I'm just not telling anybody yet." He hesitated. "It doesn't have an ending yet either. I can't figure out where it goes."

Angela looked at her son, and Kambria kept that look with her ever after.

"It'll come," she said. "When it does, play it for your father."

Across the room, Mr. Hart sat with his viola across his knee. He caught Jalen's eye and nodded once, as he did at lessons whenever the boy played true.

Later, while the nurses were taking down the paper snowflakes, Kambria saw Angela beckon him over to her recliner. The old man bent low to hear her. Angela asked him a question, and he smiled and nodded.

"He blows a ram's horn at his church every Easter, at the sunrise service," Angela told her when he had gone. "A shofar. He brought it home from Jerusalem when the orchestra played there." She looked across the room at Jalen, who was loosening his bow with his head down. "I asked him to take us this Easter, if I'm still able to go. I want my boy to hear what it's going to sound like."

Kambria didn't have to ask what she meant. They had read it together at the dinner table more times than either of them could count. *…for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.* (1 Corinthians 15:52)

\* \* \*

On the second Tuesday of December, Kambria went out to the vending machines and stopped short in the doorway of the waiting room.

Celeste was sitting beside him again. She had been stopping by the waiting room on her breaks for weeks now; Kambria had seen her once or twice and told herself it was kindness.

She had two coffees, one in each hand, and she was holding one out to him, and Ezra was taking it. She was murmuring, low and warm, and leaning in a little. She leaned in toward everyone. And Ezra was laughing.

Kambria hadn't heard him laugh since the morning of the clippers. Before that, she couldn't remember. It was a tired, surprised laugh.

Celeste laid her hand on his forearm, lightly, just for a moment. She did that with everyone.

Then she took it away.

Kambria stopped at the threshold with her coins in her hand and felt the same dread she got at her bench when a sample she expected to be clean came back dirty.

She went back inside without her soda and said nothing. There was nothing to say yet. A volunteer had brought a tired man a cup of coffee. That was all.

But Celeste was not looking at Ezra as she looked at the patients. There had been hunger in her face. Kambria had seen it before, on other women in other waiting rooms.

But when she sat back down beside Angela's recliner, Angela was looking past her, through the glass doors and down the hallway, to where the corner of the waiting room was just visible. Her face was calm. Her hands were folded on the blanket over her knees, and her lips were moving. She was praying, and Kambria knew without asking that she was praying for both of them.

Angela said nothing either.
