That night, after Ezra and the children were asleep, Angela sat alone at the dinner table in her purple scarf and opened the black notebook. She turned past the pages she had already filled, past the signs and the dates and the verses she and Kambria had copied out together, to a fresh page.

At the top she wrote: *Proverbs 7.*

Beneath it, after a pause, she wrote her husband's name.

Then she bowed her head over the page.

"Father," she whispered, "he's tired and he's hurting, and she knows it. Don't let him walk through that door. Protect his mind and his ear gates, Lord, and lead him in the paths of righteousness, whatever it costs me." She was quiet a long moment. "And her too. Somebody sent her. Let her be found."

## Chapter 4: For Ezra, When You're Ready

> *And Israel stretched out his right hand, and laid it upon Ephraim's head, who was the younger, and his left hand upon Manasseh's head, guiding his hands wittingly; for Manasseh was the firstborn.* — Genesis 48:14

**Word study: *wittingly* — שָׂכַל** Hebrew *sakal* (Strong's H7919). To act wisely, with insight, knowing exactly what you are doing. Old Jacob was nearly blind, but he crossed his arms on purpose, and the younger son received the greater blessing.

The old man Jacob was dying, and his eyes were dim with age, so that he could not see. Joseph brought his two sons to the bedside, and the old man reached out for them in the dark. He found their heads with his trembling hands and rested them there, crossing his arms so that his right hand lay on the younger boy, and he blessed them. When he had finished blessing all his children, he gathered up his feet into the bed, and yielded up the ghost, and was gathered unto his people. (Genesis 48:10–16; 49:33)

\* \* \*

For a while that spring, it looked like they had won.

Angela finished her last round of chemotherapy on an overcast Tuesday in February. The nurses on the sixth floor lined the hallway and clapped while she rang the brass bell by the door, three times. Mr. Harold, Angela's friend from the recliner next to hers, cheered loudest. Kambria cried. Ezra stood at the end of the hallway in his work jacket and clapped along with everyone else, and when Angela turned and looked for him, he gave her a small, proud nod. It was the closest he had let her see him come to the infusion room in all those months.

She had surgery in March. Radiation in April. And on the first warm day of May, her oncologist, Dr. Sandoval, came into the exam room smiling and said the words they had been praying for, or that Angela had been praying for: *no evidence of disease.*

In the parking garage afterward, Ezra sat behind the wheel of his truck with both hands on it and didn't start the engine. Angela watched him and waited.

"Honey?"

"Give me a second," he said. His voice was rough. He kept his face turned toward the window so she wouldn't see his eyes, and she let him have that.

That summer was the best they'd had in years. Angela's hair came back soft and curly, a shade darker than before. They took the kids to the Outer Banks for a week, and Ezra taught five-year-old Mia to jump the waves while Angela watched from under an umbrella, laughing. Jalen, seventeen now and nearly as tall as his father, brought his cello and practiced on the porch of the rental house every evening at sunset. The unfinished melody had grown longer. It climbed higher now before it fell back. Ezra caught himself listening to it from inside the kitchen, and once, when Jalen hit a high note and held it, Ezra almost went out to tell him it was good. But he didn't.

On their last afternoon a storm came in off the ocean. They waited it out on the porch, all four of them, and watched the rain blow sideways across the dunes. When it passed, the sun came out low behind the house, and Mia jumped off the bench and pointed.

A rainbow stood over the water, the whole arch of it, from one end of the beach to the other. Above it was a second one, fainter.

"Mama! Two of them!"

Angela took Mia's hand and walked her down the wet boardwalk to the sand. Ezra followed with his coffee. Jalen stayed on the porch, but he set the cello down to look.

"You know what that is?" Angela knelt so her face was level with Mia's. "That's God keeping a promise. After the flood, He put His bow in the clouds and told Noah, every time you see this, I remember."

"Remember what?"

"That He keeps His word, baby. Every single time."

Mia thought about that. Then a butterfly came across the dune grass, dark, with a purple shine on its wings when the light caught them, and it landed on Angela's knee. Mia held her breath.

"Purple," she whispered. "That's your color."

"It sure is."

"Where did it come from?"

So Angela told her. She told her about the caterpillar that eats and eats, and then hangs itself up and wraps itself in a little case and goes still. "It looks like it died," she said. "Anybody walking by would think so. But it didn't. It was waiting. And when the time came, it came out new, with wings."

Mia looked at her mother's hair, short and dark and curly, and then back at the butterfly.

"Like you," she said. "You came out new."

Angela laughed, and then she stopped laughing, and pressed a knuckle under each eye. She pulled Mia into her lap. The butterfly opened and closed its wings twice, then lifted off and went out over the water toward the rainbow, and Mia waved at it until she couldn't see it anymore.

Ezra stood a few steps behind them in the wet sand. He was happy. Then he saw the back of Angela's neck, thin under the new curls, and he was afraid. He said nothing.

\* \* \*

In August, Angela's back began to hurt.

She blamed the beach chairs at first, and then the new mattress, and then her age. She told no one for three weeks. When she finally told Kambria, Kambria drove her to the hospital that same afternoon for scans.

The cancer was back. It was in her spine, her hips and her liver. Dr. Sandoval sat down across from them in the small consultation room, which was how Ezra knew before the doctor even spoke. Doctors only sat down for the worst news.

"Stage four," Dr. Sandoval said, her voice low and even. "We can treat it. We can buy time. But I want to be honest with you both about what we're treating toward."

Angela nodded. She was calm. She reached across the space between the chairs and took the doctor's hand. "Thank you for not dressing it up, Doctor," Angela said. She held the doctor's hand in both of hers. "I would rather know. Now tell me how we spend the time."

Ezra stood up, walked out of the room, and went down six flights of stairs to the parking garage. He sat in his truck for an hour and hammered the steering wheel with his fist until his knuckles were bruised purple. He didn't cry. He couldn't. Something in him had locked shut a long time ago, the day an Army carton came home to Old Ferry Road with his father's things in it, and his father's watch among them, stopped at 3:17. The watch had been on his wrist since he was sixteen. The carton sat on the shelf over his workbench, behind the paint cans, where he did not have to look at it.

When he finally went back upstairs, Angela was sitting in the waiting room with her purse on her lap, waiting for him. She didn't ask where he'd been. She just stood up, slipped her hand through his arm, and said, "Let's go home, honey. Let's go home and tell the kids."

\* \* \*

By October, the hospice nurses had set up a hospital bed in the living room, by the big back window that looked out on the yard and the studio. Angela had asked for that spot. She wanted to see the leaves turn, she said. She wanted to hear Jalen practice.

And the people came.

They came every day, all day, until Ezra lost count. Pastor Grant came every morning with his worn Bible and his pocket calendar, and told the family plainly what each day was likely to bring. Teachers from Angela's school came with casseroles. Her old class sent a box of handmade cards so heavy the mail carrier had to bring it to the door. Rosa from the infusion center came with a knitted blanket. Lionel Hart, Jalen's teacher, came every evening after school and went straight out to the studio, and some nights Ezra could hear the two of them out there until late, the cello and the viola, playing for her through the open window. Kambria came every single evening after work and stayed until Angela fell asleep.

And every time someone came, Ezra watched his wife do the same thing.

She prayed for them.

She was weaker every week. By the end of October she could barely lift her head off the pillow. But when a visitor sat down beside the bed, Angela would ask them one question, "What can I pray about for you?", and then she would close her eyes and do it, out loud, by name, while they sat there with their coats still on.

She prayed for Pastor Grant's arthritis and his son in the Navy, while she was the one dying. She prayed a young teacher through a crying jag about a classroom she couldn't control. Elijah, Ezra's oldest friend, the man who joked his way through every hard thing in his life, sat down beside the bed with his cap in his lap, and Angela asked him her question, and Elijah opened his mouth to make a joke, and nothing came out. She prayed for him anyway. Ezra watched from the kitchen doorway as Elijah bowed his head and wept into his cap. She prayed over Lionel Hart, low and urgent, and the old man closed his eyes and nodded, and nodded again.

One morning, Pastor Grant found Ezra in the kitchen afterward, pouring coffee he wasn't going to drink. The old minister leaned against the counter and shook his head, a bemused smile on his face.

"You know what the Book of James says?" he asked, his voice low. "'Is any sick among you? let him call for the elders of the church; and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord…' (James 5:14)" He nodded toward the living room. "That's why I come every morning, son. I'm the elder. I'm supposed to be praying over her." He let out a soft laugh. "And every single morning, she prays over me."

Ezra didn't answer. He stared down into his coffee.

"Thirty-five years I've been a pastor," Pastor Grant went on. "I've sat at a lot of deathbeds. I've never seen anybody less sick than that woman in there. Her body is failing. But her soul is the healthiest thing in this house." He rested a hand on Ezra's shoulder. "'…though our outward man perish, yet the inward man is renewed day by day.' (2 Corinthians 4:16) That's her. She's not the sick one here."

He didn't say who was. He didn't have to. He squeezed Ezra's shoulder once and went out to his car, and Ezra stood alone in the kitchen.

He was the one with the strong back and the clean blood test at his last physical. And standing there with his coffee gone cold, listening to his dying wife pray over a crying stranger in the next room, he thought of his father at Pilgrim Rest, raising holy hands on Sunday morning that he would raise against his mother by Friday night. And the woman who was dying had been praying for his healing every day of their life together.

He remembered the dinner table: her head bowed over every meal for years, her left hand resting open on the cloth beside his plate. He had never once covered it. He'd told himself it was a church thing. His father's thing. And she had never once taken it back.

\* \* \*

On a Sunday in early November, Ezra's mother came.

Loretta was seventy now, with a voice that had sung alto in church choirs for fifty years. She had prayed for her son every morning, and especially the year his father left for the war and never came back. Ezra loved her, and he let most of her phone calls go to voicemail, and they both knew why.

She asked him to wait in the kitchen. He was surprised, but he went.

Through the doorway he watched his mother sit down beside Angela's bed and lean close to the pillow. Then she spoke too low for Ezra to hear.

Angela listened. Tears ran down her face. She nodded, and then she did something Ezra would see again on the nights he couldn't sleep. She picked the black notebook up off her lap, the one she wrote in every night, and pressed it against her chest with both arms.

When his mother came into the kitchen, Ezra asked her what it was.

Loretta looked at him. Grief was in her face, and an older thing under the grief. "Something between me and her," she said. "And between you and God, when you're ready."

She put her hand on his cheek. She hadn't done that since he was a boy. Then she picked up her handbag and went home.

\* \* \*

Two days later, on a cold, clear Tuesday afternoon, Angela asked for him.

The kids were at school. The hospice nurse had stepped out to the porch. The house was quiet except for the furnace and the slow tick of the kitchen clock. Ezra pulled a chair up beside the bed and sat down, and Angela turned her head on the pillow and studied him in silence. She was so thin now. Her eyes looked enormous in her face.

Then she reached under the blanket and drew out the black notebook and held it out to him with both hands.

It was heavy. The cover swung back an inch as he took its weight, and he saw a page of her round hand with a single word printed small in the margin, Selah, and beside it a Strong's number, and a box drawn around one line. He shut it. He had seen her writing in it for a year, late at night at the dinner table, but he had never asked what was inside. On the front cover, under the two words she had written there the night she bought it, she had added three more:

*For Ezra, when you're ready.*

"What is it?" he whispered.

"Everything I want you to know." Her voice was barely above a whisper. "Everything Kambria and I found. Everything I prayed for you."

"I'll read it tonight."

"No." She shook her head. "Not tonight. Not because I asked you to." She pressed it against his chest and held it there until he closed his arms around it. "When you're ready, you'll know. And it will be there. And when you finally reach for Him, honey, He'll send you the Comforter. You won't have to carry any of it by yourself."

He wanted to say something. He wanted to tell her he would be ready, that he would read every word, that he would become whoever she'd been praying he would become. But the words stuck behind the locked door, and all he could do was nod.

That night, after the kids were asleep, he stood in the front hallway turning the notebook over and over in his hands. Then he opened the hall closet, reached up to the top shelf, and pushed it all the way to the back, behind the winter coats and a box of Christmas lights, where he wouldn't have to see it.

He closed the closet door. He stood with his hand on the doorknob. He knew he was putting away the last thing she had ever asked of him.

\* \* \*

Angela began to leave them the week before Thanksgiving.

Kambria saw it first. She had come straight from the lab, and she stood at the foot of the bed in her coat, listening to Angela's breathing. Years in hospital wards had taught her that sound, and Ezra watched her face change. She said nothing for a moment. Then she came and put her hand on his shoulder.

"It's going to be tonight," she said. "Maybe early morning. You should call your mother. And wake the kids if you want them here."

They sat with her through the night. Loretta came and sat by the window, praying under her breath with her eyes closed. Mia, five years old, fell asleep curled up at the foot of her mother's bed. Jalen sat in the corner with his cello and played barely louder than a whisper: an old setting of the hundred and twenty-first psalm at first, and then, near two in the morning, the melody that was his own. It climbed, searching. It fell back. It climbed again, higher than ever before, and held there, trembling, and stopped. It still didn't have an ending.

Toward morning, Kambria touched Ezra's arm and nodded toward the bed. Then she gathered up Loretta and Jalen and led them into the kitchen, and the room was empty except for Ezra and his wife and his sleeping daughter.

Angela's breathing had grown slow and shallow, with long pauses in between. Ezra sat down in the chair where a hundred visitors had sat, and kept his hands on his knees.

Then her hand moved on the blanket.

So weak he thought he'd imagined it. The fingers stirred, and uncurled, and lay open on the wool, turned toward him.

Ezra looked at it, and every grace he had ever sat through came down on him at once: the bowed heads, the open hand beside his plate, his own hands kept in his lap like evidence.

He took her hand in both of his.

Her fingers were cool and light as paper, and they closed. With whatever she had left, Angela held on.

He had cried once since he was eight years old, on the floor of a studio he built with his son, and never in front of her. It broke out of him now, all of it, and he bent over their hands with his shoulders shaking.

"I'm here," he whispered. "Angie. I'm right here."

He had no words for God. But from somewhere under thirty years of silence, from the front pew at Pilgrim Rest, the old words came up on their own, and he heard his own voice say them out loud, cracked down the middle, to the God he had refused at that table every night of their marriage.

"'*The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul…*'" (Psalm 23:1–3)

He lost the next line. He could not see.

Her lips moved. Her eyes stayed closed and her voice was only breath, but he bent close and heard her finish it for him.

"*…he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name's sake. Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me…*" (Psalm 23:3–4)

She drew one more breath and spent it on His name. "Jesus."

Then her eyes opened, once, and found him, and the smile started on one side, slow, the way it had at the fair with sugar on her fingers, and took its time getting to the other. It cost her everything. She gave it to him anyway.

They were the last words she said, and the last thing she gave him.

Her breathing slowed. It paused. He waited for the next breath, and waited, and it didn't come. Outside the big back window, the sky over the studio was beginning to pale. Mia slept on at the foot of the bed. In the kitchen, his mother was weeping into a dish towel.

Her fingers were still closed around his. He didn't move. He sat there with her hand in both of his until the window went from gray to white, as if, for as long as he held on, there was still something to hold.

\* \* \*

They buried her that week, on a cold, bright morning, beside the church where she had taught Sunday school for fifteen years.

The day began with Mia's hair.

Mia came downstairs in her black velvet dress with a comb in one hand and two yellow ribbons in the other and held them up to her father. Two puffs. Angela had done them every morning of her life: part down the middle, a dab of the coconut cream, two puffs high and even, a yellow ribbon on each. Ezra had watched it a thousand times from the kitchen doorway. He had never done it himself.

He tried. His big hands, that could set a door plumb by eye, could not make the parts come straight. The left puff came out lopsided and low. Mia looked at herself in the hall mirror and her chin began to shake, and she said, very quietly, "That's not how Mommy does it," and Ezra stood behind her with the comb in his hand and had nothing to say to that.

Kambria redid them in the church bathroom, kneeling on the tile in her good stockings, while Mia held perfectly still and watched her in the mirror to make sure she got it right.

The church was full. Angela's last class, fourth graders now, sat in the front rows on the left, in their winter coats, every one of them holding a card. A boy in the second row waved at the casket when they wheeled it in, a small, hopeful wave, and his teacher put her hand on his arm and he put his hand down.

Joe and Pat had driven down from Erie through the night. Joe sat on the aisle in a dark suit and a pressed checked shirt, his silver hair combed straight back, and he did not move once during the whole service. He looked at the casket the way he had looked at every joint Ezra ever cut in that house: as if he expected it to be true. Pat sat beside him in her small gold cross, and every few minutes she leaned her shoulder against his, and he let her.

Pastor Grant preached from Proverbs 31. He read it slowly. When he came to the twenty-eighth verse he stopped and looked up from the pulpit at the second pew.

"'*Her children arise up, and call her blessed.*'" (Proverbs 31:28)

Mia stood up.

She stood up on the pew in her velvet dress and her two yellow ribbons, because she was five, and the pastor had said *arise*, and she had always done what the Bible said. She stood there in front of three hundred people, waiting to be told what to say.

The whole church came apart. Somebody in the back let out a sound that wasn't a word. Pat put both hands over her mouth. Pastor Grant held on to the pulpit and couldn't go on, and for a long time the only sound in that sanctuary was grown people trying not to be heard.

Jalen reached up and took his sister around the waist and lifted her down into his lap, and held her there, with his chin on top of her head and the ribbons against his face, and stared straight ahead at the casket.

Ezra sat on the other side of them and did not move.

At the grave, Jalen played "Amazing Grace." He made it through the first verse and the second. On the third, *Through many dangers, toils, and snares*, the bow caught on the string and stopped, and he sat there on the folding chair in the cold with the cello against his knee and his face working, and could not find the note. Behind him, Mr. Hart lifted his viola and played the line, quietly, one bar, until Jalen found it again and took it back from him. He finished it alone.

When they lowered the casket, Mia pulled on Kambria's coat.

"It's cold down there," she said. "Mommy doesn't have her blanket."

Nobody answered her. Kambria knelt down on the frozen grass and held her, and Mia let herself be held, and kept watching the hole.

Ezra didn't cry at the grave. Elijah stood at the back with his cap crushed in his fist and not a joke in him, watching his friend's face, and later he told his own mother it was the worst thing he had ever seen: a man at his wife's funeral with a face like a house after the power's been cut.

\* \* \*

That night the house was full of food nobody had cooked and silence nobody could fill.

Mia would not go to bed. Ezra carried her up at nine, still in the velvet dress, the yellow ribbons crushed flat from the car seat, and she climbed out of his arms and knelt down on the rug beside her bed, the way she had every night of her life, and folded her hands on the quilt.

Then she looked up at him and waited.

Every night it had been Angela down there on the rug beside her. Two sets of folded hands. *Now I lay me down to sleep*, and then the long list: Daddy, Jalen, Grandma Loretta, Grandma Pat and Pop Joe, Miss Kambria, Mr. Walt, the boy at school who cries, the dog on Otis Street. And last, every night, Angela laid her hand on top of Mia's head and blessed her with the old words from Numbers, the priest's blessing, and kissed her where the two puffs met and said, *Goodnight, my love.* Ezra had heard it a thousand times through the wall. He had never once come in.

"Mommy always started it," Mia said. "So it's your turn."

He knelt. His knees cracked on the floorboards. He looked at her small brown palms pressed together, the knuckles still sticky from the funeral cake, and he opened his mouth.

Nothing.

He tried again. The words were right there, *Now I lay me*, five words, a child could say them, his child said them, and they would not come out of him. They sat in his throat like a stone in a pipe.

Mia waited. She was so patient. She had learned that from her mother too.

Ezra leaned forward and kissed her on the forehead, right at the part where the two puffs met, and when he pulled back his face was wet and he couldn't stop it.

"Maybe you can do a prayer for me instead, baby," he whispered.

Mia looked at him for a moment, very seriously. Then she got up off her knees.

He was still kneeling, so for once they were the same height. She stepped in close and reached up and laid her small hand flat on top of his head, the way her mother had laid hers on Mia's every night of her life. Her palm was warm and a little sticky. He felt it there, and the air would not go down.

"*The LORD bless thee, and keep thee,*" Mia said.

She said it in Angela's rhythm. Not her own sing-song: her mother's. The same pauses in the same places, the same little lift on *keep*.

"*The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.*" (Numbers 6:24–26)

Then she leaned forward and kissed him on the top of the head, right where her hand had been, and said, in her mother's voice, "Goodnight, my love."

Something gave way in his chest like a floor.

He got to his feet somehow. He tucked her in with hands that would not hold still. He walked out. He pulled her door shut behind him and stood in the dark hallway with his fingers on the knob.

Through the wood he heard her start her list, alone, slower than usual. Jalen. Grandma Loretta. Grandma Pat and Pop Joe. Then a long pause.

"And God, please help my daddy. He forgot the words."

He let go of the knob.

He went down the stairs in the dark. The hospice company had come for the bed while they were at the cemetery, and where it had stood for seven weeks there was a rectangle pressed into the living-room carpet, four deep dents from the wheels, the pile flattened pale in the shape of where she had been. He stood at the edge of it and could not step in.

He took out his phone and found it without looking: a video, nine seconds long, that Angela had sent him from the sixth floor during her fourth round of chemo. He had been sitting in the waiting room at the time, in the gray vinyl chairs. She had known exactly where he was, and exactly why he couldn't come in. He had watched it once, felt something catch in his throat, and put the phone face down on his knee. He had never answered her.

He cast it to the big television across from the rectangle in the carpet, turned off every lamp in the house, knelt on the floor in front of the screen, and pressed play.

Her face filled the dark room, close and a little blurry, lit gold by the lamp beside the infusion recliner. Her glasses had slid down her nose. She was wearing the soft purple scarf. Behind her, faintly, Mr. Harold grumbled at his crossword.

"Hey, honey," she said. "It's me. I know you're out there worrying. Stop it. I'm okay." She tipped her head and gave him the look over her glasses she gave her third graders when they were being silly. "God's got me. And I've got you." Then the smile broke, wide and bright and completely unafraid, starting on one side and taking its time getting to the other, and she laughed, and her hand came toward the camera, and the video ended on her face in the middle of that laugh.

Nine seconds.

He played it again. Again. On the fourth time through, the thing in his chest that had held since the hospice bed let go all at once. When her hand came toward the camera he leaned forward and pressed his face against the glass, and for one blurred second her hand was on his cheek, and Ezra Patterson broke open like a dropped jar.

He cried for her smile. He cried for every August and every paper plate of fried dough. He cried for every grace he had sat through with his hands in his lap, for the one prayer he had managed at the very end when there was nothing left to give her, and for the five words he could not give his daughter tonight. He cried with his face against the cold screen until the glass was wet beneath his cheek and there was nothing left in him at all.

*Can you hear me, Angie?*

*I keep looking for you. I know you're gone. I stood at your grave this morning and watched them lower you down, and I still look for you. I hear a car door and think it's you home from school. I smell coffee and think you made it. I reach across the couch cushion for a hand that isn't there.*

*Since you left, I've been traveling somewhere I've never been before. I don't know what to call it. It's a shadowed country, and the roads all go down. There are signs along the way, and I've read them all. Grief. Then anger. Then a long road called Nothing, where I can't feel anything at all. The dark there has a weight to it, a pull, like gravity. It holds me down in the mornings. It won't let me get up. I keep walking, looking for you, but you're not here, Angie. I've looked everywhere. This isn't where you went.*

*I remember your hand on the blanket that last night. Opening. Reaching for me. I finally took it, and you held on. But I keep asking the same thing, over and over, in the dark.*

*Did you reach for my hand as I reached for yours? Or were you reaching for Someone else, Someone I couldn't see, standing on the other side of the bed?*

*And if you were, why won't He reach for me?*

A floorboard creaked behind him.

Mia stood at the foot of the stairs in her yellow nightgown with her teddy bear hanging from one hand, the ribbons gone, her hair loose. He could not tell how long she had been there. He made no move to wipe his face. She crossed the dark room in her bare feet, stepped right into the rectangle in the carpet without stopping, stood beside him, looked at the frozen picture of her mother, and said, "Play the part where she laughs."

He played it. Mia watched with her mouth a little open, and when Angela's hand came toward the camera, Mia lifted her own hand and laid it flat against the glass, over her mother's, beside his wet cheek. Neither of them spoke. When it ended she climbed into his lap, bear and all, and was asleep before it could start again, and he sat on the floor in the dark with her until his legs went numb.

At the top of the stairs, Jalen stood in his socks and watched them both. He didn't come down. After a while he went back to his room and closed the door very quietly, so his father would never know he had seen.

In the morning, before anyone was up, Ezra wiped his face off the television with his sleeve. A small handprint stayed low on the glass. He could not make himself clean it.

He carried his coffee down the front hallway and stopped in front of the closet. Behind it, on the top shelf, behind the winter coats, was her notebook, with his name on the cover in her hand. He did not open the door.

He would not reach to that shelf again for a year. And by the time he did, his children would be gone.

## Act 2 — The Fall

## Chapter 5: Red Sky

> *The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come.* — Joel 2:31

**Word study: *terrible* — יָרֵא** Hebrew *yare'* (Strong's H3372). To fear, to be afraid, to stand in awe. The day of the LORD is called terrible because it will make the whole earth afraid. It comes from the same root as the fear of the LORD, which is the beginning of wisdom. One fear comes too late. The other saves.

*…Stretch out thine hand toward heaven, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even darkness which may be felt. And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days: They saw not one another, neither rose any from his place for three days: but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.* (Exodus 10:21-23)

\* \* \*

After the funeral, the house went quiet in a way Ezra had never heard before. It was not empty. The kids were there. But nobody hummed in the kitchen anymore, nobody called up the stairs, and her gray cardigan stayed on the hook by the back door where she had hung it the last day she walked, because none of them could make themselves take it down. Ezra slept on the couch with the news on low and told the kids it was his back.

The news ran over him all night. A ceasefire in Ukraine that lasted two days. A thin, dark-haired man in a gray suit standing behind the chairman's chair at the Organization for World Peace, saying nothing. A new flu, and white tents in hospital parking lots. Phoenix rationing water. Fields in California left unplanted. None of it had anything to do with him. Angela would have said all of it did.

The grief came in pieces. His hand reaching across the cushion for her every morning before he remembered. Twelve cups of her peach yogurt lined up in the refrigerator, because he kept buying it. Her phone, still plugged in on the counter, lighting up with Jalen's text from the school lot, *can u get me at 4 today*, and twenty minutes later, *nvm*. And Ezra at two in the morning, typing to it himself, *Where are you. Come home. I'm sorry*, lying in the dark while it buzzed against the counter ten feet away, once for every message.

The week before Christmas it went down to nine degrees. At eleven at night he drove to the church, climbed the chained cemetery gate, and spread his heavy canvas work coat over the frozen mound of her grave, tucking the edges into the clay with his bare hands. *It's cold down there. She doesn't have her blanket.* He left it there. He never went back for it.

By New Year's his belt was three notches tighter, and the studio windows had been dark for a month. Jalen had not touched the cello since the funeral.

One evening in February, he came in from the garage and found Mia alone in the front hall, standing by the door in the last ashen light from the window beside it.

She was wearing her mother's shoes. They were Angela's black Sunday shoes, with the low square heels, and Mia's small feet were lost inside them. She stood on the old pine floorboards with her head bowed, the front of her dress bunched in both fists against her chest, studying her feet with great seriousness.

"Baby," he said. "What are you doing?"

She kept her eyes down. "Practicing."

"Practicing what?"

"Walking where Mommy walked." She took a step in the big shoes, and then another, and the heels knocked on the boards. "They're too big right now," she told him. "But Mommy said I'll grow into them."

Ezra had to hold on to the door frame. He didn't trust himself to speak, so he didn't. He stood and watched his daughter walk the length of the hall in her mother's shoes, one slow knock at a time, with her head bowed the whole way, and he thought he had never seen anything so small look so certain of where it was going.

On the wall beside her hung the small framed drawing he had bought on one of their anniversaries, at a fancy gallery downtown. The man at the door was holding a tray of champagne. Angela had stopped in front of this one and gone quiet, and he had paid for it before they left. The next weekend she made him hang it three times. "Higher. No, lower. Is that level to you?" He had walked past it every day since without once really looking. He looked up at it now: a little girl standing in her mother's shoes. In the bottom right corner, it was signed by the artist, Michael Banks.

\* \* \*

Kambria came by every Sunday after church with a casserole and the mail. "Pastor Grant asked about you again," she said at the door every time. "We'd love to see you there, Ezra." And every week he said, "Maybe next Sunday," and they both knew he meant never.

On the counter, under a pile of unopened sympathy cards, lay the one card he had opened. A pressed lavender flower on the front, and inside, in looping handwriting: *Thinking of you and holding space for your grief. You don't have to carry this alone. — Celeste.* And a phone number. He hadn't called it. He hadn't thrown it away, either.

\* \* \*

On the first Saturday in March, Mia made dinner.

She had been planning it all week with her grandmother. It was boxed macaroni and cheese and hot dogs cut into coins, with a bowl of grapes in the middle, and she had set three places with real napkins, folded into triangles as Angela used to fold them. Jalen came in from the studio and sat down without a word. Ezra sat at the head of the table, in front of a plate he had no appetite for, and felt his stomach tighten at the sight of the folded napkins.

Then Mia bowed her head, and reached out both her hands.

She did it exactly as her mother used to. Her right hand went to Jalen, and he took it. Her left hand lay open on the table, palm up, reaching toward her father.

Ezra stared at it.

Twelve years he had left that hand lying open on the table. He thought of the hospice blanket, and how long it had taken him to finally reach, and how short a time he'd had to hold on.

He reached out and took his daughter's small hand in his.

Mia squeezed. Across the table, Jalen looked at their two hands, and then at his plate, and held his sister's a little tighter.

"Dear Jesus," Mia said in her clear, careful voice. "Thank You for the macaroni. Thank You for Daddy and Jalen and Grandma. Please tell Mommy we miss her. And please help Daddy not be sad. Amen."

"Amen," said Jalen.

Ezra could not say it. His throat had closed. But he held on to Mia's hand long after the prayer was over, until she giggled and said, "Daddy, I need it to eat," and he let her go.

Afterward, while she carried her plate to the sink, he stood at the refrigerator with the dish towel in his hand. The calendar there was in Jalen's handwriting, and one square was circled twice in red marker: *Thursday, April 16. RECITAL. 7 PM.* "You're coming, right, Daddy?" Mia said from the sink, not turning around. "Jalen said you're coming."

"I'll be there," Ezra said.

She held up her little finger over her shoulder without looking, and he hooked his own around it.

\* \* \*

That night, he fell asleep on the couch earlier than usual.

The house had gone quiet for the night. The kids were in bed. Out in the studio, Jalen had been playing late again; he played late most nights now, and the last thing Ezra heard before he drifted off was the melody: the slow, grieving one, low on the cello's deepest string. It had changed since Angela died. It went lower now, darker, before it began to climb. And it climbed higher than it ever had, searching, reaching, until it held one long, trembling note at the very top.

Then it stopped. It still didn't have an ending.

Ezra slept.

When he opened his eyes, the room was red.

Not dim. Not dark. *Red.* A deep, glowing crimson light filled the living room from wall to wall, pouring through the big front window and lying across the carpet and the couch and his own hands. It colored everything: the lamp, the television, the pale rectangle on the carpet where the hospital bed had stood.

And it was silent. Completely silent. No furnace. No traffic. No cello.

Ezra eased himself upright. He could hear his own pulse. He got up off the couch, and walked to the front window, and looked out.

The sky was red.

The whole sky, from one edge of the world to the other, was the color of blood. And hanging in the middle of it, low and enormous above the rooftops across the street, was the moon. It was huge, bigger than he had ever seen it, and red too, a deep, smoldering red. Its light lay over the street and the houses and the bare trees, and nothing moved anywhere.

He stood at the window, and he felt it.

He knew what it was, and he would not name it. There was no voice and there were no words, only a pull on his heart, steady and strong. Out there beyond the red sky and the burning moon, Someone was looking straight at him, through the glass, through the night, through every locked door inside him, and calling him by name.

*Ezra.*

He took a step back from the window.

*No,* he thought. And then, out loud, his voice hoarse in the red silence: "No."

He woke up on the couch.

The living room was dim and colorless and ordinary. The television was murmuring to itself. Through the front window, the sky over the rooftops was black and full of stars, and a thin white moon hung over the trees, small and pale and nothing at all like the thing in his dream.

The couch cushion under him was damp. His hands were shaking. He sat forward on the couch with his head in his hands and pulled air in through his teeth until his pulse let go of him.

A dream. Just a dream. Grief did that to people. He'd read about it somewhere.

But he couldn't get back to sleep.

\* \* \*

Sometime after three he gave up and went upstairs.

He hadn't been in their bedroom in months, getting his clothes from the laundry room so he wouldn't have to. Now he stood in the unlit doorway, and the room still smelled faintly of her, of the lavender lotion she kept on the nightstand. He turned on the small lamp by her side of the bed.

Her Bible was there, on the nightstand, where it had always been. Worn soft at the edges, the gold letters almost rubbed off the cover. No one had touched it since before the hospital bed came. Ezra had walked past it a hundred times and never let himself look at it.

He picked it up because the dream had shaken him, and because it was the only thing in the room that was still hers. He sat on her side of the bed with it in his lap and thought of her hands holding it every Thursday night for six years at the dinner table.

He flipped through it and found the page quickly, a place that had been opened many times before.

A sheet of paper lay tucked between the pages, folded in half, soft with age.

He unfolded it.

It was a child's drawing in crayon. A house: their house, with its crooked porch light. Above it, a sky colored red from edge to edge, the crayon laid on in thick, waxy strokes. At the center of the red was a small yellow circle, with light pouring out of it. And in the window, Mia had drawn a small rectangle, and inside it, a brown shape lying on a couch.

Beneath it, in Angela's neat, round handwriting, it said:

*Mia, age 4. "That's what the sky does when Jesus is almost here. That's Daddy on the couch. He doesn't see it because he's sleeping."*

Ezra's hands began to shake again.

He looked at the date Angela had written in the corner. It was from more than a year ago, before the diagnosis, before the chemo, before any of it. Before the couch became his bed.

He bent over the page he had found. One verse was underlined, twice, in Angela's blue ink, the same blue as the spiral notebook she kept for Israel, and beside it, in the margin, she had written a single word: *Ezra.*

*The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come. (Joel 2:31)*

He sat on his wife's side of the bed until the sky outside the window began to lighten, holding the drawing in one hand and her Bible in the other, and he did not move.

On his wrist, his father's watch still said 3:17. It had not moved in all these years.

Neither had he.

\* \* \*

The phone rang at seven.

He let it go to voicemail. It rang again. On the third time he answered it, because only one person on earth called three times in a row.

"It's my birthday today," Loretta said. No hello. "Seventy-one. I'm not asking you, Ezra. I'm telling you. You're going to put those children in that truck and drive out here, and you're going to eat at my table, and you're going to help me make it."

He opened his mouth.

"Angela's pizza," his mother said, and her voice broke on the name and came right back. "The one I taught her. I've got the yeast. You bring yourself."

The line went dead.

Ezra sat on the edge of the bed with the drawing in his lap and the phone in his hand and the sky going pale in the window. For the first time since the funeral, there was somewhere he had to be.

## Chapter 6: The Deacon

> *Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.* — Colossians 3:21

**Word study: *discouraged* — ἀθυμέω** Greek *athumeō* (Strong's G120). To lose heart, to be broken in spirit. It is built from *a-*, without, and *thumos*, the passion and fire inside a person. A child who is provoked long enough does not only grow angry. Something in him goes out.

*Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD… And if any man said unto him, Let them not fail to burn the fat presently, and then take as much as thy soul desireth; then he would answer him, Nay; but thou shalt give it me now: and if not, I will take it by force. Wherefore the sin of the young men was very great before the LORD: for men abhorred the offering of the LORD.* (1 Samuel 2:12, 16-17)

\* \* \*

On Sunday, his mother's seventy-first birthday, Ezra put his children in the truck and drove out to Cedar Hollow, which he had not done since the funeral.

The city fell away behind them. The houses got farther apart. Past the last stoplight the county road gave up and turned to gravel, and Mia pressed her face to the window and counted cows out loud, and Jalen, in the back seat, took one earbud out to listen to her. It was the first time in a month Ezra had heard either of them sound like a child.

Loretta Patterson still lived in the white frame house on Old Ferry Road in Cedar Hollow where Ezra had grown up. The porch steps sagged in the same place. The chicken coop out back still leaned toward the creek. Inside, the plastic runner in the hallway was the same, and over the couch the same framed photograph still hung: Deacon Calvin Patterson in his Sunday suit, a white carnation in the lapel, one big hand on an open Bible at the deacons' table at Pilgrim Rest.

Ezra had stopped looking at that picture the year he was eight. He walked past it now without turning his head.

The house smelled of yeast. In the kitchen a big blue bowl sat on the counter under a damp dish towel, and the little television by the bread box was on with the sound low: Bishop Roland Sterling, twenty thousand members and a billboard over the Beltway, smiling into the camera, saying, "Sow your seed into this ministry today, and watch what God does with your harvest." Loretta reached past it and clicked it off without looking.

"Jalen, baby, take your sister out to the coop. There's eggs need finding." She waited until the back door banged. Then she pulled the towel off the bowl. The dough had risen high and pale and domed, pressing at the rim.

"Wash your hands," she said.

"Mama, I—"

"I'm seventy-one years old today, Ezra Calvin Patterson. Wash your hands."

He washed his hands.

She dumped the dough onto the floured counter, and it sighed as it went down. She showed him once: heel of the hand, push it away, fold it back, quarter turn. "Not like you're sanding it. Like it's alive. Because it is." He did it wrong. She slapped flour on the counter and made him do it again. Hands that could plane a door to a thirty-second of an inch did not know what to do with something that gave back.

"This was hers," Loretta said, watching him work. "Angela's. Friday nights. She called me the first year you were married, said, 'Mama Loretta, Ezra says nobody makes pizza like his mother, and I need to know what he means.' I drove into the city with a bag of flour and this bowl. She had flour to her elbows and she was laughing the whole time. Every Friday after that, for twelve years, that girl made this dough." She pushed a strand of gray hair back with her wrist. "She told me you never once said it was as good as mine."

"It was better."

"I know it was. You should have told her."

He kneaded. The dough went smooth under his hands, warm and soft, and the kitchen was quiet except for the slap and push of it and the chickens complaining out back and Mia's voice rising, *I found one! Jalen, I found one!*

"Put your weight in it," Loretta said. Then, in the same voice, without looking up from the pan she was oiling: "You've been dreaming."

His hands stopped.

"Don't stop. It'll tighten up." She set the pan down. "Your daddy dreamed too, at the end. Did you know that? Before he went over. He'd wake up at night shouting."

Ezra pressed the heel of his hand into the dough and pushed it away and folded it back. He looked through the doorway into the front room, at the photograph over the couch.

"Mama," he said. "Was he ever, at home, the man everybody thought he was at church?"

Loretta wiped her palms on her apron. She let the question sit, the way she always had. She folded the dish towel in half, and in half again.

"No, baby," she said finally. "Not one day of his life." She took the dough from under his hands, gently, and turned it once, and gave it back to him. "Keep working it. I'll tell you while it rises."

\* \* \*

Calvin Patterson worked for the railroad. Six days a week he left the house before dawn in his steel-toed boots and his gray work jacket and walked to the rail yard at Hollis Junction, where he coupled freight cars and threw switches in the bitter weather and came home after dark smelling of creosote and diesel. He was strong, and he was good at the work, and the men on his crew were a little afraid of him.

On Sundays he was Deacon Patterson.

Pilgrim Rest Church sat at the crossroads in Cedar Hollow, a red-brick building with a white steeple and a sign out front with changeable letters. In 1988, when Ezra was six, the sign said: *HELL IS HOT. JESUS IS COMING. ARE YOU READY?*

On Sunday mornings the sanctuary was full. Four hundred people packed the pews in their best clothes, the women in wide hats, the men in three-piece suits, and the air was thick with perfume and heat. Ezra sat in the front pew in a clip-on tie that pinched his neck. His mother sang alto in the choir. And his father sat at the deacons' table below the pulpit, in the place of honor, with his Bible open in front of him. Beside the pulpit hung the number board, black felt with white slide-in numbers: the hymn across the top, the psalm for the day under it, and the verse beneath that. Ezra could find his place in the book by those numbers before he could read the words around them, and he found it faster than anyone in the pew.

Calvin Patterson was a big man with a big voice, and when he led devotion before the sermon, the building shook. He could quote scripture for an hour without once looking down at the Bible in front of him. He knew more of it by heart than the pastor did, and everyone said so. He lined out the old hymns in his deep, rough voice, and he prayed long and loud about sin, about drinking and lust and the fire waiting for anyone who didn't repent, and the congregation shouted back, "Pray, Deacon! Tell it!" At the end of every service, when the pastor called for the closing prayer, Calvin stood at the front and lifted both hands high, and four hundred people lifted theirs with him. Ezra lifted his too, when he was small. Then he learned what those same hands did behind the front door on Friday nights, after payday. When he was eight, sitting in the front pew, he slid his hands under his legs and sat on them through the whole closing prayer, and he promised himself he would never lift his hands to God in any church for as long as he lived. He never told anyone why. He had kept that promise ever since.

At six, in the front pew, Ezra was terrified of his father, and terrified of God, and could not have said which was which.

\* \* \*

After service, the deacons counted the offering in the church office, and the last one to count was always Calvin.

One Sunday when Ezra was seven, he went looking for his father to ask if he could have a soda from the fellowship hall, and the office door was open a crack. Through the gap he saw his father alone at the big wooden desk with the offering plates in front of him, counting stacks of bills. He watched his father take a thick fold of twenties off the top of one stack and slide it into the inside pocket of his suit jacket. Then another.

Calvin looked up and saw his son's face in the gap of the door.

He neither jumped nor looked ashamed. He stood up, walked over, opened the door, and looked down at Ezra without a flicker of expression.

"What you see in this office," he said, his voice low and pleasant, "stays in this office. You understand me?"

Ezra nodded. He didn't understand. But he never told anyone. Not his mother, not the deacons, not Angela. He carried it for all those years, the picture of his father's big hand sliding the church's money into his jacket while the choir was still singing in the next room.

\* \* \*

At home, the Deacon was a different man.

In Cedar Hollow, people called him a man of God. Church mothers brought him sweet potato pies. Men stopped him on the sidewalk to shake his hand and ask him to pray for their sons. The railroad gave him a plaque for twenty years without a lost day, and the church gave him another for service, and he hung them both in the front hallway where every visitor would see them. But behind the front door on Old Ferry Road, he was an unjust man. He bought himself new suits every spring and gave Loretta forty dollars a week for groceries and told her to make it stretch. He decided who was right in every argument, and it was always him. He never said he was sorry. When anything went wrong at the yard or at church, somebody at home paid for it. Loretta and Ezra lived with a man the four hundred people in the pews never met, and they knew better than to tell anyone.

What Calvin had at home was a bottle.

He kept it in the cabinet over the refrigerator, behind the cereal, where the church would never see it. On weeknights it was one glass, sometimes two, after supper. On Friday nights, after he cashed his check, he stopped at the liquor store out at Hollis Junction on the way home, and by the time his boots hit the front steps everyone in the house knew what kind of night it was going to be.

Some Fridays Calvin was so drunk he could not stand, let alone drive, and when the cupboards ran empty it was Ezra who went for the groceries, sitting on a stack of phone books in the cab of the truck, barely able to see over the steering wheel.

Calvin did not need a reason. Spilled milk was enough. A look was enough. Loretta's voice a little too loud on the phone was enough. He hit with his open hand first and then his fist, and he hit Loretta more than he hit Ezra, and when Ezra was old enough to stand between them, he hit Ezra for standing there.

And while he did it, he quoted scripture.

"'Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands,'" Calvin would say, breathing hard, slurring the words, while Loretta held her jaw at the sink. "'Children, obey your parents in the Lord: for this is right.' You hear me, kid? This is the Word of God."

Ezra heard him. He learned the verses before he learned to read, and he learned them with the back of a hand. He knew, even then, that his father had them wrong. No one who had sat through as many sermons as Ezra had could miss what his father always left out: *Husbands, love your wives… ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath… (Ephesians 5:25; 6:4)* Calvin never read that part out loud. To Ezra at eight, God was a big man with a loud voice who quoted the Bible while he hurt you. God took the money when he thought no one was looking. God was one man in front of the church and another man behind his own front door.

Later, after Calvin had passed out on the couch, Loretta would slip into Ezra's room in the dark. She would kneel by his bed and lay her cool hand on his face over the bruise and pray for him in a voice so low he could barely hear it. Some nights she cried while she prayed.

"Your daddy's sick, baby," she told him once. "The drink makes him sick."

Ezra lay there and let her pray. But he couldn't understand why she was praying to the same God his father quoted. It seemed to him like asking the man with the bottle to make the hurting stop.

School was no refuge, though he tried to make it one. Ezra carried the house with him through the doors every morning, folded small, the way he carried his lunch. He learned which shirts had sleeves long enough. He learned which mornings to say he had fallen off his bike. He learned that a teacher who bent down and asked, "Is everything all right at home?" wanted him to say yes, and he said yes, because the man whose name was on the plaque in the church hallway would be waiting on the other side of any other answer. Who would believe a boy over Deacon Patterson? Who in that whole neighborhood would even try?

He stopped wanting to be like the other children, and then he stopped trying to be near them. He ate lunch at the far end of the table, and after a while he ate it on the back stairwell, where nobody came. He quit going out to recess. He sat on the cold step with his knees pulled up and watched the other boys run, as if he were watching them through a window. Something gray settled on him that year and did not lift, and it did not lift on weekends either, because the weekend was Friday night. A boy that age should not have known the word *tired* the way he knew it.

There was no one to turn to. That was the thing he understood most clearly, long before he had the words for it. His mother was in the same house taking the same blows, and he would not add his weight to hers. The church mothers patted his head and told him what a blessing his daddy was. His teachers saw a quiet boy with good manners and no friends. And the only God he had ever been taught to call on sounded exactly like the man on the stairs. So he called on no one, and he got very good at it.

He had not yet read the psalm that described him, but it was already true of him. *I looked on my right hand, and beheld, but there was no man that would know me: refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul.* (Psalm 142:4) He only knew that he was a child and tired in a way that sleep did not touch.

There was one thing in that house that Calvin never managed to ruin, and it came out of the oven on Sunday mornings.

Loretta got up before dawn to make her dinner rolls, and by the time Ezra came down the stairs the whole house smelled of warm flour and butter. The kitchen windows were fogged. A dish towel lay over the pan, and under it the rolls sat in rows, golden-topped, shining where she had brushed them with butter. She never measured. She worked the dough with the heel of her hand, folded it and folded it again, and would never say how. Women at church asked her for the recipe every year at the fellowship dinner, and every year she smiled and said, "Some things you keep." When she tore one open for Ezra it came apart in flaky layers, soft and smooth and sweet with butter, and for as long as it lasted in his mouth he forgot to be afraid. Even Calvin ate them quietly, on those mornings, and said nothing at all.

Years afterward he would meet a verse that sounded to him like that kitchen. *O taste and see that the LORD is good: blessed is the man that trusteth in him.* (Psalm 34:8) He had tasted first. The trusting came much later, and it came slowly.

Whatever else that house taught him, it taught him to respect his elders. *Yes, ma'am. No, sir.* He stood when an older person came into a room. He gave up his seat on the bus. He never talked back to a church mother, not even the ones who patted his head and told him what a blessing his daddy was, and he kept his eyes down and his voice low when the deacons spoke. Loretta required it, and the church required it, and Calvin required it with his hand. But it took root in Ezra deeper than any of them knew, and it outlasted the man who had beaten it into him. Thirty years later he would still call the old man across the street *sir*, and still go quiet and respectful in front of a gray head, even when he was angry enough to break something.

It was in the Book, too, plain as a nail, in the nineteenth chapter of Leviticus, in a line he did not read until he was grown and recognized as already his: *Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.* (Leviticus 19:32)

It was never that Ezra failed to love the beauty around him. He saw it all: the fogged kitchen windows, the light coming through the church's tall glass on a Sunday, the grain in a plank of scrap wood he found and kept under his bed. He loved it quietly, and never said so, in case someone took it. What he could not do was accept the house those things sat inside. He would not call it his, and he would not call it normal, and so he lived in it the only way he knew, which was out of sight. He kept to the far end of the table and the back stairwell, to long sleeves and short answers.

If there was a place for a boy like that, the psalmist had named it. *Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble.* (Psalm 32:7) Ezra had yet to learn whose hiding place it was.

The day he came out of it he was fifteen. He carried his tray past the stairwell door and sat down in the middle of the long table, and stayed. He would not be that boy again, folded small and waiting to be passed over. Whatever it cost him, he would stand where people could see him.

Jesus had told the crowd on the hillside: *Ye are the light of the world. A city that is set on an hill cannot be hid.* (Matthew 5:14)

\* \* \*

The worst night came in October of 1990, a few weeks after Ezra turned eight.

It was a Friday, and for once Ezra was walking home with something to carry.

That week he had written his name on the sheet taped outside the gym at Coretta Elementary, under the heading *Boys' Basketball*, the pencil shaking a little in his hand. He had never played. There was no hoop at the house on Old Ferry Road and no one to throw a ball with, and at practice it showed. He traveled every time he picked the ball up. It slipped through his fingers or bounced off his shoes, and the other boys, who had been playing since they could walk, laughed, not meanly. The coach blew his whistle and told him to keep his elbow in.

At the end of that Friday's practice, with the sun going orange in the high gym windows, the coach lined them up for free throws. Ezra stood at the back of the line with his stomach tight. When his turn came he bent his knees the way he had been shown, and he shot, and the ball rose in a lopsided arc and dropped through the net without touching the rim.

For a second nobody said anything. Then the coach said, "Well, look at that," and somebody slapped him on the back.

He walked the mile of gravel home with that one shot in his chest like something warm he was trying to keep alive. He played it over and over: the ball leaving his fingers, the soft sound of the net. He was going to tell his mother. He might even tell his father, who liked sports on television, who might for once look up.

A lopsided shot in a school gym that nobody saw but a coach and a few boys. It was small. It was also the only thing all year that was his. *For who hath despised the day of small things?* (Zechariah 4:10)

He heard them from the yard. The front door was shut, and it did not matter; the sound came through the clapboard. His father was home hours early, drunk by four in the afternoon, and he was already shouting before Ezra got his key out of his pocket.

"...four hundred of them, and not one says thank you! You think this house runs on prayer? Every dime in here is mine, you hear me, Loretta? Every dime!"

A smaller voice: "Calvin, please. The boy will be home."

Ezra stood on the top step with his hand on the knob. Then he opened the door anyway.

He dropped his bag in the doorway. His mother was on the floor of the hallway with her hand over her mouth and blood between her fingers.

Ezra walked past her and stood in front of his father.

He did not decide to do it. He was there, between them, eight years old and in his school shoes on the plastic runner, his school jacket still zipped to his chin, looking up.

Calvin stared down at him, swaying. Then he reached into the pocket of his work jacket and took out a pistol: a .357 Magnum, heavy and black and long in the barrel, the one he kept in a shoebox on the closet shelf and told Ezra never to touch. He thumbed back the hammer. He put the end of the barrel against Ezra's forehead.

It was cold. Ezra would remember that to the end of his days: how cold the metal was, and how it shook.

Loretta made a sound behind him. Ezra did not turn around.

He looked his father in the eye.

He was not afraid. He waited to be afraid, and the fear never came. What came instead was a flat, hard tiredness. He was sick of it. He was sick of Friday nights, and of his mother's face at the sink, and of the verses, and of the fear itself, and in that moment some small, cold part of him thought that if his father pulled the trigger, at least it would be over. And underneath that lay a second thing, one he understood only halfway: if he looked down now, if he cried or begged or stepped aside, it would never stop. Not for him, and not for her. So he did not look down.

The barrel trembled against his skin. His father's eyes were red and wet and wild. The kitchen clock ticked. A car went by outside. Ezra could smell the whiskey and the diesel on him.

Then Calvin's face changed.

It broke open. Ezra saw him see it: the boy, the gun, the blood on his wife's hand, and himself. His finger came off the trigger. He lowered the pistol and slammed it down on the hall table so hard the lamp jumped, and he stood there breathing with both hands braced on the wood. Then he turned and stumbled out the front door into the last of the daylight and left it standing open behind him.

Ezra closed it. He picked up the gun with both hands, because it was too heavy for one, and put it in the kitchen drawer under the dish towels. Then he got a wet washcloth and knelt down beside his mother on the floor.

That was the night Ezra understood that nobody was coming. Not his father, and not his father's God.

He never told anyone about that night. Not Angela. Not anyone. The shot he had made that afternoon went unmentioned too; it belonged to a boy who had been left somewhere in that hallway.

One person came that night, though he never knew what he had come for. Elijah Brooks was the boy from the next house down Old Ferry Road, a head taller than Ezra and twice as loud, and on the night the gun came out of the shoebox he did the one thing nobody else on that street did. He came. He had stolen his father's car, a 1970 Barracuda his daddy had fitted up to look like the black car in the horror movie he'd watched fourteen times, with the stripe down the hood, the scoop, and an engine that announced you two blocks away. Elijah was ten years old and had to sit on a phone book to see over the wheel. Ezra had come out to sit on the front step in the cold with no coat, and had not gone back in. Elijah saw him there under his mother's lit window, and he leaned across and shoved the passenger door open and said, "Get in."

He didn't ask. He drove them to Whitlock Creek Park, past the old bowling alley with its sign hanging by one bolt and its windows gone, and the two of them sat below the overpass with a pair of borrowed poles and a coffee can of worms, and fished for catfish until the light went. They caught three. Then Elijah let the engine roar and turned the radio up as loud as it would go, and Ezra, eight years old, put his arm out the window into the cold and laughed harder than he had laughed in his life.

They took the long way home, over the railroad tracks and past the jail and up onto the overpass they had been fishing under all evening. On the far side the road dropped toward a parking lot, and a man came around the corner in a pickup, on their side of the line. Elijah yanked the wheel. The Barracuda swung and overcorrected and the back end came around, and then there was a tree. Ezra remembered the sound of it. He remembered Elijah's head going through the windshield. He remembered the quiet after, and the radio still playing, and the smell of gas and cut grass, and thinking, with perfect clarity, that the feeling was back.

Elijah lived. He lay in the hospital for six days with his head wrapped and his jaw wired, and Ezra, with fourteen stitches in his forehead and a story ready for his mother, sat by the bed through most of them. Elijah's father mourned the car for a year and never once raised his voice about it, because the boy had nearly died in it. The doctors said it should have killed them both. On the fifth day Elijah wrote on a napkin, in crooked letters, *Luck or a reason?* and Ezra turned it over a good while before he wrote back, *Don't know.* He had printed it in square block capitals, every letter the same height. They never decided which. They stayed friends every day after that.

*A man that hath friends must shew himself friendly: and there is a friend that sticketh closer than a brother.* (Proverbs 18:24) *And who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?* (Esther 4:14)

\* \* \*

After that night, the house went silent.

Calvin came home the next afternoon, sober and gray in the face, and did not say a word about it. There was no apology and no word of any kind. For days he came and went without speaking, and ate his supper without looking up, and slept on the couch in front of the television with the sound turned low. Tanks in the desert. Soldiers loading onto airplanes. A map of a country called Kuwait.

Calvin had been in the Army at eighteen, before the railroad, before Ezra was born. He had told the story of those years at church a dozen times: how he had been a soldier for his country before he was a soldier for the Lord.

In December, he announced that he was going back.

He told the congregation first, on a Sunday morning, standing at the deacons' table. His voice filled the sanctuary.

"Church, I have been called. My country is calling men of faith and courage, and I wore its uniform once, and I will wear it again. I can't sit here and talk about courage while other men's sons go to the desert in my place."

The church leapt to its feet. People cried. The choir sang.

Ezra, in the front pew, knew it was not courage. He had seen his father's face in the hallway that night. His father was not going to war. He was running from his own front door.

Calvin told Loretta and Ezra afterward, in the car.

Ezra was eight years old. He sat in the back seat and listened to his mother stifling her sobs in the front, and his father saying "It's done, Loretta, it's already done," and Ezra caught himself counting the Sundays until January, and slid his hands under his legs.

\* \* \*

They saw him off at the bus depot in Hollis Junction on a raw, sleeting morning in January 1991.

There were other families there, other soldiers, other wives crying and kids holding homemade signs. Calvin wore his uniform. He looked bigger in it than he did in his Sunday suit. He hugged Loretta and kissed her cheek. Then he turned to his son.

Ezra had decided in the car that he was going to do something brave: hold his father's hand.

He had never done it before. Calvin was not a man who held hands. But all around them, other children were holding on to their fathers, wrapping their arms around their legs, and Ezra wanted that, for just one day, to feel the warm love of a complete family. So he stepped forward and reached up and held out his hand, open, palm up, to his father.

Calvin's eyes dropped to it.

Then he reached out and patted Ezra twice on the top of the head.

"You're the man of the house now," he said. "Men don't cry."

Then he picked up his duffel bag and got on the bus.

Ezra stood on the cold concrete with his hand still held out in front of him, open and empty. Then it fell back down to his side. He returned to his mother's side and stood there with his head down. He watched the bus pull out of the station. He watched it turn the corner. He didn't cry. His father had told him not to.

\* \* \*

In the kitchen on Old Ferry Road, all those years later, Loretta pulled the pizza out of the oven, Angela's pizza, the crust blistered and brown, and set it on the stove top between them, and sat down across from her son with flour still on her apron. Out back, Mia was showing Jalen every egg she had found, one at a time, by name.

"I'm going to ask you again," she said. "Because you didn't answer me the first time. You've been dreaming."

Ezra looked up at her, startled.

"I know that look, baby. I've seen it on you since you were a little boy." She folded her hands on the table. "You want to tell me about it?"

He meant not to. But he found himself telling her anyway: the red room, the red moon, the pull at the window. Mia's drawing in Angela's Bible. The verse with his name in the margin. He told it in a monotone. When he was done, his mother sat without speaking while the kettle came to a boil behind her.

"He's calling you," she said finally.

"Who? God?" Ezra laughed, a short, ugly sound. "Mama, I grew up in that church. I know all about God calling. I watched Dad do it every Sunday. Then he went home and got drunk and hit you."

"Your father was not God."

"He talked like he was."

"Yes," Loretta said. "He did. And that is the worst thing he ever did to you. Worse than the drinking. Worse than his hands." She reached across the table, and for a moment Ezra thought she was going to take his hand. Instead she laid her hand on the table between them, palm up, open, and left it there. "Your father knew every word in that book, Ezra. And not a single one of them ever reached all the way into his heart."

Ezra looked at his mother's open hand on the table. For a long moment he didn't move. Then, reluctantly, he took it, and it was warm, and he let her keep it.

\* \* \*

The knock had come on a Saturday in early March 1991, a few days after the ground war ended.

Ezra answered the door. There were two men on the front steps in Army dress uniforms, with their hats tucked under their arms. One of them asked, gently, if his mother was home.

He remembered the sound Loretta made. He remembered her sliding down the wall of the hallway until she was sitting on the plastic runner. He remembered one of the men kneeling beside her. The rest of that day was gone.

The box came six weeks later.

It was a plain cardboard carton sealed with brown tape, with PATTERSON, PERSONAL, SEND HOME printed across the lid in Calvin's own block capitals, pressed so hard the marker had bled into the cardboard. He had packed it himself in the last days before the ground war, the Army's letter said, and the Army had added what was found on him, and it had come home without him. Loretta opened it at the dinner table with a steak knife while Ezra watched. Inside were his father's things. A folded uniform. A shaving kit. A packet of letters to the other deacons of Pilgrim Rest, all about church business. A Bible: black leather, gold-edged, Calvin's name stamped on the cover.

Tucked inside the Bible's front cover was the church program from his last Sunday, the one with "Deacon Calvin Patterson, Our Soldier of the Cross" printed under his photograph on the front, folded carefully so it would not crease. There was no picture of Loretta. There was no picture of Ezra.

At the very bottom of the box, wrapped in a handkerchief, an Army tag tied to its strap, was the watch.

It was a heavy steel watch with a black face, the one Calvin had worn every day of Ezra's life. The crystal was cracked straight across. The hands had stopped at 3:17.

The letter from the Army said his father had been killed by artillery fire. One of the soldiers who came to the door had said that the watch had been on his wrist when he was hit, and had stopped then.

Ezra picked it up. It was too big for his wrist, and too heavy. He held it in both hands, stared at the stopped hands, and felt nothing.

Then he watched his mother fold the flaps of the carton shut over the rest of it, one at a time, and press the brown tape down with her palm. She carried it to the hall closet and set it on the top shelf, behind the winter coats, and stood there with her back to him.

The Sunday after the funeral, Pilgrim Rest took up a special collection for the Patterson family. The pastor read the total from the pulpit, and the church stood and clapped for the deacon who had given his life for his country. Loretta sat in the choir loft with her hands folded in her lap and her eyes on the floor. Ezra sat in the front pew and did not clap.

He was eight years old. He was holding a dead man's watch. That night he slid it onto his own wrist, though it was too big and did not run, and then he took it off again and slept with it under his pillow. The box stayed on the shelf, and over the years he stopped seeing it.

He started wearing the watch when he was sixteen, when his wrist was finally big enough to hold it. He never had it repaired or replaced the cracked crystal. He wore it every day for twenty-eight years, stopped at 3:17, and when people asked him why he wore a watch that didn't work, he said, "It was my father's," and they always nodded, satisfied.

That wasn't the reason. Ezra himself could not have said why he wore it.

\* \* \*

He left the kids asleep in his old room, on his mother's promise to bring them home in the morning, and left her house just after dark.

He skipped the turn for home and drove on down Old Ferry Road, because after what his mother had said he needed to see it again, until the old red-brick church came up on the corner. It had closed six years ago. The steeple was still there, but the white paint had weathered to the color of dishwater and was peeling off in strips. Plywood covered the windows. The sign out front had lost most of its letters. The only words still on it said: *FOR LEASE.*

Ezra parked across the street and turned off the engine and sat looking at it.

*Did you ever love me, Dad?*

*Did you ever love Him? Or was it all a show, the Sunday suit and the Bible and the shouting, every word of it, all for the four hundred people in the pews?*

*I held out my hand to you. At the bus station. I was eight years old and I held out my hand. Did you even see it? Did you feel anything at all when you patted me on the head and turned away?*

*I sat at my own table for twelve years and never once took my wife's hand when she reached for me. I only learned how at the very end, when it was almost too late. And now she's gone, and I'm the one who keeps reaching, in the dark, for a hand that isn't there.*

He sat in the truck until his hands were cold.

Then he took his wallet out of his back pocket and opened it. Tucked behind his driver's license was a cream-colored card with a pressed lavender flower on the front. He had moved it there from the kitchen counter a week ago, because he wasn't ready to throw it away.

He turned it over. The phone number was written in looping blue ink.

He looked at the dead church. He looked at the stopped watch on his wrist. Then he took out his phone and dialed.

It rang twice.

"Ezra," Celeste said. "I was hoping you'd call."

## Chapter 7: The Strange Woman

> *With her much fair speech she caused him to yield, with the flattering of her lips she forced him.* — Proverbs 7:21
>
> *Notwithstanding I have a few things against thee, because thou sufferest that woman Jezebel, which calleth herself a prophetess, to teach and to seduce my servants to commit fornication, and to eat things sacrificed unto idols.* — Jesus, Revelation 2:20

**Word study: *fair speech* — לֶקַח** Hebrew *leqach* (Strong's H3948). Learning, teaching, instruction, from a root meaning to take hold of.
