*"And in the days of these kings shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed…" (Daniel 2:44)*

She read the words until she could have recited them. Then she wrote one more line beneath them, and drew a box around it, as Angela did.

*The stone is coming.*

## Chapter 10: Ten to One

> *…be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.* — Daniel 3:18

**Word study: *serve* — פְּלַח** Aramaic *pelach* (Strong's H6399). To serve, to worship, to pay reverence. In Daniel's Aramaic, serving a god and worshipping him are one word. The three young men knew that bowing once, just to get along, was already service.

King Nebuchadnezzar set up his image of gold on the plain of Dura, and he sent for every prince and governor and captain and judge and treasurer in the empire to come to its dedication (Daniel 3:1-2). They came from every province and stood on the plain in their finest robes (Daniel 3:3). Then a herald cried aloud, "To you it is commanded, O people, nations, and languages, That at what time ye hear the sound of the cornet, flute, harp, sackbut, psaltery, dulcimer, and all kinds of musick, ye fall down and worship the golden image" (Daniel 3:4-5). Whoever would not bow would be cast that same hour into the midst of a burning fiery furnace (Daniel 3:6). The music played, and the whole plain went down on its face (Daniel 3:7). Only three young men were left standing: Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego (Daniel 3:12). They were brought before the king in his fury (Daniel 3:13), and they offered no plea and no argument. They said only that their God was able to deliver them: "But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods" (Daniel 3:17-18).

\* \* \*

On the Sunday after the statue, Kambria sat in the fourth pew on the left at Mount Zion Christian Center, Angela's church on Rhode Island Avenue, in the seat beside the one that had been Angela's.

Nobody sat in Angela's seat. It had stayed empty since the funeral, going on a year now, and the women who came early to save their places walked past it with their eyes averted. Kambria laid her Bible on the cushion beside her every Sunday, as she used to when Angela was running late, and picked it up again after the closing prayer.

Mia sat on her other side this morning, in a purple dress with her hair in two puffs, swinging her patent leather shoes. Loretta had driven her in from Cedar Hollow because Ezra was "working." Loretta sat at the end of the pew in her Sunday hat and said nothing about where her son was, and Kambria didn't ask.

Before the service started, Mia reached across Kambria's lap and patted the empty cushion beside the Bible with her small hand. "Mommy's saving it," she whispered. "For Daddy. For when he wakes up."

Kambria had to look down at her hands after that.

Pastor Grant came to the pulpit at eleven-thirty. Pastor Xavier Grant was sixty-one years old, a gentle, gray-haired man with reading glasses he was always pushing back up his nose. He carried a pocket calendar and a fountain pen, and he answered every question he was asked plainly and honestly, even the hard ones. He had been Angela's pastor for fifteen years. He had come to the house every morning in her last weeks, and she had prayed over him instead of the other way around, and he had preached her funeral and wept through the last half of it.

"Turn with me," he said, "to the twelfth chapter of Genesis."

His sermons always ran long, and this one was no different. He preached for forty-five minutes on God's promise to Abraham: *And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. (Genesis 12:3)* He preached on Romans 11, where Paul asks whether God has cast away His people Israel, and answers, *God forbid. (Romans 11:1)* He preached that the God who keeps His promises to Israel is the same God who keeps His promises to the church, and that a Christian who loves the Bible ought to love the people God chose to carry it.

He preached it well. He preached it with his whole heart, and Kambria believed every word of it. She had read those same chapters with Angela at the dinner table. She wrote *Genesis 12:3* and *Romans 11:1–2* in her notebook and underlined them both.

Then, near the end, he took off his glasses and folded them and held them in his hand.

"Church, some of you have seen the news this week," he said. "There's going to be a great gathering in Jerusalem the first week of November. Leaders from all over the world, all the nations together, coming to talk about peace and about a common moral law for all mankind." He smiled. "Now, I don't know what will come of it. But I know the Bible tells us to *Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee. (Psalm 122:6)* So when you go home today, I want you to pray for that gathering. Pray that God will use it."

"Amen," said the church.

Kambria didn't say amen. Her pen hung over her notebook and did not come down.

\* \* \*

She caught him in the fellowship hall afterward, by the coffee urns, where the coffee was burnt, as it always was.

"That was a good word, Pastor," she said.

"Well, thank you, Sister Kambria." He took her hand in both of his. "You doing all right? I know this time of year is hard. It's almost a year now."

"It's almost a year." She held on to his hand a moment. "Pastor, can I ask you something about the end of the sermon? About the gathering in Jerusalem?"

"Of course."

"You said pray that God will use it." She set the question down plainly. "But peace on whose terms? A common law for all mankind, written by who? Because I've been reading about it. And I don't think it's going to say Jesus is Lord."

Pastor Grant considered her over the top of his coffee cup. Then he set the cup down and drew her aside, away from the urns, to the window by the coat rack where nobody was standing.

"No," he said. "It isn't."

Kambria stared at him.

"I've read Daniel too, Sister. And Second Thessalonians, and the thirteenth of Revelation. I was reading them before you were born." He polished a lens on his tie. "A law for all mankind with His name left off it. A peace that comes in through the side door. I know what that looks like."

"Then why did you tell them to pray God would use it?"

"Because He will. He uses everything." He looked out the window at the parking lot, where families were buckling children into car seats. "Kambria, I have four hundred people out there. Half of them are hanging on by a thread. Some of them don't know the Lord yet, and some of them think they do. If I stand up there and preach fire every Sunday, the ones who most need to hear it will stop coming, and they'll never hear the rest." He turned back to her. "Paul told Timothy to pray for kings and for all that are in authority, because God 'will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.' All men. That's who I preach to. I'm not called to call the judgment down on anybody. I'm called to turn the light on and let God show them what's in the dark. The ones who are watching will see it."

In the margin of her notebook, under *Genesis 12:3*, she wrote: *1 Tim. 2:4. He sees. He chose mercy.*

\* \* \*

That night she ate supper alone, the television muttering in the corner.

She lived in a small brick duplex in Brookland, with a spare room she used for her notebooks and a kitchen just big enough for one table and two chairs. She had bought the second chair for Angela. It was the chair Angela used to sit in when they met here instead of at Angela's house, on the Thursdays when Ezra had the TV too loud.

The evening news came on at six. The anchor, a silver-haired woman with a calm, serious voice, had a great deal to get through.

The Euphrates was at its lowest level in recorded history, she said. Dams upstream in Turkey held back what was left, and farmers in Iraq were walking across a riverbed where boats used to go. In one place the falling water had uncovered the ruins of a city that had lain under the river for three thousand years.

Kambria stopped chewing.

Then a clip from a debate in Virginia. Lucas Thorne, the law professor running for the Senate, calm and handsome in a dark suit, said the country needed "one moral standard that every American can live by, whatever they believe."

Then Jerusalem. A hotel high on the Mount of Olives called the Olivet Crown, long and curved, all pale stone and dark glass, with workers on scaffolding hanging banners. *The Council for Universal Moral Law: Opening Session, Jerusalem,* the caption said. *November 2–6.* Two hundred and fifty delegates from more than a hundred and forty countries were coming to agree on a short list of moral principles that, in the words of one organizer, "every person on earth can live by, whatever they believe." A president. Two prime ministers. A prince from the Gulf. Rabbis and imams and ministers in their collars, all smiling for the cameras together.

Kambria put down her fork.

"The principles are based on the Seven Laws of Noah," the anchor said, and a law professor in a bow tie came on to say that five of the seven would pass without a fight. "The difficult conversations will be around the other two: blasphemy and idolatry. How do you define idolatry in a document meant for the whole world? Some traditions would consider the worship of a human being as God to fall under that heading. So the drafters have some delicate work to do."

"Thank you, Professor," the anchor said, and moved on to the weather.

Kambria didn't hear the weather.

*The worship of a human being as God.* She knew exactly who he meant. Every person at Mount Zion that morning had sung to Him. Angela had died with His name on her lips.

She reached across the table for her notebook. Her hand was shaking, and she made it stop.

Then, because the hotel on the mountain would not leave her alone, she picked up her phone and found the Council's own website. Somebody was paying for all of it: the hotel, the flights, the banners. She scrolled to the bottom of the page. There was a long list of sponsors: universities, foundations, two governments. The last name on the list was in the smallest type of all. *The Meridian Trust, Dubai.* No logo. No link. When she searched for it, she found a post-office box in Dubai and nothing else. She wrote it down.

\* \* \*

She dated a clean page. *October 25, 2026.* Then she wrote down everything she could remember from the broadcast, as exactly as she could, as she logged a sample at the lab. *Council for Universal Moral Law. Jerusalem. Nov 2–6. Olivet Crown hotel, Mount of Olives. 140+ nations. 250 DELEGATES. Seven Laws of Noah. Idolatry: "the worship of a human being as God."*

Under it she wrote the rest of the broadcast, because it belonged on the same page. *Iran: two more cities. Third wave. Formula recall, salmonella. Arizona, taps dry nine days.* And at the bottom, on a line by itself: *Euphrates. Lowest in history. Ruins showing in the riverbed.* She stayed on that line until the words stopped moving. Then she wrote two references beside it, *Revelation 9:14* and *Revelation 16:12*, and under them, because she would not put words in God's mouth: *Not yet. Watch.*

Then she opened her Bible to Genesis 9 and read it through twice, every word God spoke to Noah when he came out of the ark. Be fruitful and multiply. Every moving thing shall be meat for you. Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed. And the bow in the cloud, the token of a promise God made to never again destroy the earth by water. She counted. There was no list of seven anywhere in it. There were no courts, no law against blasphemy, no law against idolatry. The Seven Laws of Noah did not come from Genesis. They came from the Talmud, from rabbis writing more than a thousand years after Moses, who drew them out of the text and gave them Noah's name. Under the broadcast notes she wrote, and underlined it: *NOT IN GENESIS. Rabbinic tradition (Talmud). They call it Noah's. God never wrote it.*

She went back over what she had written, line by line. Then she went into the spare room and came back with two of her older notebooks, the third and the sixth, and laid them open on the table side by side.

In the third notebook, years back, in Angela's round handwriting, there was a newspaper clipping about the Seven Laws of Noah and a group that was working to spread them among non-Jews. Angela had written underneath it: *Good laws. But watch what happens to the seventh. Watch who defines "idolatry."* Angela had drawn a box around that line, as she drew a box around one line on every page, the one she most wanted to remember. And under that, in Kambria's own hand: *Revelation 13:15. Worship the image or die.*

In the sixth notebook, there was a verse she had copied out some while later, after she had read more about the Noahide movement, because she wanted to remember what the real promise said.

*In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you. (Zechariah 8:23)*

She read it aloud in the quiet kitchen. Ten men out of all the nations.

She knew the verse. It was from Zechariah, and it was a beautiful promise. It was about the day the true King would reign in Jerusalem, when the nations would stream to Him and ask to learn His ways. It was about Jesus. She and Angela had been sure of that.

And now, in the week before that promise, ten men from every nation were packing their suitcases for Jerusalem, to a hotel built on the mountain where His feet were going to stand, to write a law that might call worshiping Him a crime.

"It's the counterfeit," she whispered. "It comes first. It always comes first."

She wrote it down. *The counterfeit comes before the real thing. Ten men from every nation. Right promise, wrong king.*

Then she read it over once more and weighed it, for Angela had always weighed what she wrote.

Pastor Grant had been right that morning. God had not cast away His people. The Jewish people were still the apple of His eye, the land was still the land He had promised to Abraham, and every word of that promise still stood: *I will bless them that bless thee.* Nothing she had seen on the news changed one letter of it. The families who would pray at the Western Wall that week had done nothing to her. Neither had the grandmothers of the World Diocese lighting candles for their grandchildren, or the Muslim cab drivers she saw kneeling on their prayer rugs in the hospital parking lot at dawn. They were sheep having no shepherd, and she had been one too. Most of them were only following the people they had been taught to trust, and she could not find it in her heart to blame them for it.

It was the shepherds she was watching. The men in the robes and the dark suits at the front of the room, who had read the same Scriptures she had and knew better, and who were leading the whole flock toward a table with no Christ at it. They would write a law for the whole world and call it God's old covenant with Noah, made new, though a covenant God had already made was not theirs to remake. God had said what He thought of shepherds like that through the prophet Ezekiel: *Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! (Ezekiel 34:2)* The flock would not answer for its shepherds. The men at the front of that hall would answer for what they did with the truth they were given. So would she.

\* \* \*

The phone rang that evening. It was Walt. Walt never called twice in one week.

"You seeing this?" he said.

"I saw it."

"I set type for the *Star* the night they signed the Babylonian Bylaws," Walt said. His voice was rough. "I set the headline myself. Seventy-two-point Bodoni, all caps. PEACE. I was proud of that headline, Kambria. I went home and told my wife I'd set a piece of history." He cleared his throat. "Now I don't know what I set."

"Walt."

"A law for the whole world. Every nation at one table. And every religion on earth at the same table, smiling for the cameras." She heard newspaper rustling on the other end, and then something that might have been a cough. "I'm an old man. I've read that book my whole life. I always thought I'd understand it better than this when it finally happened."

"I don't think anybody understands it better than this," Kambria said. "I think we just watch."

"Watch for what?"

Her eyes returned to Daniel 3, open on the table in front of her.

"For the music," she said.

\* \* \*

After he hung up, she sat with her Bible open and did not read it, and then did.

She read the whole third chapter of Daniel out loud to the empty chair across the table. She read about the herald and the music and the plain full of people going down on their faces. She read about the three who stayed standing. She read their answer to the king, and she read it twice, because it was the part she had always loved the most.

*If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. (Daniel 3:17-18)*

*But if not.*

They hadn't known whether God would save them from the fire. They had only known that He could, and that they would not bow either way.

Then she read what happened next. The king heated the furnace seven times hotter than it had ever been heated, so hot that the soldiers who threw the three young men in died at its mouth. And then the king leaped up from his throne in astonishment.

*Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. (Daniel 3:25)*

Kambria touched the page.

She thought of Angela on the sixth floor, with the drip taped to her arm, reading Psalm 23 aloud to a room full of strangers. *Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me… (Psalm 23:4)* Angela had walked into the fire. And she had not walked in alone.

She thought of Ezra across the city, in a house with the curtains closed, working on a Sunday that nobody believed was work.

She bowed her head at the dinner table and prayed for him by name, as Angela used to, every Thursday night for all those years. She prayed for Mia in her purple dress and for Jalen in his dorm downtown. She prayed for Walt alone with his newspapers, and for Pastor Grant, who saw all of it and chose mercy. She prayed for Loretta. And then, because she had promised Angela she would, she prayed for herself.

*Lord, when the music plays, keep me standing.*

When she lifted her head, it was dark outside the window. She turned to the last page she had written on and added one more line beneath, in deliberate letters.

*But if not.*

## Chapter 11: The House of the Gate

> *And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.* — Genesis 11:4

**Word study: *name* — שֵׁם** Hebrew *shem* (Strong's H8034). A name, a reputation, renown, the mark of who someone is. At Babel men set out to make a name for themselves. In the very next chapter God calls one man out of that world and tells him, "I will bless thee, and make thy name great" (Genesis 12:2).

After the Flood, the families of Noah's sons spread out across the earth, and they all still spoke one language (Genesis 10:32; 11:1). As they journeyed from the east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they dwelt there (Genesis 11:2). They learned to bake bricks hard in the fire and to bind them with slime from the tar pits (Genesis 11:3), and they said to one another, "Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name" (Genesis 11:4). They did not build it to find God. They built it so that they would never need to look for Him again. And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower which the children of men had built (Genesis 11:5). He saw that they were one people with one language, and that nothing they set their minds to would be withheld from them (Genesis 11:6). So He confounded their language, so that no one could understand his neighbor, and He scattered them from that place across the face of the whole earth (Genesis 11:7-8). They left the city half built. And its name was called Babel (Genesis 11:8-9).

\* \* \*

The story came on the radio on Tuesday afternoon, while Kambria was driving home from the grocery store.

She almost missed it. It was the last item before the traffic report, read off fast by a young man with a train to catch. Ahead of next week's opening of the Council in Jerusalem, he said, delegates from more than a hundred and forty nations would stop first in the Gulf, for a morning of prayer and fellowship at the House of the Gate. The ceremony would be broadcast live on Wednesday. Then he moved on to an accident on the Beltway.

Kambria pulled over on Rhode Island Avenue and sat with the engine running.

She knew that name. She had not heard it spoken out loud in years, but she knew exactly where it was written down.

\* \* \*

The spare room in her duplex had one window, one lamp, and a bookshelf of pine boards that Ezra had built for her one Christmas, the screw holes plugged and sanded so she could never find them. The bottom shelf held her notebooks. There were nine of them now, standing in a row in the order she and Angela had filled them: the red one, the blue one, the green one, two black ones, a brown one, the gold one for the church, a gray one, and the newest, which lived in her bag.

She pulled out the fourth one, the first of the two black ones, and sat down on the floor under the lamp with it in her lap.

She found the page at once. The tape had yellowed at the corners, and the photograph had faded a little, but it was all still there.

It was a color printout of a picture Angela had found online in the spring of 2023. Angela had printed two copies in the library at her school, on the good printer, and brought them to the dinner table on a Thursday night, one for each of their notebooks. *So we both remember,* she had said.

The picture showed three buildings standing together on a wide platform of pale stone, on an island in the Persian Gulf, with the sea and the sky behind them. All three buildings were the same height. All three were plain, square, and white, the color of sand in the sun. One was a mosque, with a long row of slender columns along its front. One was a church, its walls cut with narrow vertical slats that let the light in. One was a synagogue, wrapped in a screen of latticework. Between them lay a garden and a shallow pool, and paths that led from each door to the other two.

Under the picture, in her own handwriting, Kambria had copied out what the caption on the website had said. *The House of the Gate. On the Persian Gulf. A mosque, a church and a synagogue on one shared foundation.*

Below that, the notes went on down the page, in two hands.

In Kambria's print, cramped to fit the margin: *Feb 2019. Pope Francis visits the UAE, the first pope ever to set foot on the Arabian Peninsula. Signs the "Document on Human Fraternity for World Peace and Living Together" with the Grand Imam of al-Azhar. The Vatican endorses it. The UAE announces this house in honor of it. The International Collective declares Feb 4 the International Day of Human Fraternity.*

In Angela's round, careful cursive, underneath: *Three houses. One foundation. Whose?*

And then Kambria again, pressing harder this time, as she remembered pressing: *Rome at the center. Every faith under one roof. Jesus offered as one way among many.* Under that she had written out two verses in full. The first was what Jesus said to Thomas the night before He died: *I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. (John 14:6)* The second was Paul's question to the church at Corinth: *And what agreement hath the temple of God with idols? (2 Corinthians 6:16)*

Last of all, Angela had added one more line, and drawn a small box around it.

*For other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ. (1 Corinthians 3:11)*

Kambria read the page twice. Then she sat on the floor of the spare room with the notebook open on her knees, and the grief she had kept folded since the funeral came open. It was Angela's handwriting that did it. It was the little box. The second copy, in Angela's own notebook, had the same box in the same place, and beside the picture Angela had penciled the number of Kambria's page, 41, the only page number she ever wrote in that book, so that each copy could be found from the other.

She let herself cry for a minute. Then she wiped her face, got up off the floor, and carried the notebook to the dinner table.

\* \* \*

She remembered the Thursday night they had taped those pictures in.

Ezra had been in the living room that night with a ball game on, and he had come into the kitchen at halftime for a beer and looked over Angela's shoulder at the photograph.

"That's nice," he had said, and he had meant it. "Clean lines. Look at that stonework. Who built it?"

"A government over in the Gulf," Angela had told him. "It's a mosque, a church and a synagogue, all on one base. So everybody can worship together."

Ezra had shrugged. "Sounds all right to me. Better than everybody blowing each other up." He had looked at the two of them, at their open Bibles and the tape and the scissors, and he had smiled his half smile. "What's wrong with that?"

Angela hadn't argued; she never did. She had only said, "Nothing's wrong with people being kind to each other, honey. It's what they build the kindness on that I'm watching."

He had gone back to his game. And Kambria had thought, at the time, that Angela was being a little too careful, a little too suspicious of something good. Three buildings in a garden, a long way away. People being kind to each other. What harm was in that?

She did not think so anymore.

She laid her hand flat on the page, over Angela's little box, and sat there until the light changed.

\* \* \*

That night she was at the hospital until dawn.

The third wave of the new flu had filled the emergency department for a week, with patients on stretchers lining the hallways, and the Centers for Disease Control had sent a small team in to swab the sickest of them and find out why this wave was meaner than the last two. Kambria had answered outbreak calls in that emergency department for years. Now she worked in a borrowed room off the hospital's microbiology lab, with a sequencer and a cooler of samples. At a quarter to three it finally went quiet, and she took her break in the staff lounge, a narrow room with a refrigerator, a coffee maker, two sagging couches and a television bolted high on the wall. The television was always on. No one ever claimed the remote.

Tonight it was on one of the cable news channels, and the ceremony at the House of the Gate was already underway. It was a quarter to eleven in the morning there. The sun was bright, and the three white buildings stood on their stone platform exactly as they did in the picture in her notebook, except that now the platform was full of people.

Kambria set her coffee down and didn't pick it up again.

The delegates walked in slow procession along the paths between the houses: men and women in dark suits, in robes, in turbans and skullcaps and clerical collars, in the white kanduras of the Gulf. A choir was singing somewhere out of sight. The camera moved along the line of faces and settled on the long pool in the middle of the garden, where three religious leaders stood side by side at the water's edge: a white-bearded imam, a bishop of the World Diocese in a black cassock and purple sash, and, in the middle, a tall, silver-haired rabbi in a black coat and a white prayer shawl. The words along the bottom of the screen named him: Rabbi Matteo Arcangeli, envoy of the Rabbinical Court of Jerusalem and president of the new Council.

The anchor's voice murmured over the pictures. The three men would light a single lamp together, she said, a lamp of olive wood and brass made for the occasion, which would be carried to Jerusalem the next week and lit again on the opening night of the Council. "Organizers are calling it the Lamp of the Three Houses," she said. "A symbol of one light shining through every tradition."

The three men put their hands together on a long taper and lit the lamp. The crowd on the platform applauded. Some of them were crying.

The door opened. Celeste took the other couch, a cup of tea in her hands. She had come down from the sixth floor to help with the flu surge like half the volunteers in the building, and looked up at the screen. Her face was soft and glowing in the blue light of the television.

"All of Abraham's children under one roof," she said. "I've been waiting my whole life to see something like this."

"Not all of them," Kambria said.

Celeste looked at her, surprised. "What do you mean?"

Kambria weighed her words. Celeste had been good to Angela, and she did not want to wound her.

"The church in that garden is just one more door," she said. "If Jesus is one door among three, then He's not who He said He was. He said He was the only way to the Father. Either that's true or it isn't. You can't put it on a shelf next to the other two and call it the same light."

Celeste smiled, the smile she gave frightened families, warm and even as a hospital lamp.

"I know that's what your tradition teaches," Celeste said. "I respect that so much, Kambria. I really do. But I think when you go deep enough into any of them, you find the same thing at the bottom. The same Light. Jesus was a beautiful teacher. He'd want this. He'd want everybody at the same table."

"He does want everybody at the same table," Kambria said. "But He said He will set the table. *That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom.* That's Jesus. Not the kingdoms of men setting a table for Him."

Neither of them spoke. On the screen the choir began another song.

Celeste turned her cup in her hands, and Kambria noticed her wrist.

A new red string was knotted three times around it.

Kambria thought of the small silver car parked at the curb outside Ezra's house that Monday, and the string hanging from its mirror, knotted three times, catching the sun.

She told herself it proved nothing. She looked away from Celeste's wrist and back up at the television, and she did not ask the question in her mouth, because she was afraid of the answer, and because she had no right to ask it. Ezra was a grown man and a widower, and who he spent his time with was his own business. That was what she told herself.

"I've got a family waiting for me upstairs," Celeste said finally, standing up. She squeezed Kambria's shoulder on her way to the door. "Get some rest after shift, okay? You look so tired, honey. You carry too much."

Then she was gone, and Kambria was alone with the television.

\* \* \*

The broadcast cut away from the garden to a reception hall inside one of the buildings, where the delegates were filing past a long table to sign something bound in white leather. Then a reporter in a linen jacket faced the camera, with the three white houses behind him, and began to explain who had paid for all of it.

Kambria only half listened. She was watching the people behind him. She was thinking about Angela's box.

Her phone buzzed in her pocket. It was a news alert from the *Post*, with a photograph.

She opened it.

The photograph had been taken that morning, on the stone platform, in front of the church. A tall man in a pale gray suit stood with one hand resting on Rabbi Arcangeli's shoulder and the other raised toward the crowd, palm out, as if he were taking an oath. He was in his early sixties, lean and tanned, with close-cropped silver hair and an easy, handsome face. He was smiling. Arcangeli was smiling beside him, and the imam and the bishop stood a step behind them, and behind them all the three white houses shone in the sun.

The caption under the photograph read:

*Adrian Crowe, founder of the world's largest digital-currency exchange, welcomes international delegates to the House of the Gate on Wednesday, ahead of next week's opening session of the Council for Universal Moral Law in Jerusalem. Crowe, a Philadelphia native whose company is headquartered on the Gulf, personally covered the travel costs of all 250 delegates. "Every family has its quarrels," Crowe told them. "But we all live in the same house. It's time we started acting like it."*

Kambria read the caption three times.

She knew the name only vaguely, from the business pages: the oil fields in Venezuela, a fund, a fortune the papers had stopped bothering to estimate. In all her years it had never come near a church. And yet here he was, standing at the center of the photograph, at the center of the platform, with his hand on a rabbi's shoulder. Two hundred and fifty delegates, from a hundred and forty nations, had flown halfway around the world at his expense to stand where he told them to stand.

She studied the man's face. It was a pleasant face. He looked like a man who remembered the names of people's children.

She went back to the borrowed lab and finished her night. She logged forty samples, and loaded the sequencer, and labeled the cooler for the morning courier to Hyattsville. But all night, under everything she did, she kept seeing that raised hand.

\* \* \*

She drove home at seven-thirty in the morning, with the sun coming up over the slate roofs on Twelfth Street, and instead of going to bed she sat down at her dinner table in her clothes from the night and opened her laptop.

It took her less than an hour to learn what the rest of the world apparently already knew.

Adrian Crowe was sixty-three years old. He had been born in Philadelphia, the son of a bus driver, and had gone to Wall Street at twenty-two with one suit off a Wanamaker's clearance rack. He had made his first fortune trading currencies before he was thirty. He had made his second, much larger one building an exchange for digital money, and now governments used it to settle their debts with one another. He lived in a penthouse in Dubai, within sight of the tallest building on earth, and he ran his company from a tower down the coast, a short drive from the three white houses. He gave away hundreds of millions of dollars a year. He had paid to rebuild a hospital in Gaza and a school in Ukraine. When the administration took control of Venezuela's oil fields, his fund had put up the largest private stake in the new operation; his chief of staff, a quiet man named Alexander Vale, had signed the papers, and the two of them had made more money from it in one year than most countries did. He did not drink, and he did not marry, and he almost never gave interviews. The few profiles of him she could find described him as brilliant, private, charming, and generous, and every one of them used the word *visionary*.

Near the end of one long magazine article, a reporter had asked him what he believed in.

*"I believe in peace,"* Crowe had said. *"Not as a dream. As an engineering problem. Most of the wars in history were fought over two things: money and God. Give the world one honest system for the first, and one shared table for the second, and you take away the reasons people have for killing each other. That's not religion. That's arithmetic."*

Kambria read it out loud to the empty kitchen.

Then she went looking for the thing that had been bothering her since Sunday night. It took her another hour. The Meridian Trust had no website, but it had a filing. A journalist in London had posted a scanned page from a Dubai company registry on a forum for reporters who followed money, and Kambria found it on the fourth page of her search. The Trust had three directors. Two were lawyers with offices in the Emirates. The third was listed only by an initial and a surname. *A. Vale.*

She knew the name. It was in the article she had just read, two paragraphs above the quote about arithmetic: Crowe's chief of staff, the quiet man who had signed the papers in Venezuela.

She pushed back from the screen. It proved nothing. A trust in Dubai had helped pay for a peace conference, and the man behind the trust worked for the man who had paid for the delegates' flights. That was all. She printed the filing, and the photograph from the *Post*, and went into the spare room and taped them side by side on the bare wall over her desk. Under them she wrote on an index card, in marker: *WHO PAYS?*

One system for money. One table for God.

She pushed the laptop aside. She opened the black notebook from 2023 to the page with the yellowed tape, and she turned to her newest notebook, the ninth, and laid them side by side on the table, the old photograph beside a clean page.

She dated the clean page. *October 28, 2026.* Underneath it, she wrote: *The House of the Gate.*

Then she wrote the name. She printed it in capitals, alone in the middle of the line, and looked at it.

*ADRIAN CROWE.*

Beneath the name she copied out every word of the caption, and every word of the quote from the magazine. Then, under those, she wrote out the verse she had been thinking of since the radio first spoke on Tuesday afternoon.

*Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name… (Genesis 11:4)*

She kept her eyes on it.

She thought of the three white houses, all exactly the same height, so that none of them stood above the others.

She thought of the lamp of olive wood and brass, on its way to Jerusalem.

She thought of the man in the gray suit with his hand raised, and of a name she had barely noticed before last night, already on every screen in the world.

Kambria picked up her pen again. Underneath the verse, she drew a small box, as Angela used to, and inside it she wrote one line.

*Somebody always wants to make a name.*

Then she printed the photograph from the *Post* a second time and taped it to the new page with a strip of tape from the kitchen drawer. She set the two notebooks side by side again: the yellowed picture from years ago, and the new one. The same three houses, the same white stone, the same sea behind them. Only now there was a man standing in front of them.

She closed both notebooks and rested her hands on top of them. They were steady.

"Lord," she said out loud, "who is he?"

The kitchen was quiet. Outside, a bus went by on Twelfth Street, and somebody's dog was barking.

She bowed her head and prayed as Angela had taught her, for Mia and Jalen first, and then for Walt, and last and longest for Ezra.

When she lifted her head, the photograph from the *Post* was still open on her laptop, and she reached to close it, and stopped.

She had looked at the faces. Everyone looked at the faces. She had not looked at the edges.

She made the picture bigger, and then bigger again, until the faces broke apart into squares. At the far right edge of the frame, cut off at the shoulder, someone was standing just behind Crowe: a gray sleeve, a hand holding a leather folder against a chest. The face was out of the picture. Only the arm was in it, and the hand, and the wrist, where the sleeve had slid back an inch.

Around the wrist was a thin red string, knotted three times.

Kambria sat in the thin dawn light and looked at it until the words stopped being words.

Somebody standing at Adrian Crowe's shoulder was wearing it too.

## Chapter 12: The Morning Paper

> *Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets.* — Amos 3:7

**Word study: *secret* — סוֹד** Hebrew *sod* (Strong's H5475). A secret, a counsel; at its root, a circle of close friends sitting together and talking in confidence. God does not shout His plans across a crowded street. He tells them to the ones who sit with Him. "The secret of the LORD is with them that fear him." (Psalm 25:14)

In the days of Jeroboam king of Israel, there was a herdsman in Tekoa named Amos, who kept sheep and gathered sycomore fruit, and had no thought of being a prophet (Amos 1:1; 7:14). The LORD took him from behind the flock and sent him north to Bethel, to the king's own house of worship, to tell the people what was coming (Amos 7:15). Amaziah the priest came out to stop him: "O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: But prophesy not again any more at Bethel: for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court" (Amos 7:12-13). And Amos answered, "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was an herdman, and a gatherer of sycomore fruit: And the LORD took me as I followed the flock" (Amos 7:14-15). Then he told them the worst of it. The days would come, saith the Lord GOD, when He would send a famine in the land: not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water, but of hearing the words of the LORD (Amos 8:11).

\* \* \*

Walt Simmons woke at a quarter after five, the same as every morning for as long as he could remember, without an alarm.

He lay a minute listening to the house. The furnace ticked. A car went by on the wet street. On the other side of the bed, the quilt was smooth and tucked tight under the pillow, just as his wife had always made it, and as he still made it every morning, though nobody slept on that side anymore. He had stopped reaching for her in the dark years back. He still noticed every morning that he didn't.

He got up in stages, the only way his knees and the wired breastbone from Brandick would let him. He put on his robe and his slippers and went down the stairs one at a time with his cane hooked over his wrist and his free hand pressed flat to the fresh scar under his robe, twelve days out of Brandick.

The murmur the doctors had been listening to for ten years had turned out to be a valve giving way. On the first Sunday in November, David from two doors down had found him on his kitchen floor with the newspaper still in his hand and called the ambulance, and the ambulance took him to Brandick Memorial, the old heart hospital on the hill, because it was the nearest cardiac unit. A surgeon there opened his chest that night and rebuilt the valve with her own two hands. Brandick had been mending hearts since before Walt was born. There was a brass plaque in the lobby with the founding family's name on it, and under it a line from Scripture that he had read three times on his way out the door: *I will restore health unto thee, and I will heal thee of thy wounds.* (Jeremiah 30:17) He had come home that Thursday against the surgeon's advice, forbidden to drive or lift anything heavier than a coffee cup. He had lifted the percolator every morning since.

In the kitchen he filled the dented pot, set it on the burner, and stood by the stove until it began to knock. Then he went out on the porch for the papers.

There were three of them, the same three he had taken for decades: the *Post*, the *New York Times*, and the *Wall Street Journal*, each in its own plastic sleeve, scattered across the steps where the boy had thrown them from his car. He was not supposed to bend. He bent for each one anyway, with one hand pressed flat to his chest. It was still dark. The streetlights were on, and the air smelled like wet leaves and somebody's chimney.

Across the street, at Ezra's house, the porch light was burning.

It had been burning every night since the summer. Walt knew who left it on. He had seen Mia do it, standing on her toes to reach the switch by the front door in her nightgown, every evening at dusk. He had never asked her who it was for. He thought he probably knew.

He went back inside and poured his coffee, black, into the brown mug with the chip in the handle. He spread the papers across the dinner table in the order he always read them. Then he took the small black Bible out of the pocket of his robe, where he had left it the night before, and laid it open beside the *Post*. He set a red pen next to it. He had been reading the Bible and the morning paper side by side at this table for longer than some of his neighbors had been alive.

The red pen was a habit from the shop, where a mistake that got past him would be printed half a million times by morning. He had never lost it. Every morning he read the paper with a red pen in his hand, and he corrected it. He circled the misspellings. He fixed the dates. Twice he had mailed his corrections to the editor, and twice the editor had printed them.

Lately the pen had found a second use.

\* \* \*

The *Post* had the Jerusalem story on the front page again, below the fold.

A week had passed since the Council for Universal Moral Law closed in Jerusalem, and the delegates had gone home. But they had left something behind. The paper said a working committee would stay on in Jerusalem to draw up "a binding framework for shared moral standards among nations," to be signed by every member state the day it was ready. A spokesman called it "the first truly global covenant." There was a photograph of the committee seated at a long white table, smiling.

Walt read the article twice. He found no misspellings in it. He picked up the red pen anyway, and in the margin beside the word *covenant* he wrote, in small square capitals: *DAN. 9:27.*

*And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week… (Daniel 9:27)*

On the business page, under a story about grocery prices, the *Post* said bread had gone up for the eleventh month in a row. The wheat harvest had come in short on three continents. Walt circled the price of a loaf and wrote beside it, in red: *REV. 6:6. A measure of wheat for a penny.*

He turned the page.

The *Journal* was the one he understood least and read most carefully. On the second page of the markets section, under a picture of a man in a gray suit with his hand raised, the headline said that Adrian Crowe's exchange was offering a single digital settlement system to the central banks of forty-one countries, free of charge for the first five years. *One ledger for the world,* Crowe was quoted as saying. *No more borders on money.* Walt did not understand half of the article. He understood the verse, though. He wrote it out in full in the margin, because it was too important to abbreviate: *…that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark… (Revelation 13:17)*

Below it on the same page was a smaller story. A consortium led by Soren Salazar, whose satellites carried a third of the world's phone calls, had signed a ninety-nine-year lease with the government in Nuuk for the whole north coast of Greenland: rare-earth mines, deepwater ports for the new Arctic shipping lanes, and ground stations for his satellites dug into the ice, where the cold would run his servers for nothing. Two American presidents had tried to buy the island and been told it was not for sale. Salazar had not offered to buy it. He had offered to run it. Walt wrote in the margin: *DAN. 11:39. Divide the land for gain.*

He turned the page, and his coffee had gone lukewarm and bitter, and he didn't get up to warm it.

\* \* \*

At twenty to seven, the front door across the street opened, and Ezra came out.

He was carrying a travel mug and his tool bag, and he walked down to the truck without looking left or right, as he did every morning now. Ezra's color was good and his shoulders easy, and Walt, who had watched him walk to that truck every morning for years, had not seen him carry himself like that since before Angela got sick. Ezra opened the truck door. Then he stopped, and turned around, and looked back at the porch light still burning over his front door in the overcast morning. He stood there. Then he went back up the steps and switched it off, and came down again, and drove away.

At ten after seven, Mia came out with Loretta, in her purple coat with the hood up, swinging her lunch box. She saw Walt in his kitchen window, as she did every morning, and she waved with her whole arm. Walt held up the *Post* and waved it back at her, same as always. It was the best part of his day, and he had never told anyone that.

The school bus came and took her. The street was quiet again.

Walt looked down at the Bible lying open beside the paper. He had been reading the minor prophets all week, one a day, as he always did in the fall, and this morning it was Amos. He had read it fifty times. He read it again now, as he used to read a proof.

*Surely the Lord GOD will do nothing, but he revealeth his secret unto his servants the prophets. (Amos 3:7)*

He looked from the verse to the newspaper and back again. Jerusalem. A covenant for the nations. A lamp for the children of Abraham. One ledger for the world. Every bit of it was printed in that small black book in his hand, and had been for two and a half thousand years, and every bit of it was on the front of the morning paper.

\* \* \*

Kambria knocked at a quarter to eight, still in her agency fleece from an all-night run at the lab, with a bag of groceries on her hip.

Since Brandick she came by twice a week on her way home from the hospital, and she brought him milk and bread and the oranges he liked, and she took his blood pressure at the dinner table whether he wanted her to or not. He still insisted he didn't need any of it, and the cuff was waiting on the table whenever she came in.

She wrapped it around his arm and pumped it up, and while she watched the needle she read the margins of the papers upside down. He saw her eyes go from *DAN. 9:27* to the circled loaf of bread to the long line in red across the *Journal*.

"One forty over eighty-eight," she said. "You've been drinking coffee."

"I've been drinking coffee since Nixon."

She let the air out of the cuff and turned the *Journal* around so she could read it right side up. She read the article about Crowe, and the verse he had copied beside it, and said nothing. Then she took the kitchen scissors from his drawer without asking, cut the article out along the margin, dated the back of it, and slid it into the back of the ninth notebook, the one that lived in her bag.

"All my life I've read that Book," Walt said. "Every morning, right here, with the paper next to it." He tapped the Bible with one crooked finger. "Kings and battles. Babylon and Persia. Things that happened a long time ago to people who weren't me." He ran his eye down the margins. "I used to read the Bible like history, Kambria. Now it reads like the morning paper."

Kambria took the chair by the window, across from him. She looked tired, and older than she had looked in the summer, but her eyes on him were kind.

"Walt," she said. "Do you pray about it?"

He picked up the red pen and put it down again.

"I read it," he said.

"That's not what I asked."

"The Lord knows what He's doing. He doesn't need an old man telling Him how to run things."

"It isn't about telling Him anything," she said. "It's about talking to Him."

Walt folded the *Journal* in half, and then in thirds, edges squared, as he folded everything. "You'll be late getting to bed," he said. "You've been up all night."

She searched his face. Then she got up and put the milk in his refrigerator, and the oranges in the bowl on the counter, and at the door she turned around.

"I'm praying for you, Walt," she said. "Every night. You can't stop me."

"Never tried," he said.

She went out. He heard her car door close out front, but not the engine. She sat out there sometimes before she drove, with her head bowed over the wheel. He knew what she was doing, and he did not look.

\* \* \*

He sat at the table with the papers folded and the Bible open and the kitchen clock ticking over the stove.

He had come close once. Every night for weeks he had sat in a plastic chair beside a hospital bed at Capital General, with his wife's hand in his and the machines breathing for her. Near the end she had whispered, *Walter, will you pray with me?* and he had said, *You pray, honey. I'll listen.* She had prayed for him.

On the last day the doctors came in together, and he had known what they were going to say before they said it. He had buried her that spring, and after the funeral he had come home to this kitchen and opened this Bible and gone on reading it every morning. He had never stopped reading it. He had never once talked to the One who wrote it. Reading, he could do. Reading never told him no.

He had read every word of the prophets fifty times. He could tell you the dimensions of the image on the plain of Dura and the number of Daniel's weeks and the names of the nations that would come down out of the north. And until Kambria started coming by, the chair across the table from him had sat empty for years.

He turned, without quite knowing why, to the ninth chapter of Daniel, where he had taught Kambria to count the weeks on the bench a few weeks back. He found the verse he had skipped over that day, the one that came before all the numbers.

*In the first year of his reign I Daniel understood by books the number of the years, whereof the word of the LORD came to Jeremiah the prophet, that he would accomplish seventy years in the desolations of Jerusalem. (Daniel 9:2)*

That was him. That was exactly him. He had understood by books. He had done the arithmetic.

He read the next verse.

*And I set my face unto the Lord God, to seek by prayer and supplications, with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes… (Daniel 9:3)*

Walt read it through twice. He sat with the red pen in his hand. He knew there was a word missing from his margins, and that it was not a verse.

Then he closed the Bible, and put it back in the pocket of his robe, and got up and washed his cup.

He was drying it at the sink when he saw the car.

It was a gray Chevrolet Malibu, parked at the curb three houses down, a man's gray sleeve resting on the driver's door, on the far side of the street. He had noticed it earlier that morning, when he went out for the papers, and thought nothing of it; people parked where they liked. It had not moved since. Its engine was running. He could see the thin white breath of the exhaust in the cold.

Kambria's little car pulled away from the curb and went down the street toward Rhode Island Avenue.

A moment later, the gray sedan pulled out and went after her.

Walt stood at the sink with the cup in one hand and the dish towel in the other until both cars were gone. Then he went back to the table and picked up the red pen. He had read the plate as it passed. He read everything. He wrote it in the margin of the *Post*, beside the story about the Jerusalem framework, in square capitals.

It was the first thing he had written in a margin in all those years that was not a verse or a correction. He sat looking at it, and hoped he was a foolish old man.

## Act 4 — The Watchman

## Chapter 13: Blow the Trumpet

> *But if the watchman see the sword come, and blow not the trumpet, and the people be not warned; if the sword come, and take any person from among them, he is taken away in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at the watchman's hand.* — Ezekiel 33:6

**Word study: *watchman* — צָפָה** Hebrew *tsaphah* (Strong's H6822). To lean forward and look into the distance; to keep watch and wait. It is the word for a man on a city wall, straining his eyes toward the road. A watchman is not a man who knows the future. He is a man who will not stop looking.

Ezekiel was a priest who never served in the temple. The Babylonians had carried him away from Jerusalem with the other captives, and he lived among them at Tel-abib, by the river Chebar (Ezekiel 1:1; 3:15). When the word of the LORD first came to him, he went and sat among the exiles where they sat, astonished, and remained there seven days (Ezekiel 3:15). At the end of the seven days the word of the LORD came to him again, and he was made a watchman unto the house of Israel (Ezekiel 3:16-17). If he saw the sword coming and gave no warning, the wicked would die in their iniquity, and their blood would be required at his hand (Ezekiel 3:18). Ezekiel had grieved with the captives for seven days. Now he had to tell them what was coming, and he knew most of them would not want to hear it (Ezekiel 3:7).

\* \* \*

Kambria slept badly on Saturday night.

She had come home from Walt's on Friday at eight in the morning, still in yesterday's clothes from the lab, and lain down on top of the covers, and stared at the ceiling until noon. All that day and the next, she kept coming back to the same things. She thought about the margins of his newspapers. *DAN. 9:27. That no man might buy or sell.* She thought about the old man folding the *Journal* into thirds with the edges lined up exactly, to avoid answering her. On Saturday she scrubbed a bathroom that was already clean, and she went to bed again at nine, and before dawn on Sunday morning she gave up.

She made coffee in the dark. The small oil lamp on her kitchen windowsill was still burning; she kept it filled and lit every night, and nobody but Angela had ever asked her why. *So someone out there can always see a light on,* Kambria had told her once, and Angela had laughed, and then stopped laughing. At the table she laid out her Bible and the heavy blue Strong's Concordance Angela had given her for her fortieth birthday, its spine split from use, and found the place by the ribbon.

She read the prophets in order, a chapter or two every morning. She had been in Ezekiel since October. This morning the ribbon was at chapter thirty-three.

She read the first six verses, and then she put her cup down.

*Son of man, speak to the children of thy people, and say unto them, When I bring the sword upon a land, if the people of the land take a man of their coasts, and set him for their watchman: if when he seeth the sword come upon the land, he blow the trumpet, and warn the people… (Ezekiel 33:2-3)*

She knew the passage. Every Christian who had ever read prophecy knew it. She and Angela had underlined it years ago in the gold notebook, with a star in the margin. But she had never read it before dawn, so soon after the Council closed in Jerusalem, with Walt's red pen still before her eyes.

She pulled the concordance across the table.

The first word she looked up was *watchman*. She ran her finger down the long column until she found Ezekiel 33:6, and then the number beside it, and then the number in the Hebrew dictionary in the back. *6822. Tsaphah.* To lean forward. To peer into the distance. To observe, to watch, to wait for.

Kambria read it twice. Every watchman she had ever pictured stood tall and calm on a wall. The word said otherwise: a man leaning forward, straining, his eyes on a road nobody else was watching.

The next word was *warn*. She found the verse and the number. *2094. Zahar.* She read the definition, and then she read it again with her finger under each word. *To gleam. Figuratively, to enlighten by caution. To admonish, to teach, to warn. To shine.*

To shine.

She leaned back from the page. The concordance listed every place the word appeared, and she went down the list one by one, as Angela had taught her, turning the thin pages of the Bible to each verse. Most of them were in Ezekiel, the watchman chapters, *warn* and *warn* and *warning*. Then, near the bottom of the column, she found one that was not about warning at all.

Daniel, chapter twelve, verse three. The last chapter of Daniel, the end of the end.

*And they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament; and they that turn many to righteousness as the stars for ever and ever. (Daniel 12:3)*

*Shine.* The same word. *Zahar.*

Kambria laid her palm on the page. In Ezekiel the word meant to warn a man that the sword was coming. In Daniel it meant to shine like the sky. It was the same word, from the same root, in the same Hebrew Bible, and she had read both verses a hundred times and never once known they were joined.

She saw Angela on the sixth floor, the infusion line taped to her arm, holding Celeste's hand and promising to pray for her. She saw Angela at the dinner table on Thursday nights, her hand held open for her husband at every meal, and never withdrawn, even when he left it lying there. Angela had never preached at anyone.

She turned back to Ezekiel and read on to verse nine, the one she had always skipped past because she had never believed it was meant for her.

*Nevertheless, if thou warn the wicked of his way to turn from it; if he do not turn from his way, he shall die in his iniquity; but thou hast delivered thy soul. (Ezekiel 33:9)*

She read it three times.

For so long she had carried every person she loved, and never once set them down. Ezra. Walt. Elijah at the bar. Her sister in Richmond. The people at the lab. She had gone to bed every night feeling that if they were lost, it would be because she had not found the right words. The verse said otherwise: her part was to blow the trumpet. Whether they turned was between them and God. *…whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear… (Ezekiel 2:5)* She had read that one too, in Ezekiel's second chapter, and never understood it as mercy. It was mercy. It meant she did not have to be God. She only had to be faithful.

The knot she had carried for months came loose, and she wept a little at the table, the coffee going cold at her elbow.

Then she opened her newest notebook to a clean page and wrote the date at the top. *November 15, 2026.* Under it, in pen, she wrote three lines.

*Tsaphah: lean forward. Keep looking.*

*Zahar: to warn is to shine.*

*Blow it. Whether they hear or not. Then leave them with God.*

\* \* \*

At seven she picked up her phone to check the weather, and saw that Jalen's video had passed a million views.

She had posted it herself, at eight minutes to midnight in April, from her car outside the Pattersons' house, an hour after Jalen had said she could. *Untitled. Jalen Patterson, cello.* It had found eleven thousand people by morning, and then it had gone quiet for the summer, as most things did. In September a cellist in Seoul with a famous name had shared it, and the numbers had started to climb again. Now, sometime in the night, it had crossed a million.

She scrolled through the newest comments. A nurse in Accra. A trucker in Alberta. A father in Toronto who wrote that he had driven four hours that morning to see his son. A woman in Ohio who said she had played it at her husband's funeral. The sound engineer from Lisbon, again, who had played it for her whole studio. And underneath almost every one of them, in a dozen languages, the same question.

*Who isn't here?*

*Who was he talking to?*

*Please tell us who "someone who isn't here right now" is.*

Kambria knew. She had been sitting in Row C with her phone held up, and she had watched Jalen's eyes go to the empty seat on the aisle with *DAD* written across the program in black marker, again and again, all through the piece. She had sent Jalen the file that same night, for the drive he was making his father. Whether Ezra had ever found it, she could not say.

She started to type an answer. She deleted it. It was not hers to tell.

She put the phone down on the table, face up, and stared at it until the screen went dark on its own. Then she picked it up again and opened the settings for her voicemail.

Before she recorded anything, she called Angela.

She did it some mornings. Not often. Angela's greeting had still been on the line all summer, bright and hurried, a classroom bell going off behind it: *It's Angela, leave it at the beep, love you.* Kambria never left anything. She only listened and hung up.

This morning a stranger answered for her. *The number you have dialed is not in service.*

Kambria held the phone away from her ear and looked at it. Somebody had finally shut off the line. Somebody had been right to. She thought of Ezra awake on that couch at that hour, and wondered if he knew yet, and hoped he did not.

Then she recorded her own, once, with her thumb shaking on the button.

"Hi, you've reached Kambria. If you're hearing this and I don't call you back, it already happened. Don't be afraid. It's not too late. Read Joel 2:32. Call on the name of the Lord."

If she was taken, people would call her. Ezra would call her. Walt would call her. Nobody would get a recording of a stranger telling them she was not in service. They would get her voice, and the way out.

She pressed *Save*.

\* \* \*

After church she called her sister. Monica, three years older, a real estate agent in Richmond with two teenage boys, answered from a Harvest Basket aisle where the eggs had been gone for two weeks. Kambria told her about the Mall and Jerusalem, and Monica said "mm-hm" the way she did to clients.

"Grandma told us on that porch in Petersburg and I believe it harder every day. Jesus is coming back. I want you ready when He does."

"Kam, you sound like Grandma's revival tent. I love you. I'm just not doing this in the middle of Harvest Basket."

"Then do it later. Read Joel 2:32. That's all I'm asking."

"Okay," Monica said, the way she said it to her boys when they asked for what they would not get.

Kambria sat in her car in the church lot with her sister's voice still in her ear. The sadness was older than the call. Then she remembered the verse. *…thou hast delivered thy soul. (Ezekiel 33:9)* She had blown the trumpet. She said her sister's name out loud to God, and started the car.

\* \* \*

On Monday night she went to Rooney's.

She had not been inside a bar in years. Rooney's was a narrow room on the corner of Twelfth Street, six blocks from the Pattersons' house, with a long wooden bar, a jukebox nobody played, and a television over the register. The bartender, a heavy, gray-bearded man named Sal, looked up when she came in, still in her coat, and raised his eyebrows. Two men at the far end were already too drunk to sit straight on their stools. Paul's list from Galatians came to her without her asking for it, the one she and Angela had copied into the gold notebook: *drunkenness, revellings, and such like… (Galatians 5:21)* She put it away; she had not come to judge.

Elijah Brooks was on the stool nearest the door, where he had sat every night since last winter. He was Ezra's oldest friend, his coat on the next stool to save it for nobody, and when he saw her his face broke into a wide, delighted grin.

"Well, look at this," he said loudly, so the whole bar could hear. "The doomsday club has sent a delegate."

A couple of men down the bar laughed. Kambria took off her coat and took the stool beside him.

"Ginger ale," she told Sal.

"Ginger ale," Elijah repeated, with deep sorrow. "Sal, you hear that? She came all the way to a bar for ginger ale. That's how you know the end is near."

"I came to talk to you," Kambria said.

"To me?" Elijah laid a palm over his heart. "Kambria. I'm touched. Are you finally leaving the church for me? Because I've been waiting for years."

"I came to tell you something," she said, "and then I'll leave you alone. I promise."

Her tone stopped his smiling. Then the smile came back, thinner. He turned his glass in a half circle on the wood and waited.

So she told him. She told him the same things she had told Monica, plainly, in order. The Council. The drafting committee it had left sitting in Jerusalem. The verses in Daniel, and what Walt had worked out on the bench across from the statue. "Jesus is coming back, Elijah," she said. "Not someday. Soon. And there's a day when it'll be too late to get ready. This isn't that day. That's why I'm sitting on this stool."

Elijah listened without interrupting, a thing she had not known him capable of. When she was done he said nothing. Over the register, Sal had the news on with the sound up. He had kept the sound up since the summer. An earthquake had struck a mountain town in Peru during the Sunday Mass, and the bell tower of the old church lay across the plaza in pieces. Men in hard hats were passing stones hand to hand, and women stood behind the tape with their rosaries, waiting for names. Beneath the pictures, the crawl went on by itself without anyone reading it: Iran, the flu, a ferry lost off Manila.

"You know what I said to Ezra once?" Elijah said finally. "Right here. This stool." He tapped the bar. "I said, if it was true, wouldn't there be a sign? Wouldn't we know?" He laughed, a short ugly sound.

Kambria didn't answer. She looked up at the television.

Elijah looked at it too. He watched the men passing stones until the picture changed. For a few seconds his face was bare: no joke, no grin, nothing to hide behind. Kambria saw how frightened he was, and had been, for years.

"What am I supposed to do, Kambria?" he asked, and for once he was not joking.

"Call on Him," she said. "That's all. Call on the name of the Lord. He'll do the rest."

He held her eyes past the end of the joke. Then the grin came back, all at once.

"Write it down for me," he said. "In case I forget. I'm an old man. My memory's going."

She took a pen out of her purse and pulled a napkin from the stack by Sal's elbow. She put the date in the corner, as she did on everything, and set the numbers down before the words. On it she wrote, in a cramped, careful hand: *Joel 2:32. Romans 10:13. For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.*

Elijah took the napkin and folded it in half, and then in half again. He took out his wallet, and put the napkin in behind his driver's license, and patted it.

"For emergencies," he said, and winked.

"For emergencies," Kambria said.

She finished her ginger ale and put a five-dollar bill on the bar. She was putting on her coat when Elijah spoke again, without looking at her.

"He doesn't come in much anymore," he said. "Ezra."

Kambria stopped with one arm in her sleeve.

"Hasn't for months. He's got somebody." Elijah shrugged. "Don't ask me who. He won't say. I asked him, and he just looked at me." He turned his glass on the wood. "I've known him since I was ten years old, and he won't tell me her name. You know what that means."

Kambria thought of a small silver car parked at the curb outside Ezra's house in October, with a red string hanging from the mirror. She said nothing and finished putting on her coat.

"Goodnight, Elijah," she said.

"Goodnight, doomsday." He raised his glass to her without turning around. "Drive safe. Don't get raptured on the Beltway."

\* \* \*

On Tuesday night she was back at the hospital.

Most of what her team had sent up to Hyattsville was the flu, the same strain as the first two waves, only meaner. But on Monday afternoon, three samples from a nursing home in Petworth had come back as something else.

Kambria ran them twice. It was a bacterium, the kind that causes pneumonia, and it would not die. It shrugged off every antibiotic on the panel, even the last two, the ones doctors kept locked away for when nothing else worked. She had seen resistant germs before; every lab had. What she had never seen was its genes. There were pieces in it from organisms that did not live in the same places and had no way to meet, lined up neatly in a row. When nature mixed things, it made a mess. This was not a mess. It was tidy.

She ran it a third time.

Then she pulled the three patients' charts. She had the access; the federal agreement gave her team every record they asked for. Three women, all over eighty, all from the same nursing home on Georgia Avenue. All three had been enrolled in October in a free wellness program, run at the home by a company called Verity Health: vitamins, blood pressure checks, and a nasal spray to "support seasonal immunity." Kambria knew the name. Verity Health Labs in Rockville was the contract bench that ran the agency's overflow sequencing; half her confirmation runs for years had gone through its doors, stamped clean. So had the Ohio isolate, two years ago, with the patch nobody could explain. It had not occurred to her to wonder who owned it. She looked it up on her phone, standing by the sequencer. Its website was clean and white and said almost nothing. At the very bottom, in small gray type, it said that Verity Health was a portfolio company of the Meridian Trust, Dubai.

She stood in the hallway with the phone dark in her hand.

Then she wrote her report and flagged it urgent and sent it up the chain. And before she logged off, she did something she had never done in all her years at the Centers for Disease Control. She copied the raw files onto a thumb drive from her own purse, every read from all three samples, and she zipped the drive into the inside pocket of her coat. It was against every rule she had ever signed. She knew that. But the same quiet voice that had told her to photograph a license plate in October told her that the report might disappear, and that the files might disappear with it.

In the ninth notebook, under the date, she wrote one line. *Pestilence, like Rev. 6:8: a pale horse. Pangs, not the seal. Matt. 24:7-8.* Under it, smaller: *Verity Health. Meridian Trust. Vale.*

Then she tried to tell the people she worked with.

She did not stand up in the break room and preach; she had promised herself she wouldn't. She waited until people came to her, and when they asked her how she was holding up, she told them the truth. She told Dana, her partner on the outbreak team, while they loaded the sequencer. She told two of the hospital's young lab techs at the coffee maker. She told a respiratory therapist named Paul, who had been raised Pentecostal and laughed and said his mother told him the same thing every Easter.

Most of them listened politely and changed the subject. Dana told her, kindly, to keep it out of the lab. One of the young techs, a quiet man named Tomás who had only been at the hospital since August, waited until the others had gone, and then asked her, without looking at her, if she could write down "that verse." She wrote it on the back of a specimen requisition. He folded it into the pocket of his scrubs and got back to work.

Celeste came into the break room at a quarter to three with a cup of tea, and her red hair pinned up, and her cheeks pink from the cold of the parking garage. She had been glowing for weeks. Everyone had noticed it. She sat down beside Kambria and put a hand on her shoulder.

"I heard you've been telling everyone the world is ending," she said, and smiled.

"Not ending," Kambria said. "Changing. He's coming back."

"Oh, honey." Celeste squeezed her shoulder. "That's fear talking. You know it is. Fear isn't from God, Kambria. Angela used to say that."

Kambria looked at her. Angela had said it. She had said it on the sixth floor, to a frightened woman in the next recliner, with Celeste standing right there smoothing a blanket.

"Fear isn't," Kambria said. "Warning is."

Celeste laughed, low and musical, and gave her shoulder a pat. Her phone buzzed on the cushion. She glanced down at the screen, and a warmth crossed her face, and then she turned the phone over so the screen was facing down.

Kambria had seen a man do exactly that, at his own kitchen counter, in the spring.

She looked away.

\* \* \*

That morning, when she got home from the hospital, she did not go to bed. First she took down the heavy blue concordance Angela had given her for her fortieth birthday, the one with the split spine, slid the thumb drive down inside the spine where the binding had come loose, and taped the spine shut with packing tape, as Angela had mended her own. Then she put the book back on the shelf between the others, where it had always been.

She sat under the oil lamp in the window with the ninth notebook open, and read back over the last three days. Monica, in Harvest Basket. Elijah, with the napkin in his wallet. Tomás, with the requisition in his pocket. Dana, who had told her to keep it out of the lab. Celeste, who had turned her phone face down. She dated every line now. If it ever came to it, someone would need to see when she knew.

There was one more person.

She had told herself for weeks that it was not her place. He had made himself very clear. Every Sunday he took the dish and shut the door. She had let that be her answer, because it was easier, and because she was afraid.

She thought of the verse she had read at four on Sunday morning. *His blood will I require at the watchman's hand.* She looked at the second line she had written on Sunday. *Zahar: to warn is to shine.*

Angela had left him a notebook. She had written it for him, every page of it, in her round, patient handwriting, and she had written on the cover *For Ezra, when you're ready.* And he had put it in a closet the night she gave it to him, and he had not opened it in a year.

How much time was left, Kambria could only guess. She only knew there was less than there had been.

She wrote one more line beneath the rest, and underlined it twice.

*Thursday. Ezra.*

She was reaching for the light switch when her phone chimed on the table.

It was an email from the agency's case system, the automatic kind, with no name at the bottom. *Your submission regarding specimen cluster DC-1117 (Petworth) has been reviewed and closed. No further action is required.*

Kambria read it standing up. Then she sat back down and read the time stamp.

She had flagged the report urgent at nine minutes past two that morning. In all her years, no urgent report had ever reached a reviewer in less than three days.

This one had been closed at two thirty-one. Twenty-two minutes after she sent it.

Nobody read that fast. Nobody even found it that fast. Not unless they had been sitting there, at two in the morning, waiting for it to come in.

## Chapter 14: The Door

> *Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.* — Jesus, Revelation 3:20

**Word study: *knock* — κρούω** Greek *krouō* (Strong's G2925). To knock, to rap on a door with the knuckles. In Revelation 3:20 it is in the present tense: I stand, and I am knocking, and I keep on knocking. He does not knock once and go away.

In the Song of Solomon, a young bride lies asleep at night, though her heart is awake, and she hears her beloved knocking at the door (Song of Solomon 5:2). He asks her to open to him, for his head is filled with dew (Song of Solomon 5:2). She does not rise; she has put off her coat and washed her feet, and she asks how she can dress again and soil them (Song of Solomon 5:3). He puts his hand in by the hole of the door, and her heart is moved for him (Song of Solomon 5:4). At last she rises to open, her hands dripping with myrrh upon the handles of the lock (Song of Solomon 5:5). But her beloved has withdrawn himself and is gone. She seeks him and cannot find him; she calls him, and he gives her no answer (Song of Solomon 5:6).

\* \* \*

Kambria parked across the street from the Pattersons' house a little before six on Thursday evening, and sat in her car with the engine off.

She had not slept much. She had spent most of the afternoon at her dinner table, writing down what she wanted to say, crossing it out and writing it again. The page was in her coat pocket now.
