She already knew she would not read from it. She had brought it anyway, as she brought a list of questions to her own doctor and then forgot all of them the moment he walked in.

It was nearly dark. The streetlights had come on along the block, and the air smelled of wet leaves and someone's fireplace. Across the street, the porch light was already burning over the Pattersons' front steps. Mia turned it on herself every evening at dusk, up on her toes by the door. Everyone on the street knew that. Nobody switched it off before morning.

In the brick house directly behind her, a curtain moved. Kambria looked over her shoulder and saw Walt standing at his kitchen window in his brown cardigan, with a coffee mug in his hand. He regarded her through the glass. Then he raised the mug, just slightly, and let the curtain fall.

She had told him on Wednesday that she was going. He had called it neither a good idea nor a bad one. He had only said, "Thursday's his night out. Go early."

She locked the car and crossed the street.

\* \* \*

Mia opened the door before she could ring the bell.

"Miss Kambria!"

Mia threw both arms around Kambria's waist and held on. She was in pajama pants and a sweatshirt with a cartoon fox on it, and her hair was in two puffs, and she smelled like crayons and macaroni and cheese. A brown teddy bear with one ear worn shiny hung from her hand by its paw.

"Hey, baby girl." Kambria knelt on the porch and hugged her properly. "Hey. Look how tall you got."

"I'm drawing," Mia announced. "Come see. Grandma went home already. Daddy's in the shower. He's going out."

She took Kambria by the hand and pulled her inside, through the front hall and into the kitchen, before Kambria could decide whether she was allowed in.

The kitchen looked as it always had. The same yellow curtains Angela had sewn herself. The same scratched table. The same chair at the end, Angela's chair, with nobody in it. A flyer from the spring was still pinned to the refrigerator with a magnet shaped like a strawberry: *Senior Recital. Thursday, April 16.*

Mia climbed onto her chair and picked up a red crayon. Before her on the table lay a sheet of paper with the beginnings of a picture: their house, the porch light drawn crooked, and a black sky colored in from edge to edge.

"That's our house," Mia said. "At night."

"I see," Kambria said. "It's beautiful."

Mia bent over the paper. In the middle of the black sky she began to draw a circle, and then to fill it in with the red crayon, pressing hard, going around and around. Kambria watched the circle darken and take a shine from the wax.

"What's that?" Kambria asked. Her voice came out thin.

"The moon," Mia said, without looking up. "It's going to be red. I'm making it for Daddy. I'm going to put it on the fridge so he sees it." She pressed harder. "He doesn't look at my pictures anymore. But he'll see this one, because it's on the fridge."

Kambria pressed her knuckles to her lips.

She knew the verse. She had copied it into her notebook a dozen times. *The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and the terrible day of the LORD come. (Joel 2:31)* She had copied the one after it a dozen times too, and she said it to herself now, silently, sitting at Angela's dinner table with Angela's daughter coloring beside her. *And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered… (Joel 2:32)*

Upstairs, the shower turned off.

\* \* \*

Ezra appeared on the stairs a few minutes later in a clean, pressed shirt that was new to her, with his hair still damp. He smelled of cologne. He stopped in the kitchen doorway when he saw her, and for a second his face showed nothing but surprise.

Then it closed.

"Kambria," he said.

"Hi, Ezra."

"It's Thursday."

His phone lay on the counter by the bread box. It lit while he stood there and buzzed once against the laminate, and Kambria read a single line on the screen before his hand came down and flipped it face down. *C: Left the light on for you.*

No one she knew went by a single letter. She did not let herself wonder.

"I know. I'm sorry. I won't stay long." She stood up. "Can I talk to you for a minute? On the porch?"

He looked at Mia, who was coloring and pretending not to listen. He looked at the clock on the stove. Then he walked past Kambria without a word, through the front hall, and opened the front door, and held it for her.

She went out. He came out after her and pulled the door almost shut behind him, so that it stood open a few inches. The porch light was bright over their heads. The air was cold.

"What is it?" he said.

She had the page in her pocket. She did not take it out.

"I'm going to say it plainly," she said. "And then I'll go. I promise." She took a breath. "I think it's very close, Ezra. Everything Angela and I wrote down for years. The statue on the Mall. The Council in Jerusalem. The committee it left sitting. Daniel. Ezekiel. All of it. It's not coming someday. It's coming now." She heard her own voice shake, and she made it stop. "I think the Lord is coming back for His people, very soon. And I don't think you're ready."

Ezra's hand closed on the doorframe. He didn't say anything.

"She left you a notebook," Kambria said. "Angela. It's in the hall closet. I know you know it's there. Every page of it is for you. She wrote it for you in that bed when she could barely hold the pen. She wrote *When you're ready* on the cover." Her eyes were stinging. "Ezra, I don't think there's time to wait until you're ready. Please. Open it. Tonight. Before you go wherever you're going."

"Don't," he said, very low. "Don't tell me what Angela wanted."

"I'm not telling you. She told me. She told me herself, at that table, the week before she died. 'When he's ready, Kam, make sure he finds it.'"

"I know where it is."

"Then open it."

"Time for what?" His voice rose. "That's what I want to know. You said there isn't time. Time for what, Kambria? The end of the world?" He laughed, a short, hard sound. "You and her. All those years. Every Thursday night at my dinner table, with your Bibles and your clippings and your colored pens. Every week, it was coming. Every week, it was the end. I came home tired from work every Thursday, and my kitchen was a prayer meeting." He stopped. His voice dropped. "And she died anyway. All that praying. All those notebooks. She died anyway."

"She didn't die anyway," she said. "She died ready."

He stared at her.

"She died holding your hand," Kambria said. "She died with the name of Jesus in her mouth. She wasn't afraid. You were there. You saw it. That wasn't her losing, Ezra. That was her going home. And she wanted you to be able to come too. That's all that notebook is. It's her holding her hand out to you one more time."

She thought she had reached him. His eyes filled, his mouth tightened, his hand on the doorframe began to shake. He looked down at the porch boards, and she saw the man who had stood in the doorway of that room with his arms folded, trying not to fall apart.

Then he looked up, and the anger was back.

"Get off my porch," he said.

"Ezra..."

"Get off my porch. Get off my property. I mean it, Kambria." His voice was rough and low. "Don't come back here with this. Don't bring it to my door again. Not for Mia, not for Jalen, not for anybody."

"Please," she said.

He stepped back inside, and the door closed in her face.

She heard the lock turn.

\* \* \*

She stood on the porch.

She lost count of the seconds. The porch light buzzed over her head. A car crept by on the wet street. She lifted her hand to knock again, and held it there, inches from the wood.

She did not knock.

She stood with her hand raised, and she thought of a verse she and Angela had read together at the dinner table on the other side of that door, more times than she could count. *Behold, I stand at the door, and knock… (Revelation 3:20)* She had always pictured that door as a church door, or the door of a stranger's heart. She had never pictured it as a front door on a street in Northeast Washington, with a porch light that a six-year-old switched on every night. She had never pictured Jesus standing there knocking with His hand raised, as hers was raised now, after the lock had turned.

He did not leave. That was what the verse said. He stood there, and He knocked, and He kept on knocking.

On Ezra's porch she understood a little of how God felt. She had thought she knew what it was to love someone who would not open the door. She had not known anything.

She lowered her hand, and sat down on the top step, and put her face in her hands, and cried.

After a while, she heard a tapping behind her. She looked up. Mia was standing at the big front window in her fox sweatshirt, with the teddy bear tucked under one arm. She had pushed the curtain aside. She was looking out at Kambria very seriously, and she pressed her free palm to the glass.

Kambria got up and went to the window, and pressed her own hand against the other side.

They stayed that way, palm to palm through the cold glass. Then a voice called Mia's name from inside the house, low and tired, and the curtain fell back, and she was gone.

\* \* \*

When she turned around, Walt was coming across the street.

He came one step at a time, his cane in one hand, the other held out for balance, and he did not look both ways. He was wearing his slippers. Eighteen days out of Brandick, he had no business on anybody's steps. He came up the walk to the bottom of the porch steps and stopped there, winded, and looked up at her.

"Well," he said.

"I knocked," she said. Her voice broke on it.

"I saw." He held out a folded handkerchief, white and pressed. "Here. It's clean."

She came down the steps and took it, and settled on the bottom step, and he lowered himself down beside her one inch at a time, grumbling, until he was settled on the cold brick with the cane propped against his shoulder. Behind them, the porch light buzzed.

"Jeremiah was put in a pit for less," Walt said after a while. "They let him down in the mud with ropes. All he did was tell them what was coming."

Kambria laughed in spite of herself, a wet, broken laugh, and wiped her eyes with his handkerchief.

"Did he get out?"

"An Ethiopian pulled him out. Rags under his arms so the ropes wouldn't cut him." Walt looked out at the street. "Nobody in Jerusalem lifted a finger. It took a foreigner."

They sat without talking. The cold came up through the brick.

"Walt," she said. "Will you pray with me?"

He was quiet for so long that she thought he had not heard.

"You pray," he said finally. "I'll sit here."

So she prayed. She prayed out loud, on Ezra's front steps, with her hands folded around Walt's handkerchief, and Walt sat beside her with his eyes open, looking at the street. "Father, it's Kambria, on his steps again. Open that closet door. Whatever it takes, Lord, open it. Hold Mia at that window. Keep Jalen in his dorm. Keep Loretta, who has prayed for her boy every morning for years. And there's a woman he's going to see tonight. I don't know her name. You do. Keep her, too." Her voice was almost gone. "And Lord, the old man sitting beside me. You've been knocking at his door longer than I have. Walter Simmons. Amen."

Walt kept his eyes open. But when she said his name, she felt him go rigid beside her, and he stayed that way until she said amen.

A little before eight the front door opened behind them.

They both stood up. Ezra came out with his keys in his hand and his coat over his arm, and he stopped when he saw them on his steps. No one spoke. Then he walked down past them, close enough that Kambria could have touched his sleeve, and he looked at neither of them. He got into his truck, and backed out of the driveway, and drove away down the street toward Sixteenth.

Walt watched the taillights go.

"I'll walk you to your car," he said.

On the drive home, on Rhode Island Avenue, she noticed the headlights behind her. A gray Chevrolet Malibu, a few car lengths back. She would not have thought anything of it, except that it had been parked in front of Ezra's house when she came out, with the engine running, and now it was here. She turned off onto a side street without signaling. The headlights turned too. She pulled into a gas station and sat at the pump with the engine running, and the sedan rolled past without stopping, its windows too dark to see in. She watched its taillights until they were gone. Then she wrote the plate number on the back of her hand in pen, because she did not trust herself to remember it, and drove home the long way.

\* \* \*

Jalen called her at ten.

She was at the kitchen table with the lamp lit and the notebook shut. She had not been able to open it. When the phone rang and she saw his name, she was so afraid of what he might say that she almost let it go to voicemail.

"Miss Kambria?" His voice was low; she could hear a roommate's music through the wall behind him. "Mia FaceTimed me. She said you were crying on our porch."

Kambria closed her eyes. "I'm sorry, sweetheart. I didn't mean for her to see that."

"What happened?"

So she told him. She did not tell him everything his father had said. She told him that she had asked his father to open his mother's notebook, and that he had said no, and that she had sat on the steps for a while afterward with Mr. Simmons. Jalen listened without saying anything. When she was done, the line went so silent that she checked whether the call had dropped.

"He'll open it," Jalen said.

"Jalen..."

"He will. Mom said. She told me, at the end. She said he'd be ready one day, and I had to be patient with him, because he was a slow builder." He laughed a little, and it caught in his throat. "She said that. A slow builder. But he finishes everything he starts. Everything. I never saw him leave anything half done."

Kambria wiped her eyes with the back of her hand.

"I'm coming home Tuesday night," Jalen said. "For Thanksgiving. Grandma's doing the dressing, and Mia's making place cards." He hesitated. "Will you come Thursday? For dinner? I know how he's been. But it's my house too. Mia wants you, and I want you to come."

She could not answer.

"I'll come," she said. "I'll bring the macaroni and cheese."

"The baked one? With the crust?"

"The baked one."

"Okay." She could hear him smiling. "Okay. Thursday."

After he hung up, she sat at the table until the kettle clicked off. Then she opened the ninth notebook to the page from Tuesday night, the one with Ezra's name underlined twice at the bottom. She drew a line through *Thursday*. Underneath it she wrote Jesus' words, in pen, all the way through.

*Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me. (Revelation 3:20)*

She numbered the page in the corner and wrote the reference small in the margin, 3 and 20, the way she marked anything she would want to find again at three in the morning. And under the verse, one more line.

*I knocked once. He is still knocking.*

Below it, smaller, she wrote the things she did not want to lose by morning. *Thurs. 11/19, 8:04 p.m. Ezra left for "C." Text on his counter: "Left the light on for you." Gray Malibu on Walt's street. Then behind me. Same car. Plate is on my hand.*

She left the lamp burning in the window and went to bed.

In the small hours she woke up, and did not know why.

The house was quiet. The furnace ticked. She lay listening, then went to the front room in her bare feet and stood beside the curtain without touching it.

Across the street, under the streetlight that had been out since summer, a car was parked with its lights off. A gray sedan. Inside it, low, she could see the small blue glow of a phone screen, and then it went dark.

The numbers she had written on the back of her hand that evening had faded, but she could still read them. She held her hand up to the edge of the window, where the glow from the porch light next door came in.

They matched.

She stood in the dark beside the curtain, making no more sound than the curtain did, and prayed without a sound while the car sat there and nothing happened. Toward four its engine started. It pulled away from the curb without turning on its headlights, and went down the street, and turned the corner, and was gone.

She did not go back to bed. She kept her seat until it was light, with her back to the wall and the lamp burning in the window, and her Bible open in front of her, and the front door where she could see it.

## Chapter 15: The Leopard's Plaza

> *After this I beheld, and lo another, like a leopard, which had upon the back of it four wings of a fowl; the beast had also four heads; and dominion was given to it.* — Daniel 7:6

**Word study: *leopard* — נְמַר** Aramaic *nemar* (Strong's H5245). A leopard, from a root that means to be spotted. The leopard is the stealthiest of the great cats, and it hunts by waiting, still and patient, until the moment it moves. Daniel saw it with wings on its back, faster still.

In the first year of Belshazzar king of Babylon, Daniel had a dream and visions of his head upon his bed, and he wrote the dream down (Daniel 7:1). He saw the four winds of heaven strive upon the great sea, and four great beasts came up from the sea, diverse one from another (Daniel 7:2-3). The first was like a lion and had eagle's wings (Daniel 7:4). The second was like a bear, with three ribs in its mouth between its teeth (Daniel 7:5). The third was like a leopard, with upon its back four wings of a fowl and four heads, and dominion was given to it (Daniel 7:6). The fourth beast was dreadful and terrible and strong exceedingly; it had great iron teeth, it devoured and brake in pieces, and it had ten horns (Daniel 7:7). Daniel's spirit was grieved in the midst of his body, and the visions of his head troubled him (Daniel 7:15). He kept the matter in his heart (Daniel 7:28).

\* \* \*

Mrs. Clarice Bell was eighty-one years old, and she was dying, and she knew it.

She had come in by ambulance on Friday night from the nursing home in Petworth, the same one, with a fever of a hundred and four and a blood pressure that would not stay up. Kambria had been called in from home at midnight to take the samples herself, her badge and login already dead since six, so a night tech had to let her in. By four in the morning the antibiotics had done nothing at all, and the doctor had come and gone, and the family had been called. Kambria knew why, and could not tell anyone in the room. There were six of them now in the treatment room off the trauma bay: two daughters, a son in a bus driver's uniform, and three grown grandchildren, standing against the walls because there were only two chairs.

Mrs. Bell was a birdlike woman with white hair braided close to her head and a gold cross on a thin chain at her throat. She had not spoken in an hour. At a quarter to five she opened her eyes, and looked around the room at her children, and then she found Kambria by the bed rail, in her mask and gown with the swab kit in her hands, and held out her hand.

Kambria went to her and took it.

"You a praying woman?" Mrs. Bell whispered.

"Yes, ma'am."

"Then pray for me, baby. Pray me home."

Kambria looked at the family. The older daughter nodded, already crying. The son took off his cap.

So Kambria prayed. She held Mrs. Bell's hand in both of hers, and she prayed in a murmur, as Angela had prayed over everyone who sat beside her bed. "Father, thank You for eighty-one years of Clarice Bell. Thank You for these children. Take away her fear, Lord, and her pain." She prayed the twenty-third psalm, and the old woman's lips moved with her on *I will fear no evil*. Then she said, "Lord Jesus, You said in Your Father's house are many mansions, and You went to prepare a place for her. Receive her now. In Jesus' name."

"Amen," said Mrs. Bell, and the whole room said it with her.

When Kambria looked up, Celeste was standing in the doorway with a stack of folded blankets in her arms. She stood looking at the family, and at Mrs. Bell, and at Kambria with the old woman's hand in hers. Her face was soft and sad. Then she set the blankets down on the counter and went out without a word.

Mrs. Bell died at six-ten in the morning with her son holding one hand and her older daughter holding the other. Afterward, in the hallway, the son gripped Kambria's hand and could not speak, and the younger daughter hugged her and said, "Thank you for praying with Mama. That's all she wanted."

Kambria walked out to the parking garage at a quarter to seven with the swab kit in a sealed bag for the courier, and sat in her car with the engine off, and did not think about the doorway at all. She thought about the phone call.

Francesca Moretti had called her on Wednesday night, a little after ten, from an unfamiliar New York number.

It had taken her a moment to place the voice. Francesca had worked two benches down from her in Hyattsville for years: a tall, quick, dark-haired microbiologist from South Philadelphia who hummed old hymns under her breath while she worked and brought a tray of her grandmother's cannoli to every office party. She had moved up to New York years ago, and been loaned from there to the new health security office of the Organization for World Peace. Kambria had sent her one file in all that time: the Ohio isolate, with the patch nobody could explain. Francesca had written back that it matched nothing she knew and she would keep looking. Then nothing.

Kambria had written to her on Monday night, three careful lines through the one personal account she trusted, asking only whether anything like Petworth had crossed her desk. She had not expected an answer.

"You asked me Monday if anyone up here had seen a cluster like this," Francesca had said. Her voice was low. "So I went looking. The Petworth report was on a server I'm not cleared for. By this afternoon it was pulled back and sealed. And Kam, somebody saw me open it." A pause. "Kam, I have to see you. Not on the phone. Can you come up?"

"Francesca, I've got work. I can't just..."

"Then come for the weekend." Francesca's voice, always so steady, had shaken. "Saturday. Four o'clock. The diner on Second Avenue at Forty-Fifth, the one with the red booths. Get a hotel. Make it look like a weekend in the city. Please."

Kambria had told her she would think about it. She had thought about it for two days, and decided it was too much, and never called back.

Now she sat in the cold car in the hospital garage with Mrs. Bell's swabs in a sealed bag on the passenger seat, and she knew why the antibiotics had done nothing, and she thought of the son who had taken off his cap.

She took out her phone and bought a train ticket.

\* \* \*

She slept for two hours, showered, and packed a bag for one night: a change of clothes, her toothbrush, her Bible, and the ninth notebook. She booked the cheapest hotel she could find near Grand Central, two hundred and eighty-nine dollars she did not have to spare, and told no one where she was going.

The Northeast Regional left Union Station at five minutes past eleven. She had a window seat and her Bible open on her lap to the seventh chapter of Daniel, and she did not read it. She kept seeing Mrs. Bell's hand reaching for her across the bed.

Her phone buzzed as the train pulled out of the tunnel. *Celeste: Heard you're taking a weekend away. Rest, sis. Safe travels.*

Kambria read it three times. She had told the front desk she needed Saturday for a personal day, and nothing more. The front desk must have said something. That was all it was. She typed a thumbs-up, and deleted it, and let the phone go dark on her knee.

At half past two the train slid into Penn Station, and she was in New York.

The city was already dressed for Christmas. On the side of a building a screen four stories tall played an ad in which glossy young people danced on a rooftop with drinks in their hands, and nobody's eyes were quite awake. *Lovers of pleasures more than lovers of God,* Kambria thought, and was ashamed, because their hearts were not hers to read. She prayed for them instead. She left her bag at the hotel, and at ten to four she walked into the diner on Second Avenue.

\* \* \*

Francesca was not there.

Kambria took the last red booth at the back, facing the door, the one Francesca would have taken, and ordered a cup of coffee, and waited. Four o'clock came. Then four-fifteen. Then half past. She called the New York number, and it rang and rang, and went to a recorded voice that said the customer was not available. At five o'clock the waitress came to refill her cup for the third time. She was a heavy, gray-haired woman with reading glasses on a chain, and she looked Kambria up and down over the rims.

"You waiting on the tall girl?" she said. "Dark hair? Talks fast?"

Kambria sat up. "Yes."

"She's been in every day this week. Same booth. Sits facing the door, orders tea, doesn't drink it." The waitress set the coffee pot down on the table. "She didn't come in yesterday, or today. But Thursday she gave me something. Said a lady might come in on Saturday with a notebook and ask for her, and to give it to her if she did." She looked at the notebook on the table beside Kambria's cup. "I'm guessing that's you." She lowered her voice. "Two men in suits came by Friday, asking after her. Flashed a badge so fast I couldn't read it. I told them I'd never seen her. I don't know why. I didn't like how they stood."

She went to the register and came back with a plain white envelope. On the front, in blue ink, was a single letter. *K.*

Kambria waited until the waitress had gone. Then she opened it.

Inside was a key on a ring with a small brass tag stamped *4C*. A business card from the health security office of the Organization for World Peace, with Francesca's name on the front, and on the back, in Francesca's quick, looping hand, an address: *312 East 43rd. Tudor City.* And a folded sheet of notebook paper with nothing on it but five lines, written in pen.

*Genesis 6:4.*

*Daniel 7:7.*

*Daniel 7:24.*

*Revelation 17:12.*

*Revelation 6:8.*

That was all. No note. No explanation. Five verses, in the order Francesca had written them.

Kambria sat motionless in the red booth with the paper in her hands. Francesca had trusted neither a letter nor the phone. She had trusted that the woman who wrote everything down would know how to read.

She opened her Bible on the table and began.

*There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.* (Genesis 6:4) The days before the flood. The mighty men. The men who made a name.

*After this I saw in the night visions, and behold a fourth beast, dreadful and terrible, and strong exceedingly; and it had great iron teeth… and it had ten horns.* (Daniel 7:7)

*And the ten horns out of this kingdom are ten kings that shall arise: and another shall rise after them…* (Daniel 7:24)

*And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet; but receive power as kings one hour with the beast.* (Revelation 17:12)

*And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him. And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth.* (Revelation 6:8) The word *death* there, she knew, could be read *pestilence*. She did not think the seal itself had opened, not yet. This was the beginning of sorrows, the birth pangs of Matthew 24:7-8, the shadow of the pale horse before the horse.

She wrote the five verses into the ninth notebook, and under them, one word from each.

*Renown. Ten. Another. One hour. Pestilence.*

Mighty men. Ten of them. And another who would rise after them. And a sickness.

\* \* \*

Tudor City was a cluster of old brick towers on a rise above First Avenue, with gothic windows and stone gargoyles. It was dark by the time she got there. From the end of Forty-Third Street she could see down onto the long row of flagpoles along First Avenue, and beyond them the tall green-glass slab of the International Collective, lit floor after floor.

The doorman at number 312 was watching a game on his phone. He looked up when she came in.

"Four C," Kambria said, and held up the key, and walked to the elevator as if she lived there. He went back to his game.

The hallway on the fourth floor was quiet and smelled of radiator heat. Kambria stood outside 4C longer than she meant to with the key in her hand. She thought about knocking. Then she thought that if Francesca were inside, she would have come to the diner, and she put the key in the lock.

The apartment was compact and scrupulously clean. Too clean. There was no laptop on the desk by the window, only the square of dust where one had been. The desk drawers held nothing. The file box under the desk had been cleared out, its lid set neatly beside it. In the kitchen there was a single mug upside down in the dish rack, and a calendar on the refrigerator from a parish in South Philadelphia, turned to November. Saturday the twenty-first was circled in blue ink. *K, 4 p.m.*

Somebody had been here before her. Somebody had taken everything Francesca had worked on and left the rest exactly where it was, so that anyone who came looking would see a tidy apartment and a woman who had simply gone away.

But they had not taken the Bible.

It was on the nightstand in the bedroom, a worn black Bible with a cracked spine, handed down, by the look of it, from some South Philadelphia grandmother. Kambria picked it up. It fell open in her hands to the place it had been opened most. Daniel, chapter seven. Verse twenty-four was underlined in blue pen, and in the margin, in the same loops, two words: *the ten.*

Two sheets were tucked between the pages, folded small.

The first was a glossy printed program on heavy cream paper. *The Organization for World Peace. Flag Ceremony and Presentation of the High Council of the Technate. Sunday, November 22. Twelve noon. Visitors' Plaza, International Collective Headquarters.* Inside, on the left page, were the speakers: Adrian Crowe, Executive Chairman. Alexander Vale, Secretary to the High Council of the Technate. On the right page, under the heading *The High Council of the Technate*, was a list of names. Kambria counted them. There were ten. Beside each name was a line of small type. The chief executive of the company that ran the power grids for half of Europe. Soren Salazar, the founder of the largest network of satellites in orbit, who had leased the top of Greenland that month. The head of the firm that made most of the world's computer chips. The man whose company held the cloud servers of forty governments. The woman who ran the biggest payment network on earth. A food company that fed a billion people. A shipping company. An artificial intelligence lab. A data company that bought every frame from the cameras going up at every intersection in Washington. And the last one, a health technology firm. *Verity Health. A portfolio company of the Meridian Trust.*

Ten men and women. Not one of them elected. Not one of them a king. And every one of them holding some piece of the machinery the whole world ran on.

*Ten kings, which have received no kingdom as yet.*

The second sheet was a printout of a single screen from some internal system, the header cut off. Kambria read it twice, standing in the bedroom of a woman who was not there.

*Organism designation: PALE. File created: September 30. Distribution: Office of the Secretary to the High Council of the Technate. Field clusters expected: four. Status: monitoring. Public communication: none until framework in place.*

Below it, in Francesca's pen, a list. *Petworth (DC). Care home, Manila. Refugee camp, Kherson. Hospital, Belém (Brazil).* And under that, underlined twice: *Created SEPT 30. First case OCT 19. They knew before it happened.*

Kambria found herself sitting on Francesca's bed.

September thirtieth. Three weeks before the first resident of the nursing home in Petworth got sick. Somebody had opened a file on a germ that did not exist yet, and named it after the fourth horse of Revelation, and sent it to the office of the man who signed Crowe's papers. *Field clusters expected: four.*

Expected.

She thought of the three old women on Georgia Avenue, and the free nasal spray in October, and the small gray type at the bottom of a clean white website. She thought of Mrs. Bell.

She could not move. Then she put both sheets back inside the Bible exactly where she had found them, and then, after a moment, took them out again and put them inside her own Bible instead, and put Francesca's Bible back on the nightstand, open to the same page. She turned off the light. She locked the door behind her.

In the lobby, a man on the bench by the mailboxes turned a page of his newspaper, and the doorman looked up from his game.

"You a friend of hers?" he said.

Kambria stopped. "Yes."

"Two guys from her office came Thursday night for her stuff. Said she got transferred overseas, real sudden." He shrugged. "Nice lady. Always said good morning. Didn't say goodbye." He went back to his phone. "Funny. They didn't have a moving truck."

Kambria walked back to her hotel through the cold, along Forty-Second Street past Grand Central, with her Bible clutched in both arms, and did not look back until the hotel doors had closed behind her.

\* \* \*

She let herself into the hotel room a little after nine and stopped in the doorway.

The tag she had hung on the knob that afternoon, *Do Not Disturb*, hung reversed. Her bag sat on the luggage rack exactly where she had left it, zipper closed. But the zipper had been open when she left, one corner of the sweater showing, the way she always left it. She had not moved it. Her clothes inside were folded now. Perfectly. In thirds, like a store.

Nothing was missing. That was how she knew they had been looking for something, and that what they wanted was not in the room. It was in her head.

She wedged the desk chair under the doorknob, took the notebook and the Bible onto the bed, and did not sleep.

She sat cross-legged on the narrow hotel bed with the lamp on and everything laid out on the blanket in front of her: Francesca's five verses, the program with its ten names, the sheet with the word *PALE* across it, and the ninth notebook open beside them. Below her window, Forty-Fourth Street hissed and honked all night.

She worked it as she would have worked an outbreak at the bench, one link at a time, and wrote each link down.

*Meridian Trust, Dubai. Pays for the Council in Jerusalem (the sponsor list). Director: A. Vale.*

*Verity Health. Owned by Meridian. The agency's contract lab: every sample I have sent since July went to their bench in Rockville. Free "wellness" program, Petworth, October. Nasal spray.*

*The germ. Nothing kills it. Genes put together. Four clusters.*

*File PALE. Created Sept 30, before the first case. Sent to the Secretary to the High Council of the Technate: Vale.*

*High Council of the Technate: ten. Verity is one of the ten.*

*Francesca: gone. Two men with a badge. Man on the lobby bench: gray overcoat, fifties, newspaper.*

She went down the list once, and then again. Then she wrote beneath the list, and drew a box around it, as Angela used to:

*Not proof. A picture. But the picture has a name in the middle of it every time.*

Past midnight she got down on her knees on the thin carpet, elbows on the bed, and prayed for Francesca until she could not find any more words. Then she prayed for herself, because she was afraid, and she told God so. *I'm a woman with a notebook. Show me what You want me to see, and give me the courage to see it.*

She fell asleep like that, against the bed, and woke at six with the lamp still on.

\* \* \*

By half past eleven on Sunday she was standing in the crowd on First Avenue, across from the International Collective.

There were police barriers along the sidewalks and news trucks with their masts up. A stage had been built on the Visitors' Plaza, inside the gates, under a white canopy. Along the back of the stage stood a row of ten white chairs, all exactly alike. Beside the tallest flagpole, where the blue flag of the International Collective hung, a second pole had been raised. It was bare.

The crowd was bigger than she had expected. Some had come to cheer, with signs: *ONE WORLD. BUILD THE FUTURE. NATIONS ARE THE PAST.* Some had come to protest, and the police kept them down the block. Most had come the way she had, alone, with their phones held up.

The front rows inside the gates were roped off for invited guests, and she could see them clearly. They were not diplomats. They were the richest men in the world, in overcoats that cost more than her car, a prince from the Gulf, two presidents, a film star. They sat with their legs crossed, cool and silent. They had already paid for what was on the stage.

*The mighty men which were of old,* Kambria thought. *Men of renown.*

At noon, the ten came out first.

They walked onto the stage in a line, in dark suits, and took the ten white chairs, and sat. Kambria checked the program in her coat pocket against their faces, one by one, as far as she could tell from the street. The grid. The satellites. The chips. The servers. The payments. The food, the shipping, the machines that think, the cameras. The last chair, at the end of the row: a thin woman with silver glasses. *Verity Health.*

Then a choir began to sing, an anthem written for the day, enormous, brass and drums and a hundred voices, about light and children and a world without borders. It never named anyone. There was no Lord in it, and no God, and no King. When it ended, Kambria could not remember one line of it.

Adrian Crowe walked out onto the stage, and a thin, dark-haired man in a gray suit walked beside him, half a step behind. They had the same walk, she thought, the same slight lean into every stride, and she could not have said why she noticed it.

Kambria knew the second man before she looked at the program. She had never seen his face. But she had read his initial on a filing from Dubai, and his title in a missing woman's Bible, and she had stared for an hour one morning at a gray sleeve at the edge of a photograph. *Alexander Vale.*

Vale went to the podium first. He did not smile. He read the charter of the High Council of the Technate in an even voice, and did not once lift his eyes to the crowd. When he turned the page, his cuff slid back from his wrist, and Kambria saw it on the big screen when the camera moved in, because she had been waiting weeks to see it: a thin red string, knotted three times. The arm at the edge of the photograph. When he finished he stepped back and to the side, and folded his hands, and was still.

Then Crowe took the podium.

He was taller than she had expected, lean and tanned, in a charcoal suit with no tie, his silver hair cut close. He did not use notes. He put both hands on the sides of the podium and looked out over all of them, the crowd and the princes and the building behind him, and he held his peace until the crowd began to shift its feet.

"For eighty years," he said, "this building has been the place where the weak came to complain about the strong."

There was a murmur in the crowd, and then, from the roped-off rows, a few men laughed.

"It passed resolutions. It held meetings about meetings. It sent letters to dictators and waited for them to write back." He did not turn around to look at the green glass tower behind him. "I am not here to ask its permission. I am here to relieve it of a burden it was never strong enough to carry."

The applause from the front rows was slow, and certain.

"Nations are an old idea," Crowe said. "Elections are a slow one. Every four years you choose between two men who do not understand the machines that keep you alive. The people on this stage behind me understand them. They built them." He swept one hand back toward the ten white chairs. "The power in your walls. The money in your hand. The food on your table. The satellites over your heads. The cure in your medicine cabinet. The ice at the top of the world, that three governments quarreled over for fifty years, is cooling the servers that keep your hospitals open tonight. They did not ask a parliament before they built any of it. And they will not need one to keep it running." He smiled with his mouth only. "Order. Peace. Safety. That is what we are offering the world. And the world, I promise you, is ready to say yes."

He looked down at the front rows, at the men in the expensive coats.

"Some of you already have," he said.

The men in the front rows stood up and applauded him. The crowd behind them followed.

But Kambria was not watching Crowe.

She was watching the ten.

While Crowe spoke, every one of them sat looking straight ahead, politely, at the back of his head. But twice, when the applause rose, she saw it: the thin woman from Verity Health turned her head a few degrees, not toward Crowe, but toward the gray-suited man standing still at the side of the stage. And Salazar, the satellite man, did the same. And then a third. They were not waiting for Crowe to tell them what to do. They were waiting for Vale.

*And another shall rise after them.*

Kambria rubbed her arms as if the room had a draft.

Crowe and Vale raised the flag together, side by side, each with a hand on the rope. It was white, with a gold circle in the middle and a gold olive branch inside it. As it climbed the pole beside the blue flag of the International Collective, the wind came in off the river and caught it, and it opened all at once and stood out stiff and bright, and it was higher. Only by a few feet. But it was higher.

Crowe looked up at it with his chin lifted, a king on a coin.

At the side of the stage, Alexander Vale was not looking at the flag. He was looking at Crowe.

\* \* \*

The crowd broke up slowly. Kambria let it carry her down First Avenue, and then she turned back, and when the gates opened for visitors at three, she walked in.

The stage was coming down. Men in work gloves were stacking the ten white chairs. The two flags hung side by side over the half-empty plaza, stirring in the wind off the water. Kambria walked to the middle of the plaza and stopped, and took out the ninth notebook, and turned to the back.

There was a photograph taped there, printed off a news site years ago and moved from notebook to notebook ever since. It was this plaza. In the photograph, on the very spot where she was standing, stood a sculpture: a great cat, a jaguar, painted in bright patterns of red and gold and blue, crouched on a pedestal, with four enormous wings rising from its back. Under it, in her own handwriting, she had copied the caption. *A gift from the state of Oaxaca, Mexico, presented to the International Collective as a guardian for international peace and security. December 2021.* The sculpture had been taken away months later. But she had kept the picture, because the minute she saw it, she had thought of Daniel.

She opened her Bible and read it standing there, in the wind.

*After this I beheld, and lo another, like a leopard, which had upon the back of it four wings of a fowl… (Daniel 7:6)*

She turned the pages forward to Revelation, to the thirteenth chapter, and read the beast John saw rising from the sea. *And the beast which I saw was like unto a leopard, and his feet were as the feet of a bear, and his mouth as the mouth of a lion: and the dragon gave him his power, and his seat, and great authority. (Revelation 13:2)*

And then the seventeenth, the verse Francesca had written down. *And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings… These have one mind, and shall give their power and strength unto the beast. (Revelation 17:12-13)*

She looked up from the page. A winged leopard, set up on this plaza as the guardian of the peace of the nations. A new flag over it today, higher than the old one. Ten chairs on a stage. And a man who stood to the side and watched, while the ten turned their heads toward him.

*One mind.* Kambria wrote it in the notebook. Then, under it: *Give their power unto the beast. Whose beast? Crowe's? Or the one who rises after?*

Four verses above the ones she had copied stood a line she had read a hundred times and never once made sit still. *The beast that thou sawest was, and is not; and shall ascend out of the bottomless pit… and they that dwell on the earth shall wonder, whose names were not written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, when they behold the beast that was, and is not, and yet is.* (Revelation 17:8)

She copied it under the others and set its three small clauses in a column, the way Walt set a column of figures. *Was. Is not. Yet is.* A kingdom that had been, and was gone, and came again? A man? She could not tell, and she did not try to make it fit anything she could see on the plaza.

She did not know. Daniel had not known either, when he first saw it. *I considered the horns (Daniel 7:8),* he had written. He had looked, and kept looking, and asked.

She turned to a clean page and dated it. *November 22, 2026.* And under it:

*The leopard's plaza. A new flag, higher. Ten chairs. "Order. Peace. Safety."*

*For when they shall say, Peace and safety; then sudden destruction cometh upon them…* (1 Thessalonians 5:3)

*…and by peace shall destroy many… (Daniel 8:25)*

*Francesca. Gone. PALE. Sept 30. They knew.*

When she closed the notebook and looked up, the plaza was nearly deserted. One of the workmen was folding a white chair. A security guard was talking into his radio by the gate.

And by the railing across the plaza, in a dark gray overcoat, a man stood watching her, his hands in his pockets.

She had seen him once before. In the lobby of 312 East Forty-Third Street, the night before, sitting on the bench by the mailboxes, reading a newspaper, when she came down from the fourth floor.

He did not look away when she looked at him. He only watched her, as Vale had watched Crowe.

Kambria put the notebook in her coat, and walked to the gate without running, and kept walking.

\* \* \*

She made the five-oh-five train at Penn Station with four minutes to spare.

She sat in the window seat with her bag on the seat beside her so no one would sit there, and her Bible on her lap with the two folded sheets inside it, and watched the lights of New Jersey go by in the dark. She thought of Francesca alone somewhere, if she was anywhere. The ten chairs. A germ that had a name before it had a victim. Mrs. Bell.

She bowed her head against the cold window and prayed for Francesca again.

Somewhere south of Philadelphia, her phone lit up in her lap. It was an email from the hospital: a meeting, eight o'clock tomorrow morning, fourth floor, mandatory. She read it four times. Then the phone buzzed again.

It was a text from a number with no name. There were no words in it. Only a photograph.

It was a picture of her, taken that afternoon: a woman in a navy coat standing alone in the middle of the Visitors' Plaza, with a notebook open in her hands and the two flags above her head.

A second text came while she was still looking at it.

*Go home, Kambria. And stay there.*

She lifted her eyes from the screen, slowly.

Three rows back down the aisle, a man in a gray overcoat sat with a newspaper open against his chest. He did not turn the page. He did not look up. He did not need to.

## Chapter 16: Divisive

> *Then shall they deliver you up to be afflicted, and shall kill you: and ye shall be hated of all nations for my name's sake.* — Jesus, Matthew 24:9

**Word study: *hated* — μισέω** Greek *miseō* (Strong's G3404). To hate, to detest, to persecute. The same word Jesus used when He said, "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you." The hatred in this verse is not for anything the believers have done. It is *for my name's sake*: for His name alone.

Daniel was preferred above the other presidents and princes because an excellent spirit was in him (Daniel 6:3). His enemies could find no occasion against him, *except we find it against him concerning the law of his God* (Daniel 6:5). So they had the king sign a decree, and Daniel, when he knew the writing was signed, went into his house, and his windows being open toward Jerusalem, kneeled three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, *as he did aforetime* (Daniel 6:10).

\* \* \*

The email had come on Sunday night, while her train from New York was somewhere south of Philadelphia, and she had gone over it again and again by the light of her phone.

*Please report to the hospital's administrative offices, fourth floor, at 8:00 a.m. Monday. This meeting is mandatory.*

At five minutes to eight on Monday morning she parked on the third level of the hospital's staff garage, in the corner by the stairwell where she had parked every day since the flu response began, and rode the elevator up to the fourth floor.

The office was at the end of a carpeted hallway that smelled of new paint. Linda Marsh, the director of Kambria's lab at the Centers for Disease Control, was sitting behind the desk. She had driven in from Hyattsville before dawn. A man she had never met sat in the chair beside her, with a laptop open on his knees and a hospital lanyard that said *Human Resources*.

"Have a seat, Kambria," Linda said. She did not smile; she seldom did, but she had always been fair, and she looked at Kambria now with what might have been sorrow.

Kambria sat.

"This is Greg Tallis, from the hospital's HR office," Linda said. "I'm going to let him explain why we're here."

Greg Tallis was young, with careful hair and a careful voice. He turned his laptop a little toward her so she could read along.

"As you know," he said, "the hospital system adopted new Inclusive Spiritual Care Standards earlier this month. They're aligned with the interim principles the Council adopted at its opening session in Jerusalem, which our board formally endorsed. They apply to everyone who works in this building, including outside partners. Your team signed the agreement when the agency set up here."

"And our department adopted the same guidelines soon after," Linda said. "Every federal employee got the training module."

Kambria remembered the module. It had been forty minutes long, with soft piano music and a woman's soothing voice, and she had clicked through it on her phone in the lab at three in the morning.

"A complaint was filed on Saturday, and it came up through the Director of Special Operations and Infectious Disease Control," Greg said. "Because you're a federal employee, it landed with your agency as well as with us. Actually, it's a pattern of concerns. That you've been engaging in religious proselytizing with patients and their families. And that you've made statements to colleagues, in shared spaces, to the effect that only one religion is true, and that people of other faiths, or no faith, are..." He glanced at the screen. "Going to be punished. Several staff members have said they found this hostile. Divisive was the word used."

Kambria looked at him. Then she looked at Linda.

"A dying woman asked me to pray," she said. "On Saturday morning. Her whole family was in the room. Her son took off his cap."

"We're aware of the incident," Greg said, choosing his words. "And we understand the impulse. Nobody is questioning your compassion. But the standards are clear. Chaplaincy requests go to the chaplaincy office, and staff are asked to offer support in a way that's inclusive of all traditions. Closing a prayer in the name of a specific deity, in a way that implies exclusivity..." He spread his hands. "Some people experience that as harm."

"She asked me," Kambria said. "She had a cross around her neck."

"I understand."

"And my login stopped working on Friday," Kambria said. "At six o'clock in the evening. I tried to pull up the Petworth files from my phone and it told me my account had been suspended." She looked at Greg, and then at Linda. "Mrs. Bell didn't come in until Friday night. I didn't pray with her until Saturday morning. Who suspended my account before anybody had anything to complain about?"

Greg looked at Linda. Linda looked at the desk.

"I don't know anything about that," Linda said, lowering her eyes. Kambria believed her. Linda was in the dark, and she was the director of the lab.

"In the staff lounge," Kambria said slowly, "a friend asked me what I thought about the ceremony at the House of the Gate, and I told her. That's the statement? That I believe Jesus is the only way to the Father? Because He said it. That's not my idea. That's in the Bible."

Greg Tallis studied his screen.

Linda leaned forward and folded her hands on the desk. "Kambria," she said gently. "You're the best scientist I have. You know that. You've been the best in my lab for all these years. This isn't about your work. Nobody has ever said one word about your work." She paused. "But Atlanta is watching every complaint under the new guidelines. And you've been telling half this hospital the world is ending. Dana called me about it on her own, last week, before any of this. People are frightened."

"They should be," Kambria said. "I'm not trying to scare them. I'm trying to warn them. Those are different things."

"To them, right now, they're the same thing."

Greg cleared his throat. "The hospital is withdrawing your access to the building, effective today."

"And the agency is placing you on paid administrative leave pending a review," Linda said. "It's not a disciplinary finding. It's a pause. Usually two to four weeks." She held out her hand. "I'll need your badge."

"And the Petworth samples?" Kambria said. "The bacterium. Did anyone read my report?"

Linda's eyes went to the window and came back. "That's been reassigned," she said. "It's not your concern now."

For the first time, someone else spoke.

"Dr. Whitfield. How was New York?"

Kambria had not noticed him. He sat by the window in a chair pulled back from the desk, a pale man in a navy suit with a manila folder shut on his knee, and nobody had introduced him. Linda's eyes avoided him. Greg Tallis had stopped fidgeting with his pen.

"I'm sorry?" Kambria said.

"Your train ticket. Union Station, Saturday, eleven-oh-five. Penn Station, Sunday, five-oh-five." His voice was pleasant. "Did you see someone? Anyone you'd like to tell us about?"

The room waited.

"I took a weekend in the city," Kambria said. "I saw a parade of flags. I prayed in a hotel room."

"Of course." He opened the folder an inch, and closed it. "Thank you, Doctor."

That was all. But Linda was staring at her desk now like a woman who has been told to stop looking.

Kambria stayed where she was.

She thought of the old men in Babylon going through Daniel's records, page by page, looking for anything they could use. *We shall not find any occasion against this Daniel, except we find it against him concerning the law of his God. (Daniel 6:5)* In her Sunday school Bible there had been a picture of those men, in turbans, with scrolls; she had colored their robes purple.

She unclipped her badge from the lanyard around her neck. Her photo on it was years old. She had shorter hair in it, and she was smiling. She laid it on the desk in front of Linda.

"Can I ask who made the complaint?"

"Complaints under the standards are confidential," Greg said. "To protect the reporting party."

Kambria nodded. She stood up. At the door she turned around.

"Linda," she said. "Can I tell you something? Not as your scientist. Just as me."

Linda looked at her, and nodded.

"He's coming back," Kambria said. "Soon. I'm not saying it to be divisive. I'm saying it because I love you, and I've worked beside you all these years, and I'd never forgive myself if I hadn't said it once."

Linda didn't answer. But she didn't look away either, and her eyes were wet when Kambria closed the door.

\* \* \*

Celeste was waiting by her car.

The staff garage was raw and concrete-gray and smelled of exhaust, and Kambria's car was where she had left it. Celeste was leaning against the driver's door in her coat, with her red hair down and her arms folded against the cold. When she saw Kambria coming, she straightened up, and her face filled with sorrow. Her coat had fallen open, and clipped inside it, where Kambria had never seen it on the sixth floor, hung a blue lanyard and a federal badge: CELESTE MOORE. DIRECTOR, SPECIAL OPERATIONS AND INFECTIOUS DISEASE CONTROL. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Kambria read it twice.

"Oh, honey," she said. "I'm so sorry."

Kambria stopped a few feet away from her.

"You heard already," she said.

"I didn't hear." Celeste uncrossed her arms. "I knew." She took a breath. "I'm the one who said something, Kambria. I'm not going to hide it from you. You deserve better than that. And Friday night, your login. That was me too. You were pulling files that were not yours to pull. I couldn't let you keep going."

"You told them I prayed with Mrs. Bell." Kambria did not raise her voice. "You shut me out on Friday, before Mrs. Bell was even admitted. Before there was anything to complain about. You had the complaint ready, and you were only waiting for something to hang it on."

Celeste did not deny it.

"I told them you've been frightening people. For weeks." Celeste's voice was soft and earnest. "Tomás came to me, after you talked to him. He's nineteen, Kambria. He couldn't sleep. You told Dana and Paul and half the lab that they were going to be left behind. And then I walked into that room and saw you praying over that poor woman's family, telling them only Jesus..." She shook her head. "I love you. You know I do. I did this because I love you. You're exhausted. You haven't been yourself since Angela. You need rest. Nobody is punishing you. This is a chance to rest."

"Angela prayed for you," Kambria said. "Every Tuesday. She told you she would, and she did. She was still praying for you the week she died."

"I know."

"You sat with her every Tuesday. You sat by her bed. You knew her husband was sitting out in that waiting room alone." Her voice broke. "You were never just a volunteer."

"I did volunteer," Celeste said. "Every word of that was true. It just wasn't all of it. Atlanta asked me to keep an eye on the sixth floor long before Petworth, and I chose the one woman there I knew I could love." She said it gently, as if it were a gift. "I trusted *you*, Kambria."

Celeste's smile held a second too long.

"You can still trust me," she said. Then, lower, so that it barely carried across the concrete: "Let Petworth stay reassigned. Whatever Francesca left in your hands, put it down. I know what she left you."

Kambria's fingers went numb on the strap of her bag.

"I never said her name," she said.

"No," Celeste agreed softly. "You didn't."

Behind them, an engine echoed up the ramp. Headlights swept across the concrete pillars, and a pickup truck came around the corner from the second level and slowed to a stop in the lane behind Celeste. It had a ladder rack on the back and a dent in the tailgate, and Kambria knew it. She had parked behind it in a driveway on a quiet street every Sunday for a year, with a casserole dish on the seat beside her.

Celeste glanced over her shoulder, and her face changed. It went warm and young.

"That's my ride," she said.

Ezra was behind the wheel.

He saw Kambria. She watched him see her. His hands tightened on the wheel, and for one second their eyes met through the windshield in the flat fluorescent light of the garage. Then he looked away, straight ahead, at nothing.

Celeste touched Kambria's arm lightly. "Get some rest, okay? I'll call you." She walked around to the passenger side and got in. Kambria watched her lean across the seat and kiss him, quickly, on the mouth. Ezra neither kissed her back nor pushed her away. He sat rigid, eyes straight ahead, and when she had settled back into her seat he took his foot off the brake and drove down the ramp, and the sound of the engine went around and around the concrete levels until it was gone.

Kambria stood alone in the garage.

The small silver car at the curb outside his house in October, with the red string hanging from its mirror. The new shirt on Thursday night, and the cologne. Elijah, turning his glass on the bar: *He won't tell me her name. You know what that means.* Celeste, glowing for weeks. Celeste, turning her phone face down.

She had watched it begin. A hospital waiting room, two cups of coffee, a hand laid lightly on his arm. She had seen the hunger in Celeste's face that day and told herself it was kindness, because that was easier, and she had said nothing. Not to Ezra. Not to Angela. Not to Celeste. And now Revelation 12:10 came back to her whole: *the accuser of our brethren… which accused them before our God day and night.* Celeste had not shouted. She had wept, and called it love, and filed it with a signature. Kambria thought, too, of Romans 14:13: *that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.* Celeste had not blocked Ezra's road. She had only laid herself across it, soft and warm, where a grieving man would not see her until he had already fallen.

Kambria got into her car and closed the door and sat behind the wheel. She left the engine off. She knew what Angela would have said, had she been there in that garage. Angela would have said, *Pray for her, Kam.* And Kambria could not. Not yet. She sat in the unheated car, and for many minutes she could not pray at all.

\* \* \*

On the way home she stopped at the Harvest Basket on Rhode Island Avenue, because she was out of milk.

The shelves were half bare. Handwritten signs hung in the dairy aisle: *LIMIT 1 PER CUSTOMER*. In the baby aisle, where the formula used to be, there was a row of naked metal shelves and a laminated recall notice. A young mother stood in front of the gap with a baby on her hip, reading it twice.

"Try the drugstore on Twelfth," Kambria said. "They had some on Friday."

She stood and looked at the stripped shelves. *A measure of wheat for a penny.* Walt had written it in red in the margin of the business page some days back, and she had read it upside down at his table and thought it was a long way off.

\* \* \*

At home, in the daylight, she saw what she had been too tired to see on Sunday night. The deadbolt had been locked, as she left it. Nothing was broken. Nothing was missing. But in the spare room the stack of notebooks on her desk had been squared up, edges even, and Kambria never squared anything. The printed filing from Dubai was still taped to the wall, but the tape had been peeled back at one corner and pressed down crooked.

On her pillow, on the bed in her bedroom, lay a glossy color photograph. It was her spare-room wall, shot from above, every string and headline and verse sharp as a surgical field. Written on the white border in a neat hand was a time stamp. *Monday, 8:14 a.m.* She had been sitting in Linda Marsh's office at eight-fourteen.

She paused just inside the door without turning on the light.

Then she went to the shelf by the kitchen table and took down the blue concordance. The packing tape on the spine had not been touched. She ran her thumb down the spine and felt the hard, flat shape of the thumb drive still inside it, and her shoulders loosened. She put the book back exactly where it had been. She checked every window. She put a kitchen chair under the knob of the back door, as her grandmother used to, and felt foolish, and left it there.

That evening her phone would not stop buzzing. It was the Mount Zion prayer chain, forty women who for years had texted each other about casseroles and hospital visits, and tonight every message carried the same link to the same story from Channel 4. Kambria pressed play.

The story was about the standards. Everyone's, now: a school district in Oregon had suspended a teacher for leading a prayer at a football game, a video platform had removed several thousand sermons for "hateful conduct." The picture changed to a church sanctuary, and Kambria sat forward. She knew the pulpit. She knew the wooden cross on the wall behind it, and the stained-glass window with the lamb.

It was Mount Zion. It was Pastor Grant.

A few seconds of his sermon played with the sound low, and she knew which one it was. She had been in the fourth pew on the left. *Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. (John 14:6)* Pastor Grant leaned on the pulpit with both hands, as he always did, and spoke evenly, without anger.

The clip ended. The picture cut to a man in a beautiful gray suit on a stage in front of thousands, hands lifted. *Bishop Roland Sterling, Kingdom Harvest Church.* "The only thing God cannot bless," he said, warmly, to great applause, "is division."

Kambria closed the video. The phone went on buzzing in her lap, one message after another, and she turned it face down on the cushion.

She got up and went to the spare room and came back with the ninth notebook, and she sat at the table and wrote, in pen, one verse under another, without stopping: three of Jesus' warnings, and Nebuchadnezzar's furnace between them.

*…ye shall be hated of all nations for my name's sake. (Matthew 24:9)*

*…yea, the time cometh, that whosoever killeth you will think that he doeth God service. (John 16:2)*

*And whoso falleth not down and worshippeth shall the same hour be cast into the midst of a burning fiery furnace. (Daniel 3:6)*

*If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you. (John 15:18)*

She looked at what she had written. It was only beginning. She knew that. Paul had written that something was holding it back, and would go on holding it back, until it was taken out of the way. She did not think it would be taken out of the way much longer.

\* \* \*

She could not stay in the house with that photograph on the pillow. A little before nine she drove to Mount Zion and found one light on in the basement.

Pastor Grant was alone in the fellowship hall, stacking folding chairs against the wall, four at a time, slower than he used to. He looked up when the stair door opened, and set the chairs down.

"Kambria," he said. "Sister Bell's son is a deacon at Shiloh. He called me this afternoon to tell me what you did for his mother, and then what happened to you after." His voice was tired and kind. "How are you, child?"

She started to say she was fine. Then she sat down on one of the chairs he had not stacked yet, still in her coat, because he was her pastor, and she told him everything. Mrs. Bell, Linda's office, the badge on the desk. The garage. Ezra's eyes through the windshield, and the truck going down the ramp.

He unfolded a chair across from her and sat, with his hands on his knees. He listened without a word. Then: "They took my sermon down. Twenty-two people have called today to tell me they're sorry. I told each of them what Jesus told His disciples. *If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you.* We're not being treated any worse than He was, Kambria. We're being treated the same. That's not a punishment. That's fellowship."

She cried then, under the low ceiling where Angela had started a Thursday study with fourteen women, with her face in her gloves.

"Now," Pastor Grant said. "Let me pray for you. And then you're going to do the hardest thing, which is pray for her."

"I can't."

"I know. Do it anyway. Not because she deserves it. Because He told us to. *Bless them which persecute you: bless, and curse not. (Romans 12:14)* Say it until you mean it."

He laid a hand on her shoulder and prayed for her there, as he had prayed over Angela every morning in her hospice bed.

"Father, this is Your daughter Kambria. She laid down her badge this morning and did not lay down Your name. Hold her tonight. Heal what was done to her, and give her what she cannot find by herself: a heart for the one who did it. In Jesus' name."

When he said amen, she said it with him. He turned off the basement light, locked the side door behind them, and stood on the walk until her car started.

\* \* \*

At eleven o'clock that night, Kambria went to her kitchen window.

The window over the sink faced east, toward the rooftops of Brookland and the dark line of trees along the railroad tracks. The oil lamp sat on the sill where it always sat, burning low. She moved it to the counter. Then she unlatched the window and pushed it open.

The November air came in all at once. Down the block a dog was barking, and a car door slammed somewhere, and the air smelled of frost.

She knelt on the kitchen floor, on the old linoleum, with her elbows on the edge of the counter and the chill on her face. She had opened it because Daniel had, and because he had gone on praying the same way he always had, with the decree signed and the lions waiting. *…as he did aforetime. (Daniel 6:10)* She wanted to pray now exactly as she had before.

She prayed for Ezra first, as she always did. She prayed for Mia and Jalen, and for Loretta, and for Walt, and for Elijah with the napkin in his wallet, and for Monica and her boys, and for Tomás, and for Linda Marsh, and for Mrs. Bell's family. She prayed for Pastor Grant and Mount Zion.

Then she knelt on the linoleum, eyes closed, saying nothing more.

"Lord," she said finally. "I don't want to. You know I don't want to." She swallowed. "Bless Celeste. Keep her. Open her eyes. Don't let her be lost. In Jesus' name."

She felt nothing when she said it, no forgiveness, no warmth. She felt hollow and tired.

She said it again anyway. Then she got up off the floor, and closed the window, and put the lamp back on the sill.

She was turning off the kitchen light when her phone lit up on the counter.

It was Ezra. In a whole year she could not remember him writing first. He had answered her messages, when he answered at all, with one word or a thumbs-up. She stood in the unlit kitchen and looked at his name on the screen until it dimmed before she opened it.

There was one word.

*Sorry.*

That was all. No name, no reason, nothing after it. She could not tell whether he meant the garage, or the closet, or the porch on Thursday night, or a year of casseroles taken at the door. Nor could she tell if he meant it at all, or if he had been drinking, or if Celeste was asleep in the next room.

She sat down on the kitchen floor with her back against the cabinets and the phone clutched in both hands, and she cried harder than she had in the church with Pastor Grant, or on Ezra's steps. And she did not know, even then, whether she was crying because it was so little, or because, after a year, it was something.

## Act 5 — The World Darkens

## Chapter 17: The Mountain

> *And they gathered themselves together against Moses and against Aaron, and said unto them, Ye take too much upon you, seeing all the congregation are holy, every one of them, and the LORD is among them: wherefore then lift ye up yourselves above the congregation of the LORD?* — Numbers 16:3

**Word study: *holy* — קָדוֹשׁ** Hebrew *qadosh* (Strong's H6918). Set apart, separated, sacred. Its root means to be cut off from the common and given to God alone. A thing is holy because God has chosen it and set it apart for Himself. When Korah said that everyone was holy, he was not lifting everyone up. He was saying that no one had been set apart at all.

*And they rose up before Moses, with certain of the children of Israel, two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown… And they took every man his censer, and put fire in them, and laid incense thereon, and stood in the door of the tabernacle of the congregation with Moses and Aaron… and the glory of the LORD appeared unto all the congregation.* (Numbers 16:2, 18–19)


\* \* \*

On Tuesday morning, Walt called at nine and told her to come over.

He gave no reason. He had never once, in all the years she had known him, asked anyone to come over. She had told him everything on Monday night, on the phone, and when she finished he had said only, "Tomorrow. I'll make the coffee."

It was a sullen, windless morning, two days before Thanksgiving. At the Pattersons' the porch light was off and the driveway was empty. In the big front window hung a paper turkey made from a traced hand, the fingers colored red and orange and brown, and across the bottom Mia had printed, in careful capitals, *I AM THANKFUL FOR MY FAMILY*.

Walt had two cups poured and the small television turned to face the table. He was three weeks out of open-heart surgery at Brandick Memorial, his breastbone wired shut, and he had poured the coffee anyway, one-handed, against orders.

"Have a seat," he said.

She sat in the chair across from his.

"I should have told you." He said it to his cup. "The woman. I saw her car outside his house in October, and then again. More than once. I figured it wasn't my business. I figured you'd find out, and be hurt, and I didn't want to be the one who did it." He rubbed his mouth. "That was cowardly. I'm sorry, Kambria."

She laid her hand over his old, spotted one. "It's all right, Walt."

"It's not. But thank you." He took the hand back and nodded at the screen. "Jerusalem. They've been on it all morning. I wanted you to see it with me."

\* \* \*

The picture was the Mount of Olives in the late afternoon: the long ridge east of the Old City, the olive trees, the white tombs stepping down toward the Kidron Valley. Across the valley the Temple Mount burned gold. At the top of the ridge stood a long, low building of pale stone and dark glass, its name in brass over the doors: *THE OLIVET CROWN*.

*JERUSALEM: COUNCIL FOR UNIVERSAL MORAL LAW CONVENES.*

Two hundred and fifty delegates. The Council, back in session, seated now as a permanent body. Buses crawling up a narrow road, men in suits and robes and clerical collars stepping down into the cameras. Then the Council's president, Rabbi Matteo Arcangeli, tall and silver-haired at the top of the hotel steps.

"For too long," he said, "the children of one God have stood apart, each claiming to hold the only door. Today we take down the walls. Every tradition here is holy. Every one of them. No tradition may stand above the others and call itself the only way."

Applause. The camera drifted over the third row and stopped on a finely cut charcoal suit. Bishop Roland Sterling, clapping with the rest, wiping his eyes. Then Senator-elect Thorne on the steps, hand in hand with the rabbi, smiling for the lenses. The first resolution, adopted unanimously: religious claims to exclusive access to God were "a root cause of division and violence in the modern world."

Walt thumbed the sound off.

"Every tradition here is holy," he said. "Every one of them. I know when a man is quoting something, Kambria."

"I don't think he knows he's quoting it."

"He knows."

She had already turned the pages. She knew the place; she had headed the page in her notebook in the spring, *THE MOUNTAIN*. "Walt. Listen to where they're standing. This is the hill where the disciples asked Him, *What shall be the sign of thy coming?* This is where He went up, and where the angels said He'd come back the same way. *And his feet shall stand in that day upon the mount of Olives.* (Zechariah 14:4) Right there, on those steps." She scrolled with her thumb. "I looked up the hotel. They cut the access road straight through the oldest Jewish cemetery in the world. Three thousand years of graves, facing the Temple, waiting to be first up when the Messiah comes. The buses drove over the broken stones this afternoon."

Walt took off his glasses.

*Behold, O my people, I will open your graves.* "They built a road over the resurrection," he said.

"Two hundred and fifty men signing a law for the whole world about who's holy, on the exact mountain where—"

"Kambria."

Something in his voice stopped her.

He had not moved his head. His eyes had gone to the front window, over her shoulder, and his hand had closed around the handle of his cane.

"Don't turn around fast," Walt said.

\* \* \*

She turned around slowly.

Across the street, at the curb in front of the Pattersons' empty driveway, a gray Chevrolet Malibu idled with its headlights off. The windows were dark. She knew the dent in its rear bumper. She knew the plate; it was written on the back of her hand again, in pen, because she had stopped trusting paper.

Behind it, a small silver car pulled to the curb. A thin red string swung from the rearview mirror.

The driver's door opened. Celeste stepped out in a camel coat, red hair loose, carrying a covered pot in both hands with a dish towel folded over the lid. She bent to the window of the Malibu and said something. The man inside never turned his head. Then she straightened and looked across the street and up at Walt's front window, and smiled, as if she could see straight through the glass.

"She's coming," Kambria whispered.

"Kitchen." Walt was already on his feet. He did not lean on the cane; he lifted it, like a man who meant to use it. "Back in the kitchen. Shut the door. Don't come out till I say."

She went. The kitchen door was an old hollow-core thing with a glass knob. She pulled it nearly closed and stood against the refrigerator with her hand over her own mouth, and listened through the gap.

The bell rang once. Walt let it ring again before he crossed the room.

The chain rattled. A crack of cold air.

"Mr. Simmons!" Celeste's voice was a light, warm bell. "Good morning. I'm so sorry to bother you. I saw Kambria's car out front and I thought, well, she mustn't have eaten. I brought soup."

"Her car's out front because she parked it there," Walt said. "That's all a car tells you."

"I only want to see her. Five minutes."

"She isn't receiving."

"Mr. Simmons." The warmth did not leave her voice. It thinned. "I know she's in there. I'm not here to fight. I'm here because I'm worried. She isn't well, and she's a long way down a road with no one to pull her back. You're a sensible man. You've had your own troubles." A pause, and a softer note. "The heart. At your age, with a winter like this coming. Such a hard thing, an old man alone."

In the kitchen Kambria's nails went into her palm.

When Walt answered, it was in the voice he used on proofreaders.

"Ma'am. I've been threatened by better. Take your soup."

"It's not a threat. It's a kindness." Something clinked: a pot set down on the porch boards. "Tell her it's still warm. Tell her I'll be thinking of her Thursday." The voice came closer to the crack. "And tell her Francesca sends her love."

The door shut. The chain slid home.

Heels clicked down the steps. A car door. An engine. Another engine. Walt did not move until both had gone, and then he turned the deadbolt, and leaned his forehead against the wood.

Kambria came out of the kitchen shaking.

"She said Francesca," she whispered. "She said it again."

"I heard."

Then Walt opened the door a foot and pointed at the pot with his cane, and Kambria carried it in to the table. He took off the lid.

Chicken and rice. Carrots cut small. A bay leaf riding the top.
