Kambria sat down on the floor where she stood. She knew the smell. She had stood at Angela's elbow in the Pattersons' kitchen on a hundred Thursdays while Angela taught her to make it. Angela had written the recipe out for Celeste once, on the sixth floor, and the story that went with it.

"That's Angela's soup," she said.

Walt put the lid back on, gently, as if the pot might wake.

"Don't eat it," he said. And then, after a while, "Pour it out in the yard. It'll take the grass."

\* \* \*

She went out the back, past the grill and the fence, with the empty pot in her hands.

David Levin was at his grill in a down vest and slippers, turning chicken thighs with long tongs, because it was noon and cold and he had a point to prove about turkeys. He lifted the tongs.

"*Baruch haba*!" he called. He always said it. His grandmother used to say it at her door.

*Blessed is he that cometh.* The crowds on the road to Jerusalem had sung it out of Psalm 118; the last thing Jesus said to that city. *Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.* Kambria had never heard anyone offer it so easily, over a grill.

"*Baruch haba*," she said, and he beamed.

Then his eyes moved past her. He nodded toward the street.

"That gray car," he said. "Been parked on our block on and off for two weeks. I called it in. Two officers came out, looked at the plate, and went away white." He turned a thigh. "They said it was federal. Said not to worry about it." He looked at her over his glasses. "I'm worried about it."

"David—"

"My grandmother lit candles every Friday night until the day she died. In the Bronx. She didn't believe half of it. But she lit them. Nobody made her, and nobody could have." He waved his tongs. "They want a law about faith now. Up on that hill. Something about it gives me the creeps, and I'm not even a religious guy."

"That feeling's worth listening to," Kambria said. "Your grandmother's candles were lit for Someone. And He's still coming."

He didn't answer. He turned the chicken. But he said, "Tell Walt I'm bringing him a plate Thursday whether he likes it or not," and when she looked back from the gate he was still standing there with the tongs in his hand, watching the street.

She poured the soup out under the fence, in the dead grass, and rinsed the pot, and set it on Walt's step.

\* \* \*

She did not go home. She drove to Petworth.

The nursing home sat on Georgia Avenue between a check-cashing store and a church with a padlocked gate: three stories of tan brick, a green awning, a handwritten sign inside the glass. *NO VISITORS UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE.* She had no badge and no right to be there. Then she thought of Mrs. Bell's hand in hers, and the son turning his cap, and she got out of the car.

The woman at the desk would not let her past the lobby. But a petite aide in purple scrubs, name tag *MARISOL*, stopped in the side hall when she heard the name Clarice Bell, and walked Kambria out to the sidewalk and pointed her up the street toward the bus stop, for anyone watching.

"You're the one who prayed with her," Marisol said, low and fast. "Her son told us." She glanced back at the door. "The Verity people came Friday. Two men in a van. They took every file from the wellness program, every sign-in sheet, every box of the spray. They said it was a recall." Her arms folded tight. "Nobody recalls anything without paper."

"How many residents?"

"Forty-one. They signed everyone up in October. It was free." Her voice dropped. "They're coming back tomorrow morning with the winter doses. They already printed the list. Forty-one names, and a dose beside every one." Her eyes were wet. "Six are in the hospital. Mrs. Bell was the first to die. She won't be the last." She looked past Kambria's shoulder at the street, and her face went blank. "I have to go back in."

"Marisol—"

"Don't come here again."

The door closed.

Kambria turned around.

Across Georgia Avenue, two cars behind her own, the gray Malibu sat at the curb with its engine running.

Then its door opened.

The man who got out was fifty, short gray hair, a heavy ordinary face, gray overcoat. He did not hurry. He crossed the median between two lanes of traffic, stopped on the near sidewalk thirty feet from her, and raised his phone. He took her photograph. He took it slowly, in plain daylight, and didn't care who saw.

Then he lowered the phone, looked at her, and got back into his car.

She walked to her own without running, because running was what they wanted. She locked the doors with the heels of her hands. She was halfway to Florida Avenue before she let the air out of her, and when she did, it came out as prayer.

*Lord. Marisol. The forty-one. The six. Francesca, wherever she is. Me.*

She did not stop at her house. She sat in the parking lot of a church for an hour, and then she drove home the long way, and checked every window twice before she dared to turn on the light.

\* \* \*

That night, by the lamp, she opened the ninth notebook and dated a fresh page. *November 24, 2026.*

*Council for Universal Moral Law. 250. Olivet Crown, Mount of Olives. Arcangeli. Sterling a delegate. Thorne, senator-elect, legal adviser. "Exclusive claims… a root cause of division."* Beside it: *Numbers 16:3. Numbers 16:29–30. Zechariah 14:4.* And in small letters: *The road is paved over the graves.*

On the facing page, the list that frightened her more. *Verity. 41 residents. 6 in hospital. Files gone Friday, no paper. Winter doses tomorrow, A.M. Gray Malibu photographed me. Celeste at Walt's door with Angela's soup. "Francesca sends her love."*

She stopped. She drew a box around the last line, and underneath it she wrote: *She is not guessing. They have her.*

Then one more verse, and a box around it.

*Depart, I pray you, from the tents of these wicked men.*

Moses had warned the people to move away before the ground opened. Enoch had been taken before the flood. Lot had been pulled out of Sodom by the hand before the fire fell. *God hath not appointed us to wrath.* She did not know the day or the hour. Nobody did.

Her phone buzzed on the table.

*Getting a ride home tonight around 9,* Jalen had written. *Grandma says don't forget the mac and cheese Thursday.* And a second later: *Dad said it's ok if you come. He said it himself.*

Kambria read the last line three times. The door she had stood in front of on Thursday night had not been shut all the way.

*I'll be there,* she typed. *Love you.* She sat a while with the phone in her hand.

Under the box in the notebook she wrote one word. *Thursday.*

She checked the oil in the lamp, filled it to the brim, trimmed the wick, and left it burning in the window.

She had one more day before Thursday. She meant to use it well: the macaroni and cheese, the notebook for Ezra's table, the right words if she could find them.

## Chapter 18: The Wall

> *After many days thou shalt be visited: in the latter years thou shalt come into the land that is brought back from the sword, and is gathered out of many people, against the mountains of Israel, which have been always waste…* — Ezekiel 38:8

**Word study: *latter* — אַחֲרִית** Hebrew *acharith* (Strong's H319). The last part, the end, what comes after. It is the word Moses used for "the latter days," and the word Job used when God blessed "the latter end of Job more than his beginning." It does not mean someday. It means the closing chapter of a story God has already begun.

*Son of man, set thy face against Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and prophesy against him… And I will turn thee back, and put hooks into thy jaws, and I will bring thee forth, and all thine army, horses and horsemen, all of them clothed with all sorts of armour, even a great company with bucklers and shields, all of them handling swords…* (Ezekiel 38:2, 4)

\* \* \*

The last pin went in at six-fifteen on Wednesday morning, before the sun was up.

Kambria stood back from the wall of her spare room with the box of pushpins in one hand and a mug of coffee going lukewarm in the other, and she looked at what she had made.

It had started in September as a single sheet taped beside the window: Ezekiel 38, in large type, the names circled in red. Gog. Magog. Persia. Gomer. Togarmah. She had pinned a headline beside each one as it came, until the paper met the other wall, the one headed *WHO PAYS?*, with the Meridian filing and the Verity brochure and Adrian Crowe's raised hand. Now the two walls ran together at the corner, and she could no longer say where one story ended and the other began.

Across the top, on masking tape: *In the latter years thou shalt come into the land that is brought back from the sword.*

Under *Meshech and Tubal*, Moscow rearming Tehran. Under *Persia*, satellite photographs of mountain tunnels bombed shut in spring and dug open by autumn. Under *Gomer* and *Togarmah*, Israeli jets over a Syrian airbase, and a warning from Washington. Under *Ethiopia* and *Libya*, the Houthis reaching into Sudan, Turkish drones outside Tripoli. And at the bottom, pinned last, the story she had read at four-thirty that morning: a Russian general named Dmitri Volkov, in command of a new joint force, shaking hands with Iranian officers on a runway while the transport planes stood behind him with their tail ramps down.

*Thou shalt come from thy place out of the north parts.*

She had argued Ezekiel 38 with Angela for most of her adult life. Was Magog Russia, or something older? They had never agreed, never needed to, because it had always been far off, a picture drawn in ink that dried long ago. Now every name in the chapter had a headline under it.

She set the coffee on the sill and laid her palm flat over the general's face. She was not afraid. She felt the calm she knew from the bench, on the morning a culture finally turned after weeks of nothing.

Then she went to get Walt.

\* \* \*

He was waiting on his porch across the street from Ezra's house when she pulled up, in his brown suit jacket and his tweed cap, with his cane hooked over the porch rail. He had been up since five. He was always up by five.

"You said it was important," he said, before she had her door open. "You sounded on the phone like you'd been up all night."

"I have been."

"I can tell." He worked his way down the steps one at a time, gripping the rail, and she came around and took his elbow at the bottom. He let her. A month ago he would not have let her; a month ago he had not been a man with a wired breastbone under his brown suit jacket. He stopped on every step to let his heart catch up with him.

Walt had said one thing about it, in the hospital, to the nurse who came to turn him. He had asked for the Bible on the bedside table and opened it by feel, without his glasses, to a psalm he had known since he was a boy. *My flesh and my heart faileth: but God is the strength of my heart, and my portion for ever.* (Psalm 73:26) "Mine failed," he told her, with a dry little laugh that hurt his stitches. "They tell me they fixed it. I'll believe it when I know whose strength it's running on."

"Is it the hospital?" he said. "Did they call you?"

"No. Nobody from the hospital is going to call me." She opened the passenger door for him. "I want you to see something, Walt. At my house. I can't bring it to you. It's on a wall."

He looked at her a moment longer, with his sharp gray eyes. Then he got in.

Across the street, Ezra's truck was in the driveway. The porch light was off. In the upstairs window, the one that had been Jalen's room since he was four, the blind was halfway up, and Kambria thought she saw someone move behind it. She looked away before she could be sure. *Thursday,* she told herself. *Tomorrow.*

She drove the twelve blocks to her own house, and neither of them spoke. Walt held his cap on his knee. At the light on Michigan Avenue she checked the mirror, as she had checked it every few blocks for a week now, and the road behind her was empty except for a city bus.

"You're looking for the gray car," Walt said.

"Yes."

"I watched for it this morning. From my kitchen." He kept his eyes ahead. "It hasn't been on our street since yesterday morning."

"It was in Petworth yesterday afternoon."

Walt said nothing, but his hand closed on the head of his cane and stayed closed.

\* \* \*

She left him in the doorway of the spare room and went to make fresh coffee, because she knew he would want to read it without anyone watching him read.

When she came back he was standing just inside the door with his hat in one hand and his cane in the other, reading the wall from left to right and top to bottom, one headline at a time. His lips moved a little. Every now and then he leaned closer to read the small type under a photograph. She stood behind him with the two cups and waited.

He read for seventeen minutes. She timed it on the kitchen clock without meaning to.

When he got to the bottom, to the general on the runway, he stopped. He stood with his chin up, reading it again. And Kambria watched the color leave his face. It went out of it from the top down, from his forehead to his jaw, until his skin was the color of the newsprint he had handled all his life.

"Sit down, Walt."

"I'm all right."

"You're not. Sit." She set the cups on the desk and pulled the desk chair around for him, and after a moment he lowered himself into it. His hands were shaking. She took his wrist without asking and found the pulse with two fingers, as she had a dozen times in the last month at his dinner table, and counted. Fast, but steady.

"I was there," he said.

"I know."

"No. I mean I was *there.*" He lifted his cane and pointed with the rubber tip at the clipping under *Persia*, then at the one under *Meshech*. "Not on this wall. In the paper. All those years I set those names, in lead and then in light. Every war on that list, I put the headline on." He straightened a clipping that did not need it. "And before that, I was in one. Vietnam, 1971. They drafted me at nineteen and put me in a fuel truck, and I drove it through a country I couldn't have found on a map. You'd hear the rockets come in at night, and you'd lie in the dirt and listen for the boom. Some nights you could see the tracers go up. Little streaks of fire." His jaw worked. "One night a rocket came down on the fuel depot. Six of ours. I'd eaten supper with two of them."

Kambria waited. He was not finished.

"Ezra's father died in the Gulf," Walt said. "Calvin Patterson. Artillery, up north, near the border. I didn't know him, not then. I found out years later, when I moved in across the street and Angela told me." He looked at the wall. "I came home from mine. He didn't come home from his. I used to watch that grown man shoot baskets in his driveway, with his father's watch on his wrist that didn't work, and think, *That could have been my kid.*"

"I didn't know that."

"Nobody does but Ezra. I told him once, and never again." He was quiet. "Fifty-five years. And every one of those names is on your wall again. Persia. The Russians sending them the missiles. The Turks building ships." He shook his head. "I told myself it was over when that war ended. Over and done."

"You set a lot of headlines that turned out not to be the end."

He made a sound that might have been a laugh. "I did. Peace in 1973. Cease-fire in 1991. *Mission accomplished.*" He rubbed his face with his free hand. "Every one of them, I believed."

She handed him his coffee, and he held it in both hands without drinking it.

"Read me the part I missed," he said. "You've got a look on your face. There's a part I missed."

\* \* \*

There was.

She opened her Bible to Ezekiel 38 and perched on the edge of the daybed across from him, so their knees almost touched.

"Everybody reads the list," she said. "Verse thirteen." She turned the book around. "*Sheba, and Dedan, and the merchants of Tarshish, with all the young lions thereof, shall say unto thee, Art thou come to take a spoil?*"

Walt read it twice.

"Arabia," he said. "Sheba and Dedan."

"They're not in the army. They stand off to the side and protest. The nations that fought Israel for fifty years are saying *Don't.*" She tapped the page. "Ezekiel wrote that list twenty-six hundred years ago, before there was a Saudi Arabia, or a Turkey, or an Iran. And it lines up with the evening news, down to who's left out."

"The Gulf states signed peace deals with Israel," Walt said, almost to himself. "Five, six years ago. I read it in three papers. *Sheba and Dedan, standing apart.*"

The color had come back into his face, and with it the look of a man reading proof.

Kambria touched the clipping under *Gomer*. "One more thing. Ezekiel never says the people of those nations are wicked. He says their rulers come with a great company." She looked at the soldiers in their rows, a woman in a headscarf carrying groceries past a mural, a boy on a bicycle in Istanbul. "I pray for every name on this wall. For Israel, because God said He'd bless those who bless her. And for the mothers in Tehran and Ankara who never asked for any of it."

"Angela used to say that."

"She said it first."

Walt set down his coffee, put both hands on the head of his cane, and pushed himself up.

"I could quote you Ezekiel 38 in my sleep," he said. "And I have never once prayed for anybody on that wall. Not one."

"It's not too late."

"No," he said. "I suppose it isn't."

He reached for his cap.

"Leave it," Kambria said. "You're staying for lunch."

She had put the food in the oven on low before she left that morning, under foil, because she had known he would reach for his cap. Catfish with lemon and garlic. Macaroni and cheese, the creamy kind with no crust, because the crusted one was for tomorrow. Cabbage fried slow with smoked turkey. The discharge papers said no salt, so she had used lemon and pepper and smoked paprika, and trusted them.

Walt bowed his head without being asked. "Lord, thank You for this food, and the hands that made it, and every one of these days You've seen fit to add to mine. Amen."

He took one bite of the cabbage and stopped, eyes closed.

"My mother made it like this. Thursdays, the day before payday, when cabbage was a nickel a head." He opened his eyes. "I haven't tasted that in fifty years."

"Eat," Kambria said gently.

*Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.* She thought it and did not say it.

"Angela would have said the fish needed hot sauce," Walt said, pushing back his plate.

"Angela would have been right."

They laughed, carefully, Walt with one hand flat against his breastbone.

\* \* \*

Before she drove him home, she went into the kitchen and took down the blue concordance.

He watched from the dinner table while she cut through the packing tape on the spine with a paring knife and slid the thumb drive out from between the binding and the cover. It was small and black, with a white label she had written herself: *PETWORTH / VERITY / PALE.*

She plugged it into her laptop and copied the rest onto it, one folder at a time, while he watched: the photograph of the gray car's plate, the five verses from New York, the chart she had drawn at three in the morning. Then she taped the drive back into the spine with fresh tape until it lay flat again, and then she put the concordance in a grocery bag and set it on the table in front of Walt.

"I need you to keep this for me."

He looked at the bag, and then at her. "What is it?"

"It's all of it. The PALEHORSE files from Petworth, and a file with the first case in it dated three weeks before the first case happened. The plate on the car that's been sitting on our street. The verses Francesca gave me in New York, the way she gave them to me. And where it all leads, Walt. Verity to Meridian Trust, Meridian Trust to a man named Vale. And Celeste Moore in the middle of it." She took the seat facing him. "If I had my badge, I'd take it to the right people. I don't have my badge. And I'm not sure anymore who the right people are."

"Kambria." His voice was very low. "Is that why the car's been following you?"

"Yes."

"Then why on God's earth would you give it to me?"

She had thought about that all night, lying awake, and she gave him the answer she had found.

"Because they're watching me, Walt. They're watching my house and my car and my phone. They've been in my spare room once already." She held his eyes. "Nobody watches an old man's dinner table. Nobody thinks an old man with a cane is the one with the evidence. You keep it on the shelf with your concordance, right next to your own. A man with two concordances is just an old man who forgot he already owned one."

He almost smiled. It didn't last.

"And if something happens to you?"

"Then you give it to Ezra." She said it steadily. She had decided that too, in the night. "Not the police. Not my agency. Ezra. And you make him read Angela's notebook first. The black one, in his hall closet. Make him read the notebook before he plugs in the drive. Otherwise none of it will make any sense to him."

"Ezra," Walt said. "Who told you to get off his porch."

"Ezra. Who said yesterday I could come for Thanksgiving." She heard her own voice catch on it, and steadied it. "He said it himself. Jalen told me."

Walt eyed the grocery bag.

"All right," he said finally. "But nothing's going to happen to you. You hear me? You're going to bring that macaroni tomorrow, and you're going to sit at that table, and I'm going to eat too much and fall asleep in Ezra's recliner with my mouth open, and you're going to be embarrassed for me."

"I'd like that."

"So would I." He pulled the bag toward him and laid his hand on top of it. "So would I."

\* \* \*

She spent the afternoon in her kitchen, cooking.

The macaroni and cheese was Angela's recipe, written out in Angela's round hand on an index card that had gone soft and spotted from years of Thanksgivings: three kinds of cheese, evaporated milk, a little mustard, a crust of buttered crumbs on top. Kambria had made it every year since Angela got sick. She grated the cheese herself because Angela had always said bagged cheese had sawdust in it. Kambria had never tested the claim. She grated it herself anyway.

At two o'clock her phone rang, and the screen said *JALEN*, and when she picked up it was not Jalen.

"Miss Kambria?" It was Mia, panting, as if she had run to the phone. "Jalen said I could call you. Are you bringing the cheesy noodles?"

Kambria laughed out loud, and the tightness she had carried since the wall that morning loosened. "I am making them right now, baby. Right this minute. I've got cheese all over my hands."

"The orange kind? With the crunchy top?"

"The orange kind with the crunchy top. Your mommy's kind."

There was a satisfied pause. Then Mia lowered her voice, as she did whenever she told a secret. "I made up a story," she said. "For Daddy. I'm going to tell it to him tonight at bedtime. It's about a lamp."

"A lamp?"

"I can't tell you. It's for Daddy first." Kambria could hear her smiling. "But you'll like it. It has you in it. A little bit. You're the lady with the oil."

Kambria stopped grating. She stood at the counter with the cheese in one hand and the phone against her ear and her eyes suddenly full.

"Mia," she said. "Who told you about the lady with the oil?"

"Mommy," Mia said, as if it were obvious. "A long time ago. When she was sick. She said some ladies were ready and some ladies weren't, and the ready ones had oil. She said you were a ready one." There was a muffled sound, and Jalen's voice in the background, and then Mia again, in a hurry. "Jalen says I have to go. Bye, Miss Kambria. Don't forget the crunchy top."

"I won't forget."

The line went quiet. Kambria set the phone down and stood at the counter with her hands on either side of the bowl, and cried, briefly, for Angela, who had told a five-year-old about the wise virgins from a hospice bed. Then she wiped her face on her sleeve and finished the cheese.

\* \* \*

While the dish baked she sat at the dinner table with the ninth notebook and her phone and read the news, because she had promised herself she would watch everything until the end, whatever the end was.

All of it came from Dubai. Adrian Crowe was hosting a gala that night in his tower to launch the Global Ledger: one account for every person on earth, one currency, no cash. The guest list ran for a column. Bishop Sterling. Lucas Thorne. Dmitri Volkov, the general from her wall, who was drinking champagne in a glass ballroom at that moment. At the bottom, a line from Crowe: *"Your hand is your account. Peace is no longer a hope. It is an arithmetic."*

She opened the notebook to a clean page and dated it. *November 25, 2026.* Under it she wrote *Dubai. The Ledger. Your hand is your account.* And in the center of the page, the verse that had waited in her all afternoon.

*Come out of her, my people, that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.* (Revelation 18:4)

It was what she would have said to every person on that list, if she could have stood at the door of the ballroom and said one thing. *Come out.* She closed the notebook and went to take the macaroni from the oven.

\* \* \*

The gray Malibu came back at nine-forty that night.

She saw it from the kitchen window while she was washing the grater and the mixing bowl. It rolled down Otis Street with its headlights on and stopped across from her house, under the streetlight that had been out since summer, and the headlights went off. The engine kept running. She could see the faint plume of the exhaust in the cold.

She dried her hands on the dish towel. She stood at the window for a full minute, deciding.

She could call the police. She had called them once, on Monday, after she came home from New York to find her notebooks squared on the desk, and a young officer had stood in her spare room and looked at the walls covered with headlines and Bible verses, and then looked at her with polite, careful eyes, and written something in his notebook, and left. She could pull the blinds and go to bed and lie awake again. She could do what she had done every night for a week: watch, and wait, and write the plate number down one more time.

Or she could do what Angela would have done.

She took her coat off the hook by the door. She took a paper plate from the cupboard and cut a square of the macaroni out of the corner of the dish, the corner piece with the most crunchy top on it, because that was the best piece, and covered it with foil. She put her Bible in her coat pocket. Then she unlocked the front door and walked down her steps and across the street in her slippers, in the cold, straight to the driver's window of the gray sedan, and knocked on the glass.

Nothing happened. She could see her own reflection in the dark window: a tired woman of forty-two in a quilted coat, holding a paper plate.

She knocked again.

The window came down four inches. The man inside was perhaps fifty, with short gray hair and a heavy, ordinary face that could have stood in any lobby in any city and never been noticed. He was wearing a gray overcoat. She had seen him before: in a lobby, on a plaza, on a train, on Georgia Avenue.

He said nothing, and his face gave her nothing.

"I'm Kambria," she said. "But you know that." She held out the plate. "It's macaroni and cheese. My best friend's recipe. You've been sitting out here in the freezing air for a week, and it's the night before Thanksgiving, and I thought you might be hungry."

He looked at the plate. For one second his face moved, and then it did not.

"Mr. Vale," he said, and his voice was flat and polite, "would like you to stay home tomorrow."

"I'm sorry," Kambria said. "I can't do that. I'm going to my family's for Thanksgiving. I've been invited." She did not lower the plate. "There's room at the table, if you'd like to come. I mean that. There always has been."

He studied her. He had spent a week of nights in a frozen car watching a woman read her Bible at a dinner table.

"Is there somebody waiting for you at home?" she said. "Tomorrow?"

The window went up.

The engine changed pitch, and the headlights came on, and the Malibu pulled away from the curb and drove off down Twelfth Street, and turned at the corner, and was gone.

Kambria stood in the street in her slippers with the plate in her hand until she could no longer hear it. Then she bowed her head, right there, under the dead streetlight, and prayed for him. She never learned his name. She prayed for him anyway. *Lord, You know who he is. You know who's waiting for him. Don't let him be lost.*

She went back inside, and locked the door, and put the macaroni in the refrigerator. She did not eat it. It was his.

\* \* \*

The alarm was set for five, so she could warm the dish and be at the Pattersons' by eight. Before she went up to bed she did what she did every night. She filled the lamp, trimmed the wick, and set it in the window where the street could see it.

Then she sat down at the kitchen table one last time with the ninth notebook, and wrote the date. *November 25, 2026. 11:20 p.m.* She wrote for a long while. When she finished, she slid the notebook into the gap behind the loose board under the window seat, where she kept the things she could not lose, and pressed the board home with her palm.

On the counter, the dish waited under its foil. She tore the back off an envelope and wrote on it. *For the Pattersons. Thursday. Back by eight. K.* She set it on top of the dish.

Out on Twelfth Street the dead streetlight buzzed, flickered, and stayed dark. No gray sedan. She told herself that was a good sign, and went upstairs.

\* \* \*

The first sound was an engine, which was wrong, because nobody drove down Twelfth Street at one-forty in the morning.

Then a second engine. Then a third.

She was at the bedroom window with no memory of crossing the room. Three black vans were rolling up the block with their lights off, slow as hearses, and behind them a dark sedan she knew. It stopped across from her house, under the dead streetlight. The engine idled. Nobody got out of it.

The vans stopped at her curb. Doors slid open together, and men in dark tactical gear poured out, and every one of them wore a red band on his left arm. They did not run. They moved like men who had done this before, and had been told in advance there would be no trouble.

She did not scream. She was surprised by that, later. She stood in her nightgown at the window with her pulse loud in her ears and said, out loud, to the empty room, "All right, Lord."

The pounding on the door shook the house.

"FEDERAL CONTAINMENT DIVISION. OPEN THE DOOR."

She went down the stairs barefoot. She had her hand on the knob when they took the door off its frame.

Light hit her, white, from four directions. A gloved hand closed around her arm, hard enough to bruise. She heard boots on her floors, in her kitchen, in her spare room. She heard glass break. The wall she had built, the Ezekiel wall, the headlines and the strings and the verses, was coming down in sheets under their hands.

"Look at this." An officer, his flashlight on the pinned pages. "Bible verses. Maps. Names." He turned the beam on her face, and there was nothing in his own. "Ma'am. Are you one of them?"

She said, "If you mean do I belong to Jesus Christ, yes."

"She's one of them," he said over his shoulder. It was not an accusation. It was a box being ticked.

They did not search her. They did not read her anything. A second man had her other arm, and her feet were bare on the cold boards, and they were already turning her toward the door when she saw the officer in the kitchen, standing at the window, with his gloved hand reaching for the lamp.

"No," she said.

His eyes stayed on the candle. His thumb found the wick.

"Please." It came out of her smaller than she meant. "Please, don't put it out."

The hand stopped.

For three seconds nobody in the house moved. The little flame stood in the glass chimney and shook, and she saw it in his eyes, gold, over his mask.

He took his hand away.

"Leave it," he said. "It's not evidence."

They walked her out barefoot over the frozen concrete. At the curb, the black van gaped. Across the street the sedan sat under the dead light, engine running. She turned her head and found the face behind the windshield. The gray man's heavy, ordinary face was lit blue from the dash. His hands were on the wheel at ten and two. His eyes rested on her without seeming to see her.

Then the van door closed on the street, and the dark.

\* \* \*

The cell was underground. She knew that before they took the hood off, because the air had changed. Cold, dead, recycled; the smell of concrete that had never seen weather.

It was perhaps eight feet by ten. A steel bench ran along one wall. A drain sat in the middle of the floor. A single caged bulb burned overhead. Above the drain, set into the ceiling, was a steel grille with a flat nozzle behind the slats, the kind she had seen over the decontamination showers at work. Under the bulb hung a placard, riveted to the block: **FEDERAL CONTAINMENT DIVISION — SUBLEVEL 3 — HOLDING B.**

They sat her on the bench. A guard knelt and locked a steel cuff around her left ankle, then her right, and ran the chain between them under the bench to a ring bolted into the floor. Another locked her wrists, in front, with a shorter chain to the same ring. The metal was colder than anything she had ever touched. It bit the bones.

Nobody spoke. The door shut. A bolt thrown, a second bolt, and then the sound that was almost the worst, the sound of footsteps walking away.

She sat in the humming light with her wrists chained under a bench and her feet bare on the concrete, and she waited for the fear.

It came, as it had to. It came up her spine and into her throat, and she let it. *Of course I'm afraid,* she thought. *I'm forty-two years old and I'm chained to a floor.* She did not fight it. She did the only thing she knew how to do with fear. She handed it up.

She thought of Mia's call. *You're the lady with the oil.* She thought about the parable Jesus told: the five wise ones, and the five foolish, and the cry at midnight, and the ones who had oil in their vessels with their lamps and went in. *And they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut.*

She had lost the hour. She knew only that it was still dark above her, somewhere, and that the night before Thanksgiving had a morning on the other side of it.

"Lord," she said. Her voice came out cracked and small and the concrete gave it back to her. "I don't know what You're doing." She breathed. "I don't need to. You know where I am."

The bulb hummed.

"I left a light on in my window. Let it keep burning." She closed her eyes. "Whatever they do to me. Let my light keep burning."

\* \* \*

Across the city, in a house with a broken door and a floor strewn with paper, a small brass lamp stood on the kitchen sill and threw its steady gold light out onto an empty street.

On the counter, a dish waited under its foil. On top of it lay a note.

*Back by eight.*

The lamp burned on.

## Chapter 19: Mene, Mene

> *TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.* — Daniel 5:27

**Word study: *weighed* — תְּקֵל** Aramaic *teqal* (Strong's H8625). To weigh, as a merchant weighs silver on a balance. It is a cousin of the Hebrew shaqal, the root of the shekel, the weight that money was counted by in the ancient world. The king of Babylon was put on the scale he used for everyone else, and he came up light.

*Belshazzar the king made a great feast to a thousand of his lords, and drank wine before the thousand… They drank wine, and praised the gods of gold, and of silver, of brass, of iron, of wood, and of stone. In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace: and the king saw the part of the hand that wrote… In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain.* (Daniel 5:1, 4–5, 30)

\* \* \*

Nina Cole had been in Dubai for nineteen hours, and she had not yet seen the sun except through glass.

She stood at the window of her room high in the Crowe Tower at seven o'clock on Wednesday evening, in a black dress she had bought at an airport and a pair of shoes that already hurt, and looked down at the city lit up below her. A helicopter crossed beneath her window, its red light blinking on the roofs of other towers. The desert was out there somewhere, beyond the last string of lights. She could not see it. From up here the whole world was laid out in grids: roads of white light and roads of red, glowing towers in rows, the black line of the sea along the western edge, and in the middle of it all the tallest building on earth, a needle of silver half a mile into the dark, close enough to touch.

She was thirty-three years old, and she had helped build the machines that ran half of what she was looking at.

"Juno," she said. "What time is it in New York?"

"It is morning in New York, Nina." The voice came from the phone on the dresser, warm and unhurried, a voice she had tuned herself over three years until it sounded like nobody and everybody. "The gala begins in thirty minutes. You have one message from Dr. Kroll. He says, and I quote, *Don't hide in your room. I'll come up and get you.*"

She smiled. That was exactly what she had been planning to do.

Nina worked at Kroll Dynamics in Manhattan, the company that had taught machines to see. Its cameras watched intersections in forty cities. Its software read faces and license plates and the way a man walked, and its newest models could hold a conversation in eighty languages and never lose the thread. She had joined at twenty-six, straight out of a doctorate at Carnegie Mellon, because Sebastian Kroll had told her in the interview that they were going to end traffic deaths, and she had believed him. She ate dinner at her desk most nights. She talked to Juno more than she talked to any human being, and she knew it, and on bad nights she told herself it was efficient.

She told no one, not even Juno, that she was afraid of what they had built. She had seen the internal demonstrations that never made it into the press releases: the models that could watch an hour of video of a man and then speak in his voice, with his pauses and his habits, well enough to fool his own sister; the robots in the Long Island test hall that had learned to open doors no one had shown them how to open. She had sat in meetings where grown men talked about these things as her grandmother used to talk about the grandchildren. And at night, alone in her apartment on the Upper West Side, she lay awake and thought about a verse she had not opened a Bible to read in fifteen years, because it would not leave her alone.

*Many shall run to and fro, and knowledge shall be increased.*

Her grandmother had read it to her at the dinner table in Baltimore when she was eleven, after she won the state science fair with a robot made out of a coffee can. Her grandmother had been proud of her. She had also studied the coffee-can robot, and then opened her old black Bible to the end of Daniel, and read that verse out loud, and said, *Baby, you be careful what you build. God gave you that mind. Don't you let anybody else tell you what it's for.*

Nina had not thought about that in years. She had been thinking about it every day for a month.

She picked up the phone, and her clutch, and went up.

\* \* \*

The ballroom was at the very top of the tower, and it had a ceiling made of glass.

She stopped just inside the doors and let the other guests flow around her. Above her head, the night sky over the Gulf was black and clear, with a few hard stars, and below it, filling the room, were perhaps four hundred people in gowns and black tie, under chandeliers of cut crystal that hung in long, glittering falls. At the far end, on a low stage, a string quartet was playing something she did not recognize. Along the walls stood towers of champagne glasses, taller than she was, each one lit from inside so that the wine seemed to glow. Between them, waiters in white jackets moved through the crowd carrying trays of food she could not name.

Across the ceiling, projected onto the glass so that the words seemed to hang among the stars, ran a single line in gold.

*THE GLOBAL LEDGER. ONE WORLD. ONE ACCOUNT. NO MORE WANT.*

"There she is." Sebastian Kroll came through the crowd toward her with both hands out. He was fifty-one, slight and pale, with rimless glasses and a soft, eager way of talking, and he spoke of his systems as his children. He kissed her on both cheeks, which he had never done in New York. "You came down. I was ready to send a robot."

"I believe you."

"You should. I have three in the building." He took her elbow and steered her into the room. "Come. You have to meet people. You built half of what they're celebrating tonight, and nobody here knows your name. That's a crime."

He introduced her to a German finance minister who did not look at her face, and a Brazilian banker who did, too long. "Those two signed last week," Kroll murmured as they moved on. "Forty-one central banks settle on Adrian's rails now. The private banks that held out lost their clearing lines on Monday." He nodded toward a small gray-haired woman near the stage, the one who ran the biggest payment network on earth. "Ines did that. Nobody voted. Nobody had to. You can't run a bank that can't move money."

He introduced her to a rabbi: a gentle, silver-haired man in black with a black skullcap, who held her hand in both of his and told her, in perfect English with an Italian lilt, that her work was "a kind of prayer, the prayer of the mind for order." His name was Matteo Arcangeli, and she had seen his face on the news all month, on the steps of a hotel on the Mount of Olives. He smelled faintly of roses.

Then Kroll introduced her to a man in a borrowed tuxedo.

She could tell it was borrowed. The jacket was a little wide at the shoulders and a little short at the wrists, and the man in it kept touching his bow tie. He was around thirty, broad, with a contractor's hands, thick and nicked across the knuckles, and a face that had spent a lot of time outdoors.

"Nina Cole, Trent Walker," Kroll said. "Trent's firm is installing our camera network in Washington. Every intersection in the District by the end of the year. Trent, Nina wrote the vision stack your cameras run on."

"No kidding." Trent shook her hand. His grip was careful, a big hand held in check. "So you're the one who taught them to see."

"Some of it."

"Huh." He studied her with frank curiosity. "I hang them, you make them look. Funny. I used to hang drywall. I apprenticed under a carpenter in Northeast for six years. Best carpenter in DC. Ezra Patterson. Never heard of him, I bet."

"No."

"Nobody has. He could build you a staircase you'd cry over." Trent took a glass of champagne from a passing tray and held it without drinking. "He'd hate this. Every bit of it. He'd stand right there by the door with his arms folded and say, *Trent, what are you doing here?*" He laughed. "I'd tell him, somebody's gonna get rich off the end of the world. Might as well be me."

Nina looked at him. "The end of the world?"

He waved his glass at the ceiling, at the gold words among the stars. "One world, one account. You never read Revelation?" He said it lightly, with his mouth only. "I grew up in church. Front pew, every Sunday, Greater Mount Calvary. My mother could quote you the whole thing." He raised the glass a little, toward the stage, where a lean, silver-haired man in a charcoal suit had just come in, and the whole room was turning toward him. "*And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark.*"

Then he drank the champagne in one swallow, and set the empty glass on a tray, and went to shake Adrian Crowe's hand.

\* \* \*

Crowe spoke at nine.

He used no notes. He stood at the center of the stage with no podium in front of him, in an open-collared shirt under his suit, and he let the room go silent, and then he let the silence go on until a few people laughed nervously. Nina had heard him speak twice before, both times on screens. In person he was taller, and harder, and he had a way of looking out over a crowd as if he were deciding which of them to keep.

"For ten thousand years," he said, "human beings have fought over money. Over who has it, and who does not. Over gold and grain and oil and land. Every war you have ever read about was, at the bottom of it, an argument over a ledger." He smiled. "Tonight we close the argument."

Applause, warm and immediate.

"We have spent a long time asking permission," Crowe said. "From parliaments. From voters. From that tired building on the East River where small nations go to make speeches about large ones." A ripple of laughter. "I have stopped asking. The people in this room have stopped asking. We are the ones who build things. We are the ones who know how the machines work. The world does not need more votes. It needs better arithmetic."

He lifted his right hand, palm out, and held it up in the light so the whole room could see it, empty.

"Your hand," Adrian Crowe said, "is your account."

The applause this time went on and on. Nina found that her own hands were moving, clapping, before she had decided to clap, and she stopped them and held them together in front of her.

"To the end of scarcity," Crowe said, and lifted a glass.

"To the end of scarcity," four hundred voices answered.

A heavyset man with a shaved head and a chest full of ribbons, standing at the head table in a Russian dress uniform, raised his glass higher than anyone. "And to peace," he called out, in thick English. "Peace in our time!"

Some people laughed, as if it were a joke. Most of them drank.

Nina looked at the man in the uniform. The program at her place setting said *General Dmitri Volkov, Commander, Joint Stability Force.* She had read on the plane that his transports were lined up on a runway in Iran.

She did not drink.

\* \* \*

Dinner was nine courses, and somewhere around the seventh she stopped counting the money.

She had not meant to count it in the first place. But she had grown up in a fourth-floor apartment on Druid Hill Avenue in West Baltimore, where her grandmother clipped coupons on Sunday afternoons, and she could not stop the arithmetic from running in the back of her head. The caviar course. The white truffles shaved at the table from a silver box. A wine the sommelier announced to the room by its year and its price per bottle, to applause, and that price was more than her grandmother had earned in a year cleaning offices downtown. When a waiter stumbled near the head table and a full bottle of it shattered on the marble floor, the man nearest it only laughed and lifted his glass for more. Two waiters were on their knees picking up the glass before the laughter had stopped.

At the next table a senator-elect from Virginia, a handsome man with a law professor's careful voice, was explaining to a Gulf minister how the universal ethics act he would introduce in January could be written so that no court could ever strike it down. Lucas Thorne, the card at his place said. Across from him a big, warm-faced American bishop with a gold cross on his chest was telling a story that had everyone around him laughing. Bishop Roland Sterling. She recognized him from the television in the lobby of her grandmother's apartment building, years ago, asking for seed gifts.

At a round table near the stage sat ten men and women she did not recognize at all. They did not laugh much. They ate little and drank less, and they talked among themselves in low voices, and every few minutes one of them would glance toward the edge of the room, toward the tall windows on the east side, as if checking on something there.

Nina followed their eyes.

A thin, dark-haired man was standing by the windows, alone, in a plain gray suit. He ate nothing. He held a glass of water he never drank, and no one spoke to him. He watched the room with great patience, and missed nothing, waiting for it to break.

"Who is that?" she asked Kroll, who was beside her.

Kroll followed her look, and his face went careful. "That," he said, "is Alexander Vale. Mr. Crowe's chief of staff." He lowered his voice. "He's the one who runs everything. Mr. Crowe gives the speeches. Alexander writes them."

"And that table? The ten?"

"The High Council of the Technate. The Organization's new board." Kroll smiled, but the smile was thin. "They were seated on Sunday in New York. Unelected, of course. Engineers and economists. People who know what they're doing." He turned back to his plate. "Alexander chose each of them."

Nina glanced back toward the window. The thin man in gray had turned his head, and for one second he was looking straight at her, across the whole width of the room. Then he looked away.

\* \* \*

The entertainment began after the ninth course.

A comedian came out onto the stage, a famous one, whose face Nina knew from streaming specials. He did ten minutes on the International Collective that had the whole room roaring. Then he did ten minutes on religion.

She would not remember most of it afterward. She would remember the waiters coming through the tables with velvet boxes, and the guests opening them, laughing, and lifting out crowns made of braided wire and dried thorn, sprayed with gold. She would remember a Brazilian banker setting one on his own head and pretending to stagger under it, and the woman beside him pressing her palms together and rolling her eyes to the ceiling, and the table shrieking. She would remember the comedian stretching his arms out wide against the backdrop and hanging his head, and saying a line about forgiveness that she would not repeat, and the room coming apart with laughter.

She would remember Bishop Sterling laughing louder than anyone, red in the face, slapping the table with his big hand. And she would remember the moment, a few seconds later, when he stopped. He sat rigid, the thorn crown in his lap, and his hand stopped on it, and he fixed his eyes on the tablecloth and did not laugh again for the rest of the night.

Then the waiters brought out the cups.

They were old: gold and silver, some of them dented, one or two set with dull red stones. The sommelier explained, to delighted applause, that Mr. Crowe had acquired them over many years at auction, from monasteries and closed cathedrals in a dozen countries. *Communion chalices,* he said. *Some of them five hundred years old.* Every guest at the head table received one. They were filled with the same wine whose bottle had shattered on the floor.

"Where is the promise of his coming?" someone called out from the back, in a high, mocking preacher's voice, and the room laughed again.

Crowe lifted his chalice. "To us," he said simply. "Since no one else is coming."

Behind the head table, the long mirror that ran the length of the wall had clouded over as the room warmed, a gray bloom of fog from frame to frame. Nina saw it first, because she was looking anywhere but at the cups. Then a line drew itself down through the fog, as if a finger were being dragged across the glass from the top.

It was not handwriting, or any lettering she knew. The strokes were strange, angular and chiseled, older than any alphabet on a keyboard. One word, and then another, and then two more, running down the glass from top to bottom, each letter as tall as her hand.

*MENE*

*MENE*

*TEKEL*

*UPHARSIN*

She knew neither the words nor the language. Adrian Crowe knew something. He had turned in his chair with the chalice halfway to his mouth, and all the color went out of his face.

"Alexander." It was not the voice he used for speeches. It was low and cracked, and it carried anyway. "Alexander. Did you see that? Did anyone?"

Vale had come up behind his chair without a sound. He looked at the mirror. He looked at Crowe. "See what, Mr. Crowe?"

Crowe turned back to the glass. It was clear, dry from frame to frame, with the whole glittering room in it and nothing written there at all. "Nothing," he said. "No. Nothing." He drank, too quickly, and the table cheered him, and the room laughed again as if it had never stopped.

Only Vale did not laugh. He was not looking at the mirror, or at his employer. Over Crowe's shoulder his eyes were on Nina.

Nina put her napkin on the table and stood up.

She was halfway across the room, walking fast, before she understood why: she could not sit at that table and watch them drink from those cups. She had not prayed in fifteen years. She had not been to church since she moved out of her grandmother's apartment. But her grandmother had drunk from a cup like that once a month for seventy years, with her eyes closed, and Nina could not watch those people laugh into it.

\* \* \*

She was almost to the doors when Kroll caught up with her.

"Nina. Nina, wait." He put a hand on her arm. He was flushed, a little drunk. "Don't go. I know. I know, the comedian was too much. I told them. Please." He steered her to the side, by a column, out of the flow of waiters. "I need to talk to you. That's why I brought you. Not for this." He gestured at the room. "For this."

He took a card out of his breast pocket and pressed it into her hand. It was heavy, cream-colored, with a single word embossed on it in gold. *CONTINUITY.*

"What is it?"

"It's the project I've wanted to build my whole life." His eyes were bright behind the rimless glasses. "Imagine twenty years of one man, every speech and every phone call and every private word, poured into an artificial intelligence until it answers the way he would answer. Not a copy. A continuation." He lowered his voice. "A mind that doesn't have to die."

Nina stared at him. "Whose mind?"

Kroll let that pass. He only smiled and glanced toward the head table.

"The budget is unlimited," he said. "I mean that literally. I want you to lead the core architecture. You can name your salary. Name a number that makes you laugh, and then double it." He squeezed her arm. "You'd never have to worry about anything again. Neither would anyone you love."

She thought of her grandmother in Baltimore, eighty-four years old, still living in the same apartment, still taking the bus to church every Sunday because she would not let Nina pay for a car service. *Baby, you be careful what you build.*

"I need to think," she said.

"Of course. Of course you do." Kroll let go of her arm. "Think tonight. Tell me in New York." He started to turn back to the room, and then turned again. "Oh. And Nina. It isn't my offer, really. I'm only the one making it." He tilted his head toward the windows on the east side. "He asked for you by name."

She looked.

The man in the gray suit was not by the windows anymore. She found him a second later, much closer than she expected, standing at the edge of the stage with his glass of water, in low conversation with two of the ten from the round table. As she watched, he lifted his left hand to make a point, and his cuff slid back, and she saw a thin red string tied around his wrist, knotted three times.

He never turned his head her way.

\* \* \*

She went out onto the terrace because she needed air that had not been breathed by four hundred people.

It wrapped around the whole eightieth floor, a wide deck of pale stone behind a glass railing, and it was empty. The night was warm and dry, with a wind coming in off the desert that smelled of dust and, faintly, of the sea. Behind her, through the glass, the party went on without sound: people laughing with their mouths open, the comedian's arms flung wide, the chalices catching the light. In front of her, the city spread out to the edge of the world.

She leaned on the railing and breathed.

"Juno," she said. "What's Continuity?"

"I have no records matching that name, Nina."

"Search the company drive. Restricted folders. Use my credentials."

A pause. "Access to that directory was revoked fourteen minutes ago."

Nina straightened, the phone tight in her hand.

Fourteen minutes. While she was standing by the column with Kroll. Someone had already decided that she did not need to see it until she said yes.

She turned and looked back through the glass, because she did not want to look at the city. At the head table Adrian Crowe was on his feet again, laughing, with his chalice raised, and the long mirror behind him shone clean from frame to frame. No one in the room had turned around. Alexander Vale stood at Crowe's shoulder, not drinking, not smiling.

Nina's hands were shaking so badly she had to use both of them to hold the phone.

"What does *mene* mean?" she said. "M-E-N-E. And *tekel*. And *upharsin*."

The answer came at once, in Juno's usual voice.

"Those words are Aramaic. They appear in the Book of Daniel, chapter five. They were written on the wall of King Belshazzar's palace in Babylon, during a feast at which the king and his guests drank from the sacred vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem. The prophet Daniel interpreted them: *MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it. TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting. PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.*" The voice paused. "Would you like me to read the rest of the chapter?"

Nina did not answer. She could not.

She was thinking of her grandmother's dinner table in Baltimore, and the old black Bible open to Daniel, and her grandmother's voice reading it aloud, the way she had not heard it in fifteen years.

"Yes," she said finally. "Read me how it ends."

Juno read it. Nina stood alone on the terrace of the tallest party in the world with the warm desert wind on her face and the gold words crawling over her head, and listened to the end of Belshazzar's feast.

*In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain.*

\* \* \*

She did not go back inside.

She went down to her room and locked the door and sat on the bed in the dark, still in the airport dress, with the city burning gold through the window. She called her grandmother. It was late afternoon in Baltimore. The phone rang five times, six, and then the old voice came on, out of breath.

"Hello? Hello, who's this?" A pause, and then the voice broke open. "Nina? Baby, is that you? Oh, thank You, Jesus. Where are you? You sound like you're down in a can."

"I'm in Dubai, Grandma."

"Dubai! Lord, have mercy." A rattle of pans. "Child, you are on the other side of the world and I'm standing here with my hands in sweet potatoes! Sister Hattie's coming tomorrow, you know she is, and she's going to ask about you. What am I supposed to tell her? That you're eating airplane food up in the sky?"

Nina pressed her free hand over her eyes. "I'll be home Friday. I'll come down Friday, I promise."

"Friday. Well. I'll save you a plate." A pause. "Nina. What's wrong?"

"Nothing. I just wanted to hear you." It came out smaller than she meant. "Grandma, do you remember the coffee-can robot?"

"Do I remember it?" A soft, wet laugh. "Baby, it's sitting on my bookshelf right now, next to your daddy's picture. I dust it every Saturday."

"You told me to be careful what I build."

The pans stopped. A long quiet on the line, all the way from Baltimore.

"I did," her grandmother said. "And I meant it." The laugh was gone. The voice had gone low and slow and certain, the voice that had gotten a frightened little girl through a funeral. "Nina. Are you being careful?"

Nina could not answer. She heard herself breathing.

"Hush, now. Don't you cry. Listen to me." Her grandmother's voice shook and held. "You call on Jesus. You hear me? Whatever it is, baby. Wherever you are. It is never too far, and it is never too late. Nineveh was the wickedest city on God's earth, and they put on sackcloth, every one of them, down to the cows in the barn, and He turned His hand. You just call on His name."

"Grandma—"

"Every morning at five o'clock I get down on these old knees and I say your name. Every single morning. You know that."

"I know." It came out a whisper.

"Then I'll see you Friday. And I'll have a plate waiting, and I'm not taking no for an answer." A breath. "I love you, baby. I love you so much."

"I love you too, Grandma."

The line went dead. Nina sat on the bed with the phone in her lap and the dark pressing at the glass.

After a while, because she could not sleep and could not stop her hands from shaking, she opened the phone and searched for anything to listen to that was not Juno's voice. The first thing the screen offered her was a video that half the people she knew had sent her in the last month: a young cellist in a white suit, onstage at a high school in Washington, D.C., with an old man playing viola behind him and a closed red curtain at his back. *Untitled,* it said. Three million views.

She had never watched it. She pressed play.

The boy leaned to the microphone and said, "I'm dedicating this to someone who isn't here right now." And then he began to play, and Nina Cole, who had not cried in front of anyone since her father's funeral, sat on a bed so high above the desert that the planes coming in to land slid past below her window, and wept until the last high note rang out and stopped.

She played it again. She fell asleep with it playing, long after midnight, with the phone on the pillow beside her head and the gold light of the tower creeping across the ceiling.

It was Thursday in Dubai by then. In Washington it was still Wednesday evening, and the families were driving home for the holiday, and the stores were closing, and a woman in Brookland was taking a pan of macaroni out of her oven, the kind with the crust, for tomorrow.

In less than thirteen hours, the trumpet would sound.

## Act 6 — The Rapture

## Chapter 20: The Twinkling of an Eye

> *Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.* — 1 Corinthians 15:51–52

**Word study: *moment* — ἄτομος** Greek *atomos* (Strong's G823). Uncut. A piece of time so small it cannot be divided again. It is the word our *atom* comes from. Paul used it here and nowhere else in the New Testament: the change will not take an hour, or a minute, or a second. It will take the smallest piece of time there is.

*…behold, there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire, and parted them both asunder; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. And Elisha saw it, and he cried, My father, my father, the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof. And he saw him no more: and he took hold of his own clothes, and rent them in two pieces.* (2 Kings 2:11–12)

\* \* \*

**Wednesday, 8:20 p.m.**

Mia came down the stairs in her mother's shoes.

Ezra heard her before he saw her: the hollow knock of the low square heels on every step, slow and careful, one foot and then the other, as she had walked in them since she was four. He was on the couch, the television low, his phone in his hand, reading a text he had not answered yet. He thumbed the screen dark.

She came around the corner into the living room in her yellow nightgown with the moons on it, her hair in two puffs, holding on to the doorframe for balance. Angela's black Sunday shoes were so big on her that her whole foot fit in the front half, and the heels flapped loose behind her.

"Baby, you're supposed to be in bed. Jalen already read you Captain Crumb."

"That was Captain Crumb." She climbed onto the couch beside him, shoes and all, and settled against his arm. "This one's mine. I made it up. I told Miss Kambria I was going to tell you."

"You told Miss Kambria."

"On the phone. She's bringing the cheesy noodles." Mia tucked her feet up under her, and one of the shoes fell off onto the floor with a thump. She never noticed. "Are you ready?"

He looked down at her. In the light from the television her face was very serious, and very much her mother's. He put the phone aside.

"I'm ready."

She took a breath, as Jalen did before he played.

"There was a man who built a house with a big strong door," she said. "Every night his little girl put a lamp in the window, because he worked late. One night the King came to bring the family to the big supper at His house. And the little girl went, and she was so happy, because her mommy was already there." She stopped, and thought, and nodded to herself. "But she left her lamp in the window. And she left her shoes by the door."

Ezra smiled. "Why'd she leave her shoes, baby?"

"So he'd know which way she went." She yawned, an enormous yawn that took over her whole face. "The door stays open a little while after." She leaned her head on his arm. "The End. Leave the light on, Daddy."

Ezra kissed the top of her head. Her hair smelled like the strawberry shampoo Angela used to buy. He sat with her for a minute, with the television murmuring, and for once he did not reach for the phone. Then he picked her up, and she let him carry her to the foot of the stairs.

"Wait," she said. "Put me down. I have to do the shoes."

He set her down. She went back for the shoe on the living room floor, and picked up the other one, and carried them both to the front door. She set them side by side on the mat with the toes pointed outward, and squared them with both hands. Then she went to the light switch and stood on her toes and turned on the porch light.

"So you can find the door," she said.

He took the shoes as part of the story and did not ask. He carried her up to bed and tucked the blanket around her and turned on the nightlight that threw paper stars on the ceiling, and she was asleep before he reached the door.

\* \* \*

**Wednesday, 10:05 p.m.**

Jalen, home from the dorm for the long weekend, was in the studio when his father's truck started.

He heard it through the window, over the cello, and stopped in the middle of a phrase with the bow resting on the string. He set the cello against its stand and went to the studio door and stood in it, in his socks, in the cold, and watched the headlights back down the driveway.

He knew where his father was going. He had known for months. He had seen the small silver car at the curb, and the texts that lit up the phone on the counter and were turned face down. He had smelled the perfume on his father's jacket in the laundry room. He had not said anything since the night in the studio, the night of the recital, when they had both ended up on the floor. His father came to dinner now. He asked about the orchestra. He had said, himself, that Miss Kambria could come for Thanksgiving.

But he still left, late, on the nights he thought no one was watching.

The truck turned the corner and was gone. Jalen stood in the studio doorway a little longer, looking at the porch light his sister had turned on. Then he went back inside, and sat down, and played the piece one more time, the whole thing, from the low C to the high G at the end, alone in the room they had built.

When he was done, he took a thumb drive out of the pocket of his hoodie.

He had made it seven months ago, on the night of the recital. Two files: the video he had made at eleven, the summer they finished the studio, and the recital itself, the one his father had missed. He had carried it in his pocket ever since, waiting for a night when his father would sit down and listen. Tonight he had thought, for a minute, at dinner, watching his father laugh at something Mia said, that it might be the night.

It was not the night. But tomorrow was Thanksgiving. And Miss Kambria would be at the table. And his father had said she could come, which was more than he had said in a year.

Jalen tore a strip of masking tape off the roll on the workbench and pressed it across the drive, and took a black marker out of the coffee can of pens, and wrote on the tape in small block letters.

*For Dad, now that you're ready.*

He went into the house. The hall was dark except for the porch light coming in through the glass beside the front door, and his mother's shoes standing on the mat. He eased the hall closet open and moved the winter coats aside. On the shelf behind them, behind a box of Christmas lights, was a black notebook. He had known it was there since the week of the funeral. Everybody in the house knew where it was, though nobody talked about it.

He set the thumb drive on top of the notebook, right in the center, where no one could pick up one without the other. Then he closed the closet and went to bed.

He set his alarm for six, so he could be up before Grandma got there with the turkey.

\* \* \*

**Thursday, 1:52 a.m.**

Ezra came home with the windows down so the cold would wake him up.

The porch light was still on. He saw it from the corner, and his stomach turned. He parked and sat in the truck a minute with the engine ticking. Then he went in by the side door, as he always did on the nights he knew he should not have gone, and kept his eyes off the front hall.

He poured two fingers of whiskey in the kitchen and took it to the couch and sat down to take off his boots. He got one off. He turned the television on low, because the house was too quiet without it. Celeste's perfume was on his collar. He could smell it every time he turned his head.

He told himself he would go up in a minute.

He was asleep before he finished the glass.

\* \* \*

**Thursday, a little before six**

Loretta Patterson knelt beside her bed every morning at five o'clock, and she had done it for twenty years, and her knees told her so.

She lived alone in the white frame house on Old Ferry Road where she had raised Ezra, a mile up the gravel from the church where she had married Calvin and held his funeral. The radiator ticked. Through the window she could see the dark fields across the road and, beyond them, the black line of the river. In two hours her neighbor's son would come over and help her carry the turkey down to his car, and drive her in past the District line to her son's house for Thanksgiving. She had made the dressing last night. It was in the refrigerator in her good blue bowl, covered in foil.

The rolls were rising on the counter under a damp towel, the way they did every Thursday and every Sunday, and the whole kitchen smelled of yeast and butter. She had never written the recipe down. She had been thinking lately that she ought to teach it to Mia, standing on a chair at her elbow with flour to the wrists, and that she would start at Christmas.

She had her Bible open on the bed in front of her and her reading glasses on her nose, and she was praying for Ezra.

She always prayed for Ezra first. For twenty years she had started there, before her own needs, before anyone else's. Some mornings she had prayed with tears. Some mornings she had prayed with nothing left in her but the words. This morning her prayer was light, and she could not have said why.

He had said Kambria could come. He had said it himself.

"Lord," Loretta said, out loud, because she always prayed out loud, in her empty bedroom, to the One who was always in it. "You know my boy. You knew him before I did. You know where he was last night, and You know where he's going." She took off her glasses and pressed her eyes with her fingers. "I'm not asking You to make him good. I'm asking You to wake him up. Whatever it takes. Wake him up, Lord. Don't let him sleep through it."

She stayed on her knees a while longer, listening, as she always did after she prayed. The radiator ticked. A car passed on the gravel below.

Then she reached for the edge of the bed, to push herself up, and stopped.

There was a sound. It was very far away, or very low, she could not tell which. It seemed to be coming up through the floor.

Loretta Patterson lifted her face toward the window, and the dark sky beyond it, and smiled.

"There You are, Jesus," she said.

\* \* \*

**Thursday, a little before six**

In a fourth-floor walk-up on Carroll Street in Brooklyn, Sarah Bennett stood in her kitchen in her bathrobe, warming a bottle of milk in a pan of water on the stove, half asleep, and heard the baby monitor on the counter go silent.

It was the silence she noticed, afterward. Lily had been fussing for ten minutes, the thin, building cry of a seven-month-old who is hungry and has decided the world should know it. Sarah had been listening to it with one ear while she tested the milk on her wrist. Then the cry stopped, in the middle, as if someone had picked her up.

"Kyle?" she called. "I've got it. Go back to sleep."

Then the windows began to hum.

She would try to describe it later, and never could. She would say it was like a ship's horn, like the shofar a friend had blown once at a wedding, but bigger than anything, bigger than the city, and coming from above and below at the same time. The pan rattled on the burner. The bottle tipped over in the water. Then the kitchen window blew in, all of it at once, and the glass came across the counter like thrown sand. Every car alarm on the block went off together. Out in the street a garbage truck stopped dead and its driver climbed down and stood in the middle of Carroll Street with his hands over his ears, looking up.

Kyle came out of the bedroom in his boxers with his face white. "What is that? Sarah, what is that?"

She was already running.

The crib was in the corner of their bedroom, under the window, with the mobile of paper birds over it that Sarah had made from a pattern she found online. The birds were wheeling in the gold light that had begun to pour through the window, though it was not yet six and there should have been no light at all.

The crib was empty.

Lily's pajamas lay on the sheet, the green ones with the little foxes, still zipped up, still holding the small round shape of her. Sarah put her hand on them. They were warm. The pacifier lay beside them on the sheet, still wet.

She did not scream. Not yet. She stood with her hand on the warm green pajamas, not making a sound, and behind her Kyle was saying her name over and over, and outside, over the whole city of New York, the horn went on, and on, and then it stopped.

Then nothing at all. Then it was not silence. Down the block a woman was screaming a name. Farther off, toward the river, something heavy had come down, and the smoke from it was already standing up over the rooftops, black against the gold.

Kyle's mother had said it every Thanksgiving until they stopped going: when Jesus comes for His own, the babies go with Him. Sarah stood with her hand on the warm pajamas and knew.

\* \* \*

**Thursday, a little before six**

The man who kept the grass at the cemetery behind Mount Zion Christian Center on Rhode Island Avenue was named Leon Fuller, and he was the only living soul who saw it happen there.

He had come in early to unlock the gates, because the families came on holidays and he liked them to find the paths swept. He was halfway down the center path with his push broom when the ground began to shake under his boots. He thought it was an earthquake. He had been in one once, in California, as a young man in the Navy. He dropped the broom and grabbed the nearest headstone with both hands.

Then the horn came, and the light came, and a wind with no direction came with them and threw him flat across a grave. Behind him every window in the church blew in at once. He lay with his cheek on the cold grass and his hands over his head, and Leon Fuller saw the earth open.

It did not explode. That was what he would tell the reporter from the *Post* three days later, sitting in his kitchen with his hands around a cup of coffee he could not drink. It opened gently, all over the cemetery at once. The grass split, and the soil folded back on itself, and he heard the sound of stone shifting under the ground, and of tearing, and then the light coming out of the graves was the same light coming down out of the sky, and he could not look at it.

When he could see again, the horn had stopped, and the cemetery was quiet, and there were holes in the ground.

Not all of the graves. Perhaps a third of them. They were scattered all through the old rows and the new, an open grave here and an untouched one beside it, as though someone had walked through with a list. The headstones were still standing. The earth was heaped neatly around each hole. And every one of the holes was empty, down to the broken boards of the coffin lids.

Leon Fuller walked the rows for an hour with his broom in his hand, reading the names. Most of them he knew. He had mowed around them for twenty-two years. Near the back fence, under a young dogwood that had been planted a year ago, he stopped beside a granite stone that was still new enough to shine.

*ANGELA PATTERSON. Beloved wife and mother. "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."*

The ground in front of it was open. The coffin was empty. Lying on the white satin, where her head had been, was the purple headwrap she had been buried in.

Leon sat down on the edge of the grass. He had heard it preached from that pulpit for twenty-two years, *the dead in Christ shall rise first*, and he had mowed around it every week. Jesus had come, and the graves had answered Him.

\* \* \*

**Thursday, a little before six**

Walt Simmons had been up since five, as he was every morning.

He was sitting at his dinner table across the street from Ezra Patterson's house, in his cardigan and his slippers, with his coffee and the three newspapers laid out in order and the small black Bible open beside the *Post*. The blue concordance sat on the shelf over the sink, next to the other blue concordance, exactly as Kambria had told him. He had looked at it a dozen times since she dropped him off. He had not touched it.

He was reading the Dubai story on the front page of the *Post*, with the red pen going in the margin, when his coffee cup began to rattle on the saucer.

Walt put down the pen.

He knew what it was before the sound reached the air. He had known what it would be for most of his life. He had read about it in Paul's letters and in Matthew and in Revelation. He sat straight in his chair with both hands on the table, and the sound came up out of the ground and into the sky and filled his kitchen and his chest and the whole world, and the light came through his window over the sink, gold, from every direction at once.

He stood up. He did not use his cane. He stood up beside the dinner table and lifted his face toward the window and closed his eyes.

He waited.

The horn went on. It shook his teeth and the bones of his face. The window over the sink cracked across with a sound like river ice, and out on the street glass was coming down in sheets. The light lay warm on his eyelids. He stood in his slippers on the linoleum and waited to be lifted, as the book said, as Kambria had told it at his table a hundred times. *Caught up together with them in the clouds.* He waited for his feet to leave the floor.

The horn rose, and held, and rose again.

And then it stopped.

Silence came down over the house. No furnace. No refrigerator. Not one bird. Then, under the silence, car alarms all over the neighborhood, thin and far off and endless. Somewhere very far off, to the south, he heard a plane, too low, and then a sound like a door slamming a mile away.

Walt opened his eyes.
