He was standing in his kitchen. His coffee had spilled across the *Post* and soaked into the Dubai story. His cane was hooked over the back of his chair where he had left it. His slippers were on the linoleum, and his feet were in them.

He turned his hands over.

Then he looked out the window, across the street, at Ezra Patterson's house, where the porch light was still burning over the front steps in the dark, and where, a few minutes later, from somewhere behind the house, in the backyard, a man's voice began shouting his children's names into the sky.

It had been Jesus. He had come for His own, exactly as He said He would, and Walt Simmons was still here.

\* \* \*

**Thursday, 7:14 a.m.**

The night guard on Sublevel 3 found the cell at the shift check, and he did not call it in for six minutes.

He stood in the corridor with the clipboard hanging from his hand and looked through the slot in the door of Holding B. Then he unlocked it and went in, because he could not make himself believe what the slot showed him, and stood on the cold concrete where she had sat.

The bench. The ring in the floor. The chain from the ring ran under the bench and up, in a slack gray loop, to the cuffs.

The cuffs were locked.

That was what he could not get past. Both wrist cuffs still closed, the little teeth set in the ratchet exactly as he had set them himself at two in the morning, the steel still closed around the space where two wrists had been. The ankle cuffs, the same. Both pairs lay on the bench like something dropped there in the instant it was used. Beside them lay a gray nightgown, folded in the shape of a woman who had been sitting, with the sleeves still half-raised.

The door had been bolted from the outside. Two bolts. He had thrown them.

Down the corridor a second guard started shouting. Then a third. Then the whole sublevel was shouting, and he heard a man at the far end of the hall begin to pray in Spanish, and somebody else vomit, and the older officer who had been on the arrest team came pounding down the stairs and stopped in the door of Holding B with his mask pushed up.

He looked at the cuffs for a long time.

"That's the lamp lady," he said. His voice cracked. "That's the one with the lamp." He wiped his mouth. "She told us in the van. She said Jesus was coming."

---

The Director arrived at 7:31, by her own key.

Celeste Moore came down the stairs with her hair unpinned and last night's makeup smeared and a coat thrown over the clothes she had put on in the dark. She had been awake for twenty-six hours. She had gotten the call from the sublevel on the drive in, and she had told the voice on the phone that it was impossible, and she had said it again at the checkpoint, and she was saying it now, under her breath, as she stopped in front of Holding B.

She looked at the locked cuffs.

She did not say it was impossible again.

"Get me Vale," she said.

It took four minutes to raise him. The monitor on the corridor wall cleared to a view of a hotel suite, pale gold, the window behind him cracked from corner to corner, full of Dubai and a sky the color of brass, with smoke going up somewhere off to the left. Vale was in his shirtsleeves. A glass of water stood on the table at his elbow. His face was perfectly still, and his eyes were on the cell behind her before she could say a word.

"Show me," he said.

She stepped aside. A technician turned a tablet to the screen. Vale watched the footage from Holding B at 5:55 and 5:56 that morning, once, and then said, "Again." Then, "Slow."

She was sitting on the bench with her head bowed and her chained hands in her lap. At 5:56:11 she lifted her face, looking up at something the camera could not see. She smiled. Her lips moved. The light on her face went gold. The cuffs dropped, empty, onto the steel.

He watched it a third time.

"Seven of the eleven cells," the guard said from the doorway, hoarsely. "Same thing. Every one of the ones we picked up this month. The ones from the churches."

"I understand you, Officer." Vale did not raise his voice. He had not raised it once. "Nobody enters this sublevel. Nobody leaves it. Not you, not the day shift, not the Director. Seal the stairwell and remove the badge readers." He looked at the tablet again, at the cuffs falling, empty, onto the steel. "This is not a security breach."

"Alexander," Celeste said.

"No." He lifted one hand. "It is a confirmation." Something finally showed in his face. "Everything we planned for assumed this would not happen. It has happened. It will not wait for us to finish." He turned the glass a quarter turn. "I have nine days of work and I have the Chairman asking me for an account of this morning. I cannot afford the Chairman learning that his Director of Special Operations stood where you are standing, and watched what you watched, and understands it."

Something in Celeste's face gave way.

"You filed under your own name," Vale said gently. "You locked her out of the system. You sat in that room in Baltimore and read the Petworth files. You have followed this woman for three months, and this morning you stood in front of a locked cell that emptied itself, and you know what it means. I saw your face. You know it better than I do." He spoke to the technician, without looking away from her. "Is the intake chamber on this level still sealed?"

"Holding B is the intake chamber, sir."

"Of course it is."

Celeste took a step back. "Alexander. I built this. I got you the Petworth lot. I got you in the door at the Centers for Disease Control. I am the only person in this country who—"

"Yes."

"I haven't said a word! I would never—"

"I know." His voice was almost kind. "That is the difficulty. You would not. And in a week you will be unable to stop." He nodded to the guards. "I'm sorry, Celeste."

They took her by the arms. She fought them. She was stronger than they expected, and for a few seconds she got an elbow free and caught one of them across the mouth, and the corridor filled with the sound of her voice, high and raw, calling Ezra's name and then another name and then nothing. They dragged her across the threshold of Holding B. The older officer who had spared the lamp turned his face to the wall.

The cuffs were still locked. The technician had to key them open to seat her.

They closed on her wrists with a click. They closed on her ankles. The chain ran taut from the ring in the floor under the bench.

"Don't," Celeste said. She had gone very quiet. She was looking up, at the grille above the drain, and the flat nozzle behind it. "Alexander. Please. It isn't ready. You said it wasn't ready."

"It was never going to be," Vale said from the screen. "That is why I need to know that it works."

He nodded.

The door shut. Two bolts. A third was thrown from the corridor, and a red lamp came on in the frame.

In the control booth, the technician pressed a key under a taped label that read, in block capitals, **PALEHORSE LOT 3**.

Through the slot in the door, the nozzle opened. It made a sound like a kettle.

Celeste Moore screamed once.

On the monitor, in a hotel suite in Dubai, Alexander Vale turned off the sound. He watched the picture for ninety seconds, as a man watches a gauge, until the vapor had taken the camera. Then he picked up his glass of water and drank.

"Log it as a decontamination test," he said. "Date it Wednesday."


## Chapter 21: Perplexity

> *And there shall be signs in the sun, and in the moon, and in the stars; and upon the earth distress of nations, with perplexity; the sea and the waves roaring; Men's hearts failing them for fear, and for looking after those things which are coming on the earth: for the powers of heaven shall be shaken.* — Jesus, Luke 21:25–26

**Word study: *perplexity* — ἀπορία** Greek *aporia* (Strong's G640). Literally, *no way through*: the place where the road runs out. Jesus used it for the nations on the day the world loses its way and every expert in it stands at the edge of the road with nowhere left to go.

*And Moses stretched forth his hand toward heaven; and there was a thick darkness in all the land of Egypt three days: They saw not one another, neither rose any from his place for three days: but all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings.* (Exodus 10:22–23)

\* \* \*

Nina woke at noon in the airport dress with the recital still looping on the phone beside her head. She shut it off in the middle of the climb.

*MENE. MENE. TEKEL. UPHARSIN.*

By daylight the letters on the mirror seemed like steam and a long night. She showered, packed, and read Kroll's text from nine: *Car at 1:30. Think about it on the plane. S.* She did not answer it.

\* \* \*

Gate A9 at Dubai International sat under a glass roof high enough to grow olive trees in marble planters. Trent Walker was slumped in a seat there in borrowed tuxedo trousers, his bow tie stuffed in a pocket.

"Connecting to Dulles," he said, before she could ask. "I sat on my balcony all night smoking, and I quit sixteen years ago. Called my mother before dawn, her time. She didn't pick up." He turned his phone over in his hand. "She always picks up."

Nina took the seat two down from him. The board said *ON TIME*. Out on the apron a double-decker jet with the Emirates flag on its tail was swinging toward the runway. It was two-fifty-five.

"Whatever kept you up," Trent said, "will you say it out loud first? So I'm not the only one?"

She was still choosing her words when the glass began to hum.

\* \* \*

The water bottle shivered in her fist. A paper cup on the next seat crept to the edge and dropped. Then the sky outside went white, a flash with no cloud behind it, and the sound came down on the terminal: a trumpet and a thunderclap welded into one blow. The roof over the olive trees burst. The long window wall came in, in sheets.

Through the hole where the glass had been, the sky turned gold from every direction at once. The sun still hung small and white in the west, and the shadows under the parked jets thinned to nothing.

Trent had been standing at the window. He was on his back in the glass now, staring at his palms, which were full of splinters and running red. "Mama," he said. "No. Mama."

The double-decker jet never reached the runway. It rolled across the grass into the sand and stopped nose-down with its engines still screaming, and no one climbed out. Behind it a plane on final approach, wheels down, a hundred feet up, simply stopped being flown. It caught a wingtip on the concrete and went over, and the fuel lit in one long orange bloom that Nina felt through the floor a heartbeat after she saw it.

The sound quit. The glass kept falling.

Then the ground took its turn: a long roll out of the desert, and a jolt that dropped everyone still standing. Ceiling panels came down. The runway lights bent like reeds. The same shock was running under Tokyo and Lima and Lisbon. Jesus had named it on the Mount of Olives: *and there shall be famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places. All these are the beginning of sorrows.* (Matthew 24:7–8)

\* \* \*

Nina kept the next hour as a stack of pictures with the sound gone. A woman in one shoe, calling a name down the concourse. A flight attendant riding the moving walkway past the olive trees with an empty pram in front of her. A gate agent at A11 saying into her phone, in Arabic and then in English, *The captain does not answer.* A man's suit, tie and shoes laid out flat on the marble as if for the morning, a wristwatch on top, still ticking.

Trent, with his back to what was left of the window, dialing his mother and listening to it ring.

Nina did not dial. As long as she did not press her grandmother's name, it had not happened. Past the broken wall, empty cars sat with their doors open across all six lanes of the airport road. Smoke stood up over the city in one column, then a second, then a third. She thought of the gold letters crawling up the tower where she had slept. *ONE WORLD. ONE ACCOUNT. NO MORE WANT.*

*In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain.*

She pressed the name.

Eight rings, and then her grandmother, recorded at some church picnic, too loud, the way she always was with machines: *"Hey, now, this is Bernice Cole! I'm out doing the Lord's work, or I'm taking a nap. One of the two. Leave me a message, and God bless you. And Nina, if that's you, baby, eat something!"* A laugh, and someone off to the side hollering about the potato salad.

Nina called again. And again. On the twelfth try she let it play to the end, so that for ten seconds, in the middle of all that screaming, somebody was laughing in her ear. Then the phone slid off her lap, and she bent over her knees at Gate A9 and cried the way she had not cried since she was small.

\* \* \*

The world did not end that day. It cracked, everywhere at once.

Harbors in Chittagong and Valparaíso drained to mud and then filled again as a wall. Planes with empty cockpits fell, and some with their pilots still in them, because the blast had blown out windscreens at thirty thousand feet. Driverless cars rolled through red lights in Mumbai and Los Angeles. A cardiologist in Chicago started counting the cardiac arrests from the first six hours and gave it up. Men had sat down on curbs and never stood again.

In the maternity wards the cribs were empty, row on row, little blankets folded over nothing. All the children were gone. For two days nobody could say it, and after that nobody could stop. Not some of them. All of them, in every nation, of every faith and none.

And the believers were gone. Not everyone who had worn the name. The ones who had known Him. Nina's grandmother. Trent's mother. A scientist in a locked federal cell. A young cellist who had played a song with no name for someone who wasn't there.

By Friday the internet was a trickle through the satellites still up. By Friday night most of those were coming down too, long white streaks across the desert sky three nights running, and the only ones still talking were Salazar's, built to ride out a solar storm and tied to ground stations under the Greenland ice. Nina watched them fall from the roof of the airport hotel, where the stranded had been herded, beside Trent, who had said almost nothing since the gate.

"My mother read me a verse about the stars falling," he said at last. "I told her it was the dumbest thing I ever heard." Nina knew they were satellites. She let him keep the verse.

"What happened to them, Trent?"

"He came for them." He wiped his face with his bandaged hand. "Just like she said. Just like everybody said for two thousand years. And we're the ones still here."

\* \* \*

By Saturday the world had its explanations, and one channel to hear them on: the Organization for World Peace, broadcasting from Geneva on Salazar's satellites in nine languages. In the hotel lobby a London psychologist told three hundred stranded travelers that the missing had been removed "by an intelligence that is not of this world."

"First true thing anybody's said on TV all week," Trent muttered, and walked out.

Then Adrian Crowe came on, from a plain room with a gray wall and no flags.

"I will not tell you that I understand what happened on Thursday," he said. "Anyone who tells you they do is lying to you, or selling you something. But I know that the world did not end. I know that you are alive, and so am I."

The International Collective, he said, had argued for six hours and voted on nothing. The Organization had not argued. At the request of the High Council of the Technate, and with the consent of forty-one nations, it had taken emergency charge of food, fuel and medicine.

"And this morning, in Jerusalem, the covenant was signed."

The framework the Council had begun in November was finished, he said. The ten of the High Council had put their names to it before dawn, then the government of Israel, then the nations of the Collective, one after another, all morning. Seven years of peace. Israel's borders under the Organization's guard. The mountain in Jerusalem opened to every man and woman and child, and the Jews free to build there, and to offer there.

"Seven years," Crowe said. "Count them with me."

"I am asking for one thing. Order. Not obedience. Order. Register at the nearest distribution point when it opens. Your hand is your account, and your account will feed you." His voice dropped. "Peace. Order. Safety. That is my promise to you."

The lobby applauded, a few hands and then all of them. Nina kept hers at her sides. In the last second before the picture changed, she saw a thin hand in a gray sleeve resting on the back of Crowe's chair, a red string knotted at the wrist.

\* \* \*

On the far side of the world, in a county north of Baltimore, a man named Michael was taking his house apart.

The radio was still clipped to his belt, the old Army handheld he had carried home from the Gulf and never turned in, still set to the county band from his years with a badge. It had not been quiet in three days: unit numbers, addresses, *any available unit*, a dispatcher's voice going hoarse and then gone, a stranger's voice in its place. Michael had not keyed it once. On Thursday he had searched every room in the house, and the attic, and the crawl space, and the woods behind the yard with a flashlight until the batteries died. On Friday he searched them all again. On Saturday he went back up with a pry bar and started pulling up the closet floor in Daniel's room, as if a twelve-year-old could have fit under the boards.

There was nothing under the boards. He stood in the boy's room with the bar in his hand, and the radio said *any available unit*, and he swung the bar through the drywall beside the door. Then his fist. Then his fist again, and again, until plaster dust hung in the beam of the flashlight and his knuckles had left their blood on the stud.

He wrapped the hand in one of Daniel's T-shirts because it was the nearest thing. He left the hole the way it was. He reached down and turned the radio off.

On the nightstand, by the boy's reading lamp, lay the cross Daniel had worn since his baptism, small and silver on a steel chain, with the clasp Michael kept promising to fix. The boy took it off to sleep. Michael picked it up and pinched the clasp shut with his good hand, and put it over his own head, and let it hang outside his shirt.

Daniel's backpack hung on its hook by the door, the pencil case still unzipped. The tablet was in the front pocket. Michael carried it past his father's empty chair at the top of the basement stairs, the reading glasses still folded on its arm, and sat on the bottom step in the dark. It woke in his good hand on a paused video: a kid in a white suit, a cello, a high school stage. *Untitled.*

He pulled the sheet off the mixing board his father had built the winter he turned nine, plugged the tablet in, brought up the faders, and pressed play.

The cello filled the cinder-block room, a line that climbed and held and fell like somebody trying to say what he couldn't. Daniel had kept this open in the dark of his room and never mentioned it. Michael had never asked what the boy listened to. Most nights he was out the door before the boy went to bed.

Then his ears did what thirty years had trained them to do, and he listened past the cello. A big hall, half its seats soaking up the low end. A phone held by somebody in the third row, close enough to catch a breath at the top of every phrase. At the dedication the picture swung down toward an empty seat and came back up, and after that the hand holding it never moved again until the last note died.

Somebody loved that boy, Michael thought.

His face was wet. He wrote *Untitled* on a scrap in his father's square capitals and folded it into his wallet, and that night, for the first time since the twenty-sixth, he slept in his own bed.

\* \* \*

On Monday a man in a dark suit found Nina on the hotel roof at dawn. Mr. Kroll had arranged a plane. Mr. Vale had approved it. There were two seats.

"Two?"

"For you and Mr. Walker."

The jet had the Organization's gold circle on its tail and fourteen passengers aboard. Trent took the last row and watched the ocean the whole way. Somewhere over the Atlantic, the thin man in the gray suit came back from the front cabin and sat down across the table from Nina.

Alexander Vale was younger up close than she had guessed, mid-forties, narrow and pale, with black, unreadable eyes. He set down a glass of water he did not drink. The red string showed under his cuff.

"Dr. Cole. I am sorry for your loss."

"How do you know I lost anyone?"

"Everyone lost someone." He gave the glass a quarter turn. "Sebastian made you an offer on Wednesday. Before Thursday it was a project. Now it is a necessity. Frightened people need a voice they can trust. A voice that does not panic and does not lie and does not die. You know better than anyone alive what can be built now. I would like you to build it."

"Whose voice?"

Vale only smiled. "You saw how they listened on Saturday." He stood and buttoned his jacket. "Take a week. Your grandmother's building in Baltimore is still standing. I made sure of it. Go and see her apartment before you decide."

Nina had never told anyone at the company where her grandmother lived. When she turned around, Trent was watching from the back row. He shook his head, once.

\* \* \*

She took the train to Baltimore on Wednesday. Soldiers in Organization armbands stood on every platform. Every lamppost on Druid Hill Avenue wore a taped sheet, *HAVE YOU SEEN*, a photo, a name. She climbed four flights because the elevator was dead and let herself in with a key she had carried since college and never used.

The apartment smelled of burnt sugar. The sweet potatoes had boiled dry and scorched black in the big dented pot; a neighbor had turned the burner off. On the table, beside a cup of coffee gone to scum, lay the black Bible and the reading glasses. The house slippers waited side by side under the chair. The cardigan hung over its back, one sleeve still pushed up to the elbow, the way Bernice wore it to wash dishes.

The coffee-can robot stood on the bookshelf next to Nina's father in his Army uniform: a Maxwell House can, bottle-cap eyes, pipe-cleaner arms, a battery pack held on with electrical tape. She took it down. It weighed almost nothing.

She sat in her grandmother's chair. The Bible lay open to Joel, one verse underlined twice in blue, a date in the margin in that shaky hand: *For Nina. 11/25.* The day Nina had called from Dubai.

*And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered.*

She sat there until the window went dark.

\* \* \*

With one bar of signal and nine percent battery, she opened the recital, because it was the last sound she had heard before the horn.

*2,114,806,331 views.*

Two billion, in six days. The comments came in Korean and Arabic and Portuguese faster than the screen could load them. The English ones said the same things. *The cellist is gone. I played this the night it happened and couldn't stop. I don't know why this is the only thing that helps.* And in every language, one question: *Who was it for?*

On the screen the boy leaned into the microphone, and the camera wandered down to the third row, to an aisle seat with a program lying on it. Nina had watched the video thirty times and never noticed the program. She brought the dim screen up to her face. Across the top, in black marker: *DAD.*

"Juno," she said. "The cellist in the *Untitled* video. Who is his father?"

"Searching," said the warm, unhurried voice. "The performer has been identified as Jalen Patterson, eighteen, of Washington, D.C., reported missing on November twenty-sixth. His mother, Angela Patterson, died a year ago. Public records list his father as Ezra Patterson, of Northeast Washington."

The name had been said to her before. Trent, at the gala, with a drink in his hand: *I apprenticed under a carpenter in Northeast for six years. Best carpenter in DC. Ezra Patterson. Never heard of him, I bet.*

"Is he alive? Is Ezra Patterson on any list?"

"He is not listed among the missing."

The screen went black; the battery was gone. Nina sat in her grandmother's dark kitchen with the robot in her lap, and knew that the father the whole world was asking about was still here.

## Act 7 — The Way of Escape

## Chapter 22: The Hall Closet

> *And Hilkiah the high priest said unto Shaphan the scribe, I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD. And Hilkiah gave the book to Shaphan, and he read it.* — 2 Kings 22:8

**Word study: *found* — מָצָא** Hebrew *matsa* (Strong's H4672). To find, to come upon, to lay hold of what was there all along. It is the word for stumbling on something you were not looking for, and the word God uses in Jeremiah: *…ye shall seek me, and find me, when ye shall search for me with all your heart.* (Jeremiah 29:13)

*And it came to pass, when the king had heard the words of the book of the law, that he rent his clothes.* (2 Kings 22:11)

\* \* \*

For two days Ezra Patterson drove around the city looking for one reason it was not true.

On Thursday he drove. He left the house early in the morning with his boots on the wrong feet and drove out to his mother's house in Cedar Hollow, running red lights that no longer mattered because half the signals in the city had gone dark. The front door of the frame house was unlocked. He called her name up the stairs. He found her bedroom door open and her Bible lying open on the bed, and her reading glasses on the floor beside it, and a dent in the carpet where her knees had been. Her nightgown lay on the floor at the edge of the bed, as though she had been kneeling in it and had simply stood up out of it. In the refrigerator, in her good blue bowl, covered with foil, was the dressing she had made for Thanksgiving.

He stood in her kitchen and held the bowl in both hands with no plan for it. He set it back in the refrigerator and shut the door on it.

On the counter, under a damp dish towel, a pan of dough had risen over the rim and sat there unbaked. The kitchen still smelled of yeast and butter. He lifted a corner of the towel and pressed his thumb into the dough, and it did not spring back. For forty years the church mothers had begged her for that recipe, and she had never given it to anyone. Now the only hands that knew it had been called up out of this kitchen in the middle of the rising, and the dough would go on sitting there, a little more sour each hour, until there was no one left to bake it. Ezra stood with the towel in his fingers and found that he was crying over bread.

He drove past Mia's school. It would have been shut for Thanksgiving anyway; he drove past it because for two years he had driven her there every morning, and his hands knew the turns. A police cruiser sat across the front walk. The young officer leaning on its fender did not straighten up when the truck slowed; there was nothing inside to guard. Ezra had known that before he turned onto the street. The radio had been saying it since noon: not one child, not in the building, not in the city, not anywhere anyone could reach. He had heard Angela say it years ago at the kitchen table, reading from the Book, and he had heard Kambria say it on his porch with tears on her face. He drove past anyway, slowly, and didn't stop.

On Rhode Island Avenue the line outside the police station ran down the block, two hundred people holding photographs, and at the end of it a woman stood with an empty car seat in her arms. Ezra did not get out of the truck. He knew what the sergeant at the desk would write on his legal pad, and he knew that no one would call.

On Friday he drove to the hospitals.

He could not have said why. The radio said the injured were being taken everywhere and no one knew who was where, and some small part of him that would not lie down said that a hospital was a place where people turned up. He walked the halls of emergency departments where the floors were sticky with blood and the beds were lined up in the corridors: a bus driver with his arm in a splint, an old man staring at the ceiling tiles, a woman still in her airline uniform with a cut over one eye. Every bed held a grown man or a grown woman. He had known that, too, before he came.

At the big hospital in Northeast, the one where Kambria's team had worked the flu wards, a nurse with her hair coming out of its clip took his arm in the hallway. "Sir," she said, "are you looking for somebody?"

He opened his mouth to say yes, and heard how it would sound, and said nothing.

She studied his face. "Honey," she said, quieter, "go home. Whoever you're thinking of, they're not in here." She squeezed his arm once and went on down the hall.

He went back out to the parking lot. He was crossing it to his truck when a voice behind him said, low and fast, "Mr. Patterson?"

A woman in a hospital lanyard stood by the ambulance bay with her arms folded tight over her chest. Mid-thirties, scrubs under a puffy coat, a federal liaison badge turned backward so the photograph faced her ribs. He knew her face. She had stood at the back of Kambria's flu-ward briefings last winter, taking notes.

"You're looking for Dr. Whitfield," she said.

His heart kicked. "Do you know where she is?"

"No." She glanced at the building, at the glass doors, at a gray car idling at the curb with a man in it who was not looking at them. "Her badge died last Friday. Her logins, everything. Then Thursday morning, early, before any of this, two men came to my desk asking when she'd last been on this floor." She glanced at the door. "Then it happened, and nobody asked me anything after that, and I thought you should know someone was looking for her."

"Who?"

"They didn't say." She was already backing away. "Mr. Patterson, I didn't tell you this. I'm sorry about your kids."

She turned and walked quickly back through the ambulance doors. The gray car at the curb pulled out without a hurry and turned left on the avenue.

He stood alone in the lot with the cold coming up through his boots.

*If you're hearing this and I don't call you back, it already happened.* Her voice on his phone on Thursday morning, on the kitchen floor. He had told himself for two days that it was coincidence: a woman who had studied the end of the world for years and had finally gotten unlucky. He had told himself she was in some emergency room under a wrong name, or wandering a stairwell in shock. He had told himself a great many things.

Not one of them had included two men at a desk before dawn, asking when.

He did not go back to the hospitals.

\* \* \*

On Friday the power went out.

It went out at a little after two in the afternoon, all at once, across the whole of Northeast, and stayed out. The refrigerator shuddered and stopped. The furnace died. The television, which had been running the Organization's emergency broadcast for two days without stopping, went black in the middle of a sentence, and the silence it left was so complete that Ezra could hear the clock on the kitchen wall, a battery clock Angela had bought at a yard sale, ticking.

He sat on the couch and listened to it.

The porch light was out. Mia's porch light, that had burned every night since the summer. It had been burning on Thursday morning when he came out of the house, in broad daylight, and he had left it burning; he could not make himself switch it off. Now it had gone dark on its own.

And at the front door, on the mat, his wife's black Sunday shoes stood side by side with the toes pointed out.

He had seen them on Thursday morning, on his way out to the truck. He had stopped and stared at them and then stepped around them, because he did not understand, and because there was no time, and because if he picked them up and put them away he would have to think about why they were there. He had stepped around them every time he went in or out since. He could not touch them.

Mia's voice came back to him, sleepy against his arm the night before the trumpet: *She left her shoes by the door.*

And his own, not really listening: *Why'd she leave her shoes, baby?*

And Mia again, through a yawn: *So he'd know which way she went.*

He got up from the couch and went to the front door and knelt down on the mat in front of the shoes.

They were scuffed at the toes. The left heel was worn down further than the right, because Angela had always stood with her weight on her left foot when she was tired, at the stove, at the sink, at the hospital bedside. He had never noticed that until now. He put out his hand and almost touched them, and then did not, and stayed on his knees on the mat until his legs went numb.

*The door stays open a little while after.* Mia had said that too, with her head on his arm, right before she told him to leave the light on.

He did not know what that meant. He was certain it meant something, and the certainty frightened him more than anything that had happened since Thursday.

\* \* \*

Walt came across the street at dusk.

Ezra heard the cane on the porch steps before the knock, the slow thump and scrape of an old man taking one step at a time. He thought about not answering. He had kept the door shut to everyone since Thursday. Mrs. Okafor next door had knocked twice on Thursday night, crying, and he had stood in the dark hall until she went away. But the knock came again, and then Walt's voice through the wood, rough and cracked.

"Ezra. I know you're in there. I can see your truck."

Ezra opened the door.

Walt was wearing his brown suit jacket over his cardigan, buttoned wrong, and no cap, and his thin gray hair was standing up on one side. His eyes were red. He was holding a grocery bag tight against his chest with his free arm.

They stood and looked at each other in the dusk.

"You're still here," Ezra said finally.

"I'm still here." Walt's voice broke on it. "Fifty years, Ezra. Fifty years I read that book. I could quote you every word. Every sign, every chapter, every verse she ever wrote on her wall. I knew it better than the preachers. I knew it better than her." He was shaking. "And I'm still here."

Ezra had no answer. He leaned in the doorframe.

Walt looked past him, into the dark hall, and saw the shoes. His face flinched, and he looked away.

"She came to my house on Wednesday," he said. "Kambria. She drove me to her house and showed me her wall. The armies. All of it. She cooked for me. Told me she'd be at your table Thursday." His mouth worked. "Then Thursday morning I got a neighbor to drive me over, and her door was standing open. Not wide. Just open. Someone had gone through it in a hurry, and someone else had pushed it to." He lifted the bag a little. "She gave me this. She told me to keep it for her. She said if anything happened to her, I was to give it to you." He held out the grocery bag. "Not the police. You. She said it twice."

Ezra kept his hands at his sides. "What is it?"

"A concordance. There's a thumb drive in the spine. She took it out of the book and showed me, and she put it back." He wet his lips. "Every file she had on the Petworth nursing home, and on the sickness at the nursing homes, and the men behind it." Walt's hand was trembling, and the bag rustled in it. "I don't understand the half of it. She said you would, someday. She said one more thing."

"What?"

"She said to make you read Angela's notebook first." Walt looked him in the eye. "The black one. In your hall closet. She said to make you read the notebook before you touch anything else, or none of it would make sense."

The word went cold and hard in Ezra, as it always did. *Notebook.* For a year people had been trying to make him open that book. Kambria on his porch, crying. His mother on the phone on Sundays. Angela herself, in the last week of her life, putting it in his hands.

"I don't need a notebook to tell me my kids are gone, Walt."

"No," Walt said. "You need it to tell you why."

They stared at each other.

Then Walt bent, one hand on the doorframe, and set the grocery bag down on the porch beside the door. He straightened up. He looked at Ezra one more time with his red eyes, and Ezra saw that the old man was not angry with him. He was frightened, for both of them.

"She made macaroni and cheese," Walt said. "For Thursday. It's sitting on her kitchen counter with a note on it. *For the Pattersons.* I saw it through her window." He stopped. "And the lamp. The one she keeps in the window. It was lit, Ezra. In broad daylight, with the door standing open and nobody home." He turned and took hold of the porch rail. "She was coming, Ezra. She was going to sit at your table."

He went down the steps one at a time, and across the street in the dark, and Ezra waited on the step until he heard Walt's door close.

The grocery bag sat on the porch. He left it there. Then, because the night was coming on and the weather report on the truck radio had said rain, he picked it up and brought it inside and set it on the dinner table without looking in it.

\* \* \*

The house got very dark very fast.

He had never given the dark a thought. There had always been streetlights, and the glow of the city on the clouds, and the television. Now there was nothing. By six o'clock the windows were black squares, and the rooms behind him were black, and the only light in the whole house was the faint gray of the sky through the kitchen window over the sink, and then not even that.

He needed a flashlight.

He went through the kitchen drawers by feel. Batteries, rubber bands, birthday candles, a screwdriver, the takeout menus Angela had kept in a stack with a binder clip. No flashlight. He went out to the garage and felt along the workbench in the pitch dark for the big work light, and remembered halfway there that he had left it on a job site in Takoma three weeks ago. He stood in the unheated garage and swore.

Then he remembered the hall closet.

Angela had kept an emergency kit on the top shelf, behind the coats. She had put it together the winter Mia was born, after an ice storm knocked the power out for two days: a box with candles and matches and a radio and a heavy yellow flashlight. *For when the lights go out,* she had said, and he had teased her about it, and she had kept it anyway.

He felt his way back through the kitchen and down the hall. He found the closet door with his hand. He opened it, and the smell came out at him in the dark, wool and cedar and her perfume, nearly gone, in the winter coat she had never worn again after the second round of chemo, and he stood with his hand on the door.

He had not opened this closet since the week of the funeral.

He reached up past the coats, onto the shelf. His fingers found the corner of a cardboard box, and then the cold metal edge of a flashlight lying on top of it. He took it down, and found the switch with his thumb, and pressed it.

It worked. Of course it worked. She had changed the batteries every spring, on the same day she turned the clocks forward.

The beam went up into the closet, white and hard, and lit the shelf.

The emergency box was there, and a box of Christmas lights, and a stack of board games the kids had outgrown. And behind the box of Christmas lights, pushed back against the wall where he had shoved it after the funeral so that he would never have to see it again, was a black notebook.

And lying on top of the notebook, in the exact center of the cover, was a thumb drive.

He stood in the hall with the flashlight in his hand and looked at it.

He had not put it there. Of that he was certain. He had pushed the notebook back behind the Christmas lights and closed the door, and nothing had been on top of it. Now there was a small black thumb drive with a strip of masking tape across it, and on the tape, in black marker, in small, careful letters, in handwriting he knew better than his own because he had watched it grow from crayon to cursive at his dinner table:

*For Dad, now that you're ready.*

The flashlight beam began to shake.

He reached up and took the notebook down with the drive still on it, holding it level in both hands. He left the drive where it lay. He backed out of the closet with the notebook flat against his chest and the flashlight in his fist, and his legs gave out at the end of the hall, and he sat down hard on the floor, three feet from his wife's black shoes.

\* \* \*

The cover said *For Ezra, when you're ready.*

That was all. Five words, in Angela's round, careful hand, in blue ink, centered on the cover. He had seen them on the day she gave it to him, in the hospice room, when she pressed it on him and he set it on the windowsill without opening it. He had seen them again the night he shoved it into the closet. He had told himself he would never look at them again.

He lifted the thumb drive and set it on his knee where he could see it. Then he opened the cover.

The first page was a letter.

It was dated in the corner, in black ink. *November 14, 2025.* Six days before she died. The handwriting was shakier than the cover. He could see where she had stopped and started again, where the pen had pressed too hard and then too light, where her hand had gotten tired.

*My Ezra,*

*If you are reading this and I am the only one gone, then put this back in the closet, honey. It isn't time yet. Go hug our babies. Go to Jalen's recital, whatever it costs you. Let Kambria in when she knocks. I'll wait.*

*But if you are reading this and the children are gone,*

He stopped. He laid his palm over the words and sat with his head back against the wall and his eyes closed, breathing through his mouth. The flashlight lay on the floor beside him, throwing its beam across the hall, across the shoes. After a while he opened his eyes and lifted his hand.

*But if you are reading this and the children are gone, and your mother is gone, and Kambria is gone, and there was a sound in the morning that you slept through, then I need you to listen to me now, the way you never would when I was sitting next to you.*

*It is not too late.*

*I know what you are thinking. I know you, Ezra Patterson. You are thinking that you missed it, that the door is shut, that God has left you the way your father left you. That is a lie, and it is the oldest lie there is, and I want you to throw it out of the house right now.*

*He took us first because He loves us. He left you behind because He loves you too, and He is not finished with you. The door stays open a little while after. Everything that is coming now is written in this book, in my hand and in Kambria's. We wrote it down so you would know it was true when you saw it. So you would know we didn't make it up. So you would know He told us ahead of time, because He wanted you to have a way out.*

*Read it all. Read it slowly, the way you read a set of plans. Don't skip ahead. And when you get to the end, there is one more page, with your name on it.*

*I reached for you every night for twelve years, honey. Now it's your turn to reach.*

*I love you. I always did. I'm not angry. I never was.*

*Your Angie*

*P.S. Kambria wrote some of these pages too. Be kind to her. She loves you like a brother. She always has.*

He went over it twice, and a third time, with the flashlight held close to the page.

*Let Kambria in when she knocks.*

He had shut the door in her face. Not long ago, on his own porch, with Mia watching through the curtain. She had stood there in the cold with tears on her face and begged him to open this book, and he had told her to get off his property, and he had shut the door, and she had driven away.

She had been coming to his table. Walt had said it. *She was going to sit at your table.*

He turned the page.

\* \* \*

It was a list. It went on for pages.

There were two handwritings on it, side by side, sometimes on the same line. One was Angela's, round and careful. The other was small and square and slanted a little to the right, and he knew it too, because it had been on every card that came to his house for years, every birthday and every Christmas and every sympathy card after the funeral. Kambria's. Between them, down the left edge of every page, were dates, and down the right edge were verses, and in the middle, in both their hands, were the things they had seen coming.

He moved the flashlight down the first page.

*Daniel 2:31–33. A great image, gold head, iron legs, feet of iron and clay. Watch for an image. A statue. Something set up where everyone can see it. Iron and clay = nations mixed together that don't hold. K., March 2023.*

Under it, in Angela's hand, much later, in a different pen: *Kam, could it be literal? An actual statue? I keep feeling like we'll see it with our own eyes. A.*

He thought of the newspaper on Walt's table that fall. The photograph on the front page of a thirty-five-foot statue on the National Mall, gold head and silver chest and iron legs, put up by some art foundation for a festival. He thought of Kambria standing on his porch with the clipping in her hand.

He turned the page.

*Zechariah 8:23. Ten men out of all languages of the nations take hold of the skirt of a Jew. A gathering of the nations in Jerusalem. Watch for it to be organized, official. A.*

Beside it, Kambria: *And Numbers 16, Korah's company, 250 princes. If they ever gather 250 of anything on that mountain, Angie, I'm going to lose my mind. K.*

He had seen it on the television on Tuesday, before the world ended. He had walked past it on the way to the refrigerator. Two hundred and fifty delegates, at a hotel on the Mount of Olives.

He turned the page. Then another. Then another.

A peace organization that would rise above the nations and promise *Peace and safety*, with a verse from First Thessalonians beside it, and a date two years before anyone had ever heard of the Organization for World Peace.

Ezra read the date twice. His thumb was resting on the edge of the page, and it had gone numb.

A world money with no cash in it, and a mark in the right hand, and Revelation 13 copied out in full by Kambria, with a note at the bottom: *They'll sell it as convenience. Watch for someone to say "your hand is your wallet."*

He read it with the same cold in his stomach he had felt at the dinner table. Kambria had written this down years before Crowe ever said it on television, and she had called it convenience.

An army from the far north, coming down on the mountains of Israel, and in the margin, in Angela's hand: *Pray for the families in those countries. Pray for Israel. Pray for the soldiers who don't know what they're marching into.*

Then, in Kambria's square little letters, with a date in October: *Matthew 24:7. Jesus: famines, and pestilences, and earthquakes, in divers places. Revelation 6:8. A pale horse, and Death on it, and Hell following. Watch for a sickness that goes after the old, the sick, the ones with no one. Watch for the name they give it. Watch who gets paid for it. K.*

Beside it, Angela, in the faint pencil of her last weeks: *Kam, I've been thinking about the nursing homes. Be careful who you tell. A.*

He had seen the nursing home deaths on the news that fall, the quiet fever sweeping through the facilities in Maryland and Virginia, the way the anchors had called it *seasonal.* He read the line twice. *Watch who gets paid for it.* His thumb had gone numb on the page again.

And then, on a page by itself, near the middle of the notebook, a single entry in Angela's hand, written larger than the others, with a box drawn around it in black ink.

*1 Thessalonians 4:16–17; 1 Corinthians 15:51–52. The trumpet. The dead in Christ first. Then us. In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.*

*Ezra, if you are reading this page, you already know.*

*You heard it, or you slept through it. Either way, honey, it was real, and it was Him.*

He turned back through the pages with the flashlight. Every page had its box, one line on every page, drawn in black ink, though the writing around it was in Angela's blue or in Kambria's tight print. Angela had gone back through the whole book with a single pen after the writing was done. Why that mattered, he could not have explained. He only knew his wife had never done anything on a page by accident.

Ezra closed the notebook.

He sat on the floor of the dark hall with the notebook shut on his knees and the flashlight lying beside him, and his lungs would not fill. Every page was dated. Every sign was written down before it happened, months before, years before, in his wife's handwriting and in Kambria's, at his own dinner table, while he stood in the doorway in his work boots and made jokes about the doomsday club.

They had told him. They had told him every single thing.

And he had laughed.

The shame came up in him so fast he thought he would be sick. He put his head down on the closed notebook and pressed his forehead against the cover, against the words, *For Ezra, when you're ready,* and he made a sound in the dark that he had never made in his life, a sound with no words in it at all.

\* \* \*

He lost track of how long he sat there. The flashlight dimmed. Outside, the rain the radio had promised began to tap the front window.

When he lifted his head, the first thing the beam showed him was the thumb drive on his knee.

*For Dad, now that you're ready.*

He picked it up and held it in his palm. It weighed nothing. A piece of plastic and a strip of tape. Jalen must have put it there on Wednesday night, while Ezra was out. While Ezra was in Mount Pleasant. His son had gone into the hall closet in the dark and found the notebook his mother left and laid this on top of it, in the center, where his father could not pick up one without the other.

He had known. Jalen had known where the notebook was the whole time. He had known his father had never opened it. And he had put this on top of it anyway, and written *now that you're ready,* believing that one day his father would be.

Ezra closed his fist around the drive until the edges bit into his palm.

There was a laptop in the house. Jalen's, the old one, the one he used for recording in the studio. It was on the desk in his bedroom upstairs. Ezra had seen it on Thursday morning when he ran into the room and found the bed empty and the cello leaning against the wall. He could not guess whether it held any charge. The power had been out for hours.

He got up off the floor with the notebook under his arm and the drive in his fist and the flashlight in his other hand, and he stepped around his wife's shoes and climbed the stairs in the dark, toward his son's room.

He had not gone into it since Thursday. He opened the door.

The cello was still leaning against the wall by the window, with the bow laid across the seat of the chair. In the flashlight beam he could see the rosin dust, pale on the strings. On the desk the laptop was closed, and on top of it was a sticky note in the same small, careful letters as the tape on the drive.

*Dad. Charger's in the studio. Password is the date we finished it.*

Ezra read it from the threshold of his son's room, and read it again, and he did not need to think about the password.

*July 19.*

He opened the laptop. The screen woke and lit his face in the dark room, and in the corner of it, small and white, the battery icon said twenty-three percent.

It would have to be enough.

## Chapter 23: Tears of a Father

> *And said, O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee, my God: for our iniquities are increased over our head, and our trespass is grown up unto the heavens.* — Ezra 9:6

**Word study: *ashamed* — בּוֹשׁ** Hebrew *bosh* (Strong's H954). To be ashamed, to be put to confusion, to be disappointed in what you trusted. It is the word in Genesis for the man and the woman who were naked and *not ashamed*, before the fall. And it is the word in Psalm 34: *They looked unto him, and were lightened: and their faces were not ashamed.* (Psalm 34:5)

*And when I heard this thing, I rent my garment and my mantle, and plucked off the hair of my head and of my beard, and sat down astonied.* (Ezra 9:3)

\* \* \*

The battery icon in the corner of the screen said nineteen percent.

Ezra sat at the dinner table with one candle and Angela's notebook under his hand, in a house that had never been so quiet. The refrigerator had stopped humming. Her black Sunday shoes stood by the front door where he could not bring himself to move them. Nothing in all the dark was alive but the little light of the screen.

There were two files on the drive. Jalen had named them himself.

*For Dad.*

*Untitled.*

He opened the first one with a hand he could not keep still.

The picture was crooked and too bright: the studio, the summer they built it, the bare pine floor and the south window black behind him, a coffee can of nails propping up the camera.

Then a face leaned in close, too close, blocking out everything, and leaned back again.

It was Jalen. Eleven years old, in a Nationals T-shirt two sizes too big, with sawdust in his hair and a scab on his elbow, sitting cross-legged on the floor of the room they had just finished.

Ezra froze with his lungs half full.

"Okay," the boy whispered. "Okay. Is it on? It's on." He looked over his shoulder at the door, then back at the camera. "Hi, Dad. It's me. It's night, and everybody's asleep, so I have to be quiet."

He looked around the empty room, and his whole face lit. "Thank you for building this with me. You were tired every day after work, and you still did it. And you let me hang the door. Mom says you never let anybody hang a door, not even Mr. Elijah, and you let me." He grinned so wide his eyes disappeared. "It's the best room in the whole world."

Ezra's hand had found its way over his mouth. He did not remember putting it there.

The boy came up onto his knees, too happy to sit still. "You're my hero, Dad. For real. I thanked God tonight for giving me the best dad ever. I said it out loud, and I think He heard me."

Then he settled back, and his voice went soft. "And when I saw you cry I knew I had to make a song where you can turn it into joy. You will always see what we built together."

He leaned in toward the camera and lowered his voice. "It's gonna take a long time, because I have to get really good first. But I already know what it's called. I'm not telling anybody. Not even Mom. You're the only one. Okay?"

He took a breath.

"It's called 'Tears of a Father.'"

He sat back, proud of himself, and then embarrassed, and rubbed his nose with the back of his wrist. "Because of you. I love you, Dad. That's all. Bye."

His small hand came toward the camera, reaching, and the screen went black.

Ezra sat in the candlelight with his son's voice still in the room. *Tears of a Father.* Seven years. Jalen had carried that name for seven years, through every slammed door and every fight in the kitchen, through his mother's dying, through the empty seat. He had never told a soul. He had kept it for his father, as he promised, and his father never came to hear it.

He knew what it was to hold out one small thing and wait for someone to look. He had been eight years old once, walking a mile of gravel home with a single free throw like a coal in his chest, wanting his father to look up from the television. Jalen had been standing in front of him for seven years holding out something the same size, and Ezra had looked at his tool belt.

Ezra laid his forehead down on the dinner table beside Angela's notebook, and he could not lift it for many minutes.

Then, because he could not stop now, he opened the second file.

On the screen, his son walked out into the light in a white suit.

He watched his son sit down before a closed red curtain, with the old man in white behind him. He watched him search the seats, and the camera followed his eyes down Row C: Mia with her daisies, his mother in her Sunday hat, Angela's purple scarf lying across a seat. And beside it, on the aisle, a seat with a program on it, and three letters in black marker.

*DAD.*

Jalen leaned toward the microphone. His chin was shaking, and Ezra watched him make it stop.

"I'm dedicating this to someone who isn't here right now."

For one second Ezra thought of Angela. Then he saw the boy on the studio floor again, leaning close to the camera. *You're the only one.*

The cello began.

\* \* \*

It was the low line. He knew it before the second note. He had heard it through the studio wall every night for longer than he cared to count, from the couch, with the television on to cover it.

And he was in the backyard, seven summers ago, with sawdust in the creases of his knuckles and his big hands over his son's small ones on the hammer. *Let the hammer do the work, J. Don't fight it. Just let it fall.* Angela was holding the level and laughing at the bubble. He had been happy. He had known it at the time, and he had not said so to anyone.

He was in the kitchen, and Jalen was fifteen and taller than his mother, and Ezra was saying, *There's no money in music, J. A trade is something nobody can take from you,* louder than he needed to, because the child would not look away. He had meant it as love. He had said it as a verdict.

Her hand on the hospice blanket that last night, opening.

His breath came in hitches. He put his fist against his mouth.

\* \* \*

Ezra watched the camera drift, unsteady in Kambria's crying hands, down to the seat on the aisle.

Empty.

He saw his phone on the counter. *Seats saved. Row C, on the aisle. 7:00. Don't be late.* He saw his own thumb press the small yellow thumbs-up and set the phone face down.

*Where were you? Told you. Work thing.*

On the screen the curtain began to open, and fifty-eight children in white were playing behind it, and had been playing the whole time. And Ezra understood that the camera kept finding that seat because his son's eyes kept finding it.

Then the cello broke upward and held, straight and hard and pressing, calling out over a full hall to one seat on the aisle. To someone who wasn't there.

*It was never only for her.*

*It was for me.*

The bus depot at Hollis Junction. He was eight, and he was holding out his hand, and his father patted him on the head and turned his back and walked out to the bus.

His own back, every night, turned to the studio wall. He had turned away from them, every night, until the day they were gone.

*I did it. I did to him what was done to me.*

The bottle. The raised hand. The couch. The red string. The thumbs-up. The empty seat.

*I knew. I chose it. It was me.*

\* \* \*

He had nothing left to defend. Every excuse had fallen down at once, and he sat in the ruins of them and made no move to pick one up. There was only a man at a dinner table who had been called, and called, and called, and had turned his back every time.

And somewhere out past these walls the trumpet had sounded, and everyone who was ready had heard it and gone. They had not left him in anger. They had simply gone, as you go when the door is open and Someone is calling, and he had slept through the only sound that ever mattered. The candle still burned. Her shoes stood by the door. Everything in the house was still here but them.

*O my God, I am ashamed and blush to lift up my face to thee…* (Ezra 9:6)

On the screen, the cello kept calling, and Ezra could not sit still under it any longer.

He pushed back his chair so hard it fell over behind him. He stood up in the dark kitchen, and he screamed. It was one word, and it came from a place in him that had been locked since he was eight years old.

"Jesus!"

And he lifted his hands.

He lifted them high, both of them, open, over his head: the hands he had sat on in the front pew when he was eight. There was no church here. There was a kitchen with one candle and a dead refrigerator and his wife's shoes by the door. He lifted them anyway.

"Jesus, it was me," he cried. "All of it. I turned my back on her, and on my boy, and on You. I knew, and I chose it. I'm not sorry because it's late. I'm sorry because it's true. Forgive me. Wash me. I can't make myself clean. Wash me."

He did not leave any of it out.

"The bottle. The couch. The television turned up so I wouldn't hear my own boy. The thumbs-up on a text, and the empty seat on the aisle. Mia's porch light, and I walked past it. Angela's hand on the blanket, and I made her wait for it till the very end. Celeste. I laughed at Kambria on my own porch and shut the door in her face. All of it, Lord. I name it. Every bit."

And as he named them, the hard thing he had carried since he was a boy began to come loose, and then it was gone, lifted out of him. *If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.* (1 John 1:9) He was clean. He had not been clean in his whole life, and he had not known it until now.

On the screen, the orchestra had begun to rise beneath his son, and a drum was ticking, faster and faster. Ezra looked down at his father's watch. It said 3:17. It had said 3:17 for thirty-five years. The ticking ran together into one sound, and stopped. The harp sang the grieving line he had heard through the studio wall every night. It was not grieving anymore.

His knees went, and he was on the floor.

His hands were still open in front of him. He held them out into the dark.

Angela had reached for him for twelve years. At every meal, on the sixth floor, on the hospice blanket the last night of her life, she had reached for him, and he had kept his hands in his lap. Only at the very end had he finally taken hers. Now he reached, with nothing in his hands and nothing left to give, for the hands of God.

And he felt them take hold of his.

It was not a picture, and it was not a voice. It was a warmth that came over his open hands and moved up his arms and into his chest, steady, and it filled the place where the hard thing had been. He knew who it was. Angela had told him, the afternoon she pressed the notebook against his chest. *When you finally reach for Him, honey, He'll send you the Comforter. You won't have to carry any of it by yourself.* Jesus had promised it to His friends the night before He died: *I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.* (John 14:18)

The Comforter had come.

And then, at last, the tears came.

They came without any sound at first, and then all at once. He had wept for Angela all that first winter, on his knees in front of the television with her laugh on the screen. This was not that. He wept for his son and for his little girl. He wept for every night he had turned the television up. Jesus had promised it in His sermon: *Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.* (Matthew 5:4) He let it come. For the first time in his life, he did not want it to stop.

The candle burned down an inch. The house was empty and still.

And in that stillness, in the place that had been shut since the bus station, he heard it. Not with his ears. It was the same call that had come to him in the dream of the red sky, the night he stood at the window and said *No.* It had never stopped calling. He had only never been weak enough to hear it.

*Ezra.*

He sat on the kitchen floor with his open hands held out in the dark, and he answered with the last breath he had, in a voice that was barely there.

"I'm here."

\* \* \*

He woke on the kitchen floor at first light, with his cheek against the chill of the linoleum and Angela's notebook under his hand.

He had no memory of falling asleep. The candle had burned down to a puddle of wax on the saucer. The house was gray and cold, and he lay listening to the quiet and found it no longer frightened him.

He got up on aching knees. He righted the fallen chair and set it back at the table, square, where it belonged. Then he stood at the kitchen window and looked out at the backyard.

The studio stood at the back of the lot in the gray light, under the bare branches of the maple: a small building of white clapboard with a green door and a window on the south side, and a short cedar ramp they had built so Jalen could roll his cello case in on its wheels. He had not set foot in it since the night of the recital. For a year he had walked past it every day on the way to the truck, and turned the radio up in the truck so he would not hear what came out of it at night, and told himself it was a hobby.

He went out the back door in his socks, across the frosted grass, and opened the green door.

\* \* \*

The room was immaculate.

That was the first thing he saw, before anything else, before he let himself see the cello stand or the chair. Jalen had kept it clean. The pine floor was swept. The music stand was dusted. The sound panels on the walls, the ones they had glued up together that first summer, were straight and whole. The recording gear on the little desk was coiled and labeled in Jalen's handwriting. The room smelled of rosin and cedar and the faint stale smell of a room no one had been in for days.

On the wall beside the door hung the framed photograph Angela had taken the day they finished: Ezra and an eleven-year-old Jalen standing in front of the green door with their arms around each other's shoulders, both of them covered in sawdust, both of them grinning.

Ezra stood in the doorway and looked at it until he could look at the rest.

Behind the two of them in the picture, just inside the open door, was the casing they had hung together on the last day, and behind the casing, the first stud. Last night, somewhere past two, in Angela's notebook, between a grocery list and a prayer for the audition, he had read a line he did not understand: *Read Ps. 91 at supper. J. asked me twice for the chapter and verse, then wouldn't tell me why. My secret keeper.*

The night before they framed the studio, she had read Psalm 91 at supper. He remembered it now: the spaghetti going cold, and Jalen not eating, watching her mouth as she read.

He took the pry bar from the hook by the door, the one they had left there for the next project. He set it behind the left side of the casing and leaned on it. The finish nails shrieked coming out of the jamb. He had taught Jalen to set those nails. He pulled the casing away a hand's width, then a forearm's, until the trim cracked at the miter, and he did not care.

On the bare stud, in an eleven-year-old's black marker, in letters that ran downhill:

*ME AND DAD. FIRST WALL.*

And under it, small, the way Ezra numbered every stud on every plan he had ever drawn: *91 4*.

He knew the verse before he could have said it. Angela had read it over the spaghetti with her finger on the line. *He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.* (Psalm 91:4)

His son had put his father under God's wings on the first day, and told no one, and a week later Ezra had hung drywall over it without a look.

He slid down the doorframe until he was sitting on the cedar ramp in his socks, the pry bar across his knees. He stayed there until the frost on the grass had gone to water.

When he could stand, he pressed the casing back against the jamb. He did not nail it. He left the stud where he could see it.

\* \* \*

On the music stand there were two things.

The first was a letter on heavy cream paper, folded once. He opened it. At the top, in navy blue, was the crest of the Capital Philharmonic Orchestra. It was dated the ninth of November. It offered Jalen Patterson a full-time position in the cello section of the orchestra, beginning in the new year, with a salary and benefits and a line at the bottom that said the orchestra had never before offered a contract to a musician so young. Below the last line, in blue ink, stood Jalen's signature, and beside it the signature of a woman named Evelyn Shaw.

He had signed it seventeen days before he was taken. He had told no one at home, least of all the man who called it a hobby.

Under the letter, on the music stand, was the score.

It was handwritten, in pen, on music paper, a thick stack of it held together with a black binder clip. The first page was folded back over the top of the stack, so that the title was hidden. Jalen had carried it out of the house folded that way, and Ezra had not thought anything of it.

Ezra took the clip off. He unfolded the first page.

Across the top, in large letters, in the careful, laboring handwriting of an eleven-year-old boy, older than the rest of the pages and faded a little, written first, with the music added under it over the years:

*TEARS OF A FATHER*

Under it, in the same boy's hand, a verse:

*…and God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes.* (Revelation 7:17)

He knew that verse. He had heard Angela read it. She had read it to Jalen on his bed one night when he was nine, the night after his first recital, when he came crying to her about something Ezra could no longer remember, and Ezra had stood in the hall outside the door and listened. She had told him about the people in white, the great multitude who came out of great tribulation, and how God would wipe away every tear. *Every tear, baby. Yours, and mine, and your daddy's too.*

The white suits. Every player on that stage in white. He had seen it on the screen and not understood. It had been that verse. It had been a promise, standing on a stage in front of an empty seat.

Under the verse, in Jalen's grown handwriting, newer, in black ink:

*For Dad, who built the room where I found it.*

Ezra turned the pages. He could not read music, not really; Jalen had tried to teach him once, and he had lost patience. But he could see the shape of it, the low notes at the start crowded down at the bottom of the staff, and then the long climb, page after page, the notes rising. And in the margin of the rising passage, the one he had heard climbing through the wall every night for all that time and stopping, always stopping, in the same place, there was a note in small black ink, in the boy's hand.

*the night we flipped the breaker and all the lights came on*

He remembered. He remembered the night they finished the wiring, the last night, after dark, and Jalen standing at the panel with his hand on the main breaker and Ezra saying, *Go ahead, it's your building,* and Jalen throwing it, and every light in the studio coming on at once, and Jalen whooping and jumping up and down on the new floor, and Ezra laughing, really laughing, and lifting his son off his feet.

Ezra sat down on the floor of the studio, with the score in his lap and his back against the wall they had framed together, and wept.

\* \* \*

He understood it then, sitting on the floor of the room they had built. Every night through the wall, until the fall, his son had been talking to him. Words had stopped working between them the summer Angela got sick, so Jalen had stopped using them. He had come out here, to the one place his father had loved him without holding anything back, and he had played the low line because that was where they were, and the climb because he remembered the night the lights came on.

His son had not kept playing in spite of him. He had kept playing because of him.

"I heard it, J," he said, out loud, to the empty room. "I finally heard it."

There was no one there to hear him say it.

\* \* \*

He could not stay. The room was full of his son, and his son was only one of the two doors that had stood open on Thursday morning.

He ran. He crossed the frozen grass with the score against his chest and went in at the back door and up the stairs two at a time, as on Thursday, and this time he knew what he would find.

Mia's door was open. The power had taken her nightlight, and the paper stars were gone from the ceiling, and the room was gray and small and plain. Her yellow nightgown with the moons lay on the bed in the shape of a sleeping girl, the blanket still tucked around nothing. On Thursday morning he had touched it, and it had been warm.

It was cold.

He sat on the little bed and held the nightgown to his face. Strawberry, the kind Angela used to buy.

*That's Daddy on the couch. He doesn't see it because he's sleeping.*

She had said it about a crayon house. She was four years old. He had been on the couch.

*Please help Daddy not be sad.* She had prayed it over a plate of macaroni with her eyes shut, and he had not been able to say amen.

A drawing of a horse, and *That's nice, baby*, with his eyes on his phone. A red moon on the refrigerator, the wax pressed so hard it shone, made so that he would finally look at one of her pictures. A porch light she would not let anyone switch off. *So Daddy can find the door.*

On the last night, she had settled against his arm in her mother's shoes and told him the whole thing, in a story, in her clear small voice. The lamp in the window. The King. The shoes by the door. *The door stays open a little while after.* She had told him what was coming and where she would be and how to follow, and he had kissed the top of her head and thought it was a story.

*Leave the light on, Daddy.*

She was six years old. She had spent a year trying to get her father to look at her, with crayons and porch lights and prayers.

*Daddy, I need it to eat.* He had held her hand through the whole blessing, and when she asked for it back he had let it go. He would have held it forever.

He lay down on her bed with his feet hanging off the end, the nightgown against his chest and the score beside him, and he said her name. Not shouting, the way he had in the yard on Thursday. Low, as a father calls a child in at dusk.

"Mia."

No one came. He said it again, and again, until it stopped being a word.

The light in her window went from gray to gold. When he finally got up, he left her door open. A little girl had told him it would stay open a little while after, and she had never once lied to him.

## Chapter 24: I Never Knew You

> *And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.* — Jesus, Matthew 7:23

**Word study: *knew* — ἔγνων** Greek *egnon*, from *ginōskō* (Strong's G1097). To know by experience, the way a husband knows a wife and a friend knows a friend. Not to know about. The men in this verse knew a great deal about God. They had preached in His name. What they never had was Him.

*Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.* (1 Samuel 2:12)

\* \* \*

Ezra sat at the dinner table in the morning light with Angela's notebook under his hands, and his hands had nothing to do.

He had barely slept, and he was not tired. He had expected to be. Last night he had gotten down on this kitchen floor and said a thing he had never said in his life, and he had half expected that by morning it would have gone sour in him, as every good feeling always had. It had not. Nothing had come to take it back.

For thirty-five years he had believed that God was his father. Not the Father Angela talked about, not the One in her prayers. His father. Calvin Patterson. A big voice in public and a cold one at home and a back walking out the door to a bus. He had believed it so deeply that he had never put it into words, even to himself. *God is loud on Sunday and cruel on Friday, and when you need Him, He leaves.* It had been the floor under every other thing he believed. It was why he sat on his hands in the front pew at eight. It was why he had sworn never to lift them. It was why, when Angela died with her hands open, he had decided that God leaves too.

And last night, when he had been as low as a man can get, God had not been loud, and He had not been cruel, and He had not left.

The floor was gone.

He sat with nothing under him, and he was not falling. That was the strangest part. He had thought, if he ever let that floor go, he would fall forever. He was not falling. Something was holding him up, and he knew what it was, because it had taken hold of his hands on this same kitchen floor the night before.

He spread his fingers on the notebook.

There was a Bible on the table, Angela's, the soft black one with the cracked spine and the ribbons. He opened it to the back, to Ezekiel, because he remembered a verse his mother used to say when he was a teenager and furious at his father, a verse he had always thought was about someone else. It took him a while to find it. His hands were clumsy with the thin pages. Then he found it, in chapter eighteen, and someone had already underlined it, in blue ink, in Angela's hand.

*…The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.* (Ezekiel 18:20)

In the margin beside it, in Angela's round letters: *For Ezra. You are not him.*

And under that, smaller, in a different pen, added later: *And neither is God.*

\* \* \*

He drove to Arlington in the afternoon.

He never exactly decided to. He needed out of the house, and he got in the truck and found himself driving south across the city toward the river, and he let himself keep driving, because he understood where he was going and why. He had not been to his father's grave since he was nineteen, when he had gone once, alone, to shout at it.

The city was strange in the daylight. Half the traffic lights were dark, and at every intersection the drivers crept through one at a time, looking at each other, waving each other on, with a courtesy he had not known Washington had in it. There were soldiers at the bridges now, in Organization armbands, with clipboards, stopping every car. A young one with a tired face looked at his license and asked where he was going. Behind him, a man in a gray overcoat, with a small silver pin of the Technate on his lapel, was watching the truck instead of the paperwork. Ezra had last seen that face in the long mirror at Rooney's, over a glass of club soda.

"Arlington," Ezra said. "My father's grave."

The soldier looked him over. Then he handed the license back and waved him on without writing anything down. "Lot of people going out there," he said. "Lot of people."

Ezra understood what he meant when he came over the rise on Memorial Drive and saw the cemetery.

The white headstones ran away over the green hills in their rows, as they always had, thousands upon thousands of them, straight and even, all the way to the trees. And among the rows, everywhere he looked, scattered over the hillsides, were the holes.

Open graves. Hundreds of them. Perhaps thousands. The earth heaped neatly beside each one, the white stones still standing at their heads. Here one, there one, and between them a whole row untouched, and then three together, and then a long stretch with none. People were walking among them. Families, mostly, in coats, moving up and down the rows with maps and phones, stopping at a stone and bending to read it and standing there. Some of them were crying. Some of them were kneeling at the edges of the open graves with their hands over their mouths. A man in an Army uniform, an old one, with medals on the chest, was sitting on the grass beside an open grave near the road with his legs stretched out in front of him and his cap in his lap, staring into it.

Ezra parked by the road and sat with the engine off.

Then he got out and walked.

\* \* \*

It took him an hour to find it.
