He had the section number from the funeral home papers his mother had kept in a shoebox, and he had to ask a young woman in a green jacket with a rake over her shoulder, who walked with him part of the way and told him, without being asked, that she had been here on Thursday morning, early, and had seen it happen, and that she had not slept since.

"They just came up," she said. "Out of the ground. Into the light. I watched them go up." She stopped at the end of a row and pointed. "Your section's down there. Third row from the end." She looked at him. "I hope he went up, sir. I hope yours went up."

Ezra walked down the row.

The stone was like all the others: plain white marble, rounded at the top, with the cross carved in a circle above the lettering. He read it standing at the foot of the grave.

*IN MEMORY OF CALVIN JAMES PATTERSON. SFC. US ARMY. PERSIAN GULF. JUN 4 1949. FEB 24 1991.*

The grass in front of it was whole.

On either side of it, two graves down on the left and one on the right, the earth was open. He could see the broken lids at the bottom. But in front of his father's stone the grass was green and unbroken and grown over, as it had been all those years.

Ezra stood and looked at it.

He had come out here, he understood now, hoping, though he knew better than anyone that there was nothing under that stone but Virginia clay. The Army had sent home a carton and a watch. He had gotten in the truck and driven across the river hoping that he would find the ground open. That in the last hour, in the dark before the shells came, his father had cried out to God, and been heard, and gone up on Thursday morning with the rest.

The grass was whole.

The grass would not say. It could not; it had never held him. If his father had risen on Thursday morning, he had risen out of the sand of Kuwait, where no one was watching. That was the thing he would hold on to, later, on the nights he thought about it. He did not know. The Bible said the dead in Christ would rise first. What his father had done in the last hours, what God had heard out in the sand or in the dark before the guns, he could not say. He knew only that his father had known about God all his life, and that no one living could say whether he had ever let Him in.

He was not the judge of that. He had never been the judge of it, though he had judged his father every day since.

*…Shall not the Judge of all the earth do right?* (Genesis 18:25)

He knelt down on the grass in front of the stone.

He had not knelt for his father in his life. He knelt now. The ground was damp and icy through the knees of his jeans, and he put one hand on the top of the white marble, as you would put your hand on a man's shoulder, and held it there.

"Daddy," he said.

It was the word he had not used since the bus station. It came out of him with a crack in it.

"I don't know if you can hear me." He swallowed. "I was scared of you my whole life, and then I hated you. I figured God was just you with a bigger voice. Not now." He looked at the carved letters. *SFC.* Sergeant First Class. He had been proud of that, once, when he was small, before he understood. "I built a room with my boy. Let him hang the door. You never once handed me a hammer." He laughed, and it hurt. "I'm still just trying to be what you weren't."

The wind moved over the hill. Somewhere down the row, a woman was crying without a sound, over another open grave.

"I hated you," Ezra said. "I need you to know that. I hated you every day. I hated you at my wedding when you weren't there, and when Jalen was born, and every time I raised my voice at him and heard yours come out." His hand tightened on the stone. "And I did it anyway. All of it. I did to my boy what you did to me. Not the gun. Not the belt. But I turned my back on him every night for all that time, and he played that cello to my back, and I let him." His voice went. He waited until he could talk again. "So I don't get to hate you anymore. I'm not better than you. I'm just a man who got a second chance you didn't."

He bowed his head until his forehead rested against the cold marble.

"I forgive you," he said. "I forgive you, Daddy. I don't know where you are. That's between you and Him. But I forgive you. I'm not carrying it anymore."

He stayed there, forehead on the stone and hand on top of it. When he finally sat back on his heels, the sun had gone down behind the trees on the far hill, and the long rows of white stones were turning gold and then gray, and the people were walking back to their cars.

He did not get up. He looked down the long rows, at the open graves and the whole ones, and words of Jesus came to him that he had heard a hundred times in Pastor Grant's pulpit and never once heard.

*Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.* (Matthew 7:13–14)

Many there be which go in thereat. He had gone in at it himself. For thirty years he had walked the broad way with his mother's religion at his back and his hands busy and a good name in the town, and he had called it the narrow one because it was well kept and he was not alone on it. His father had walked it too. They had walked it side by side, and neither had once looked up to see where it went.

Few there be that find it. He had not found it. He understood that now, with his knees in the wet grass. It had found him, in a cold kitchen and a dark house, when he had nothing left in his hands to carry it with.

He bowed his head again.

"Lord Jesus," he said. "I don't have anything to bring You. I came out here thinking I might have something. A forgiveness. A good deed. I don't." He shut his eyes. "*All our righteousnesses are as filthy rags.* (Isaiah 64:6) I've read it all my life, and I thought it was about other men." His breath smoked in the cold. "It's me. I was dirty when I went to church and dirty when I stayed home. Nothing I did out here today made me clean. You did that, on the cross, before I was born, and You did it for me on my kitchen floor last night. I didn't earn one hour of it."

The wind moved the dry grass. He did not look up.

"So I'm not asking for what I've earned. I'm asking for mercy. That's the only thing I've got to ask for." His voice broke and he let it. "*God be merciful to me a sinner.* (Luke 18:13) That's the man in Your story, Lord, the one who stood off by himself and wouldn't lift his eyes. That's me. Be merciful to me. Be merciful to my boy, and my girl, and the ones I can't find. And if You want to use me, use me as I am. I'm weak. You know I'm weak. You told Paul, *My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.* (2 Corinthians 12:9) Then let it be made perfect in me. I'm Yours, Jesus. All of me. I've got nothing else."

He stayed bowed a long while. When he finally lifted his face, he was no longer afraid, and he could not have said when the fear had left him. Whatever the Lord asked of him, he thought, he had already laid it down on this hill.

He took his father's watch off his wrist.

He had worn it every day since he was sixteen. It had come back from Saudi Arabia at the bottom of a cardboard carton, stopped at 3:17, and he had slept with it under his pillow from the day it came, until his wrist was big enough to hold it, and it had hardly been off his wrist since. He held it in his palm now and looked at the stopped hands. 3:17. The box his father's things came in was still in his garage, on the shelf behind the paint cans, where he did not have to look at it.

He thought about leaving it on the stone.

Then he didn't. He put it back on his wrist and buckled the worn leather strap.

"I'll come back," he told the stone. "I don't know when. But I'll come back."

He stood up, and his knees cracked, and he walked back up the row in the dusk, past the open graves, toward the truck.

\* \* \*

He did not drive home right away. He sat in the truck at the edge of the cemetery with the engine running for the heat and his phone dark in its cradle on the dashboard, and he read Jesus' sermon in Matthew seven in Angela's Bible by the dome light.

*Not every one that saith unto me, Lord, Lord, shall enter into the kingdom of heaven; but he that doeth the will of my Father which is in heaven. *Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? and in thy name have cast out devils? and in thy name done many wonderful works? And then will I profess unto them, I never knew you: depart from me, ye that work iniquity.* (Matthew 7:21–23)*

He read it slowly, as Angela had asked him to read everything. Then he read on, past the place where the loud men stop reading. He read about the wise man who built his house upon a rock, and the rain descended, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat upon that house, and it fell not, because it was founded upon a rock. And the foolish man who built his house upon the sand.

He thought of the duplex on Kennedy Street he had shored up two winters back, the back wall leaning off a footing poured on fill.

He sat in the truck with the Bible lying on the wheel, as Kambria's had, and he thought: *I have built my whole life on sand. On my father. On my grief. On my own two hands.* And then he thought, with a feeling so new it had no name: *It is not too late to pour a footing.*

He reached for the phone and held down the button on its side. He had switched it off on Thursday morning and left it off through all of it: the empty rooms, the hospitals, the studio, the grave. The screen went white, then black, and then everything that had been waiting for him came in at once, a dozen messages, then twenty, buzzing against the plastic: Elijah, four times. *Ez. Ez, call me. Please. I'm losing it.* The school. The police station, an automated message, *no new information at this time.* Mrs. Okafor. A number he didn't recognize.

And at the bottom of the pile, a name he had not let himself think about since Thursday.

*Celeste: I'm so scared, Ezra. Everyone's gone. I can't be alone tonight. Please come. I need you. I'll leave the door open.*

Ezra sat in the truck at the edge of Arlington National Cemetery, with the open graves going dark on the hills behind him and his wife's Bible open on the wheel, and looked at the screen.

He knew exactly how to get to Mount Pleasant from here. He had driven it a hundred times. Twenty minutes, at night, with no traffic.

His thumb moved toward the screen.

## Chapter 25: A Way to Escape

> *There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.* — 1 Corinthians 10:13

**Word study: *a way to escape* — ἔκβασις** Greek *ekbasis* (Strong's G1545). A way out; literally, a stepping out through the end of something, the one road open when every other way was walled in. Paul did not promise the Corinthians that the wall would never come. He promised that God would cut a door in it.

*And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out.* (Genesis 39:12)

\* \* \*

The message sat on the screen in the dark cab of the truck, and the cursor blinked under it.

*I'll leave the door open.*

Ezra knew that door. Red paint, a brass knocker shaped like a hand, three steps up from a narrow street in Mount Pleasant. He knew the sound the lock made, and the lamp in the front window, and the smell of the hallway, candles and wine and something sweet underneath. He knew exactly how it would be if he went. She would be frightened, and he would hold her, and for one night neither of them would have to be alone with what had happened. It would feel like comfort. It would feel, for an hour, like the oldest kind of mercy.

His thumb was on the screen. He had started to type. *On my w*

He stopped.

It was not virtue that stopped him. He would be honest about that later, when he told it. It was Angela's Bible lying open on the wheel, which carried her handwriting in the margin of Ezekiel: *For Ezra. You are not him.* He looked from the phone to the page and back to the phone, and he understood that he could not hold both of them in his hands at the same time. One of them would have to go down on the seat.

He set the phone face down on the passenger seat. He sat with the engine running and the open graves of Arlington going black on the hill behind him.

That was when the other voice started.

It did not sound like a voice. It sounded like his own thinking, which was what made it dangerous. It was calm and reasonable and sad.

*You know what you are,* it said. *You were in her bed while your son played to an empty seat. You were in her bed the night your daughter waited outside in the wet grass. You were there when the trumpet sounded, as good as there. You slept through it. Did you think you could cry for one night on a kitchen floor and be clean? Men like you don't get clean. You had twenty years of chances. You used every one of them up.*

He tried to answer it and came up empty.

*Go to her,* the voice said gently. *At least she wants you. Nobody else does anymore. They're all gone, and they went without you, and that tells you everything. The door is shut. You heard it shut on Thursday morning. Go where a door is still open.*

Ezra put the truck in gear.

He drove north across the river with the phone dark beside him, and for the first ten minutes he had not decided which way he would turn when he reached the city. The bridges were lit by work lights on generators, and soldiers in Organization armbands waved him through without looking. The streets were dark. At the light where one road climbed toward Mount Pleasant and the other ran east toward home, he slowed almost to a stop. A car behind him flashed its lights. He sat at the fork with his blinker off.

Then he took the right fork, toward Brookland, toward the empty house, and he did not feel good about it. He felt worse, with the last warm room in the world falling away behind him.

\* \* \*

The house was cold when he came in. The power had come back on sometime in the afternoon, and then gone off again, and the clock on the stove was blinking a time that meant nothing. He lit the candle on the dinner table with a match from the drawer. His wife's shoes were still at the front door, side by side, pointed out. He left them where they were. He could not imagine moving them.

He laid Angela's black notebook and her Bible on the table and opened neither, his hands on the closed covers.

The voice had followed him home.

*There's a verse,* it said, *about men like you.*

And there was. He knew it before he went looking, because he had seen it the night before, in the notebook, in Kambria's careful print, on a page he had skimmed past without stopping because it frightened him. He opened the notebook now and turned the pages until he found it. Hebrews twelve. Kambria had copied it out under the heading *Esau*, and drawn a line under it, and written a warning beside it in red pen.

*For ye know how that afterward, when he would have inherited the blessing, he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.* (Hebrews 12:17)

He read it again.

*…he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears.*

So that was it, then. That was the answer to the question he had been afraid to ask since he got up off the kitchen floor that morning. Esau had sold his birthright for a bowl of stew because he was hungry and it was there, and later, when he understood what he had thrown away, he wept and begged for it back, and it was too late. The door was shut. Tears did not open it.

Ezra had sold his for less than a bowl of stew. For a red door in Mount Pleasant. For a couch and a television and a bottle. For the pleasure of being angry at God.

He sat at the table and felt the warmth of the night before draining out of his chest until there was almost nothing left of it. He had been so sure. He had stood in this kitchen with his hands in the air and felt something take hold of him, and he had been sure. Now he thought: *Maybe that was only grief. Maybe it was only a man so tired he would believe anything. Maybe it was just what you wanted to feel.*

His phone lay face down on the table where he had dropped it coming in. He turned it over and scrolled back through the pile from the truck, past Elijah, past the school, and found one he had missed, tucked under the first.

*Celeste: Ezra? Are you coming? I'm scared. Please.*

He looked at it. He read the verse again. He thought, *What does it matter now? If the door is shut, it's shut. Why not one more night of being held by somebody? What's left to lose?*

He stood up. He took his keys off the hook by the back door.

And with the keys in his hand, standing on the threshold, he glanced back at the table, at the notebook lying open in the candlelight where he had left it, and he saw that Kambria had not stopped writing where he stopped reading.

He had stopped at the verse, because the verse was what he had gone looking for, and it had told him what he already believed. But there was more. Under the red line, in smaller letters, there was a note, and under the note there was an arrow pointing to the facing page, where the writing changed. The facing page was Angela's.

He came back to the table with the keys still in his fist and bent over the notebook and read it standing up.

Kambria had written: *Careful. Esau sought the BLESSING with tears, not repentance. He wanted the inheritance back. He never once wanted God. He wept over what he lost, not over what he did. Read Genesis 27:41. The minute he stopped crying he planned to kill his brother.*

And under that, smaller: *The devil loves this verse. He'll hand it to anybody who's actually sorry, to make them quit. Don't let him. Turn the page. K.*

Ezra turned the page.

It was in Angela's round handwriting, in blue ink, and it was dated years ago, a Thursday in March. There was a verse at the top, written large and carefully, the way she wrote the ones she wanted to remember.

*There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.* (1 Corinthians 10:13)

Under it she had written, in smaller letters:

*For the one who is reading this in the darkest night.*

Ezra's eyes went to his hand. He opened it. The keys lay on his palm, the truck key and the house key and the little brass one for the studio, with the plastic tag Jalen had made in shop class that said DAD in raised letters.

He laughed. It came out of him without warning, one short broken sound, and then he could not stop, and then it was not laughing anymore, and he had to sit down.

Under Angela's verse, in a different ink, Kambria had added one more line, and it was the one she always added. He had heard it from her mouth a hundred times on his own porch, and he had shut the door on it a hundred times.

*And it shall come to pass, that whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered…* (Joel 2:32)

*Whosoever,* Kambria had underlined. Twice.

He sat with the keys in his hand and read the two pages, the one that said it was too late and the one that said it was not, side by side under the candle. The first page was true. Esau was real. A man could harden his heart until he could no longer turn, and Scripture said so plainly. But the voice in the truck had not read him the whole page. It had read him one verse, cut away from everything around it, and hidden the rest. It had done what his father did at the deacons' table and what the false shepherds had done in Jerusalem: it had quoted the Word to keep him from God.

He was not Esau. Esau had wanted the blessing back. Ezra did not want anything back. He did not want his old life back. He did not want the couch or the bottle or the red door. He wanted God.

He stood up and picked the phone up off the table.

He opened Celeste's last message. *Please.*

He sent no reply. There was nothing he could write to her that would be true and kind at the same time, not tonight. He would pray for her. He would pray for her as long as he lived, and he would mean it. But he could not be the one to go to her. He went into her contact and pressed the red word at the bottom, *Delete Contact*, and the phone asked him if he was sure, and he pressed it again.

Then he put the phone in the drawer under the counter, with the matches and the birthday candles, and shut the drawer.

It was not a victory. Nothing in him felt brave. He felt like Joseph running out of the house with his garment in somebody else's hand, ashamed and shaking, sure he was doing the only thing left to do. *Flee also youthful lusts…* Paul had written to Timothy (2 Timothy 2:22). Not fight them. Not reason with them. Flee.

He went back to the table and sat down. He hung the keys on the back of the chair.

\* \* \*

He did not sleep. He did not try.

He sat at the dinner table through the middle of the night with the candle and the two Bibles, Angela's soft black one and the big old family one his mother had given them on their wedding day, and he read. He read the fifty-first Psalm three times through, out loud, in a whisper, because there was no one in the house to hear him. *Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.* (Psalm 51:1) David had written it after Bathsheba, after the prophet came and told him a story about a rich man who stole a poor man's only lamb, and David had been angry about the rich man, and the prophet had said, *Thou art the man.* (2 Samuel 12:7) Ezra knew how that felt now. He had been angry at his father for thirty-five years. He was the man.

*Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.* (Psalm 51:10)

He found Job, because Angela had a note in the margin that sent him there. *I made a covenant with mine eyes; why then should I think upon a maid?* (Job 31:1) He had never heard of a man making a covenant with his own eyes. He made one, at the table, long after midnight, out loud, and felt foolish, and meant it.

Around four the candle guttered, and he lit another from its stub.

At some point near dawn he stopped reading. There was nothing left now but to do the thing the verses were all pointing at, the thing Kambria had begged him to do on his porch that fall, the thing Angela had done at this table every Thursday night for years with her hand held out to him across the tablecloth.

The night before, he had cried out to Jesus in grief. He had been dragged there. The song had broken him open, and the name had come out of him before he could stop it, and he had been heard. He believed that now. He believed it more than he had believed it last night, because the voice had tried so hard to take it away from him.

But he had not yet laid his life down on purpose, with nothing pushing him. With no song playing. With no tears to carry him. Cold, and awake, and choosing it. This was not a second beginning, for he was already His. It was surrender.

He pushed the Bibles aside. He laid both hands on the table, palms up, where Angela's hand used to lie at every grace, waiting for his.

"Lord Jesus," he said.

His voice sounded strange in the empty kitchen. He kept going.

"I'm calling on Your name. Kambria said whosoever. Angela said whosoever. I'm a whosoever. I'm not asking because I'm scared, though I am. I'm not asking because they're gone, though they are. I'm asking because You're God, and I'm not, and I've spent my whole life pretending I didn't need You. I need You. I'm not going back. Whatever it costs. Whatever's coming. I'm Yours. I'm not going back."

He said it again, slower. *I'm not going back.* And as he said it the second time, he felt the strength go out of him.

It went out of him all at once. His arms went heavy on the table. His head went heavy. The room tilted, and the candle flame stretched long and gold, and he thought, distinctly, *This is what happened to Daniel.* He had read it an hour before, in Angela's Bible, without understanding it: the prophet by the river, seeing the vision of the man clothed in linen, and *there remained no strength in me: for my comeliness was turned in me into corruption, and I retained no strength.* (Daniel 10:8) He understood it now. It was not fear. It was weight. It was what happened to a man made of dust when something that was not dust came close to him.

He tried to stand, and his legs did not hold him.

He went down sideways out of the chair. On the way down, his left arm swung out and his wrist struck the edge of the oak table, hard, and he heard the crack of his father's watch against the wood, a sharp, flat sound in the quiet. Then the floor came up, cold linoleum against his cheek, and the kitchen went away.

\* \* \*

He was not asleep. He would always be sure of that.

He was lying on his face on the floor, and he could not move, and then a hand touched him.

It touched him between the shoulders, and it set him up on his knees and on the palms of his hands, trembling, as it had set Daniel. He could not have looked up. He saw only the floor, and the floor was full of light, a light that was not the candle and not the dawn, that came from no window and threw no shadow, and was warm on the back of his neck.

A voice spoke above him. It was not loud. It did not need to be loud. It was the voice he had heard in the dream of the red sky over the rooftops, the night he stood at his front window and said *No*, the voice that had been calling him through the studio wall every night for all those nights under his son's cello. He knew it. He had always known it.

*Fear not.*

He was shaking all over. He could not stop.

*Son of man, stand upon thy feet, and I will speak unto thee.* (Ezekiel 2:1)

And he stood. He did not do it himself. Something stood him up, as his own hands had stood the first wall of the studio upright with his son pushing beside him, and held him there until he was steady.

*I have made thee a watchman.*

He heard it as clearly as he had ever heard anything in his life.

*…I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.* (Ezekiel 3:17)

The light grew until there was nothing else.

\* \* \*

When he opened his eyes, the kitchen was full of ordinary morning.

The sun was coming in low through the window over the sink, laying a long gold bar across the linoleum and over his outstretched hand. The candle had burned down to nothing and gone out. Somewhere outside, a single bird was singing, the first bird he had heard since Thursday. He was lying on his side on the kitchen floor beside the chair, with a bruise rising on his wrist where it had hit the table.

And the kitchen was ticking.

It took him a moment to understand. It was small and close and steady, a sound he had never heard from that watch on his own wrist. He lifted his left arm off the floor and looked at it.

The old crack across the crystal had split into a star. Under it, the second hand was moving.

He watched it go around once, a full minute, jerking from mark to mark, and did not let himself move. It had come home from Saudi Arabia at the bottom of the carton, stopped. A watchmaker had looked at it once. Angela had talked him into taking it off once, the only time, for a man on Georgia Avenue, for his birthday, and the man had opened the back and said the movement was sound, there was nothing broken, he could not say why it would not run. Ezra had worn it dead on his wrist every day of his life since. Now it was running.

The hands had left 3:17. For the first time in thirty-five years the watch said something else.

He had looked at it every day since boyhood. 3:17. He had never given the number a thought. It was simply the time his father's watch had stopped, the time something had happened in the desert that no one would ever explain to him.

He said it out loud to the empty kitchen, as he had said it to every stranger who ever asked why he wore a dead watch. "Three seventeen."

And under it, the words he had just heard on the floor. *I have made thee a watchman.*

Three. Seventeen. Not an hour and a minute. A chapter and a verse.

All his life the watch had been holding a Bible reference up to his face, and he had read it as the time.

He got up off the floor so fast he knocked the chair over. He grabbed Angela's Bible off the table with shaking hands and flipped toward the back, past Psalms, past Isaiah and Jeremiah and Lamentations, the thin pages sticking together under his thumb, until he found Ezekiel, and then chapter three, and then the verse, and he read it aloud, standing in the sunlight, and his voice cracked in the middle of it.

*Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel: therefore hear the word at my mouth, and give them warning from me.* (Ezekiel 3:17)

Chapter three, verse seventeen. The same numbers he had looked at every morning of his life.

He dropped to the floor with the Bible open on his knees and the watch ticking on his wrist.

His father had been wearing it when it stopped. His father, who had said the words of God at the deacons' table and never lived a line of them. The watch had stopped at the watchman's verse on the night his father died, and it had waited all those years on the wrist of a boy who hated God, and it had started again on the morning that boy said *I'm not going back*.

Angela had underlined the verse. Of course she had. In the margin beside it, in blue ink, she had written one word, and then, at some later time, in different ink, Kambria had written another under it. Angela had written: *Ezra?* With the question mark. And Kambria had written: *Yes.*

He read the rest of the chapter on the floor, and it was not gentle. *When I say unto the wicked, Thou shalt surely die; and thou givest him not warning, nor speakest to warn the wicked from his wicked way, to save his life; the same wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood will I require at thine hand.* (Ezekiel 3:18) Kambria had been one. She had stood on his porch with the clipping in her hand, and he had shut the door on her, and she had gone home and kept watch anyway, with her lamp burning in the window, until the morning the Bridegroom came.

Now her post was empty, and the city was dark, and God had handed the lamp to the last man in Washington, who didn't deserve it.

\* \* \*

Before he did anything else, he opened the notebook again.

He turned past the pages he had read, past the statue and the Council and the leopard and the Organization, past every sign the two women had written down before it happened, to the last pages, where the entries stopped. He read what came after the Rapture in the Scripture they had copied out, because now it was his to know. The seals. The trumpets. The beast that would rise and make war with the saints. The mark on the right hand and the forehead. And near the very back, on a page by itself, in Angela's hand, Revelation twenty, verse four.

*…and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; *and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.* (Revelation 20:4)*

Angela had written nothing beside it, only a small box around it, as she boxed the things she did not want to forget, and under the box she had left the rest of the page blank. Across from it, in Kambria's print, pressed hard enough to show through the page, was a single line: *This is the page with your name on it.*

Ezra read it standing at the counter in the morning light, and he understood it. The ones who had been taken on Thursday were the ones who had believed before. Angela. His children. Kambria. His mother. They had believed without seeing, and they had been kept from the hour of trial. That door was shut, and it was right that it was shut. But the book was not shut. God was still calling names. The multitude in white in Revelation seven, Kambria had written beside it, was the Church already home: *…have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.* (Revelation 7:14) What waited for the ones left behind was the other picture, the souls under the altar in Revelation six, who held to the testimony of Jesus, and the beheaded on the page before him, who would not take the mark.

They would reach that place through it, though. Not around it. Through it.

For the ones left behind, believing in Jesus the way he had believed in the Washington Nationals, or in the weather, would not hold. A hand raised once in a dark kitchen was where it started, and it was real. But something was coming that would test it with everything, the right hand and the forehead and the knee, and the only people who would stand were people who loved Him more than they loved being alive.

He picked up a pen from the jar on the counter, one of Angela's blue ones, and he wrote in the blank space under her box, in his own square capitals, pressing hard enough to dent the page.

*BELIEVE HIM ALL THE WAY. LOVE HIM ENOUGH TO DIE.*

Then he capped the pen and put it in his shirt pocket.

He was still turning pages, Revelation forward and Daniel back, hunting for he did not know what, when he came to a line in Angela's blue ink at the foot of a page, with no verse beside it: *Calvin's box. Pray Ezra opens it someday.* He read it twice. Then he thought of the box.

The cardboard carton Calvin had packed himself and the Army had sent home, his block capitals still across the lid, the brown tape gone brittle. It had come to him from his mother's hall closet and sat ever since on the shelf above his workbench in the garage, behind the paint cans, where he did not have to see it. He had not touched it in years. He could not have said why he wanted it now. The watch was running. Whatever the box had to give him, he thought, it had already given.

He went out to the garage and brought it in anyway and set it on the kitchen counter in the light.

It was lighter than he remembered. The folded uniform, the boots, the shaving kit, the packet of letters to the deacons, the black Bible with the church program tucked inside the cover. He lifted them out one at a time and laid them on the counter. At the bottom lay a folded handkerchief, and under the handkerchief, the floor of the box.

He ran his thumb along it. It was not right. He had spent his life inside other men's walls and knew when a thing was thicker than it should be. The bottom of the carton stood a quarter inch higher on the inside than it should have, and what lay there was not cardboard. It was a plate of thin plywood, cut to fit, with a hairline seam where it met the walls of the box, a seam that did not belong. A man with a pocketknife and patience had cut it and glued it in.

He took a butter knife from the drawer and worked the point of it into the seam. The old glue gave with a dry little crack. He pried, and the plate lifted away, and in the flat dark space beneath it lay an envelope.

It was long and white, gone the color of weak tea, and sealed. Across the front, in a big, looping, old-fashioned hand that Ezra had not seen in thirty-five years but would have known anywhere in the world, was a single word.

*Ezra.*

He sat down at the table with it and turned it over twice before he opened it. The flap had been sealed with cellophane tape gone yellow and brittle. He slid the butter knife under the tape and lifted it, and drew out three sheets of thin airmail paper, folded in thirds, covered on both sides in his father's cramped script, every line climbing toward the right edge.

The first line said: *Somewhere in Saudi Arabia. February 23, 1991. Night.*

His father had died on the twenty-fourth.

\* \* \*

*Son,*

*They tell us we go in before first light. I do not know if I will come back, so I am going to write you what I could not say to your face, and if I come home, I will burn this, and if I do not, I have hidden this under the bottom plate of my box, where nobody will look for it but you, and I pray it finds you when you are a man.*

*I have been in the desert for weeks. There is nothing out here but sand and sky and men waiting, and a man has a lot of time to think when he is waiting. I have done more thinking out here than in all the years before. I did not like most of what I thought.*

*I think about your mother's rolls. Of everything, that is what comes back to me out here, the smell of that kitchen on a Sunday morning. I ate them with my head down because I could not look at her and take them both. I never once told her they were the best thing in that house. If you get the chance, tell her for me.*

*I want you to know first that I am sorry. For your mother. For the nights. For the bottle and the belt and the hand. For the gun. I will never forget your face when I put that gun to your head, Ezra. You did not cry. You did not look down. You looked at me like you were already a man and I was the boy. I knew then I had lost you, and I knew I deserved to lose you. I ran away from that look. That is the truth. I told the church I was going to war for my country. I was running from my own front door.*

*Now here is the worst thing, and I am going to say it plain, because there is nobody out here to perform for.*

*I do not know God.*

*I have known about Him all my life. My mama took me to church before I could walk. I could quote you half the Bible before I was twenty. I have led devotion at the deacons' table for nine years and lined out every hymn in the book and lifted my hands at the closing prayer every Sunday so the whole church could see me do it. I have counted the Lord's money and put some of it in my own pocket and gone up front the next Sunday and prayed over the offering. I quoted "Wives, submit" to your mother and left out the next verse. I quoted "Children, obey" to you and left out "Fathers, provoke not." I used His Word like a strap.*

*And I never once knew Him. Not one day. I quoted a God I never knew.*

*There is a chaplain out here, a young white boy from Tennessee, couldn't be more than twenty-six. He held a service on Sunday in a tent, and he read Matthew seven, and when he got to the part where Jesus says, "Many will say to me in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name," and He says, "I never knew you," I had to get up and walk out of that tent. I walked out into the sand in the dark and I threw up. Because that is me. That is the whole of me, son. I prophesied in His name. I did many wonderful works, in front of people. And He never knew me, because I never let Him.*

*I have been trying to pray since Sunday. Real prayer, not the kind I do at the table. It is hard. I do not know how. I am forty-one years old, and a deacon, and I do not know how to talk to God when nobody is listening. But I am trying. I said to Him last night, Lord, I do not know You, but I want to. If You will have a man like me. And I think, I am not sure, but I think something heard me.*

*Here is what I want you to know, and this is the reason I am writing this at all.*

*The God I showed you is not God. The man you saw at the deacons' table on Sunday and in the hallway on Friday night is not what God is like. I was a liar, son. Do not believe my lie. Your mother knows Him. Watch her. She is the real thing. When she prays at night with her door shut, that is God. When she puts her hand on your face after I hit you, that is God. Not me. Never me.*

*Do not be like me. Do not learn your God from your daddy. Find Him yourself. And if you ever have a boy of your own, do not let him grow up afraid of you. Build something with him. Anything. A birdhouse. A wall. Just do it with your hands next to his. I never did that with you, and I would give anything tonight to have done it once.*

*I have to go. They are calling us out.*

*I love you. I do not think I ever said it. I love you, Ezra. I have loved you since the day you were born and I did not know how to show it, and that is on me, not on you. You were a good boy. You are a good boy.*

*If I do not come back, I hope God will let me see you again someday. I do not know if He will. But I hope.*

*Your father,*

*Calvin*

*Matthew 7:21–23. Read it, son. Then read the rest of the book, and do not stop where I did.*

Ezra stopped. He had read those same verses in the truck only hours before, and had not known they were already waiting for him in his father's hand.

\* \* \*

Ezra read it three times.

The first time he read it fast, skipping ahead, looking for the blow. The second time he read it slowly, every word, with his finger under the lines. The third time he could not see the words at all, and he read it anyway, because he knew them by then.

*Build something with him. Anything. A wall.*

He looked across the kitchen, out the window, at the white clapboard studio across the yard in the morning sun. He thought of an eleven-year-old boy with his father's black marker. *ME AND DAD. FIRST WALL.* He thought of himself on that first night in the studio, sitting in one of the folding chairs, crying, and Jalen silent beside him, and Ezra saying, *Because my dad never built anything with me.*

He put the letter down on the counter and covered his face with both hands. Under his sleeve, the watch kept time. His father had written, a night before the end, that he thought something had heard him. Ezra could not know. He hoped, and for now that was all he was given.

\* \* \*


His father had told him not to stop where he had stopped. The rest of what Kambria knew was still in her house, and he did not mean to leave it there. Early that Sunday morning he drove to her door.

It was a small brick duplex on a narrow street in Brookland, twelve blocks from his own, with a chain-link fence and a concrete stoop. The spare key still lay under the third brick from the left along the walk. He did not need it.

The door stood an inch open. The frame around the lock had been split from top to bottom, white wood showing through the paint, the deadbolt hanging by a screw. A strip of yellow tape had been pulled across the jamb and torn through, and one end fluttered in the cold.

Ezra stood on the stoop with his hand flat against the door.

Someone had come for her. Not the dark. Not the trumpet. Someone with a boot.

He pushed it open.

The house was freezing and it was wrecked. Drawers pulled out and upended, cushions slit, books flung off their shelves and lying where they fell with their spines cracked. The front room had been stripped to the floorboards. And in the spare room, where Walt said the wall had been, there was no wall.

There was a plaster ruin. Every headline and photograph, every filing and map, was gone, and in their place hundreds of little holes, the pinholes where the paper had hung, scattered across three walls like a night sky. Scraps of red yarn dangled from some of them. The desk had been swept bare. Square clean rectangles in the dust showed where a stack of notebooks had sat for years, and a ring where a mug had been. On the floor under the window lay the poster board, torn in half. He picked up the top piece. *WHO P*, and a rip.

He stood in the middle of the room and understood that this was an arrest, and not a rapture.

He had to hold the thought in both hands, because it was so much worse and so much better than what he had believed. Not gone, then. Not yet. Taken. By men, with a warrant or without one, in the night, from her own kitchen.

*If you're hearing this and I don't call you back, it already happened.* Kambria's voice, on his phone, on Thursday morning.

Maybe it had. Maybe the trumpet had found her in a cell. But the men had come first, before dawn on Thursday, and no one could tell him whether she had been rescued or only moved.

On the chair by the desk, untouched, lay her Bible. Nobody had thought it worth taking. He picked it up, and it fell open in his hands to the place it had been opened most. The left-hand page held one verse, underlined in red ink so many times the line had worn through the paper.

*For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first…* (1 Thessalonians 4:16)

He did not put it down. Then he took a laundry basket from the hall, emptied out like everything else, and laid the Bible in it with great care, on top of nothing.

He went to the kitchen.

The lamp was there, on the sill over the sink, where someone had set it down. It had burned dry. A black ring of soot crowned the chimney and the wick had gone to ash. Whoever had broken her door and torn her wall had walked past a brass lamp in a window and left it burning. He didn't understand that. He understood the dish beside it, a pan of macaroni and cheese gone dull under its foil, and the envelope propped against it, addressed in her square little letters. *For the Pattersons. Thursday. Back by eight. K.* He read it twice and put it in his shirt pocket. He left the dish where she had set it. It was hers to give.

But he wasn't done. Walt had told him: *She said to make you read the notebook first.* Kambria wrote everything down. A woman who dated every line did not leave her last pages for strangers to find.

He stood in the kitchen, in the cold, and made himself think like her.

The window seat. A cushion on the sill, a wooden bench beneath it, the sort a woman would put in a small kitchen to keep her feet out of the draft. Someone had thrown the cushion off and kicked the bench out of line, but they hadn't pulled up the boards. He crouched. On the third board from the wall, the edge of the wood was worn pale along one side by a thumbnail, again and again, until it shone.

He pressed. The board lifted.

Under it, in the dark, wrapped in a dish towel, lay a single notebook. Black cloth cover. Elastic band. The ninth.

He opened it where a ribbon marked the last page. *November 25, 2026. 11:20 p.m.* The last entry, the letters as square and even as the first. Above it, the day before, and the day before that, line after line, dated and signed, covering pages.

Before he went, he saw to the lamp. He filled it from the can under the sink, steadying the base so he would not spill, and trimmed the burned end of the wick with the kitchen scissors, and wiped the soot from the chimney with a dish towel until the glass was clear. He struck a match. The flame came up small and blue and then gold, and steadied, and he lowered the chimney over it.

He did not leave it in her window. Whoever had broken that door had left it burning, and they would be back.

He did not read the notebook there. He had heard the sound of a car outside, slow, in the street.

He set the lamp's chimney straight, the notebook inside his jacket against his ribs, and went through the front room to the stoop. At the end of the block, half hidden by a bare tree, sat a gray Chevrolet Malibu with its engine running and its windows fogged. A man's shape behind the wheel held a newspaper up before his face, and did not turn the page.

Ezra turned his back on it and went down the steps with the basket on one hip and the lamp in his other hand, the flame low behind its chimney, as if he had every right to be there. He blew the lamp out and wedged it on the floor of the cab between the basket and the seat. He took the long way home, through Brookland and Fort Totten and back across Rhode Island Avenue, and watched his mirrors, and the Malibu did not follow.

That did not mean it was not there.

On the drive, the city went by in gray. Burned-out cars on New York Avenue. A line of people outside a pharmacy, six blocks long. Soldiers at the intersections. A church on Rhode Island Avenue with its doors standing open and its lot full of cars that had not moved since Thursday, their windshields white with frost.

At the curb in front of his own house, he looked across the street at Walt's porch. The old man's curtains were drawn, but there was a light behind them.

Ezra carried the lamp up his own front steps and set it in his front window, beside the switch where Mia used to reach up on her toes in her nightgown to turn on the porch light, so that Daddy could find the door.

The notebook he put on the dinner table, under the candle. Then he went across the street, and knocked.

## Act 8 — The Tribulation Watchman

## Chapter 26: The Scribe

> *So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.* — Nehemiah 8:8

**Word study: *sense* — שֶׂכֶל** Hebrew *sekel* (Strong's H7922). Insight; understanding; the good sense that sees how a thing is put together and why. It comes from a root that means to be wise, to act with insight. The scribes did more than read the words aloud. They stopped, and explained, and kept explaining until the people could see what God meant.

*And Ezra the scribe stood upon a pulpit of wood, which they had made for the purpose… and when he opened it, all the people stood up… For all the people wept, when they heard the words of the law… neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.* (Nehemiah 8:4–10)

\* \* \*

Walt opened the door on the third knock, in his cardigan and slippers, with his reading glasses pushed up on his forehead and his cane in his left hand.

He regarded Ezra in silence. Then he looked past him, across the street, at the small gold flame burning in the Pattersons' front window.

"That's hers," Walt said. "That's Kambria's lamp."

"I filled it this morning."

The old man's mouth worked. He stepped back from the door without a word, and Ezra went in.

Walt's kitchen was just as Ezra remembered it from the few times he had crossed the street in all his years on Twelfth Street: the yellow linoleum, the percolator on the stove, the round table under the window with the newspapers spread across it in their order. Except that the newspapers were days old now. There had been no paper delivered since Thursday. Walt had laid out Wednesday's *Post* and Wednesday's *Times* and Wednesday's *Journal* anyway, in a row, with his Bible open beside them and his red pen uncapped on top, and Ezra understood that the old man had been sitting here every morning since, reading the last news there was.

They sat down across from each other. Walt did not offer coffee. Ezra put his left wrist on the table between them, palm down, and pushed back his sleeve.

Walt studied the watch, the cracked crystal and the second hand jerking around under it, and for a while he said nothing.

"That's your daddy's," he said. "That's the one that came back stopped."

"It started this morning. On the kitchen floor." And Ezra told him. He began with the text that had lit up the dark cab of his truck the night before, and he meant to go in order, and he could not keep to it. He told the old man that God had spoken to him, and that he had not earned a word of it. He told him a hand had lifted him off the linoleum when he had no strength left to stand. He told him the watch on his wrist had started again at the very verse his father never lived. Last of all he took his father's letter out of his shirt pocket and laid it on the oilcloth, and Walt read it through to the end, every cramped line, without a word.

Walt let him finish. Then he took his glasses down off his forehead and put them on, and leaned over Ezra's wrist, and peered at the watch for a full minute through the bottom of his bifocals.

Then he sat back in his chair and took the glasses off again and pressed his thumb and finger into his eyes.

"Three seventeen," he said. "I set that verse once. In nineteen eighty-one. A preacher bought an ad on the church page. Ten-point Century, two lines." He shook his head. "I could tell you where every comma goes in that chapter, Ezra. I could have told you on Wednesday. I could tell you what it means. I could tell you about the watchman and the blood on his hands. I know it better than you ever will." His voice thinned. "And it never once stood me up off a floor."

Ezra had no answer for that, so he said the only thing he had come to say.

"I'm going to read them," he said. "Angela's notebooks, and Kambria's last one. Out loud. Every night, from the beginning. I don't understand half of it yet, and I want to, and I don't think I can do it by myself." He looked at the old man. "I want you to come and read with me."

Walt was quiet.

"You know the book," Ezra said. "I don't. You can tell me where I'm wrong."

"I can tell you where you're wrong," Walt said. "I can't tell you where I'm wrong. That's the trouble." His eyes went through the window to the lamp across the street. "What time?"

"After dark. Seven."

"I'll bring my own Bible," Walt said. "Yours is too small to read."

\* \* \*

Elijah came first, though. Elijah came that same night, before Walt, before the reading had even begun.

Ezra took the phone out of the kitchen drawer at four that afternoon and sat with it in his hand at the table. He left alone the messages from the one name no longer in his contacts and scrolled past it, down to the four from Elijah, and read them. *Ez. Ez, call me. Please. I'm losing it.* And under those, sent sometime in the night, a fifth he had not seen in the truck: *never mind. dont call.*

He called.

It rang seven times. Then it picked up, and there was breathing on the line and nothing else.

"Eli," Ezra said. "It's me."

"I said don't call." The voice on the other end was thick and slow. "I said never mind."

"Where are you?"

A long pause. Then, in a voice Ezra had not heard from Elijah Brooks in all their years of friendship, a frightened boy's: "Rooney's. In the back. Sal's gone, Ez. The door was unlocked. I've been here since Friday."

Ezra drove the six blocks to Rooney's with the lamp still burning in his window behind him.

The front door of the bar stood open on its hinge. Inside it was dark and cold and smelled of spilled beer and rot. The television over the register was dead. Glass crunched under his boots. In the back room, under the one window, on the floor beside the pool table, Elijah was sitting with his back against the wall and his knees drawn up and a bottle of bourbon standing beside him, two-thirds gone. He had not shaved in days. He was still wearing the clothes he had worn to his sister's in Hyattsville the night before Thanksgiving, a brown sweater with a turkey on it that his niece had picked out for him as a joke.

He looked up when Ezra came in, and Ezra saw that he had cried himself dry.

"They took Renee's kids," Elijah said. "Both of them. Right out of the guest room. I was sleeping on the couch." He laughed, and it came out wrong. "Ez, I was on the couch. I heard it. I heard the horn. I thought it was a truck. I rolled over and put the pillow over my head."

Ezra lowered himself to the floor beside him and leaned on the same wall.

"I slept through it," he said. "I didn't even roll over."

Elijah looked at him. Then he laughed again, harder, and this time it broke in the middle and turned to weeping, and Ezra put his arm around his oldest friend's shoulders and held on while he shook.

"You said," Elijah managed. "Remember? Right out there. That stool. I said if it was true, wouldn't there be a sign. And you said—" He could not finish.

"I said Angela would want there to be," Ezra said. "I remember."

"There were signs, Ez. There were signs every night on that television. Kambria came in here and told me to my face. She sat on that stool and she told me, and I made a joke, and I bought her a ginger ale." He pressed the heels of his hands into his eyes. "I'm the guy who makes the joke. That's all I ever was. Everybody likes the guy who makes the joke." His voice dropped to almost nothing. "Where'd they go, Ez? Where'd they all go?"

So Ezra told him.

He had no notebooks with him and no Bible, only what he had read in the last two nights, and what Angela had said to him on a hospice bed, and what Kambria had shouted at him through a screen door. He told it badly, out of order, and he had to stop twice because he had lost the next part.

"They didn't die, Eli. They were taken. Jesus said He'd come back for His own. The dead in Christ first, and then the ones alive, caught up in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. That sound, that was the trumpet. Angela wrote it down. Kambria wrote it down. They told me at my own table and I made jokes. Thursday morning, at first light, on an ordinary day." He stopped. "And it's not over. The door stays open a little while after. Angela wrote that. Whoever calls on His name."

"Whoever?" Elijah said.

"Whoever."

Elijah listened to every word with his head against the wall and his eyes shut.

When it was done, Elijah was quiet for a while.

"So it's real," he said finally. "All of it. Every crazy thing she said."

"All of it."

"And it's not too late."

"It's not too late."

Elijah opened his eyes and looked at the bottle beside him. He looked at it, the bourbon that had gotten him through the last two nights. Then he picked it up by the neck and set it upside down in the dirty sink behind the pool table, and they both listened to it run out.

"I don't know how to pray," he said. "I never did. I just bowed my head at my mama's table and waited for her to stop."

"Neither do I," Ezra said. "I'm two days in. Say what's true. That's all I know so far."

So Elijah Brooks, who had made a joke about every serious thing all his life, knelt on the sticky floor of the back room at Rooney's beside an overturned barstool and said what was true. He said it in a whisper, with his forehead against the green felt of the pool table.

"God. I don't know how to do this. I've made a joke about You my whole life. About everything. I made one when she sat on that stool and told me. I'm sorry. If it's not too late, I'm here. Whatever's left of me. Please."

It was not eloquent, and it took a while. Ezra knelt beside him with a hand on his back and said nothing.

At seven o'clock, when Walt came across the street, big-print Bible under one arm and cane tapping, he found the Pattersons' front door unlocked and two men at the dinner table, one of them in a sweater with a turkey on it, both of them red-eyed, waiting for him with the notebooks stacked between them in the candlelight.

\* \* \*

They began at the beginning.

The first notebook was red, and it was older than Ezra had realized, as old as his marriage, from the first year Angela and Kambria had sat at this table. On the first page, in Angela's round hand, it said *Of the Nations*, and under it, *Matthew 24*, and under that the whole chapter was copied out in blue ink, verse by verse, with notes in the margins in two handwritings.

Ezra read it aloud by candlelight. He read slowly, because the words were new to him, and because he had decided that morning on the kitchen floor that he would not hurry this. He had never cut a board before he read the plans through, and he would not start now. When he did not know what something meant, he stopped, and Walt told him, in his dry, exact voice, chapter and verse. When Walt did not know, they looked in the margins, and usually one of the women had already asked the same question, years ago, and written down the answer.

He read the disciples on the Mount of Olives asking *what shall be the sign of thy coming*, and Jesus answering: deception first, and wars and rumors of wars, and nation against nation, and famines and pestilences and earthquakes in divers places. And beside the list, in Kambria's print, dates. Clippings taped in. The earthquake in Turkey. The new flu. The wells going dry in the West. All of it dated before it happened, years before, and then dated again, in different ink, when it did.

He read *as the days of Noe were*, eating and drinking and marrying and giving in marriage, and he thought of Rooney's, and of the jukebox nobody played, and he could not go on, and Elijah took the notebook from him and read the next verse himself, badly, with his finger under the words.

*Then shall two be in the field; the one shall be taken, and the other left.*

They stopped there the first night. None of them could go on past that verse. Walt sat with his big hands folded on top of his Bible and stared at the candle. Elijah's face was wet and silent. And Ezra closed the red notebook and laid his hand flat on its cover, and he prayed for the three of them out loud, the first time he had ever prayed for anyone but himself. He had no idea how. He said what was true.

They came back the next night, and the night after that. It became the shape of their days. In the mornings the city was a place to survive: lines for water, lines for gas, rumors of food at a warehouse in Northeast, soldiers at the bridges, the radio announcing new Organization rules every few hours. In the evenings they sat at the dinner table under one candle and read the plans.

Ezra had thought the reading would only tell him what was coming. It did that. But something else happened too, so gradually that he did not notice until it was well underway. The lies he had lived by began to come apart.

Not all at once. A wall framed wrong comes down board by board, every nail pulled. He read *Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee*, and a board came down: the one that said God leaves. He read Jesus calling, *Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest*, and another came down: the one that said he had to carry everything himself, the one he had nailed up at eight years old on a cold stairwell step, when he decided that no one was coming. It had been holding up the whole house. He read *Fathers, provoke not your children to anger*, and he put his face in his hands at the table, and the board that said it was all Calvin's fault came down, and so did the one that said none of it was. Every night something false came out of him and something true went in where it had been. Paul had a word for it, Walt said. *Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind.* Ezra wrote it on the inside cover of his own notebook, a new black one he had found in Jalen's desk, in his square capitals. RENEWING.

He was standing up straighter. His hands had stopped shaking in the mornings. He could sleep.

\* \* \*

On the ninth night, near the back of the third notebook, he turned a page and found his own name.

Angela had written it. It was dated the spring before she got sick, and it was written in her best hand, the one she kept for the ones she meant. At the top of the page she had copied a verse.

*For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the LORD, and to do it, and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments.* — Ezra 7:10

And under it, by itself, on a line alone:

*Lord, let him become his name.*

Ezra stopped reading. Walt looked up.

"What is it?"

Ezra turned the notebook around on the table so the old man could see it. Walt read it, and his face shifted, and he turned it back without a word.

"I never read it," Ezra said. "The book of Ezra. I never even opened it. My daddy named me out of it, and I never once looked to see who he was." He laughed, a little. "I figured he was a prophet. A big angry man in a robe. That's what I figured Daddy wanted me to be."

"He was a scribe," Walt said.

"What's a scribe?"

Walt reached across the table and turned the pages of Angela's Bible for him with his thick, careful fingers, past Chronicles, to the little book of Ezra, and then on into Nehemiah, the eighth chapter, and laid it open in front of him.

"A scribe," Walt said, "is a man who copies the Word down so it won't be lost. And then reads it to the people. That's all. He's not a king. He's not a prophet. He doesn't see visions. He sits with the book and writes it out and reads it out loud." He tapped the page. "Read that."

Ezra read it. The people gathered in the street before the water gate, as one man. Ezra the scribe standing on a pulpit of wood they had built for him. Opening the book in the sight of all the people, and all the people standing up. Reading from the morning until midday.

*So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.*

He read it again. Then he looked up at the dinner table: the candle, the stack of notebooks, Walt's big-print Bible, Elijah's turkey sweater, his own new notebook full of square capitals. He looked at what the three of them had been doing every night for nine nights, without a name for it.

His father had named him for a man who sat with the book and read it aloud and gave the sense. His father had given him that name and then left him for a war, and never read him a single line of it.

But God had not left. God had waited forty-four years, and taken him the long way around through every kind of ruin a man could make of his life, and set him down at last at a dinner table with a candle and a stack of notebooks, reading the Word aloud to two broken men, and had let him find out only now, on the ninth night, what his own name meant.

He laid his palm flat on the page, and Walt and Elijah let him sit.

Under Angela's prayer, last on the page, in Kambria's hand, there was one more entry, dated the week of the funeral. Two verses, one under the other, and a single word.

*Daniel 12:1. At that time thy people shall be delivered, every one that shall be found written in the book.*

*Revelation 3:5. Jesus: I will not blot out his name out of the book of life.*

*Amen.*

\* \* \*

The woman came on the twelfth night.

It was almost ten. Walt had gone home across the street, and Elijah was asleep on the couch under Angela's afghan, where he had slept most nights since Rooney's because he could not stand to be alone in his apartment. Ezra was sitting up with the fifth notebook, the one with the Feast days in it, when someone knocked on the back door, three light raps.

He took the claw hammer off the hook by the door before he opened it. He was ashamed of that later. He did it anyway.

She was standing on the back steps in the dark, a slight woman in her early thirties in a long dark coat with the collar turned up, with a laptop bag over her shoulder and a phone in her hand, its screen turned down against her coat so it would not light her face. She looked a week short of sleep. She looked at the hammer in his hand, and then at him, and she did not step back.

"Mr. Patterson," she said. "Ezra Patterson. Jalen's father."

"Who's asking?"

"My name is Nina Cole. I'm an engineer. I work for Kroll Dynamics in New York." She said it fast; she had rehearsed it on the train. "I wrote the software that runs the cameras on every corner of this city. I found you with it. I'm sorry. I have to speak with you, and I couldn't call, because they listen to the calls now." Her voice shook on the last part. "Please. I watched your son's video four hundred times. I need to know what he was playing to."

Ezra studied her. Then he hung the hammer back on its hook and stood aside, and she came into his kitchen and stood in the candlelight and looked at the notebooks on the table, and at Kambria's lamp burning in the front window, and at the wall of clippings Ezra had begun pinning up in the dining room, and she sat down without being asked.

She told him over coffee, with her coat still on.

"I was in Dubai the night before. A gala at the top of a tower so tall it had its own weather. Halfway through the toasts, words appeared on a mirror behind the head table, in a language nobody there could read." She turned the mug. "Thursday I was at the airport when the sky made that sound. My grandmother raised me. She was in her bed that morning. She's not in it now. Vale flew me home himself, and over the ocean he said her address out loud, an address I never gave anyone. Then he offered me a job. On something called Continuity." She looked at her coffee. "I said yes. What else do you say to that?"

"What's Continuity?"

"It's an artificial intelligence," Nina said. "A computer program. Kroll Dynamics is building it in a data center out in Virginia the size of six football fields, forty thousand servers, pulling more power than a city. We drive it from a control room under our building in Manhattan, and I'm writing the core of it." She turned the mug. "You feed it a person. Everything he ever said and did. Every speech, every interview, every hour of video, every email, his medical records, his voice down to the breath. It studies him until it can answer a question he was never asked, in his voice, with his face on a screen, the way he would have answered it. Not a recording. New words. His words."

"A copy of a man."

"Kroll won't call it that. He calls it a continuation. That's where the name comes from. Continuity. The man stops. The mind keeps going."

"What man?"

She looked up at him. "Adrian Crowe."

Ezra knew the name. Everyone knew it now. Crowe had been on every surviving screen in the world since Friday morning, promising order.

"Why would they need a copy of a man who's still alive?" Ezra said.

"That's what I keep asking," Nina said. "Nobody will answer it."

She set her phone face up on the table between them, and its screen lit, and a warm, unhurried woman's voice spoke out of it, a voice that sounded like nobody and everybody. "It is ten fourteen, Nina. You asked me to tell you when you had been here fifteen minutes."

Ezra stared at the phone.

"That's Juno," Nina said. "My assistant. I built her." She touched the screen, and it went dark. "She's the one who found you. I asked her who the cellist's father was, and she found the program from the recital, and the seat with your name on it, and your face at the gas station on Rhode Island Avenue on Saturday afternoon, and your truck on Memorial Drive." She met his eyes. "If I could find you this easily, Ezra, they can find you in four minutes. They just haven't started looking yet."

"Looking for what?"

"For people like you," she said. "People who know what happened. There's a list. I've seen the outline of it. Anybody who was connected to the missing in a certain way, anybody who's been flagged saying certain words in public, anybody who won't register." She reached into the laptop bag and took out a folded sheet of paper and pushed it across the table. "That goes up on every corner on Monday."

He unfolded it. It was an Organization notice, in the plain blue-and-white type they used for everything now, the gold circle at the top. *Census of the Living. All residents are required to register with the Organization for World Peace within thirty days, for the purposes of relief, rationing, and the restoration of order. Registration is quick, free and confidential.*

"Registration," Nina said, "is a face scan, a hand scan, and an account. No account, no ration card. No ration card, no food."

Ezra folded the notice up again and set it on top of the stack of notebooks. Then he opened the notebook nearest his hand, the fourth one, the one Angela and Kambria had written together, to a page near the back, and turned it around and slid it across the table to her, without saying anything.

At the top of the page Kambria had copied out Revelation thirteen, verses sixteen and seventeen. *And he causeth all, both small and great, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand, or in their foreheads: And that no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.* Beside it she had written a date, two years ago, and a note: *It will begin as something kind. Relief. Food. Order. Don't take the first step.*

Nina read it. She read it twice. Her coat stayed round her shoulders. She looked at the lamp, then at the man across the table, and she put her forehead down on the table.

"My grandma used to read me that," she said. "When I was little. I thought she was trying to scare me."

"She was trying to warn you," Ezra said. "So was Kambria. So was my wife." He looked at the lamp in the window. "I didn't listen either."

She stayed the night on the floor of Mia's room, because the trains had stopped at ten. In the morning she did not go back to New York. She called in sick, from a phone she had brought that was not her own, and spent the day reading the notebooks, with Juno shut off and face down beside her.

\* \* \*

"You never opened the bag," Walt said.

It was the next night, the first night Nina sat at the table, and the fifteenth since the old man had carried it across the street. The grocery bag still stood where Ezra had set it that Friday, on the sideboard by the dining room wall, under a dish towel. He had walked past it forty times.

"I had Angela's notebook first," Ezra said. "Kambria said read the notebook first."

"You've read it." Walt put his cane across his knees. "She asked for the notebook before the bag. She didn't ask for the notebook instead of it."

Nina had put down her fork. "What bag?"

Ezra lifted the dish towel. Inside lay a thick blue concordance with packing tape wound round its spine. He cut the tape with his pocketknife. Between the binding and the cover, in a slit someone had sliced with a razor and glued shut again, lay a thumb drive, small and black, with a strip of masking tape on it.

*Petworth.*

"Walt says she made it," Ezra said. "Some of it came from New York."

Nina held out her hand. She took the drive from him, turned it over under the candle. "Can I?"

She had a laptop in her bag with the radio card torn out and the wireless chips cut, one she called her clean room. She plugged the drive in. It asked for no password. It opened on a folder, and the folder held two hundred and ten files.

Nobody spoke while she read.

Ezra watched her face. In his years on job sites he had watched men read an inspector's report, and it was how a man looked when the worst thing he had suspected was true, and worse. She opened a spreadsheet and sat very still. She opened a scan of a government form. She opened a map, and a list of facilities, and a column of lot numbers, every one stamped PALEHORSE. She opened a photograph of a license plate, taken at night through a windshield. She opened a page of five verses, typed out in the order a woman in New York had given them, with one word pulled from each. She opened a chart Kambria had drawn by hand and scanned: Verity Health to Meridian Trust, Meridian Trust to *A. Vale*, and off to one side, joined to the rest by a dotted line, *C. MOORE.*

"Nursing homes," she said at last. "Dialysis centers. Hospice wards. Hospitals that serve the poor. Four sites. Petworth here, and Manila, Kherson, Belém. In October." Her voice had gone flat and careful. "This is a field trial."

"Of what?" Walt said.

"An organism." She turned the screen toward them. At the top of the page, in a clinical gray header: *ORGANISM DESIGNATION: PALE.* "It's an engineered pathogen. They tested it on the people nobody would miss." She did not look up from the screen. "There's a reference at the bottom. Verity Health is the contract lab. Verity is owned by Meridian Trust. And Meridian Trust..."

"One of the ten," Ezra said.

She nodded. "The ten who sit on the High Council."

Ezra reached over without a word and took the ninth notebook from beside the candle, where it had lain since the day he found it. He had read all of it. He opened it to a page near the end, dated, and turned it so Nina could read.

*November 22. The Centers for Disease Control calls it "an unusual cluster, cause unknown." Their own file calls it PALE. Rev. 6:8: "And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him." They named it themselves, Lord. Watch who gets paid for it.*

And under it, the next page, her last full entry:

*November 25. If I don't come back, the files are with Walt. Celeste is not who she says. She is Special Operations. She was in my ward to watch me. She was in Ezra's life to watch HIM. Whatever she asks him for, he must not give. Pray for her anyway. Psalm 91.*

Nina read the page twice. Her mouth went tight. "Special Operations," she said. "Who's Celeste?"

Ezra could not answer.

He could not pronounce the name. It had been two weeks since he had deleted it, and he had not said it aloud since. In the end it was Walt who said it, in his dry, exact voice, looking at the candle.

"A woman he knew."

Nina looked from one of them to the other. Then down at the laptop, and something came into her eyes that Ezra had seen in a surveyor's, before a tape was pulled tight across a ruin.

"I can look," she said.

"At what?"

"At where she is." She was already typing. "The woman who wrote that notebook. Kambria Whitfield. If the Organization took her, they logged it. They log everything. I built the thing that logs it." Her fingers stopped, once, over the keys. "I shouldn't. Every query I run tells them where I am. They will know I did this."

"Then don't," Ezra said.

"I'm doing it." Her voice was quiet. "I've done everything else they asked."

She sat with her hands on the keys for the length of one breath. She whispered a short sentence, not to either of them, and Ezra understood that she had never prayed it before and did not know it was a prayer. Then she began.

It took forty minutes. She worked through a chain of doors she had built herself, every one with her name on the lock, and the screen scrolled and halted and scrolled, and Walt dozed with his chin down and woke, and Elijah, who had come in at some point and stood in the doorway in his turkey sweater, said nothing.

"There," Nina said.

A grainy gray picture came up on the screen. A concrete room, a ceiling grille, a drain in the floor. A steel bench along one wall, a ring in the floor, a chain running from the ring to her wrists. At the bottom of the screen a stamp: *SUBLEVEL 3 / HOLDING B. 11/26. 05:54:12.*

A woman sat on the bench in a gray nightgown with her wrists cuffed to the chain. Her head was bowed. She was praying. Ezra knew the set of those shoulders before he knew the face.

"Kambria," he said.

The clock on the corner of the screen ran. 05:56:00. 05:56:08.

At 05:56:11 she lifted her face, as if someone had spoken her name. She smiled. The picture went gold at the edges. The cuffs dropped, still locked, onto the steel of the bench, and the nightgown settled where she had sat, in the shape of a woman sitting.

The room was empty.

Not a chair creaked in Ezra's kitchen.

"Play it again," he said.

She played it again. The chain, the heap, the little ringing of steel. A woman there, and then a woman not there, and in between not one second in which a person could have moved.

"She was caught up," Walt whispered. "She was caught up in the twinkling of an eye."

Ezra's hand was on the edge of the table, and he found that he was weeping and had been for some time. *In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.* He had said it a hundred times in the last two weeks, off a page, in a voice that believed.
