He had never seen it. And here it was in gray on a laptop, in a locked room under a federal building, and it had been this woman, who had begged him, on his own porch, in the cold.

*Let Kambria in when she knocks.*

He had not. She had gone anyway. She had gone from a cell with the cuffs still locked.

Nina made a sound. "Keep it running," she said. "Look at the door."

The door at the top of the frame opened at 07:14. The night guard came in alone and stood at the bench a long time. Then an older officer in the doorway, with his mask pushed up. Then the angle changed, and a different camera, on the corridor, showed the monitor on the corridor wall.

On it, a tall, thin man in shirtsleeves, in a hotel room with a cracked window, with a red string at his wrist.

He was not in the building. He was a face on a wall-sized monitor in the corridor, and the camera was looking over a technician's shoulder at it. Alexander Vale, watching by video from half a world away, and next to the technician's chair a woman in a pale coat with her arms folded, whom Ezra had held, and had wept with, and had been going to go to on Saturday night.

Celeste.

He could not hear the sound. Nina turned it on. The voices came thin from the speaker. Vale's, low and exact. Hers, shaking.

"Seven of the eleven cells," the guard said from the doorway. "Same thing."

"You said you had a handle on this," Vale said to the woman.

"It's what I told you. She's in her own faith, her own—"

"You filed under your own name," Vale said gently. "You locked her out of the system. You have followed this woman for three months, and this morning you stood in front of a locked cell that emptied itself, and you know what it means." The pause on the screen. "I'm sorry, Celeste."

Ezra was out of his chair before he had decided to be.

On the screen Celeste turned and looked straight at the camera, and her face was a face he knew better than he wanted to, and it was terrified. She said one word. He thought it was his name.

Then the picture split into four, and in one of the squares the door of Holding B stood open, and the guards took her by the arms.

Nina's hand found the keyboard. "That's enough," she said. "That's enough."

"What did they do?" Ezra said.

She turned the laptop down until the screen went dark. "I know what's in that room. I read it in the file an hour ago." Her eyes stayed on the dark screen. "It's a decontamination chamber. There's a nozzle in the ceiling."

"With what?"

Nina took a long time.

"With the label on the booth key," she said. "PALEHORSE. LOT 3."

The candle flickered. Walt had both hands flat on the table, as though the table were moving.

"What time was that?" Ezra said.

"07:41," Nina said. "The morning of the twenty-sixth."

He stood very still.

"She died on Thursday," Ezra said. "Seven forty-one in the morning."

"Yes."

"She texted me on Saturday night." He said it flatly, as if reading it off a page. "Twice. *Please come. I'm so scared, Ezra. I'll leave the door open.*"

Nobody said a word.

"Somebody had her phone," Nina said, softly. "Somebody wanted you to come."

He saw the red door in Mount Pleasant. He saw the brass knocker, shaped like a hand. He saw himself on the parkway, at the fork, with his blinker off, deciding. And he saw a gray car with a man behind the wheel holding a newspaper at the end of a block.

He sat down.

"The Lord made a way to escape," he said, in a whisper with no air behind it. "For the one who is reading this in the darkest night." He covered his face. "She wasn't calling me, Walt. She was already dead. They used her to get me to walk out my own front door."

Nobody told him it was all right. The old man reached across the table and covered one of Ezra's hands with both his own, and held it, and the candle burned down low.

At last Elijah, from the doorway, in a small voice that was only half a joke, said, "Well. Whose turn is it to pray?"

Ezra raised his head.

"Mine," he said.

He thanked God for Kambria, who had gone up from a cell with her cuffs still locked. He said Celeste's name, too, as he had promised at the kitchen table, whatever she had done; she was past his prayers now, so he gave her over to the Judge of all the earth, and it was the hardest thing he had ever done on his knees. And, after a long time, he prayed for Vale.

\* \* \*

From then on there were four of them at the table.

Ezra read them the first thing he had learned that he was certain of, the next thing he had written in his notebook. He read Galatians six: *Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.* And then John's first letter, chapter three: *Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren.*

"That's the law now," he told them. "For us. I don't know much yet. But I know that. We carry each other. And if it comes to it, we lay down our lives for each other, because He laid His down for us." He looked around the table, at the old man and the joker in the turkey sweater and the engineer in the dark coat. "It's going to come to it. You read the notebook. You know it is."

Nobody argued.

The next day Ezra went down into his own basement with a flashlight and a tape measure and a carpenter's pencil behind his ear, out of twenty years' habit, and then took the pencil from behind his ear and looked at it and put it in his pocket and took a black marker instead. He measured the long wall under the dining room, where the old coal bin had been before the house had gas heat. It was nine feet deep and twelve wide, with a brick floor and a low ceiling, and the only way into it was a small iron door that had been plastered over in the nineteen sixties.

He built a wall in front of the iron door. A false wall, framed in two-by-fours, faced with old paneling he pulled out of the garage, with a shelf of paint cans and garden tools across the front of it so that it looked like it had been there forever. One section of the shelving swung out on hidden hinges if you knew where to lift. He built it in two days. It was the most careful work he had ever done. He countersunk every screw and puttied every head so a flashlight would slide right over it.

Nina wired the room.

She brought things from New York in a duffel bag on her second trip down, a box of parts and cables she had signed out of the Kroll lab under a project number that did not exist, and she sat cross-legged on the brick floor of the coal bin for an evening with a soldering iron and a headlamp, talking to herself. When she was done there was a little steel box on a shelf against the brick, with a cable running up through a hole Ezra drilled in the floorboards and out under the eaves to a long thin antenna hidden along the gutter of the back porch.

"It's a transmitter," she said. "Low power. FM, on a dead frequency near the bottom of the dial. It'll reach maybe five miles on a good night, more if it bounces. They can find it if they're looking. They're not looking yet. They're looking at phones." She handed him a cheap microphone on a cord. "Whatever you say into that, anybody in this part of the city with an old radio will hear."

Ezra weighed the microphone in his hand.

"What do I say?"

"What you say up there every night," Nina said. "Read them the plans."

\* \* \*

They did it the first time on a Sunday night that December, at nine o'clock, with snow coming down outside.

There were four of them in the coal bin, sitting on paint buckets and folding chairs around the little steel box, with a single battery lantern on the brick floor between them and the swinging shelf closed behind them. Walt had brought a thermos. Elijah had brought the afghan from the couch and wrapped it around Walt's knees without asking, and Walt had let him.

Ezra had Jalen's thumb drive in his hand, the one with the masking tape across it that said *For Dad, now that you're ready.* Nina had copied the second file off it onto the transmitter's little computer. She looked at him, and he nodded, and she pressed a key.

The low line of the cello came out of the steel box and out along the wire and up through the floorboards and out along the gutter into the snow.

Ezra sat with his eyes closed and listened to his son. He had heard it a dozen times now. He would hear it a thousand. It did not get easier, and he did not want it to. The line climbed and fell back and climbed, and somewhere out there in the dark, in kitchens and basements and parked cars across Northeast Washington, he thought, someone was turning a dial, and stopping, because they had heard this before, on their phone, in the weeks before the world ended: a young man in a white suit, and a piece with no name.

Nina faded it down under his voice after the first minute, as they had practiced.

Ezra lifted the microphone. His hand was shaking. He held it with both hands.

"My name is Ezra," he said. "That's my son you're hearing. His name is Jalen. He was eighteen. He was taken on Thursday morning, weeks ago, with his little sister, and his mother before them, and a lot of people you loved too. I know where they went. I know why. I know what's coming next, and I know it's not too late. I'm going to read to you. I'm going to read you what two women wrote down before any of this happened, every word of it, and the Book they got it out of. I'm going to do it every night at nine o'clock, as long as I can. I'm a carpenter. I'm not a preacher. I don't know much. But I can read."

He opened the red notebook on his knee, to the first page.

*Of the Nations. Matthew 24.*

He read for forty minutes. When he finished he had nothing of his own to add, so he said the greeting Paul opened his letters with, and John opened Revelation with, the words Angela had underlined there, the ones he had decided would close every night.

"Grace be unto you, and peace."

Nina switched off the box. The lantern hummed in the quiet.

Before the greeting he had read one line over again, the line Angela had boxed on that page. Nina noticed.

"You ended on the box," she said, coiling the cable over her elbow.

"It's how she marked what to remember."

"Then say it slowly tomorrow," Nina said. "Some of the people out there are writing it down."

Then, out of the little steel box on the shelf, from the receiver Nina had wired into the same circuit to listen to the frequency, came a crackle of static, and a man's voice, very faint, breaking up, on the same dead channel near the bottom of the dial.

"Ezra? Ezra, are you still there? This is Brooklyn. It's Kyle, Ezra. Kyle Bennett, from Rooney's. We picked you up off a bounce, man, I don't know how. There's thirteen of us in a church basement on Atlantic Avenue." A burst of static swallowed the next words, and then the voice came back, and it was crying. "We heard the song. Please don't stop. Please. Tell us what happens next."

Ezra had not moved. *Kyle.* The French-literature boy with the lighter. Nina bent to the box.

"Brooklyn," a second voice said, flat and low and rough as a plank, cutting in on top of Kyle's, "give the man room to breathe. You'll burn up the channel."

"Who is that?" Ezra said.

"Somebody north of here, on the same repeater." Nina frowned at the meter. "He's good. He's clean on the signal."

The rough voice kept on. "Carpenter. Your ground's floating. I can hear sixty-cycle hum under every word you say. Somebody's got your mic stand sitting on a power strip. Plug the box into a different circuit than the lantern's charger, and stop broadcasting from a coal bin." A short silence. "And turn the mic off-axis. You're popping every p. Whoever's running the board, tell them that cello is the cleanest thing on the air tonight."

Nina laughed in spite of herself, a startled, helpless sound. Elijah slapped his own knee. "Who is that?" he whispered.

"I don't know," Ezra said. His own mouth, out of practice, had begun to smile against his will. "But he's right about the coal bin."

The voice came back once more, quieter. "Play the song again tomorrow," it said. "Same time." And it was gone.

## Chapter 27: Head Knowledge

> *Thou believest that there is one God; thou doest well: the devils also believe, and tremble.* — James 2:19

**Word study: *believest* — πιστεύεις** Greek *pisteueis*, from *pisteuō* (Strong's G4100). To be persuaded; to put your weight on something. It is the same word John uses in *whosoever believeth in him should not perish*. James is not mocking belief. He is saying that agreeing a bridge exists is not the same as walking across it, and that the devils agree with every word of the Creed, and are terrified.

*I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee. Wherefore I abhor myself, and repent in dust and ashes.* (Job 42:5–6)

\* \* \*

Walt Simmons had been a typesetter most of his working life, and he still woke every morning at four-fifteen, the hour he used to catch the bus to the *Star*.

There was no bus now. There was no paper. He woke anyway, in the dark, on his own side of the double bed, and lay listening to the house, and then got up and put on his cardigan and his slippers and went down the stairs one at a time with his hand on the rail and his cane hooked over his wrist, and made coffee in the percolator as his wife had made it for all those years, two scoops and a pinch of salt. The gas still worked, most mornings. When it did not, he made it on the camp stove Ezra had brought over in December.

Then he sat down at the round table under the kitchen window and opened the ledger.

It was a bound accounting book, green cloth, with red and blue ruled columns, the kind the *Post* had used for payroll before computers. He had found a box of them in his basement in December. On the first page of the first one, in his careful square capitals, he had written THE RECORD, and under it the verse he had set for himself.

*Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.* Habakkuk 2:2.

Every morning since December, he had written down what had happened in the world the day before, as exactly as he could find it out, with the date in the left margin and the verse it belonged to in the right. He got the news from the radio, from the Organization's broadcasts in the morning and the BBC on shortwave at night, from what Nina brought down from New York in her head and would not write anywhere else, from Elijah's runs through the city, from the line outside the relief center on Bladensburg Road. He wrote it all in red pen. Facts on the left. Scripture on the right. Nothing in between.

*WEEK 6, FROST. Organization announces Census of the Living extended 30 days. 61% of District registered. Unregistered to be "visited."* Revelation 13:16.

*WEEK 7, SLEET. Rice $41 for 10 lb. at Bladensburg relief market. Wheat futures suspended.* Revelation 6:6.

*WEEK 7, SLEET. Earthquake, Peru, 7.9. Second in 5 weeks.* Matthew 24:7.

*WEEK 8, HARD COLD. Crowe addresses Collective. Calls for "one ledger for one world." Applause 4 min.* Daniel 8:25. *By peace shall destroy many.*

*WEEK 9, HARD COLD. Fever in the nursing homes of Prince George's and Baltimore counties. "Isolated clusters." Health Directorate offers the "Verity Prevention Protocol," free, to the registered.* Revelation 6:8.

*WEEK 10, THAW. Forty-one dead in one week at a care home in Baltimore. The unregistered, turned away at the door of the clinic, are healthy. A reporter asks why. He is no longer on the air.* Revelation 6:8. *Behold a pale horse.*

It was the most useful thing he had ever done, Ezra said. Walt read from it on the air every other night, before Ezra read from the notebooks, so that the people listening could see the prophecy and the newspaper side by side, as Walt had always seen them. *This is the evening paper,* Walt would say into the cheap microphone in the coal bin, *and this is the Book that printed it first.* People wrote to them about it, in the strange ways people wrote now: notes left under the brick at the relief center, messages passed hand to hand. *Tell the old man to keep the record. It helps.*

Walt kept the record. He was good at it. He was the best in the city at it, probably. He knew where every verse was. He knew what every sign meant. On the radio, when a caller asked a question, he could answer it before Ezra had finished repeating it, chapter and verse, with the Greek if they wanted it.

And he did not pray.

He had never prayed. Not once, not in seventy-four years. Not as a boy, at his mother's knee in the cold-water flat in Shaw, where he had bowed his head and moved his lips and thought about baseball. Not at his wedding. Not in the hospital, years ago, when his wife lay in the bed with the machines breathing for her and her hand in his, and she had said, very faintly, *Walter, will you pray with me?*, and he had said, *You pray, honey. I'll listen.* And she had prayed, in a whisper, for him, and he had listened, and she had died two days later with her eyes on his face.

He knew the Book better than any preacher in Washington. He had read it cover to cover forty-one times. He had a red pen mark beside nearly every prophecy in it, a date, a clipping. He had known the Rapture was coming, he had known the season, he had read the signs on the front page of the *Post* every morning with his red pen.

And on the morning of the twenty-sixth of November he had been sitting at this table with his coffee when the horn sounded, and he was still here.

\* \* \*

They read at Ezra's dinner table every night at seven, and broadcast from the coal bin at nine.

By the end of January there were nine of them at the table, not counting the ones on the radio. Elijah, who had stopped drinking and started cooking, badly and with enthusiasm, for everybody. Nina, when she could get down from New York, which was every week or two, always by a different train and a different route, always with her phone left in a drawer at her apartment, running on Juno, so that the cameras would think she was home. Mrs. Okafor from next door, who had lost her husband and her twin daughters and had banged on Ezra's door on Thursday night and been turned away, and who came back in January and was let in. A young couple from the next block who had heard the broadcast on a car radio. A bus driver named Marcus. An old woman named Dolores who had been a member at Greater New Hope for forty years and had never once believed a word of it, and cried every night at the table because she did now and it was too late for her husband. Ezra did not let anyone tell her it was too late for her.

Walt took the end seat by the window, where he could see his own house across the street. He answered the questions. He kept the record. He brought the coffee in his thermos.

He noticed that when they prayed at the end of the night, he folded his hands and bowed his head and moved his lips and thought about the record.

No one else noticed, or if they did, they kept it to themselves. They thought of him as the old watchman, the one who had known before anyone. They brought their questions to him. When Dolores asked him, she took his hand. "Walter. Was he saved? Sixty years married. A deacon thirty of them. Tell me he went."

"The book says the dead in Christ rise first, Dolores," Walt said. "It doesn't say who was in Christ at the last. That was between him and God, in the last hour. I won't tell you what I don't know."

She held his hand across the table and thanked him. He went home that night and sat at his own table in the dark and could not get warm.

It was Ezra who said it to him, finally. Not unkindly. Ezra was not unkind anymore. It was the strangest thing about him, the thing Walt had watched happen across the street over two months and still did not entirely believe: the man who used to stand in his own front door with his arms folded and a smirk on his face now sat on the floor so Dolores could have his chair, and waited out every question to the end.

It was the second week of February. Everyone else had gone home. Walt was gathering up his ledger and his thermos, and Ezra was sitting at the table with the candle, and he said, without looking up from the notebook in front of him:

"Walt. When was the first time you prayed?"

Walt stood with his thermos in one hand and his cane in the other.

"Don't," he said.

"I'm not trying to—"

"I know what you're trying to do. I know exactly what you're trying to do. I've watched you do it to nine people." His voice came out harder than he meant. "You don't have to do it to me. I know the book. I know it better than you do."

"I know you do," Ezra said.

"I could quote you the whole road. Romans three twenty-three, Romans six twenty-three, Romans ten nine. I could quote you every verse on the Roman road and tell you who carved it. I know it, Ezra."

"I know you do." Ezra looked up at him then, in the candlelight, with eyes that were not judging him at all, which was worse. "Walt. You read me James two last week. On the air. You read it better than I could have. *The devils also believe, and tremble.*" He was quiet for a moment. "Do you tremble?"

Walt said nothing. He set the thermos down on the table so that it would not make a sound. Then he picked up his ledger and his cane and walked out the back door and across the dark street to his own house, and he did not sleep at all that night.

\* \* \*

He trembled. That was the truth of it. He had trembled since the morning of the twenty-sixth.

He trembled as the demons in James trembled, he thought, lying on his side of the bed in the dark. Because they knew. They knew exactly who God was, better than any theologian. They had seen Him. They knew every promise was true and every warning was true, and they knew precisely what was coming, and the knowing did them no good at all. It only frightened them. He knew what was in the second half of the book. He knew about the seals and the trumpets and the bowls. He knew about the mark and the image and the lake of fire. He knew, to the chapter, what happened to a man who knew all of this and did not repent. And the knowing lay on his chest at night, a locked chase of cold lead, and did nothing for him but make it hard to breathe.

He had thought, all his life, that knowing was the hard part. That the people who went to church and clapped and cried and did not know Daniel from Deuteronomy were fools, and that he, who knew, was the serious one. He had sat at his dinner table every morning for decades with the Bible beside the newspaper and his red pen uncapped, checking the world against the Word, and he had been proud of it. He had thought that was faith.

It was proofreading. That was all it was. He had proofread God for decades, and found Him accurate, and never once trusted Him with anything.

Somewhere past three he got up and went downstairs without turning on a light, and sat at the round table in the dark, and opened the drawer under it, the one he had not opened in years.

Her things were in it. He had put them there after the funeral, everything from her side of the bed and her purse and her pockets, all in one drawer, and closed it, and not opened it since. A pair of reading glasses with a cracked lens. A tube of hand cream. A rosary that had been her mother's, though she had not been Catholic. A church bulletin from Greater New Hope, folded small. A pen. And a little spiral notebook with a blue cardboard cover, the kind they sold at the drugstore for a dollar, that he had never opened, because he had known what it was and had not wanted to know what was in it.

He opened it now, in the dark, and tilted it toward the faint light from the street.

It was her prayer list. He had known that. He had seen her writing in it every night of their married life, sitting up on her side of the bed with her knees drawn up and her reading glasses on the end of her nose. Pages and pages of it, in her loose, looping handwriting, names and dates. The children down the street. Her sister. The pastor. People from the hospital. A boy from the neighborhood who had gone to prison. And on every page, on every single page, at the top, before anything else, the same name.

*Walter.*

It was on the first page, dated the year they married. It was on the last page, dated the week she went into the hospital, the handwriting shaky. All those years. Every night. At the top of every page.

Beside his name, on some pages, she had written verses. Not prophecies. She had never cared much about the prophecies; she had teased him about his newspapers and his red pen. Short verses, simple ones, the kind they taught children, most of them in Jesus' own words. *For God so loved the world.* *Come unto me.* *I stand at the door, and knock.* And on the last page, in the shaky hand, beside his name, there was a single line.

*Lord, he knows all about You. Let him know You.*

Walt Simmons sat at his dinner table at three in the morning, with his dead wife's prayer list open in his hands, and after seventy-four years of checking, he had nothing left to check.

He did not know how to pray. That was the plain fact. He knew every prayer in the Bible. He could have recited Solomon's dedication of the temple, or Daniel's confession, or the Lord's own prayer in Matthew and Luke, and noted the differences. He did not know how to say a single word to God himself, in his own voice, about his own self. He had never done it. He was afraid to.

He was afraid, he understood, sitting there, because he had always believed that if he ever really spoke to God, God would answer, and he would have to do whatever God said. That was why he had kept to the newspaper and the red pen. A man could check prophecy all his life and never once have to obey anything.

*I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear.*

Job had known everything too. Job had been right about God for thirty chapters, and his friends had been wrong, and it had not been enough. It took the whirlwind. It took God Himself, speaking, asking him questions he could not answer. *Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding.* And Job, who had understanding, who had the best arguments in the book, put his hand over his mouth.

*But now mine eye seeth thee.*

Walt got up from the table. He left his cane. He went up the stairs in the dark with both hands on the rail, one step at a time, and down the hall into the bedroom, and around the foot of the bed to her side, the side nobody had slept on for years, and he got down on his knees beside it.

Getting down took some doing. His knees were seventy-four years old, and they had never done this, and they cracked, and he had to hold on to the mattress. When he was down, he had no words. He knelt there with his forehead against the edge of her side of the bed, where her pillow still was, and the smell of her hand cream was still faintly in the pillowcase after all those years because he had never washed it, and he could not think of a single word.

So he said her words.

"Lord," he said. His voice was a cracked whisper. "I know all about You. Let me know You."

Nothing happened. No light came, no voice, and Walt had expected none; he knew from the book that it did not usually go that way.

But he kept kneeling. And after a while, he found that he could say something else, something of his own. It came out of him slow and halting.

"I proofread You," he said. "For decades. I checked You. I never trusted You. I was too proud to need You, and too scared to obey You, and I hid behind knowing. You were right about everything and I knew it and it didn't matter to me." He stopped, and started again. "She asked me to pray with her. At the end. And I wouldn't. I said, You pray, honey. I'll listen." He could not go on for a minute. "I don't want to listen anymore. I want to come. If You'll still have an old fool who knew the whole road and never walked a step of it. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm Yours. Jesus. I'm Yours."

He said the Name. He had set it in type ten thousand times. He had never once said it to anyone.

And something answered.

It was not a voice. It was not a light. Later, when he tried to tell Ezra, he would only be able to say that it was like the moment in the composing room, all those years ago, when he finished setting a long column of type and locked it into the chase and pulled the first proof, and held the damp sheet up to the light, and every letter was where it belonged. Not like that. It was that. Everything in him that had been set backward and upside down for seventy-four years, every letter of him, turned around at once and settled into its place, and he was being read. He was being read and understood, all the way through, and loved anyway. He knelt on the floor of the bedroom beside his wife's side of the bed, and he wept, for the first time since the funeral, and whether it was grief or joy he could not tell, and he did not care.

*Now mine eye seeth thee.*

He knelt there until the window turned gray.

He put his palm flat on his breastbone where the surgeon's long scar ran, and felt the new valve beat against it, steady and ordinary and not his own work. The surgeon at Brandick Memorial had rebuilt his valve. A new heart he had never asked for. *A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh.* (Ezekiel 36:26)

\* \* \*

Then he went downstairs and made the coffee, two scoops and a pinch of salt, and sat down at the round table, and opened the ledger.

He left the news for later. For the first time in the record, he wrote something else.

He wrote the date in the left margin in red. *WEEK 12, SNOW.* And then, in the space where the facts went, in his careful square capitals:

*WALTER J. SIMMONS. BELIEVED.*

And in the right margin, the verse.

*Job 42:5.*

He sat looking at it. It was the second thing he had written in his life that was not a verse or a headline. The first had been a license plate, in October, in the margin of the morning paper, and he had hoped that night that he was a foolish old man. He had not been. He was not a fool this morning either.

Then he turned the page, because there was still news to write, and the record still had to be kept.

\* \* \*

He told Ezra that evening, before anyone else came. He made no speech of it. He set the ledger down on the table and opened it to the morning's page and turned it around and pushed it across.

Ezra read it once and then again. He got up, came around the table, and put his arms around the old man, in his chair, and held on, and Walt let him. Neither spoke. Elijah came in the back door with a pot of something that smelled like burned onions and stopped in the doorway and looked at them and said, "Well, all right," then set the pot on the stove and went back out to stand on the porch in the cold for five minutes to give them the room.

That night, when they prayed at the end of the reading, Walt prayed out loud. It was not very good. He stumbled, and repeated himself, and called God *sir* once by accident, the way he had called the managing editor *sir* for decades. Dolores laughed through her tears and squeezed his hand. Mrs. Okafor said *amen* after every sentence, to help him along. And when he finished, Ezra said *amen* too, and looked at him across the table with an expression Walt had seen once before, on the face of his own father, the day he got hired at the *Star*.

On the air, at nine, Ezra handed him the microphone.

Walt had read the record on the radio every other night for two months. His voice was known now in a few thousand kitchens in Northeast Washington, the old man with the newspaper, who knew where everything was. Not a word he had put on the air was anything but a fact or a verse.

He held the microphone in both hands, as Ezra did.

"This is Walt," he said. "The old man with the record. I want to tell you something that isn't in it." He cleared his throat. "Some of you are like me. You know the book. You've known it for years. You knew all this was coming. You can tell the people around you exactly what every sign means. And you're still here, and you're wondering why, and you're scared."

He stopped. Ezra was watching him. Nina, in the corner by the transmitter, had stopped typing.

"Knowing about Him won't save you," Walt said. "I'm seventy-four years old and I just found that out last night, on my knees, on the floor by my dead wife's side of the bed. The devils know everything I know. They believe every word, and they tremble. Trembling won't save you either. You have to come to Him. Not to the book about Him. To Him. Tonight. On your knees, if your knees still bend. Mine barely do." He tried to laugh and could not quite. "That's all. That's the whole record tonight. Back to Ezra."

He handed the microphone back. His hands were shaking.

Ezra took the microphone. Nina's hand was already hovering over the keys, waiting for the reading that always came next, and Ezra set the red notebook down on his knee, closed.

"No sermon tonight," he said. He looked at the old man, who was staring at his own hands. "My son wrote something. Some of you know it already. Tonight we'll just listen."

Nina pressed the key. The low line of the cello rose out of the steel box and out along the wire and into the snow, and in the coal bin nobody said another word.

That week there were more notes under the brick at the relief center than there had been in all of January. Elijah brought them back in his coat pockets, a stack of them, folded small, and laid them on the dinner table in front of Walt. Most of them said only a few words. *I knew it too. Last night I prayed.* *My father was a pastor. I never believed him. I do now.* *Tell the old man thank you.* One of them was written on the back of an Organization ration form, in a child's careful printing. *Mr. Walt, my grandma says you are a watchman too now. Is that true?*

Walt read that one several times. Then he took out his red pen and wrote in the record, under the day's news, in the right margin, where the verses went:

*Ezekiel 33:7.* And beside it, small, the only joke he had ever written in it: *Late hire.*

\* \* \*

The news came on the fourth of March, at six-thirty in the morning, on the BBC, through the static of the shortwave set on the kitchen counter.

Walt was sitting at the round table with his coffee and the ledger, and he almost missed it, because the announcer read it at the end of the bulletin, as a curiosity, in the bemused tone the British kept for things they could not place.

"Two men are still standing in Jerusalem," the announcer said.

"They came from nowhere anyone can determine, on the morning the covenant was signed, fifteen weeks ago, and took up a position on the broad stone plaza below the Temple Mount, near the new offices of the Council for Universal Moral Law, and began to preach. They are old, and bearded, and barefoot, and dressed in rough sackcloth the color of dust. They speak in Hebrew, and in Arabic, and in English, and some say in every language at once, so that every listener hears them in his own tongue. They speak against the Council and its covenant. They have called its president a false shepherd. They call on the city to look on Him whom they have pierced.

"On the second day, the Organization's security services attempted to remove them from the plaza. What happened next is disputed. Witnesses say the first two officers to lay hands on the old men were burned, though no one can say by what. One witness, a German tourist, says that fire came out of their mouths. The officers have been taken to hospital. The two men have not moved from the plaza since.

"And on the third day, a curious meteorological footnote. The men declared, before thousands of witnesses and every camera in the city, that no rain would fall on the land of Israel until they had finished their testimony. The rainy season in Jerusalem usually runs through March. Not a drop has fallen since they said it."

The bulletin moved on to the weather in London.

He had seen a paragraph about them in December, on page nineteen of the *Post*, under a mattress sale, and turned the page.

Walt sat with his pen in his hand. He did not need to look it up. He had set it in type himself, in nineteen seventy-nine, for a full-page advertisement a church in Anacostia had bought in the Sunday paper, in thirty-point Caslon, centered, with a border of thin rules.

*And I will give power unto my two witnesses, and they shall prophesy a thousand two hundred and threescore days, clothed in sackcloth… And if any man will hurt them, fire proceedeth out of their mouth, and devoureth their enemies… These have power to shut heaven, that it rain not in the days of their prophecy.*

He wrote it down. Facts on the left. Scripture on the right.

*WEEK 15, THAW. Two men in sackcloth, Jerusalem, below the Temple Mount. Fire. No rain.*

*Revelation 11:3–6.*

And then, because it was the first thing that occurred to him to do, he set down his pen, and folded his hands on the open ledger, and bowed his head, and prayed for two old men he had never met, half a world away, who were standing on a stone plaza in the sun with every gun the Organization owned pointed at them, and telling the truth.

When he looked up, there was a car parked across the street, in front of Ezra's house, that had not been there when he sat down.

It was white, with the gold circle of the Organization painted on the driver's door. Two people were sitting in it. One of them held a tablet up to the windshield, aimed at the Pattersons' front window, where Kambria's lamp was still burning.

## Chapter 28: Whose Right It Is

> *I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it: and it shall be no more, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him.* — Ezekiel 21:27

**Word study: *overturn* — עַוָּה** Hebrew *avvah* (Strong's H5754). A ruin; a heap of rubble; a thing turned upside down until nothing of its old shape is left. Ezekiel says it three times, the strongest a Hebrew writer could say anything. The crown of David would be overturned, and overturned, and overturned, and no one would wear it rightly again until the One came to whom it had always belonged.

Zedekiah was the last king to sit on David's throne in Jerusalem. He had sworn an oath by the name of the LORD to the king of Babylon, and broken it, and he had stopped his ears against the prophet. So the word of the LORD came to Ezekiel by the river Chebar, against him: *And thou, profane wicked prince of Israel, whose day is come, when iniquity shall have an end, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown: this shall not be the same: exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high.* (Ezekiel 21:25–26)

\* \* \*

The white car with the gold circle on its door sat in front of Ezra's house for forty minutes that morning in March, and then it drove away, and it did not come back that day, or the next.

It came back on the third day with a second car behind it.

Ezra watched them from the upstairs hall, through the gap in the curtains of Jalen's room. Four of them this time, two from each car, in the soft blue Organization jackets that were meant to look like relief workers and not like police. They went up Mrs. Okafor's walk first and knocked, and she opened the door, and Ezra could see from upstairs how her shoulders stiffened. They talked to her on her step for five minutes. One of them held a tablet up to her face and she let him. Then they thanked her and came down her walk and stood on the sidewalk in front of the Pattersons' house, looking up at the front window, where the lamp was.

They skipped the knock and wrote something down. Then they crossed the street to Walt's.

Walt let them in. Ezra had told him to, if they came, so that it would look ordinary. He watched the old man's front door close behind them and stood at the window counting. Nineteen minutes. When they came out, they were smiling, and one of them shook Walt's hand on the porch.

Walt came across the street an hour later with his thermos and sat down at the dinner table and took off his cap.

"They wanted to know if I was registered," he said. "I told them I was an old man and I didn't get out much, and the relief center scared me with all the lines, and I'd been meaning to. They said they'd send someone with a mobile unit. They were very kind." He set the thermos down. "Then the young one asked me about you."

"What about me?"

"Whether I knew the man across the street. Whether I'd ever heard of a radio program at night. He said there'd been complaints from the neighborhood about interference on the emergency band." Walt looked at him. "I told him I was too old for the radio. I lied to him, Ezra. I sat in my own kitchen and lied to a boy younger than my grandson would've been, and I don't know if God forgives that."

"Rahab did it," Ezra said. "For the spies."

"I know Rahab did it." Walt rubbed his face. "Hebrews eleven thirty-one. It's in the record." He frowned into his thermos. "Knowing it doesn't make it feel any better."

That night Nina came down from New York on the late train, and she did not take her coat off, and she did not sit down.

"They have the frequency," she said. "Not the location yet. The frequency. There's a work order in the system to put three receiving vans on it, triangulating, starting Monday. Northeast quadrant." She was very pale. "I can lose the work order for a few days. I can't make it disappear. If you broadcast from this house again after this weekend, they'll be at that basement door inside an hour."

Nobody spoke.

"Then we move it," Ezra said finally.

"Move it where?"

"I don't know yet." He looked around at the twenty-three people crowded into his kitchen and dining room and hall, sitting on the stairs and the counters and the floor, because the hidden church had outgrown the coal bin in February and was outgrowing the house now. "But I know we need batteries, and lamp oil, and water filters, and a way to carry the transmitter, and we can't buy any of it, because none of us have a card." He stood up. "I'll go out tomorrow before light."

"Alone?" Elijah said.

"Alone. One man looking for one thing. Two men is a patrol."

\* \* \*

He went out at four-thirty the next morning in the truck, with the headlights off for the first six blocks.

The hardware store on Bladensburg Road had been looted in the first week after the Rapture and again in January, and he had heard there might still be something in the back. It was a long, low building of painted cinder block with a sign that said FREEMAN BROS. HARDWARE SINCE 1952, half of it shot out. Somebody had pried the steel gate halfway up and left it hanging. He parked around the side and went in through the gap with a headlamp turned down to its red setting and an empty duffel bag over his shoulder.

The front of the store was stripped to the shelving. But in the back, past the plumbing aisle, there was a stockroom with a steel door that someone had tried and failed to force, and Ezra had hung a hundred doors like it. He had it off its hinges in six minutes with a flat bar and a hammer.

Inside were things nobody had thought to steal. Boxes of D batteries, still sealed. Three cases of lamp oil. A carton of ceramic water filters, the kind you set in a bucket. Coils of rope. Tarps. He was filling the duffel bag as fast as he could, kneeling on the concrete with the red light on his forehead, when he heard the engine.

It came up Bladensburg Road fast, a deep diesel growl, far too heavy for a car, and braked hard outside, and a door slammed.

Ezra switched off the headlamp and did not move.

Boots crunched over the broken glass at the front of the store. One man, moving without waste or hurry. A white light swept across the ceiling of the main room, then down the aisles one by one, then toward the back.

"Who's there?" A man's voice, low and hard. "I can hear you breathing. Come out with your hands where I can see them."

Ezra had every reason to stay hidden. The stockroom had a back door with a push bar. He could be through it and around the side to the truck in fifteen seconds, if it was not chained. He could not tell if it was chained.

He did know something else. He had spent four months in the Word, every night, as he had once spent his apprenticeship learning to read lumber. In the Proverbs, which Angela had loved, there was a verse he had copied into the front of his notebook in January, because he had needed it for his own temper: *A soft answer turneth away wrath.* And in Hebrews there was a line about the ones who were full grown, *who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.* He had been praying for months to have his senses exercised. He did not want to run without knowing what he was running from.

He stood up with his empty hands raised, and stepped into the doorway of the stockroom.

The white light hit him full in the face.

"It's just me," he said, keeping his voice even. "It's just Ezra. I'm not armed. I come in peace."

The light held on his face. Then it dropped to his chest, and Ezra could see the man holding it.

He was big, bigger than Ezra, and dressed for war: helmet, dark plate carrier with pouches across the front, a rifle at his shoulder with the light mounted under the barrel, a pistol on his thigh, gloves, boots. His face under the helmet was weathered and bearded, nearer sixty than fifty, with eyes that stayed on Ezra's hands. He did not look like a Peacekeeper. Peacekeepers wore blue. Nor did he look like one of the gangs that had come out of the suburbs in January. He was too disciplined, and too still.

And hanging outside his vest, on a plain steel chain, swinging slightly against the dark plate, was a cross.

It was small and silver and worn smooth. In a city where the faith of Jesus Christ had been declared divisive in the first weeks and dangerous soon after, where people had been taken from their homes for less, a man was wearing it on the outside of his armor, where anyone could see.

Ezra looked at it. He could not help himself.

The man caught him looking. Then the man's eyes dropped from Ezra's face to Ezra's collar and stopped there, and a look crossed the hard bearded face, wary and then astonished.

Ezra had forgotten he had it on. A second cross, smaller, plain silver on a leather cord at his own throat. Angela had given it to him on an anniversary more than ten years back, and he had not worn it once since, until the morning the watch began to tick.

Two crosses, in a looted store, in a city where either one could get a man taken from his house.

Neither of them moved.

"You're a believer," the man said slowly.

"Since November," Ezra said. "You?"

"Since November."

The rifle came down until it pointed at the floor.

They stood in the dark hardware store looking at each other, two strangers in the wreckage of the city, and Ezra let his hands come down.

"Michael," the man said, and lowered the light out of Ezra's eyes. "My name's Michael."

"Ezra."

"I heard." Michael studied him. "You're not *the* Ezra? On the radio? The carpenter."

"I'm the carpenter."

Michael nodded slowly. "We've been tracking you since you crossed the tree line by the Arboretum. One truck, no headlights, nobody behind you. A man that alone on that road is up to something, so I came in to find out who you were, and whether you'd take everything or only what you needed." He glanced at the duffel, which held only batteries, oil and filters, and at Ezra's open hands. "I'd have bet on a looter. We've been listening to you since the first night. Me and my men. We pick you up off a repeater on a hill north of Baltimore. Every night at nine. That cello." Then his face hardened again, careful. "Show me your hands. Both sides. And your forehead. Push your hair back."

Ezra understood. He turned his wrists over in the light, backs and then palms, and pushed his hair off his forehead with both hands, and held still. No red string. No scan scar. No mark. It had not come yet, not the real thing, only the registration. But they were already checking each other.

"Now you," Ezra said.

Michael's eyebrows went up. Then a smile moved in his beard. He stripped off his gloves and held out his hands and turned them over. He pushed up the front of his helmet. Clean.

"There's two more in the truck," he said. "You want to check them too?"

"You bet I do."

Michael laughed, a short bark, startled out of him. "Good. You'd be surprised how many don't."

The two in the truck were younger, a tall Black man with a shaved head named Dorsey and a red-bearded kid from West Virginia named Pruitt, and they were clean, and they checked Ezra again, and by the end of it all four of them were standing in the first gray light beside the armored truck on Bladensburg Road, laughing, with no good reason to laugh at all. Ezra had not laughed in weeks.

Ezra looked at Michael across the hood of the truck. "You're the ground-hum man."

Michael's beard shifted. "You fixed it?"

"Took me a week."

"Took you a week." Michael nearly smiled. "I was about to drive down there and do it myself."

*Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity.*

\* \* \*

Michael helped him load the duffel. Then he leaned against the armored door with his arms folded over the cross and considered Ezra for a full minute.

"You can't go back to that house," he said.

"I've got twenty-three people—"

"I know what you've got. I've heard you every night. The old man with the record, and the joker who cooks, and the lady who cries." Michael's voice was flat and certain. "The Peacekeepers start moving through the Northeast quadrant Monday. Not the relief workers. The other ones, with the vans. House to house. Anybody unregistered goes on a bus to a processing center in Maryland, and some come back with a card, and some don't come back. They've got your frequency."

"How do you know that?"

"Because they've got mine too, and I've been running for three months." Michael pushed himself off the truck. "I'm not asking you to leave your people. I've got men. I've got trucks. I've got places all over this city and up the coast. My men will move your twenty-three tonight, a few at a time, into houses where the walls are thick and the neighbors are ours. Your old man too." He paused. "And you come north with me."

"North where?"

"Where the supply comes from." Michael held his gaze. "You've got the Word, Ezra. I've heard you. You've got more of it in four months than Grace's preacher got through in fifteen years, and I'd know. She brought every sermon home and read it to me over Sunday dinner. But you don't know how to stay alive, and you don't know how to keep anybody else alive, and you're about to have a lot more than twenty-three. You need what I've got. And God knows I need what you've got." He held out his hand. "Come and see."

Ezra thought of the coal bin, and the lamp in the window, and Walt's thermos on the dinner table. He thought of the young Peacekeeper on Walt's porch, smiling, shaking the old man's hand.

He took the hand.

\* \* \*

They moved the twenty-three that night in four trips, in a delivery van with a bakery's name still painted on its side. Walt went last. He would not go until he had seen every one of the others out the back door and into the van. Then he stood in Ezra's kitchen with his cane in one hand and his green ledger under his arm and looked around at the table and the candle and the clippings on the dining room wall, and said, "Well," and nothing else.

Michael was waiting in the back doorway. "He comes with me first," he said to Walt. "I want a look at your man before I take on his people. Then I'll send for the rest of you."

Walt looked him over: the armor, the beard, the cross. "And if you don't like what you see?"

"Then you'll have him back sooner."

Walt grunted. He put his free hand on Ezra's shoulder. "Go and learn something. Then read it to us." He went out the back door into the dark, with Pruitt holding his elbow.

Ezra took the lamp out of the front window last of all, and blew it out, and wrapped it in a towel, and carried it to Michael's truck. His own truck he left in the driveway with the keys on the seat; Pruitt came back for it the next night, and by the end of the week it was in a barn in Maryland, painted flat gray, hauling lumber for the walls.

They drove north all the next day on back roads Michael knew, the long way up through Maryland, doubling back twice, around checkpoints that Dorsey called in on a handheld radio from a mile ahead, through towns where every third house was dark and the churches were boarded up and spray-painted with the gold circle. On some of them, under the circle, a different can had added six words in black: *REPENT YE, AND BELIEVE THE GOSPEL.* Ezra knew them. It was the first thing Jesus preached in Galilee. "Houses on the line," Michael said, without slowing. "See that, and somebody within three streets will feed you." It was dusk when they crossed the Mason-Dixon line into Pennsylvania, and full dark when Michael turned off a county road onto a logging track that climbed into the South Mountain woods, bare and black.

He stopped in a clearing and cut the engine. Nothing sounded but the ticking of the cooling block.

"We walk from here," he said.

They walked a mile uphill in the dark with no lights, Michael in front and Ezra stumbling behind him over roots and rocks, until the woods opened onto a steep slope of jumbled boulders under a cliff, and Michael stopped before a crack in the rock no wider than a doorway.

Before he went in, he did something Ezra did not understand. He took a coil of fine fishing net from a pouch on his vest, nearly invisible, and strung it across the mouth of the crack, hooking it onto small eyes screwed into the rock, and touched a wire at one end to something hidden in a crevice. Then he cut two boughs from a hemlock beside the opening and laid them across the mouth, so that from ten feet away it looked like nothing but rock and a tree.

"Anything touches that net, it rings a bell inside," he said. "Deer, sometimes. But we're ready if it's not."

Inside, the crack became a passage that sloped gently downward, back into the hill, much farther than Ezra would have believed, until it opened all at once into a chamber so large his small light did not reach the far wall.

Michael lit a fire.

It was a great round room of stone, domed overhead, forty feet across. High in the center of the dome was a natural chimney in the rock, and Ezra watched the smoke rise up through it into the night while cold, clean air came down the same way and moved across his face. The firelight lit the walls orange and gold, and the walls hid it completely. From outside, Michael said, you could stand on top of the hill and never know there was a fire under your feet.

Back on the county road, in the last light, Michael had shot a grouse with a bow. He cleaned it now beside the fire, spitted it on a green stick, and turned it over the coals until the fat dripped and hissed, and handed Ezra half of it on a flat stone.

Ezra had not eaten fresh meat since November. He held it a moment, though it burned his fingers, and bowed his head over it. He didn't know the words men said over food. Angela had always said them. "Thank You," he said. "For the bird. And for him." It came out short and awkward, and he ate before it cooled.

When the meat was gone his mouth was dry as sawdust. He looked around the chamber for a jug, a canteen, anything, and found nothing, and did not ask. Michael watched him look.

"Thirsty?"

"I'll make it till morning."

Michael regarded him across the fire a while. Then he pulled a square of white cotton cloth from a pack and tossed it over.

"You won't have to," he said. "Go down that passage about thirty feet. Relieve yourself on that. All the way. Then bring it back."

Ezra stared at him.

"Well," Michael said, "you're the one that's thirsty."

He did it. When he came back holding the wet cloth at arm's length, Michael had set a small scorched tin can into the edge of the coals. He had Ezra drop the cloth into it. When the can began to steam and then to boil, Michael set a collapsible camp pot upside down over it, a pot with a little pouring spout on its rim, and tilted it just so. The steam rose into the cold pot and gathered on its inside and ran down, drop by drop, out through the spout into a tin cup Michael held beneath it.

It took twenty minutes to fill the cup. Michael handed it to him.

It was water. Clear and warm and clean, tasting of nothing at all.

Ezra did not put his face down to it. He drank sitting up, with his eyes on the passage they had come in by. He was not sure yet how far to trust the man across the fire. Michael saw it, and said nothing.

Then Ezra lowered the cup and looked into it, at the cloth and the can and himself, and he started to laugh and could not stop, and Michael sat across the fire with the corner of his mouth turned up in his beard.

\* \* \*

Over the fire that night, Michael told him a little. Only a little.

"I came home from Desert Storm and stayed in," he said. "Military police. Then SWAT, in a county north of Baltimore." He turned the stick in the coals.

The fire popped. He waited it out.

"Twenty-sixth of November I came off a night shift at six. Pulled into my own driveway. Front door standing open. Daniel's bicycle on its side in the yard." His voice did not change, and that was the worst of it. "Grace's side of the bed was made. And empty."

"Everybody who was in the book was taken," he said, staring into the fire. "Everybody who was ready. And I wasn't." He was silent. "But we still have a chance. Don't we? The ones left. Tell me that. You're the one who reads."

Ezra had been asked that question twenty times since December, at the dinner table and on the air. He had never been asked it by a man in armor in a cave.

"Yes," he said. "John saw it. A great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, standing before the throne in white robes. And one of the elders asked him who they were. And the answer was, *These are they which came out of great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.* (Revelation 7:14) That's the ones who were taken, Michael. The ones who were ready." He leaned toward the fire. "But John saw others, too. Under the altar, the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held. *And white robes were given unto every one of them…* (Revelation 6:11) That's for the ones who come to Him now, whatever it costs. God's still calling people. Jesus told the church at Sardis, *…I will not blot out his name out of the book of life…* (Revelation 3:5)"

Michael's jaw was tight. "The church," he said roughly. "When they left, the restrainer left with them. That's what Grace used to tell me over Sunday dinner. *only he who now letteth will let, until he be taken out of the way.* (2 Thessalonians 2:7) And now all hell's loose on the ones who are left."

"The restraint is gone," Ezra said. "Second Thessalonians two. The hand that was holding it all back has stepped away, and it's coming. But the Spirit didn't leave, Michael. I felt Him come. On my kitchen floor, in the dark, with my hands out, after they were all gone. The Comforter came anyway." He held Michael's eyes. "Joel says it. *…I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh… whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered…* (Joel 2:28, 32) That's not a promise for before. That's a promise for now."

Michael held his gaze across the fire. Then he bowed his head over his folded hands, and his shoulders moved once, and Ezra looked away into the dark and let him be.

\* \* \*

Michael kept him in the front of the cave for days and nights.

He called it resting up. There was nothing to do in the front of the cave but wait, and Ezra waited. Once a day a nameless man brought a tin plate of beans and a heel of bread, and left it without a word.

On the first night a young man came in shivering from the cold outside, and Ezra gave him his blanket and sat the rest of the night against the wall. On the second day there was half a loaf left over and no one in the cave but him, and he broke it in three and left two pieces on the ledge by the passage for whoever came by. When a man with a lantern asked him whether he had gone farther into the hill in the night, he said that he had walked ten steps down the left passage looking for water, and turned back when the dark began to frighten him. It would have cost him nothing to say no.

Those days were a stripping down. He sat in the dark front chamber with a candle and Angela's Bible and nothing to fix, nothing to build, no one to read to and no one to perform for, and he prayed more in those days than in the forty-four years before them. *That the trial of your faith, being much more precious than of gold that perisheth, though it be tried with fire.*

On the fourth morning, Michael came down the passage with a lantern and stopped in front of him.

"Grace and peace unto you," he said.

Ezra stood up and dusted off the knees of his pants. "And unto you."

"Follow me."

Past the great dome the cave split three ways. Michael stopped at the fork and held the lantern high so Ezra could see all three mouths.

"Pick one."

Ezra looked from one to the next. "Does it matter?"

"Not to me. Front's kept dark on purpose. Whichever one you take, forty feet in you step on a plate and a light comes on behind you." Michael tipped his head at a black notch high in the left wall. "And a man up in there has your whole left side."

"With a rifle."

"With a bow. A rifle tells the whole hill."

"You'd shoot a man for picking the wrong hole?"

"There's no wrong hole. He picks one and he gets a light. What he does in the light is up to him." Michael took the left passage. "This one. Mind your head."

At the end of it was a small chamber, and in its back wall a slab of gray rock taller than either of them. Michael set his palm flat on one spot and leaned. The slab swung inward without a sound.

Ezra couldn't help it. "Who hung that?"

"A man who'd have liked you." Behind the slab stood a steel door, and behind the door an elevator with a single brass button. "Army put in the steel. My father put in the rock."

"Your father."

"Hold the rail. It's a long way down."

When the doors opened, Ezra did not step out. He stood in the opening and stared.

Concrete corridors ran off in three directions under steady white lights. Men and women of every age went by in work clothes and sweaters, carrying crates, pushing carts, talking low. None of them wore blue.

"What is this place?"

"An old volcano. Fell in on itself before Adam." Michael stepped out and waited for him. "The Army dug into the wall of it in the fifties, for a war with the Russians that never came, and then forgot it. My father didn't forget it. Bought it for scrap in eighty-nine. Paid less than he paid for his truck." A woman with a clipboard nodded to him as she passed, and he nodded back. "He left it to me. I gave it to the church."

"Which church?"

Michael looked down the corridor at the people. "This one."

On the wall facing the elevator, painted in plain black letters a foot high, was the first half of the verse Kambria had copied under Angela's prayer:

*AND AT THAT TIME SHALL MICHAEL STAND UP, THE GREAT PRINCE WHICH STANDETH FOR THE CHILDREN OF THY PEOPLE.* DANIEL 12:1.

"Children of Thy People," Michael said. "That's what the sign says. The ones who live here just call it the Rock. My mother named me out of that verse. I never read it till December." He glanced at Ezra sidelong. "You and me both, I guess."

He put something into Ezra's hand: a smooth white stone the size of an egg, with nothing written on it.

"What's this for?"

"Nobody comes down here who isn't brought. Three days in the front, and the elders hear how you spent them. You gave away your blanket. You split your bread three ways. You told the truth about ten steps in the dark when a lie was free. And the first night, you drank with your eyes on the door." He closed Ezra's fingers over it. "Everyone who stays gets one of those. What's written on it is between you and Him."

Ezra turned the stone over. "What's on yours?"

Michael tapped the pocket of his vest, once. "Nice try."

Jesus promised it to the church at Pergamos: *To him that overcometh will I give to eat of the hidden manna, and will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.* (Revelation 2:17)

The storerooms went back farther than the lights. Sacks of rice and wheat and beans, cans and jars, water in blue drums stacked three high.

"How many does this feed?" Ezra said.

"Two hundred and twelve, as of this morning. Four years, if nobody gets greedy. Three if they do."

"And if they do?"

"Then God will make provisions for His people."

In the radio room a map of the Eastern seaboard covered one wall, crossed with lines in colored marker, the routes the supply trucks ran. Along each line sat small round stickers, each with a number in black. Michael touched each one as he passed. Four along the Baltimore line. Two in Delaware. One he did not name, in the Pennsylvania hills.

"These are our distribution channels," he said. "Each one counts. Each one guards. Each one knows only the next. No one but me knows what all the numbers mean."

"Seven," Ezra said. "Seven candlesticks."

Michael looked at him. "You counted."

"Twenty-some years of measuring twice."

"Good. We could use an eager mind and a good memory down here."

At the console, a young operator in a headset, a thin kid named Anton with a pencil behind his ear and a milk crate of burned discs under his chair, turned and said, "Boss. Peacekeeper traffic."

Michael took the headset from the young man, listened, wrote one word on the pad with his father's square capitals, and held it up for Ezra to see.

*PALEHORSE.*

"Third time this week," Michael said. "Cold-chain trucks. Registered clinics only. The dispatcher says it like a lot number. 'PALEHORSE Lot Four, staged at Fort Detrick.' I don't know what it is."

Ezra had to wet his lips. "I do."

He told him, standing in the radio room with the numbered map at his back: the drive in the spine of the concordance, the files, the nursing homes, the woman in the cell and the camera that had watched her go. When he finished Michael had put the headset down and did not seem to know what to do with his hands.

"A plague that picks its victims by the ledger," Michael said, very low. "Revelation six, verse eight."

"*And power was given unto them over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with sword, and with hunger, and with death, and with the beasts of the earth.*"

"Then there's no hiding in the registry," Michael said. "And no hiding outside it, if they decide to come after us in the same breath." His jaw set.

Michael led him down a long corridor to a steel door and stopped with his hand on it. "You've been hearing it for an hour."

Ezra listened. A deep, even hum came up through the floor. "I thought it was the lights."

"It's what runs the lights." Michael opened the door. "Water."

The door gave onto a gallery cut out of the living rock. Thirty feet below, a black stream ran fast and cold through a stone channel and turned the blades of two iron wheels set into the flow. Heavy cables climbed the wall from the wheels and ran off into the dark. Over the door, in the same black letters as the sign by the elevator:

*He shall dwell on high: his place of defence shall be the munitions of rocks: bread shall be given him; his waters shall be sure.* (Isaiah 33:16)

"I didn't pick that one either," Michael said. "I read it in January and found it was already true."

"Where's it come from? The water."

"Off the rim. Rain and snowmelt go into the mountain through a fault the old miners never found. We dammed it upstream behind a wall you could walk past all day."

"And when it floods?"

"Side channel. Sinks back into the stone. This floor's never seen an inch." He pointed down at the wheels. "Those turn the generators. Lights, pumps, fans, the radio. All of it off one creek."

"No fuel," Ezra said.

"No fuel to haul, nothing for a drone to smell, and no switch on a desk in New Jersey." Michael leaned on the rail. "That's the part I like."

Below the wheels the water stepped down through a stair of stone basins, gravel, then sand, then charcoal, then white cotton stretched on wooden frames.

Ezra looked at the cotton a long time. "That's the rag."

"Same as the cloth I gave you that first night. Only bigger."

"You could've just told me."

"You'd have forgotten it by morning." Michael pushed off the rail. "You won't forget that cloth."

Past the filter beds the channel split. Most of the water went on toward the growing rooms. A narrower arm of it turned off through a low arch, and Michael ducked under and took Ezra after it.

On the far side, three long chambers had been cut side by side into the rock, and the cold met them at the arch. Down the middle of each floor ran an open trough of black water a yard wide, moving fast and quiet, with a plank walk on either side. Shelves stood along both walls: crocks with cloth tied over their mouths, sacks of potatoes and onions on slats, wheels of hard cheese wrapped in wax, cuts of smoked meat hung from iron hooks. Every crock sat in a stone cradle that dipped into the trough, so the water ran around its belly.

At the head of each chamber, set into the ceiling over the trough, was a square iron mouth with a fan behind it, turning slow.

"Air comes down the shafts off the top of the mountain," Michael said. "The fans pull it in and throw it straight down onto the water. It runs the whole length of the room over the trough before it goes out the far end, and by then it's cold enough to see your breath in July." He held his palm under the iron mouth until Ezra did the same. "The water's what does the work. The fan just carries it."

"And in summer the water stays cold?"

"It comes out of the rock at the same temperature every month of the year. Too deep for August to find it." He nodded at the trough. "Winter's when it earns its keep. Snowmelt comes in off the rim near freezing, and this room drops to where milk keeps two weeks and meat keeps till spring."

At the end of the last chamber, a side room was packed to the ceiling with straw, and in the straw, in rows, lay blocks of gray-white ice a foot thick.

"January," Michael said. "We let the upper channel freeze in wooden forms, cut it out, and bury it in straw down here. It's still here in August. The medicine goes in that room, and anything else that won't keep." He shut the door on it and the cold stayed in. "A cold room the Lord built. All I did was dig the door and hang a fan."

Ezra pointed up at a round iron grille in the ceiling. "And those?"

"Lungs. Forty shafts to the surface, under brush and boulders and a dead oak stump. Clear day, the caps come off and the whole mountain breathes." Michael laid his palm on the passage wall and waited until Ezra did the same. The stone was warm under his palm. "The old fire, way down. It's like this all year."

In the last gallery men and women worked with hammers and chisels in a pale cloud of dust, widening a passage by lamplight. Masons, quarrymen, a few old tunnelers out of the subway. "The stone company," Michael said. "What they cut comes out as walls and steps. The rest goes up to the growing rooms, and whatever's left goes into the floors of the passages we'd rather nobody came down."

"Who taught you to build like this?"

Michael walked several steps before he answered. "My father. Always ready. Cans in the basement when other men on our block were buying lottery tickets. Water barrels. A generator he ran on the first of every month to make sure it still would. They laughed at him on the block, and at church." He tapped the wall twice with two fingers. "He used to say a man who prepares isn't afraid, he's obedient. Noah. Joseph in Egypt. He deeded me forty acres of mountain and a bunker the Army had given up on, the year I came home from the Army, with his water drums already lined up inside. He was in his chair the morning of the twenty-sixth. Now he's not."

At the next door Michael tried the handle, let go, and tried it again.

"You did that at the last one too," Ezra said.

"I count things. Doors, drums, people. My mother called it a sickness. My father called it inventory."

"What do you call it?"

Michael thought about it. "Staying alive long enough to be useful."

The gallery narrowed to a cut no wider than a man's shoulders, and Michael stopped at its mouth with his lamp held low. The channel ran on ahead of them, a hand's breadth of black water in a groove as straight as a rule.

"The masons dug this from both ends," he said. "Two crews, one working up from the water and one working down from the grow rooms, cutting toward each other by the sound of the chisels."

"How close did they come?"

"A finger's width." He kept his eyes on the channel. "We'd read how it was done before we ever picked up a hammer." *This same Hezekiah also stopped the upper watercourse of Gihon, and brought it straight down to the west side of the city of David.* (2 Chronicles 32:30) "He closed the springs outside his walls so the Assyrians would come and find nothing. *Why should the kings of Assyria come, and find much water?* (2 Chronicles 32:4) Vale's patrols have walked this whole ridge. They found a creek that runs thin in August and goes under the rock. Everything it carries comes out in one place, and that place is not on any map."

"They heard each other through the rock," Ezra said. "The two crews."

Michael looked at him. "Through the rock. That's the whole trick of this place."

The cut opened into a long hall under blue-white lamps, and Ezra smelled green before he saw it. Troughs stood in racks to the ceiling, lettuce and beans and young wheat, and water ran down the racks in a thin bright sheet, over the roots and out the far end, where it fell away through a slot in the floor. Michael did not take him down after it. The beds were not filled with earth. They were filled with stone, ground fine and sifted, the same stone the masons had taken out of the channel.

"Nothing leaves the mountain," Michael said. "Not the water, not the rock. What we cut out, we grow in." He put two fingers into a trough and let the water run over them. "The channel was Hezekiah's way of keeping a city alive through a siege. This is the same channel. It only ends in something green."

But the water did not stop at the green. Past the last rack the channel dropped through a cut in the floor, and Michael took a lamp off its hook and led him down eleven steps into a room he had saved for last.

It was a pool. Square, cut straight down into the living rock, as long as a pickup truck and deep enough to stand in to the chest. Stone steps went down into it on two sides. The channel spilled in at one end over a lip of rock, in a sheet as clear as glass, and left by a grate at the other, on its way back to the wheels. The water was so still and so clean that the bottom looked closer than it was. One lamp hung over it. Above the inflow, cut into the rock in the same black letters as the verses upstairs, was a single word.

*SILOAM.*

And along the lip where the channel spilled in, smaller, the masons had chiseled two more: *ENGEDI* on the near side of the stream and *ENEGLAIM* on the far.

"The masons named it," Michael said. "I didn't argue." He set the lamp on the top step. "Jesus spat in the dirt and put it on a blind man's eyes and told him, *Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.)* (John 9:7) Hezekiah's tunnel came out at that pool. Ours comes out at this one." He looked at the water. "Everybody who stays goes down into it. Not because the water does anything. Because He said to."

Ezra crouched and touched the letters on the lip. "What's this?"

"Ezekiel forty-seven." Michael didn't need the Book. "He sees water coming out from under the threshold of the temple. Ankle deep, then knee deep, then a river a man can't cross. It runs down into the Dead Sea, and the dead water turns sweet. *And every thing shall live whither the river cometh.* (Ezekiel 47:9) And then fishermen stand on the shore *from Engedi even unto Eneglaim*, spreading their nets." (Ezekiel 47:10)

He nodded at the near side. "Everybody knows where Engedi is. Springs over the Dead Sea. David hid in the caves there with his men while Saul hunted him." He nodded at the far side. "Nobody knows where Eneglaim is. Men have dug for it for two hundred years. One says it's a spring on the north shore. One says it's across the water in Moab. One says it's under the salt. Nobody's found it." He picked the lamp up. "The masons figured it this way. The river starts at a place everybody can find, and it ends at a place nobody can. You don't get there by a map. You get there by following the water."

Ezra stood at the edge. The cold came up off the surface into his face.

"I was baptized," he said. "At Pilgrim Rest. I was six." He heard his own voice go flat. "My father put me under. Deacon Patterson, in his white robe, with the whole church singing. He held me down a little too long. I came up choking, and he laughed, and four hundred people laughed with him."

Michael didn't say anything for a while.

"What did it mean?" he asked finally.

"That my father was a deacon."

Michael nodded slowly, as if Ezra had answered a different question, the right one. He picked up the lamp and went back up the steps and left Ezra standing alone at the edge of the water, looking at the word on the wall.

And there was one more room, with a long table and shelves to the ceiling. Michael opened it, and stood back, and let Ezra enter alone.

It was a library. Bibles, hundreds of them, in every size and binding. Concordances. Old commentaries with cracked spines. Hymnals. Children's Bibles with pictures. And on one long shelf, notebooks: handwritten copies of whole books of Scripture, Psalms and John and Romans and Isaiah, written out from memory and from borrowed pages by people who had watched the printed ones seized and burned.

"They're burning them now," Michael said from the doorway. "Not everywhere. Not yet. But in the cities the Organization's collecting them. Divisive literature. My men pull them out of the fires when they can, and out of the warehouses, and out of the empty churches. We keep the Word two ways down here: on the page, and in the heart. Somebody memorizes, somebody copies." He paused. "You ever hear about the Bibles of Petra?"

Ezra shook his head.

"My grandmother told it to me. Years ago, Christians carried Bibles into the caves at Petra, in Jordan, and hid them there, waiting for the day Israel would have to flee into the wilderness and need them." Michael shrugged. "I don't know if it's true. I live by it anyway. Every cave on my routes has Bibles hidden in it for whoever comes after us."

Ezra stood among the shelves with his hand on the long table and looked at the spines.

He thought of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, whom he had read about in January. The king had sat by the fire in his winter house and cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife, three or four columns at a time, and thrown it in the fire until it was consumed.
