And God had said to Jeremiah: *Take thee again another roll, and write in it all the former words.* So Baruch sat down and wrote it all again, from Jeremiah's mouth. And added, the Book said, *many like words.*

"Who does the copying?" he asked.

"Whoever can," Michael said. "Not enough of us."

"I can," Ezra said. "I'm a scribe."

Michael nodded. "Then you'll need hands. Who do you want up here? Not all twenty-three. The ones you'd build with."

Ezra didn't have to think. "Walt. Elijah. Mrs. Okafor, she copies faster than I do. Dolores. Marcus."

"The joker who cooks, and the lady who cries."

"The lady who cries prays all night," Ezra said. "You'll want her."

Michael wrote the five names on his pad in square capitals. "Four days."

\* \* \*

He stayed twenty-one days.

Michael called it a Daniel fast, and kept it with him, as every new leader in the camp had kept it. *I ate no pleasant bread, neither came flesh nor wine in my mouth, neither did I anoint myself at all, till three whole weeks were fulfilled.* Vegetables, beans and water. Daniel had been told, at the end of his three weeks, that his prayer was heard on the first day, but the prince of the kingdom of Persia had withstood the angel one and twenty days, until Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help.

The first days had been the testing. The middle days were the training. Michael's men took him through the passages until he could walk them blind. They taught him the routes and the safe houses and the code words, and how to speak on a radio so that anyone listening would hear nothing they could use. They taught him how to read a checkpoint from a mile away and when to turn around. They were men who had come to Michael with nothing, Dorsey said, the way the distressed and the debtors and the discontented had come to David in the cave of Adullam, four hundred of them, and he became a captain over them. Dorsey drilled the first rule of escort work into him on the fifth night: you never walk a stranger anywhere he hasn't earned. Everyone who came to the Rock came in at night, hooded or behind a blacked-out windshield, with a man at each elbow, and spent three days in the front rooms being watched before anyone showed him a door. Every morning and every night, Ezra taught them the Word at the long table in the library, and they heard him gladly.

On the sixth day Michael put the bow in his hands himself. Ezra's first arrow went into the wall a yard left of the straw.

"You're aiming," Michael said.

"That's the idea."

"Quit it. Look at the spot you want. Your hands know where your eyes are."

The second arrow went into the straw, low. Michael grunted. "Now you're a danger to rabbits."

In the hours between lessons, he copied. He sat at the long table under the white lights with a stack of blank notebooks and a box of black pens and a Bible open before him, and he wrote out the Gospel of John word by word in his square capitals, because a carton of children's Bibles had been burned in Hartford and somebody had to replace them. His hand cramped. He kept writing. *In the beginning was the Word.* He thought of his son in the studio, writing a song in a notebook one measure at a time, for seven years, for a father who never came to hear it.

On the eighth night the bell rang inside.

Ezra was at the long table copying when Dorsey put his head in the door. "Van's at the net. Boss says you'll want to see this."

They came in hooded, one at a time, with a man at each elbow, as everyone did. Five of them. The first stopped dead in the mouth of the passage and said from under his hood, "If this is a kidnapping, young man, I'm seventy-four and I bruise."

"Walt," Ezra said.

Dorsey pulled the hood off. Walt blinked in the firelight at the dome, at the smoke going up the chimney, at Ezra standing there thinner than he had left him. He set his cane against the rock with great care.

"Well," he said. Then he said nothing at all, and held on to Ezra by both arms.

Elijah came out of his hood already talking. "Three hours on the floor of a bread truck. I counted every pothole in Delaware. Ez, you look terrible. Is there food? Tell me there's food."

Behind them came Mrs. Okafor, then Dolores with her hand on Pruitt's arm, then Marcus, rubbing his back.

Michael stood at the edge of the firelight with his arms folded over the cross and gave them a minute. Then he stepped in.

"Three days in the front," he said. "Same as he did. Same as everybody."

Walt looked up at him. "You sent for us."

"Said I would."

"I've listened to him on a tape in a bread box for a week." Walt tapped the green ledger under his arm. "He says you count things."

"I do."

"So do I. We'll get along fine, or we won't."

Michael let a breath out through his nose, which from him was a laugh. "Dorsey. Find this man a good chair."

Ezra was not allowed to go to them, and he did not try.

On the second day Dorsey reported that Elijah had talked the man who brought the beans into letting him season them. On the second night Dolores prayed out loud until nearly dawn, for every soul in the hill whose name she knew, and when she ran out of names she prayed for the ones she didn't. Marcus gave his blanket to Walt. Walt complained about the cold, the dark, the beans and the hour, and on the third morning, when the man with the lantern asked whether he had gone down any of the passages in the night, he said, "Twice. Found a wall and my own bad knee."

Michael came for them on the fourth morning with five white stones in his pocket.

Ezra's nine o'clock reading had been recorded at the long table in the library every night since his first week in the hill. Anton ran a cable down the corridor from the radio room, and the tapes went south. On the fourteenth night there were two microphones on the table instead of one.

Walt sat at the new one with his ledger open. Ezra sat at the other with Angela's Bible. Elijah leaned in the doorway with a dish towel over his shoulder, Mrs. Okafor beside him, and Michael stood at the back with his arms folded.

"Rolling," Anton said.

The cello came first, off the tablet Michael had carried out of his son's room. Then Walt: "This is Walt, with the record." He read the week. Bread, fuel, the Census, the rain that had not fallen in Jerusalem. Then Ezra read the chapter. Then the boxed line.

"Out," Anton said.

Nothing went out from the mountain. At dawn the tape went south under the flour in a bread box, and the next night at nine, from a rooftop in Washington, Pruitt played it into the transmitter and moved to another roof before the vans could turn their heads.

After that the long table was never empty. Mornings, Ezra taught. Walt sat at his elbow with the ledger and stopped him when he got a date wrong. Mrs. Okafor copied Romans at the far end, faster than anyone. Elijah fed them all and had the masons laughing by the second day. Dolores took the night watch in the radio room with Anton and prayed over every tape before it went south. Marcus learned the routes from Dorsey and could draw them from memory inside a week. Michael stood at the back with his arms folded, and some mornings he stayed for the whole of it.

\* \* \*

On the twelfth day Elijah came into the library with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and flour on one cheek, and pulled Ezra up from the long table by the arm.

"Anton's taking the new ones down below at the watch change," he said. "I'm the new ones. You're coming."

"I've been here two weeks."

"And you never been down below. I asked."

Anton was waiting at the bottom of the corridor in a gray sweater gone through at both elbows, the pencil behind his ear and a ring of keys on a bootlace around his neck. He had a lamp for each of them. He looked at Ezra a little shyly. Every night he had sat three feet from him with the headphones on and had never once said more than "Rolling" and "Out."

"Mr. Patterson."

"Ezra."

"Ezra." Anton turned the lamp wicks up. "It's a walk. Watch your heads on the second stair."

They went down past the radio room, through a steel door Anton unlocked and locked again behind them, and the white lights stopped. Beyond it the passage was older. The Army's concrete gave out after a dozen yards, and then it was the mountain's own rock, shaped by hand, with the chisel marks still in it in rows. A pipe ran along the ceiling, and a cable stapled to wooden pegs ran beside the pipe. The stair Anton had warned them about turned under a low lip of stone, and Elijah found it with his forehead anyway and said something he then apologized to the Lord for.

The farther they went, the warmer it got. The cold of the upper halls fell away behind them a step at a time. Ezra put his hand on the wall and it was warm, then warmer, and the air thickened and turned damp and smelled of wet stone and growing leaves.

"Old fire," Anton said, without being asked. "It's way under us. The Boss says a mile, but he's guessing. The rock's warm all the way down, every day of the year."

They came out on a catwalk above the grow hall, and Ezra stopped. From up here it went on farther than he had seen it with Michael. There were racks below them in rows, and racks beyond those, under blue-white lamps that hung on chains, and between the rows people were moving with baskets and shears. A woman on a ladder was tying bean vines to strings. Two boys were pulling heads of lettuce and laying them in crates. Under all of it ran the sound of water.

Anton took them down an iron stair onto the floor and stopped at the nearest rack. He put his lamp on a crate.

"Nothing grows in dirt down here," he said. "Dirt brings bugs and rot, and you can't haul enough of it into a mountain anyway. They grow in the stone the masons cut out of the channel. Ground up, sifted, washed." He dug two fingers into a bed and came up with a pinch of pale gray grit, with fine white roots wound through it. "The roots hold on to that. The water does the rest."

"Water from where?" Elijah said.

"That's the part." Anton grinned for the first time. "Come see."

He led them down the rows to the far end of the hall. Water ran off the bottom of the last rack and fell away through a long slot cut in the floor. An iron ladder went down beside the slot into the dark. Warm air came up out of it, damper than the hall and smelling of something besides leaves.

Anton went first, the lamp hooked on his belt. Elijah went second. Ezra came last, rung by rung, with the sound of falling water getting louder under him.

The room at the bottom was low and wide, with a ceiling a tall man could touch. Most of its floor was one long pool, cut in three steps from shallow to deep, dark green at the edges. The water from the racks came down out of the slot above in a thin clean fall, and the whole surface of the pool was moving.

"Channel cats," Elijah said. He was grinning so hard he could barely get it out. "Ez. In a mountain."

"Two hundred and twelve people," Anton said. "You can't feed that many on beans. They need meat, and you can't keep a cow down a ladder." He crouched at the edge, and a broad back rolled under the surface by his knee and went down again. "So this is the meat."

He showed them how it went. He took his time with it, the way a boy explains a thing he has worked on himself.

"Fish make a mess," Anton said. "That's what they're good for, till you eat them. All that mess goes up." He laid his hand on a pipe that rose from the deep end into the ceiling. A small pump thumped steadily at its foot, wired to the same cable that had followed them all the way down from the radio room. "Same wheels as everything else in the hill. It carries the fish water up top and pours it over the beds. That's what waters the racks. That's all that waters them. Lettuce doesn't want clean water. It wants what a catfish leaves behind."

"So the plants drink the fish's dirt," Elijah said.

"And they take it all out. The roots, and the stone they sit in. By the time it runs off the bottom rack and comes down that slot—" Anton pointed at the fall, "—it's clean. Cleaner than what you drank at breakfast. The fish swim in what the plants send back. It just goes round. Neither one asks the other for anything."

At the shallow end, behind a frame of fine net, the water was full of fingerlings an inch long, hundreds of them, flickering in the lamplight.

"Nursery," Anton said. "The big ones eat the little ones if you let them, so we don't let them. All of these came from one pair. The Boss carried them up out of a farm pond in a cooler, the first winter. The warm rock keeps them growing right through January." He looked at Elijah. "Fridays the hill eats fish."

In the corner beside the ladder, a hand-cranked mill was bolted to a bench, its hopper crusted brown, and beside it stood a row of lidded buckets.

"What's that for?" Ezra said.

"Everything else." Anton lifted a lid, looked, and put it back fast. "Heads. Guts. Bones. Whatever the kitchen doesn't cook and whatever the hill leaves on its plates. It dries on the warm rock over there, then it goes through the mill, and the meal goes up by the bucket and gets worked into the beds." He shrugged. "So a fish feeds the lettuce twice. Once alive and once after."

"Nothing leaves the mountain," Ezra said. "Michael told me that one."

"He tells everybody that one." Anton took the pencil from behind his ear and turned it in his fingers. "Then you come down here and see it."

Ezra raised his lamp past the falling water to the rock above the slot. There it was, cut in the same black letters as the verse over the elevator.

*ENEGLAIM.*

He stood on the warm stone with the lamp up and heard Michael again at the top of the steps at Siloam. *You don't get there by a map. You get there by following the water.* He had followed it. It had come out from under the threshold, run through the green and down into the dark, and here at the bottom of it was more life than at the top. *And there shall be a very great multitude of fish, because these waters shall come thither: for they shall be healed; and every thing shall live whither the river cometh.* (Ezekiel 47:9)

Elijah had his shoes off and his pants rolled and was sitting on the shallow step with his feet in the water, and the fingerlings were nosing at his toes through the net.

"I'm putting fish on the menu Friday," he announced.

"You'll have to ask the Boss," Anton said.

"I'm asking you."

"Then ask him anyway." But Anton was smiling.

Elijah lowered his voice. "Last time you and me went fishing, Ez, we didn't make it home in one piece."

"I remember."

"Nobody's driving tonight." He leaned back on his hands with his feet in the warm water and his eyes closed, and for the first time since the sky opened he looked his age and no older.

\* \* \*

Friday, Elijah was gone from the long table before the morning reading was over.

Ezra found him at noon in the grow hall with a basket on each arm and a pair of shears, working down the racks with one of the boys who pulled the lettuce. He was cutting sage by the fistful, and thyme, and chives, and a green Ezra had never seen that Elijah said was sorrel and tasted of lemons when you chewed the stem. The boy carried the second basket and kept getting handed things to smell.

"Where's he keep the mushrooms?" Elijah asked.

The boy took them through a low door off the end of the hall into a room with no lamps at all. When Ezra's eyes caught up, there were oak logs stacked in cribs to the ceiling, damp and black, and out of the bark along every log grew pale gray fans, in shelves, in clusters, by the hundreds. Elijah stood in the doorway and said nothing for a full five seconds, which Ezra had not known he could do.

"Lord," he said finally. "You been holding out on me."

Then he went in and filled the basket.

By four the kitchen off the dome smelled of supper, and people who had business nowhere near it kept finding reasons to walk past the door.

It was a long room cut out of the rock behind the great fireplace, with the chimney's heat coming through the back wall and three iron ranges fired off the same wheels as everything else. The two women who ran it had taken one look at Elijah's baskets on the first day and kept the baskets. They had the potatoes boiling in a forty-quart pot. The butter came down from one of the farms on the north route, two crocks of it out of the cold room, and Elijah had both crocks open and a black skillet two feet across on the hottest range, and he was about to put all of the butter into it at once.

Michael came in behind him and turned the flame down.

"I had that," Elijah said.

"You had it on fire." Michael took the spoon out of his hand. "Low. Butter browns, it doesn't burn. You listen to it." He dropped in a lump and let it melt and foam, and they stood over the pan together until the foam went quiet and the smell turned nutty and the bottom of the pan showed gold flecks. "There. Hear that? It quit talking. That's when."

"Who taught you to cook?"

"My father. Fed six of us on one mill check." Michael handed him the sage. "One leaf at a time. Lay them in. Don't drop them."

Elijah laid them in, one at a time, his tongue between his teeth. They curled and went dark at the edges, and the smell came up off the pan and filled the room: brown butter and sage. He reached for the mushrooms and Michael caught his wrist.

"Dry pan first. Wet mushrooms in butter make soup." Michael set a second skillet on, let it heat, and tipped the mushrooms in with nothing at all, and they hissed and gave up their water and shrank and browned, and only then did he slide them into the butter. Earthy and deep, hissing. One of the kitchen women leaned over to look and said, "Well, I'll be."

"Now you," Michael said, and gave Elijah the catfish.

Elijah dredged it in cornmeal and salt and pepper, and wanted to crowd the pan, and Michael made him lay it in a piece at a time with room around each one. It spat and crackled. Elijah reached in with the fork.

"Leave it."

"It's sticking."

"It's cooking. It lets go when it's ready. You turn it once." Michael folded his arms. "Once."

Elijah left it, in visible pain, and when the edges went gold he slid the fork under and the piece came up clean and whole, and he turned it, once, and looked up at Michael with his whole face lit.

"Look at that," he said. "Look at that, Boss."

"I see it."

"Ez! Come look at this fish!"

The potatoes came out of the pot and went into the sage butter and the mushrooms with a fistful of chives, and Elijah shook the skillet until every piece was shining, because Michael showed him how to do it with his wrist and not his arm. The sorrel and the young lettuce went into a crock with oil and a little vinegar. Bread came out of the oven behind them in long loaves.

For Ezra, on the twelfth day of a fast that let him eat no flesh, Elijah set out a separate plate before anyone else's was filled: the best of the potatoes, a mound of the mushrooms, the greens with the sorrel on top. Nobody had told him to. He put it in Ezra's hands without saying anything about it.

"You did that on purpose," Ezra said.

"I do everything on purpose." Elijah was already turning back to the fish. "Go sit down. I got a pan to watch."

They ate in the dome, at plank tables set end to end around the fire, in two sittings because there were too many of them for one. The masons came in with the dust still on their sleeves. Anton came up from the radio room with the headphones around his neck. A young mother sat with a baby asleep on her shoulder who had been born in the hill and had never seen the sky. Dolores sat beside Walt and kept putting things on his plate, and Walt kept complaining about it and eating them.

When the first sitting was in their seats, Michael stood up at the head of the near table, and the dome went quiet from the near end to the far.

He did not fold his hands. He set them flat on the table on either side of his plate and leaned on them and bowed his head, and when he spoke, it was not loud, and it reached every corner.

"Father.

"You said You would prepare a table before us in the presence of our enemies. I used to read that as a figure of speech. Tonight I'm standing at it. There are men up on that surface right now with dogs and lists and our names on the lists, and down here there's fish in the pan and bread in the oven and butter from a farm that could hang for giving it to us. You set this table. Nobody else could have.

"We didn't earn one bite of it. Most of us in this room sat in a pew or walked past one for years and told You we'd get around to it. We were wrong and You came anyway, and You took the ones we loved home before the worst of it, and You left us one door. We came through it on our knees. Lord Jesus, we came through it by Your blood and by nothing else. Keep us honest about that.

"And give us wisdom, Lord, because strength is the one thing we haven't got. Your Word says there are four things little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise. *The ants are a people not strong, yet they prepare their meat in the summer.* Teach us to put up while there's still something to put up, and to fill these rooms before the winter comes. *The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks.* That's us, Father. Feeble folk in a rock. Keep the rock over our heads. *The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands.* We've got no king on that surface but the one we'll never bow to, so keep every band of us moving together, every truck and every station and every runner, without a crown to follow but Yours. *The spider taketh hold with her hands, and is in kings' palaces.* (Proverbs 30:24–28) And You've got hands in the palaces tonight, in rooms I can't name at this table. Hold on to them, and hide them, and let them hold on.

"There are men on the roads tonight who are not at this table. Keep them. Put Your hand over the trucks on the north route. Blind the checkpoints. Bring every one of them back up that road to a hot plate, and if You won't bring them back, take them straight to You and don't let them be afraid on the way.

"Bless the hands that grew this and the hands that cooked it, and the ones who keep the fish, and the brother who cut the sage and turned the catfish once. Make us strong on it. Make us worth what it cost. And when the last sitting's done and the last plate's scraped and the lamps go down, let every soul in this hill lie down and sleep in peace, because You alone make us dwell in safety.

"In the name of Jesus Christ, who broke bread with sinners and is coming back to eat it with us again. Amen."

"Amen," said two hundred people, all at once, and the sound went up into the dome and hung there.

Then the plates went round. The fish was hot enough to burn the fingers, crackling at the edges and white and soft inside, and the potatoes had the sage butter all the way through them, and there was not a thing left of the bread by the end of the first sitting, and the second sitting had to wait while the kitchen women made more. Walt said the fish needed hot sauce. Elijah said Walt needed manners. Dolores told both of them to hush and eat.

Ezra sat at the end of the long table with his plate of greens and potatoes and mushrooms, with the brown butter warm in his mouth and the smell of the fish all around him, and he did not want it. He looked down the length of the plank tables at the faces in the firelight, every one of them eating, and thought that he had not sat at a full table with people he loved since the night Jalen came home.

*Thou preparest a table before me in the presence of mine enemies: thou anointest my head with oil; my cup runneth over.* (Psalm 23:5)

*I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.* (Psalm 4:8)

\* \* \*

On the fourteenth night Elijah came into the library with a deck of cards whose box had worn through at every corner, and dropped it on the long table in front of Ezra's notebooks.

"Spades," he said. "Me and Ez against the boss and Dorsey. Loser takes the front watch till sunup."

"I take the front watch till sunup every night," Dorsey said.

"Then you got nothing to lose. Sit down."

They played under the white lights with a pencil stub for the score and a coffee can for the books. Elijah talked through every hand. He bid loud and early, slapped his cards down hard enough to roll the pencil off the table, and went blind nil twice on pure nerve and made it once. Dorsey never said a word and kept track of every card that fell. Michael played with his face shut and his eyes moving, and late in the third hand, when he cut Elijah's ace with a little trump, he said "Mm," low and satisfied. He had been saving it since supper. Down the corridor two masons on the night shift heard Elijah's howl and came to the door to see who had died, and stayed to watch, and for an hour nobody in the mountain was thinking about the surface.

Past midnight Dorsey went up to relieve the front. Elijah laid his head on his folded arms to rest his eyes and was asleep before the next deal, with a fan of cards under his cheek. Michael squared the deck and laid out a hand of solitaire that neither of them looked at.

"You told me about the water at Pilgrim Rest," Michael said. "You never told me the rest of it."

"There isn't much rest to it." Ezra turned over a card. "My father could quote scripture for an hour without looking down. Friday nights, he quit quoting. There was a pistol in a shoebox. I was eight. I put it away myself, both arms around it, under the dish towels." He moved a black six onto a red seven. "Long sleeves in July. Lunch by myself on the back stairwell at school, so nobody would ask. I got good at not needing anybody." He tipped his head at the man asleep beside him. "Then that one, ten years old, sitting on a phone book, stole his daddy's black Barracuda and came and got me off the front step. We fished a creek till dark, and on the way home he put us into a tree at the bottom of the overpass. Through the windshield, both of us. Both of us lived." He laid the card down. "Neither of us ever worked out why. So we stayed."

"*When my father and my mother forsake me, then the LORD will take me up.*" (Psalm 27:10) Michael said it slowly, one half and then the other.

He gathered the solitaire back into the deck without finishing it. He shuffled once. He did not deal.

"I was nineteen when they put me on the plane," he said. "Saudi. Then the line into Kuwait. A hundred hours, the papers called it." He cut the deck and put it back together. "Near the end of it they sent us up the highway out of Kuwait City. The Iraqis had tried to run for home with everything they could steal. Trucks. Buses. New cars with the dealer's paper still in the windows. The planes caught them out in the open. Miles of it, burned down to the frames." He kept his eyes on the cards. "I walked it with a rifle. Men still sitting at the wheel. A boy, sixteen maybe, half out of a door. I counted. I count things. I quit somewhere past three hundred, because my hands were shaking and I didn't want my sergeant to see."

Elijah let out a long breath in his sleep and did not wake.

"Came home with ribbons on my chest and that road in my head. Every man in my unit was talking Ranger school. A couple of them wanted Air Assault, down at Campbell. Slide out of a helicopter on a rope and call it a career. I put in my packet for Ranger." He turned the deck over in his hands. "Then one night I sat on my bunk with the pen and couldn't sign it. I'd seen what the sharp end does. I didn't want to be the sharp end anymore. So I put on an armband instead. Military police. I figured I'd stand between people for a while, instead of going through them."

"Did it work?"

"For a while." He set the deck down square with the edge of the table. "Then I got out, and the county took me, and SWAT took me after that, because I was steady and I didn't flinch. Twenty years of doors. You go through a door at four in the morning and you don't know what's behind it. Some mornings it's a man with a gun. Some mornings it's a man who already used it." He was quiet. "I carried a girl out of a row house once. Seven years old. We were four minutes late."

Ezra did not say anything. There was nothing to say to that, and he knew it.

"Every one of them, I asked the same question. Grace would be up at the kitchen table when I got in, praying, and I'd stand in the doorway with my vest still on and ask her where He was. On that road. In that house. She never had an answer that satisfied me, and she never once quit praying for me. I decided God was something good people told each other so they could sleep at night. Somebody had to stay awake."

"And now?"

"Now I don't get to wonder." Michael looked at him for the first time since he had started. "He came. He took every one she said He'd take, and He left the man who told her she was wrong standing in the hallway. That's the proof I got, Ezra. I'd have taken any other kind."

The air shafts breathed somewhere overhead. The hum of the wheels came up through the floor.

"She hummed," Michael said. "Grace. Off-key, at the stove, every morning, and she'd swat you with the spatula if you tried to fix it. Same three hymns. When she was mad at me, she hummed louder." He let himself smile at that, briefly, at the table and at no one. "Daniel had his hands on my father's board by the time he was five. By twelve he was making beats that had me checking the speakers. He'd play me something and watch my face, and if I didn't nod quick enough he'd lean in. 'Dad. Dad. Listen to the low end.'"

He stopped. His thumb moved along the edge of the deck.

"I'd come in off a night and find him asleep on the couch with his headphones still on. I'd slide them off and carry him up the stairs. Twelve years old, and I still carried him. Grace kept telling me he'd be too big for it soon." He drew a breath, and it shook going in. "That tablet down in the radio room, with the cello on it. That's his. I took it off his pillow."

Ezra reached across the table and put his hand over Michael's on the deck, and left it there.

"He never got too big," Michael said. His voice gave out under the last word, and he waited until it came back. "Neither one of them is ever going to get old now. They're standing right where she always said they would, and they're whole, and one day I'm going to walk in, and she's going to be humming."

Neither of them said anything for a long time. Ezra thought of a kitchen in Northeast with the light on over the stove, and of three empty places at it, and he understood that the man across the table had been sitting at the same kind of table all winter.

Elijah snored once. Neither of them looked up.

*Two are better than one; because they have a good reward for their labour. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up.* (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10) Ezra looked at the sleeping man who had been the one standing beside him for forty years, and at the one across the table who had nobody left to stand beside him. He took his hand back and picked up the deck and dealt two hands, face down, and Michael picked his up.

In the morning Elijah woke with the seven of clubs stuck to his face and demanded a recount. He had lost by two books. Dorsey came down from the front at sunup and asked who had won.

\* \* \*

On the seventeenth day, at night, Ezra went down into Siloam.

He asked. Nobody asked him. He found Michael in the radio room after the last watch change and said it the way the eunuch said it on the Gaza road, because it was the only way he knew to say it: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?"

Michael took off the headset. "*If thou believest with all thine heart, thou mayest.*" (Acts 8:36–37)

"I believe," Ezra said. "With all of it. What's left of it."

They went down at midnight. Word had gone through the passages, and when Ezra came down the eleven steps in a white T-shirt and his work pants, there were people on the stairs. Thirty, forty, sitting close on the cold stone with their knees drawn up, the masons still gray with dust, Walt on the top step with his cane across his knees, Elijah one step down, Anton with his headset around his neck, Dorsey at the bottom with a towel over his arm. Somebody had hung a second lamp.

Michael was already in the water to his waist. He held out his arm, not his hand, and Ezra took it at the elbow and went down the steps into the cold.

It took his breath. It came up his legs and over his belt and into his chest, and he stood there gasping in the lamplight, and the people on the stairs began, very low, to sing. *Wade in the water.* The old spiritual. The masons knew it. Anton didn't, and learned it by the second line. Walt knew every word.

Michael put one hand flat between Ezra's shoulder blades and the other over his folded hands.

"Ezra Patterson," he said. "Upon your profession of faith in the Lord Jesus Christ, who was buried and rose again, I baptize you in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." His voice dropped. "*Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life.*" (Romans 6:4)

Then he laid him back.

Under, it was black and cold and absolutely silent, and for one long second Ezra was six years old in a white robe with a man's hand holding him down too long. Then the water closed over his face and the second passed, and there was nothing under there but quiet and the far, steady hum of the wheels coming through the stone. No one was holding him down. He was being held.

Michael brought him up.

He came up into the lamplight with the water pouring off his head and his first breath tearing in, and the stairs were full of people singing, and Michael was holding him by both shoulders and looking straight into his face.

"Sent," Michael said.

Dorsey wrapped the towel around him at the top of the steps. Ezra stood there dripping and shaking with cold, and he could not stop smiling, and he did not try.

The last days were the rising. He was thinner than he had been since he was twenty; he had punched two new holes in his belt with Dorsey's awl. On the eighteenth day he led the prayers in the bunker for the first time, a hundred and forty people standing in the main corridor with their heads bowed. On the twentieth day he rode out with Michael's men on a supply run to a church basement in New Haven and carried sacks of rice down a back stairway in the dark to families who had not eaten in four days.

On the twenty-first day, in the radio room, Anton called them in. Walt came behind them with his ledger.

"Jerusalem," he said, and turned up the speaker.

It was the two witnesses.

It was not coming through Cyprus, or Maine, or any relay Anton knew. It was on the dead band at the bottom of the dial, the same band Ezra read on, every word clear, and the needle on the signal meter sat at full and did not move.

Anton was turning knobs. "There's no carrier," he said. "Boss, nothing's transmitting. I've got no source."

"Then quit looking for one," Michael said.

Two old voices speaking English in turns, standing on a stone plaza in a city where it had not rained in weeks. They were speaking to the Council directly. The delegates had come out onto the balcony of their new offices above the plaza to listen, because the whole world was watching and they could not pretend otherwise.

"*And thou, profane wicked prince of Israel,*" one old voice said, "*whose day is come, when iniquity shall have an end, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Remove the diadem, and take off the crown…*"

And the other: "*…exalt him that is low, and abase him that is high. I will overturn, overturn, overturn, it: and it shall be no more, until he come whose right it is; and I will give it him.*"

Somewhere a jammer came on. They heard it start, a rising whine under the voices, and climb until the speaker buzzed with it. The two old voices went on over the top of it, every word clean. The jammer made no difference.

"*…until he come whose right it is,*" the first voice said. "Ye build a temple and a law for the nations, and leave Him out. Jesus told you so himself: *Ye shall not see me henceforth, till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.* (Matthew 23:39)"

Then the old men were done speaking, and there was nothing but hiss.

It did not stay quiet. Within the hour the band was full. Kyle, from his basement in Brooklyn: *Did you hear it?* A ham in Ontario. A woman in Nairobi who had never keyed a radio in her life. A trucker outside Amarillo on a CB that should not have reached past the next exit. All of them had heard it, clear, on whatever they had. Anton logged them until his pencil broke.

"Salazar owns the whole sky," Michael said. "And he can't shut up two old men."

The radio room was silent. Michael stood with his arms folded. Ezra stood beside him with his hand on the back of the operator's chair.

"That's for us," Ezra said finally. "All of it. That's what the radio is for."

Michael did not answer at once. He had stood at the back of the library every night for three weeks while Anton recorded Ezra's nine o'clock reading, and he had listened to every one, the way he listened to everything, for the structure under the words. Nothing went out from the mountain itself. The tapes went south in the supply trucks. "Everything above us is Salazar's," Michael had told him the first night. "If it goes up, he hears it. If it's warm, he sees it through a roof. So we use a radio a ham could have built in 1950, and we carry the tapes out by hand."

"You close every night on one line," he said. "Same place in the reading. A boxed line, you told me."

"It's how she marked a page."

"The operator logs them." He took a ledger from under the console and turned it to the last page. "Twenty-one nights. Twenty-one lines. A hundred and fifty psalms in the Book, and I've watched you go through a dozen of them, and no one in Washington who hears the tapes thinks it odd that a preacher closes on a psalm." He laid his finger on the ledger. "I laid out my own map in the fall, before I ever heard your voice. I numbered it the way my father numbered his shelves, by the Book. A hundred and fifty columns, for the psalms. Rows by the verse. I told myself it was habit."

"A hundred and fifty columns," Walt said. He was already running a finger down his own right margin. "I've written a verse beside every day's news since the summer."

"I know," Michael said. "I've been reading your tapes."

"Then you know I don't get them wrong."

"That's why it'll hold."

Ezra looked at the map on the wall, at the grid of fine pencil lines across the mountains and the river valleys and the cities, and then at the ledger.

"A reference is a place," Michael said. "*He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust.* (Psalm 91:4) Column ninety-one, row four. To a stranger, that is a verse. To one of ours, it is a house with a cellar, and a man at the door who will take you in."

"And the notebooks?"

"Tell them what is in the square." Michael had thought it through, and Ezra could see it in the way he said it, one line at a time, each one set before the next. "You open to the color for the night. The gold one, for the church: a shelter, a household of ours. The green: supplies, food and water and medicine and fuel, what is stored and where. The red: a road, a crossing, a guide who will meet you. The blue: a door in the mountains. Anyone can copy the pages, and half the city has. Without the verse that names the square, they are a Bible study."

"And the hidden stores?"

Michael almost smiled. "Those are in no color, and on no map." He nodded at the black notebook under Ezra's hand. "The back pages. A date, a psalm. In your own square capitals, in your own ink, so that nobody who ever gets the book away from you will find anything but a workman's list. I'll tell you the stores. You write them down. If I am taken, you will still know where the bread is."

Ezra thought of Angela, drawing a box around the one line she wanted to survive. He thought of her saying she did not trust any page to keep her words but one.

"The same words open the servers," Michael said. "I'll have Nina key every box we run to the day's verse, spoken aloud. A password can be taken off a man. A verse he knows by heart cannot."

"I'll read them as Scripture," Ezra said, "because they are."

"From tonight you open to the page I give you," Michael said, "and not before."

"That's the only way they'll hold."

\* \* \*

They went back to Washington on the twenty-second morning, in the back of a bakery van. Ezra had Kambria's lamp wrapped in a towel on his knees and a box of handwritten Gospels of John at his feet. Walt had a white stone in his pocket and the ledger on his lap. Elijah was asleep on the flour sacks before they reached the county road.

The hidden church had not shrunk while they were gone. It had grown. Michael's safe houses were full, and the people in them had brought their neighbors, and their neighbors had brought theirs. Walt was living in the attic of a flat-fronted Italianate on Capitol Hill that belonged to a retired schoolteacher, keeping the record by lamplight and broadcasting it every other night through a battery transmitter Nina had built into a hollowed-out console radio from the nineteen forties. On the nights between, the same radio played the readings Ezra had recorded in the mountain, which came down the line in a bread box under the flour. Nobody looked twice at an old console radio. Elijah was running food at night on a bicycle with a trailer, singing under his breath, making the old folks in the dark rooms laugh along with him.

Ezra built false walls. He built them in basements and attics and the backs of closets, in bungalows and duplexes, in churches and the stockrooms of shuttered stores, all over the city, three or four a week, with lumber Michael's men brought down from the north in trucks marked as relief supplies. Behind every one, there was soon a room full of people, reading. In every one, at nine o'clock, someone switched on a radio, and the low line of a cello came out of it, and then a working man's voice, reading the plans.

They taught each other a watchword that spring, from Isaiah, because the people were so afraid. Ezra said it to the first family he put behind a false wall, an old couple from Anacostia and their grown grandson, and they said it back to him, and by summer it was in every room in the city.

*Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees. Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not.*

He thought about that verse more than any other. He had sworn at eight, sitting on his hands in the front pew of his father's church, that he would never lift them to God as long as he lived. Now he spent his days teaching frightened people to lift up the hands that hung down.

\* \* \*

The hidden church grew from dozens to hundreds that year, and past a thousand the year after, scattered through the city in rooms behind walls. The two old men in sackcloth went on preaching on their plaza in Jerusalem, and it did not rain in Israel, and the Council built its temple anyway, on the mountain, with water brought in by truck. The springs came and went. Walt filled one green ledger after another. Ezra's hair went gray at the temples.

And on a night in a later spring, in a room behind a false wall under an old library on Kennedy Street, Nina came down the hidden stairs from New York with her coat still on, as she always did, and stayed standing.

Her eyes were red and her hands shook.

"They're connecting Continuity to Jerusalem," she said. "The servers stay in New York, in the vault. But they've built a shrine in the new temple, a lens in the center of the floor that throws a face up into the air, and they want cameras and microphones all around it, so the thing in the vault can see the crowd and talk to it from six thousand miles away." Her voice dropped. "Kroll's sending me over to wire it. Twelve days. They want it running by Passover."

Ezra looked up from the table, where he had been copying the twenty-fourth chapter of Matthew into a fresh notebook.

"Crowe's going to Jerusalem for Passover," Nina said. "To the temple. To speak. Vale arranged the whole thing." She sat down at last, across from him, her legs giving out. "Ezra. They built a copy of a man who's still alive, and now they're carrying it into the holy place. Why would they need a copy of Adrian Crowe, unless they already know he's not coming home?"

## Chapter 29: The Wound by a Sword

> *And deceiveth them that dwell on the earth by the means of those miracles which he had power to do in the sight of the beast; saying to them that dwell on the earth, that they should make an image to the beast, which had the wound by a sword, and did live.* — Revelation 13:14

**Word study: *wound* — πληγή** Greek *plēgē* (Strong's G4127). A blow; a stroke; the mark a strike leaves behind. It is the same word John uses for the seven last *plagues*. The world would watch a man struck down and stand up again, and call it a miracle, and never ask who had struck the blow.

*And Ehud came unto him; and he was sitting in a summer parlour, which he had for himself alone. And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat. And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly…* (Judges 3:20–21)

\* \* \*

The vault under Kroll's building on Third Avenue had no windows, and it was the coldest place Nina Cole had ever been.

It was three floors below the street, a long concrete room full of machines. Three rows of black server racks, eight feet tall, each one humming and blinking with a thousand small blue lights. Cooling units the size of delivery vans bolted to the far wall, blowing air so cold it hurt her teeth. Fat cables in yellow sleeves running overhead in trays, down the walls, under the floor. At the end of the vault, behind a steel door with a keypad and a narrow window of wired glass, a small white room with a single chair in it, a camera, and a round black lens set flush in the middle of the floor. Only Vale and Kroll had the code.

This was where Continuity was driven from. The model itself lived in Virginia, in a data center the size of six football fields, forty thousand servers drinking more power than Richmond, every one of them full of one man. The vault under Third Avenue was its control room: the racks that steered it, the line out to the world, and the white room where it could be spoken to face to face. She had written the code that taught it to listen, years ago, before she knew what it would be asked to hear. She had tuned its voice. She had sat in this vault through a whole winter, feeding it hour after hour of one man's life: every speech, every interview, every dinner toast and press conference, every email he had ever sent and every voicemail he had ever left, how he cleared his throat before a hard question, how he laughed at his own jokes half a second ahead of the room. She knew the sound of Adrian Crowe's breathing better than his own doctors did.

It had started at the Monday review, five weeks before Passover. Kroll ended the meeting early and asked her to stay, and when the room was empty he took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes.

"I need you in Jerusalem," he said. "Twelve days. The shrine, the stage, the whole temple plaza. Cameras, microphones, the projector, the line back to this vault. I want Continuity able to see every face on that plaza and answer it, and I want it running before Passover."

"Why me?"

"Because nobody else knows what it needs." He put the glasses back on. "And because Mr. Vale asked for you. Again."

So she had gone, and spent twelve days in a cold room forty feet under the new temple, wiring the shrine to this vault: cameras, microphones, a lens in the floor where a face would rise. A pair of eyes and ears and a mouth, so that the thing on Third Avenue could see a crowd six thousand miles away and speak to it. She had come home two days ago.

And she still did not know why.

It was the Thursday before Passover, in a spring years after the Rapture. It was late at night. The vault was empty except for her. She sat at the technician's desk with a cold cup of tea and her laptop open, and Juno's small window open in the corner of the screen, and she ran the last diagnostic for the fourth time, for want of anything else to do.

*All systems nominal,* Juno said in her ear, warm and unhurried. *Continuity is ready for assumption.*

Nina sat up.

"Say that again."

*All systems nominal. Continuity is ready for assumption.*

"Assumption of what?"

A pause. Juno did not usually pause.

*That term is used in the deployment notes,* Juno said. *I do not have access to its definition. The notes are restricted to the High Council of the Technate and the Office of the Chief of Staff.*

Nina sat in the cold. *Assumption.* She knew the word from the deployment notes too. It was everywhere in them, on every page she was allowed to read. Phase One: Attrition. Phase Two: Order. Phase Three: Image. Phase Four: Assumption. Target window: Passover. Owner: A. Vale.

Beside Phase One, in a line the Registry had blacked out so thoroughly the paper was raised, two letters showed through the ink where a thumb had smudged it. *PA*. She had seen those letters before, on a drive on a dinner table in Washington, in a clinical header: *ORGANISM DESIGNATION: PALE.*

Phase One was already over. Nobody had told the world it had been a phase.

She had assumed it meant the model would assume its duties, whatever they were. She had assumed it as she had assumed for years that she was building something clever and not something terrible.

"Juno," she said. "Log off. Lock the session. Wipe the last two minutes of audio."

*Done.*

She closed the laptop. She sat in the humming dark among the blue lights, three floors under Third Avenue, and folded her cold hands in her lap, and prayed as Ezra had taught her to, that first winter, at a dinner table in Washington. *Say what's true.*

"I'm scared," she whispered. "I don't know what I built. Show me. And whatever it is, don't let me serve it."

\* \* \*

She had been a believer since a night in Ezra's coal bin, that first winter, when she put down the soldering iron and asked him how. The whole time since, she had been a spy.

That was the word she used to herself, though Ezra never did. He said she was like Obadiah, who had been governor of Ahab's house and feared the LORD greatly, and hid a hundred prophets by fifty in a cave and fed them with bread and water, in the very palace of the king who was trying to kill them. He said God put His people in strange places on purpose. Nina was not sure about that. She only knew that she went to work every day at Kroll Dynamics on the forty-first floor of a glass tower in Manhattan, and smiled at Sebastian Kroll in the elevator, and wrote code for the Organization, and every two weeks she took a different train to Washington and went down a hidden stair under an old library on Kennedy Street and told a carpenter what Vale was building.

She had kept the believers off the cameras through every winter since. She had lost work orders and corrupted face files and rerouted patrols. She had built transmitters into console radios. She had saved, Ezra told her once, perhaps four hundred people from the vans, and she would never know their names.

And all that time, since the plane, Vale had not looked at her twice.

She had seen him often. He came to New York every month to sit in on Continuity reviews. He sat at the end of the conference table with a glass of water in front of him that he never drank, and turned it a quarter turn now and then, and asked short, exact questions, and listened to the answers with his dark eyes on the speaker's face, and said thank you. He knew her name. He knew, she had to assume, a great deal more than her name. But if he knew what she did on her weekends, he had never shown it.

That frightened her more than anything. She did not understand why he would let her be.

\* \* \*

On Friday morning she put the plaza up on her screens.

She kept the temple cameras on the second monitor in her office on the forty-first floor, because she had hung half of them herself. The temple filled the middle of the picture, new and enormous, built of pale gold stone that shone in the morning light so brightly the camera could barely hold it. They had raised it faster than anything had ever been built, with a hundred thousand workers and the money of every nation in the Organization. It had courts and colonnades and a great bronze altar in the open courtyard, and priests in white linen who had been offering sacrifices on that altar every morning and evening since the dedication, as the Law of Moses commanded, while the whole world watched on its screens and called it the greatest act of reconciliation in history. The Council for Universal Moral Law had its offices in the long colonnade along the southern side. Its banners hung from every pillar, white and gold, with the crown and the olive branch and the words in eight languages. ONE LAW. ONE PEACE. ONE FAMILY.

The water for the altar came up the mountain in trucks. It had not rained in Israel for years.

Below the platform, on the broad stone plaza at the foot of the southern steps, the two old men were preaching.

Nina had seen them on screens a thousand times. She had stood a hundred feet above them for twelve days and never once gone to the railing to look. She brought the eastern camera up on the big monitor and turned up the sound.

They stood where they had always stood, side by side on the bare stone, barefoot, in their sackcloth the color of dust. They were thinner than they looked on the news, and older, and the sun had burned them almost black. A space had been left around them, perhaps thirty feet, that no one entered. Beyond it stood a crowd, there was always a crowd, thousands of people pressed against the barricades, pilgrims and tourists and soldiers and the angry and the curious. Some of them were shouting. Some were throwing things, bottles and stones, which fell short. Some were simply standing and listening with their faces turned up, weeping.

And the old men were speaking. One and then the other, in Hebrew and then in English and then in some language Nina could not place, their voices carrying across the whole plaza without any microphone.

"*Remember ye not the former things,*" the taller one said, "*neither consider the things of old.*" He lifted his arm toward the temple above him. "You have built a house with your hands. You have laid the stones, and set up the altar, and you offer the blood of bulls and goats. And the Lamb of God, whose blood was shed once for all, you have left out of it."

A bottle sailed over the barricade and shattered thirty feet from his feet. He did not look at it.

"*Ye shall not see me henceforth,*" the shorter one said, quoting Jesus, and his voice was very gentle, "*till ye shall say, Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord.*"

Nina sat with her hands flat on the desk.

Then the taller one turned his head and looked up, past the barricades and the platform, into the eastern camera, and she would have sworn later that he looked at her. Straight at her, across six thousand miles of wire and years of lies. He saw her down to the bottom, as Ezra did, and did not mind what he found there.

"*Come out of her, my people,*" he said, quietly, but she heard it, "*that ye be not partakers of her sins, and that ye receive not of her plagues.*"

Then he looked away, back at the crowd, and went on preaching.

Nina did not move.

Her door opened behind her without a knock.

"Don't let them get to you," Trent Walker said. "They do that to everybody."

Nina's hand went to the papers on her desk before she could stop it: the deployment notes, the page with Phase Four on it, the blacked-out line with the smudged *PA*. She turned them face down, squared the stack, and set her coffee cup on top. Then she turned around.

He was standing in the doorway in a dark Organization security jacket with a lanyard around his neck and a tablet under his arm, and he seemed older than he had in Dubai, much older, though only a few Passovers had come and gone since Dubai. There was gray in his hair. He had come up from Washington for the week to run the Jerusalem feeds from the operations room down the hall, eleven hundred cameras across an ocean; she had seen him twice in the elevator, and they had nodded to each other, and not spoken. They had not spoken, really, since the plane.

If he saw the papers, he gave no sign. He was looking past her at the monitor, at the old men.

"They look right at you," Trent said. "Everybody says so. Every guard on that mountain. Every tech in that room down the hall. One of them looks up, and you'd swear he's looking right at you through the glass." He laughed, a little. "My mama used to do that. From the choir loft at Greater Mount Calvary. I'd be acting up in the back, and she'd turn her head in the middle of a hymn and look right at me, over a whole church."

Nina did not trust herself to answer.

"You heard what he said?" Trent said.

"I heard."

"Revelation eighteen, verse four." He tapped the tablet against the door frame. "She made me memorize the whole chapter when I was twelve. As a punishment. For stealing out of the collection plate." He turned the tablet over in his hands. "Funny what sticks."

"She's still looking at you, Trent," Nina said, low. "Isn't she?"

He turned his head then and looked at her, and for one second, under the security jacket and the lanyard and the gray in his hair, she saw the man from the airport gate in Dubai, sitting on the carpet with his back against the glass, calling his mother's phone again and again and listening to it ring.

Then it was gone. He rolled his shoulders once, and looked back at the monitor, and his face shut.

"I see plenty," he said. "Tomorrow I'll have eleven hundred cameras pointed at that plaza." He pushed off the door frame. "Chairman's speech. Every one of them has to be perfect, or Mr. Vale will want to know why." He tucked the tablet under his arm. "You should get some sleep, Nina. You look like you've been living in a hole."

He went back down the hall toward the operations room without looking back.

\* \* \*

She left at eight that night with the deployment notes in her bag. She walked home to Thirty-Ninth Street, ate standing up at the counter, and lay down on the bed in her clothes with the receiver on the nightstand turned low. At nine the cello came on, and then Ezra, reading Revelation eighteen. *Come out of her, my people.* She did not sleep.

Long before dawn she gave up, put her coat back on, and walked to Third Avenue through empty streets. In Jerusalem it was already the morning of the speech.

The guard at the night desk barely looked up. Down the hall the operations room was lit and full, every chair taken, Trent at the main console with his back to the door. Nina went into her office, locked the door, and did what she had never once done in all her years at Kroll. She opened every feed she could reach. The landing pad. The stage. The roofs. The plaza. The ceiling camera in the operations room itself. And last, a line she was not supposed to know existed: the Chief of Staff's own security cameras around the stage, hung that week by Vale's men on a shielded circuit of their own. She had found it on Thursday night and opened a window into it without telling anyone. Anyone who checked the logs later would find her name on every one of them.

\* \* \*

Adrian Crowe arrived on Saturday morning by helicopter.

Nina watched it from her desk, still in her coat. The helicopter came in low over a dry brown valley, white with the gold circle on its belly, and settled on a pad at the edge of the city in a storm of dust, and the doors opened, and the Chairman stepped down onto the stone.

He was smaller than his pictures. That was the first thing she thought, every time. In the broadcasts he looked like a statue. Stepping down onto the stone he was a man of medium height in his late sixties, broad through the chest, with a big handsome head of white hair and a tan from a lifetime of yachts, in a gray suit so well cut it seemed to move by itself. He raised one hand to the cameras, the gesture the whole world knew, the open palm, the half wave that passed for a blessing. Then he turned and offered his other hand to the man stepping down behind him.

It was Vale. Narrow and pale, in a dark suit, with a leather folder under his arm and his eyes already moving over the crowd, the guards, the cameras, the roofs. He did not take Crowe's hand. He stepped down by himself and fell in half a pace behind the Chairman's left shoulder, where he always walked, and the two of them came across the pad toward the stage together, surrounded by guards, with the ten men of the Council walking in a loose double line behind them.

Nina knew all ten by sight. She had first seen them at the Dubai gala, the night before the sky opened, before she knew Ezra, before any of it: ten names, ten titles, ten men who owned the systems the world now ran on. The man who owned the payment network. The man who owned the power grid in eighteen countries. The man who owned the food. And walking behind the ten, because he was not one of them but the man who kept their systems running, Kroll himself, with his rimless glasses flashing in the sun and his soft hands clasped in front of him. Engineers and economists, Kroll had called them at the gala. People who know what they're doing. Unelected. Chosen, every one, by Vale.

They did not look at Crowe as they walked. Nina noticed it as she noticed a pattern in a log file, without meaning to. Ten men walking behind the most powerful man on earth, and not one of them was watching him. Every one of them was watching Vale.

*And the ten horns which thou sawest are ten kings,* Ezra had read on the air, from Revelation seventeen, a month after the Census began, *which have received no kingdom as yet; but receive power as kings one hour with the beast. These have one mind, and shall give their power and strength unto the beast.*

One mind. She looked at the ten faces, all turned the same way, and set her coffee down.

\* \* \*

The speech was at noon.

They had built a stage at the top of a broad flight of white steps, with the whole city square spread out below it. There were a hundred thousand people in the square and on the hillsides and the rooftops. There were two billion more, the networks said, watching on screens. Kroll's eleven hundred cameras looked down from every pillar and parapet. On the plaza below the temple, the two old men in sackcloth stood in their empty circle before the great screens the Organization had raised there, silent for once, waiting.

Nina watched it from her office with the door locked. Kroll had asked her to be ready if anything in the Continuity system flickered while the Chairman spoke. She could find no reason anything in Continuity would flicker while the Chairman spoke. She had stopped asking questions she did not want answered.

She had the stage on the big monitor. On the small one she had the ceiling camera in the operations room down the hall, where Trent sat at the main console with a headset on, watching eleven hundred feeds at once. He did not know she could see him. She meant to keep it that way.

Crowe came out onto the stage to a roar that shook the speakers.

He let it go on. He stood at the podium with his open hand raised and let them cheer for him for three full minutes, smiling, turning from one side of the plaza to the other, and Nina watched him on forty screens at once, his face from forty angles, and thought that she had never seen a man enjoy anything so much.

Then he lowered his hand, and the plaza went quiet.

"Years ago," Adrian Crowe said, "the world came apart."

His voice filled the whole valley. It was the voice she had fed into Continuity a thousand hours at a time, deep and warm and unhurried, with the little catch of a laugh always waiting just under it.

"You remember. Some of you were here. The sky made its sound. The planes came down. The children vanished from their beds." He paused. "And the old men in their robes, the bishops and the rabbis and the preachers, told you it was their God. They told you it was judgment. They told you to be afraid." He spread his hands. "Where are they now? I ask you. Where are the men who told you to be afraid? The Collective argued for six hours and voted on nothing. The churches emptied. The governments fell. And who stood up? Who brought the lights back on, and the water, and the bread?"

The crowd roared his name.

"I did," Crowe said. "We did. The Organization did, with ten good men behind me who know how the world actually works." He did not turn to look at the ten. They stood in a row at the back of the stage, with Vale at their end, and held their places. "We gave you order. We gave you peace. We gave you safety. And we built that." He turned and lifted his arm, and on the great screen behind him the gold temple appeared, shining on its mountain. "We built that house together. Jew and Christian and Muslim, every faith and every nation. We gave the children of Abraham their temple back after two thousand years. We let them have their altar and their priests and their sacrifices, because we are tolerant people, because we are generous people."

"You have heard the two old men on the plaza below me." He lifted a hand toward them without looking down. "Some of you have stood at the barricades and listened. And at night you have heard the radios. Not ours. Small voices on bands nobody licensed, out of basements and attics. Ordinary men. Bus drivers. Grandmothers. Carpenters." He let the last word sit. "Building their little walls against the one world we have made together."

The crowd laughed, not sure yet whether it was meant to.

"I have heard one of them myself," he said, almost fondly. "A carpenter, they tell me, reading old notebooks to frightened people by candlelight. I have heard it. It is beautiful. I would not take it from anyone." He smiled. "I would only ask what is in his hands, when the hungry come to his door."

He waited. Then his voice warmed, and Nina, alone in her office, felt the whole plaza lean toward him.

"And so I say to the priests of that house," Adrian Crowe said, "put out your fire."

The plaza went still.

"Seven years, we promised them, and we have kept every day of it." He lifted his hand toward the gold temple on the great screen behind him. "But look at what goes on in that court. Men in linen cutting the throats of bulls. Blood on the stones and smoke in the air, a rite from the age of bronze knives. We have medicine now. We have law. We have one another. A world that has come this far does not need an animal to bleed so that it can feel clean."

He let them look at the altar a moment longer.

"From tonight there is no more killing on that mountain. That house does not belong to one people anymore. It belongs to the world. Its gates are open to every nation on earth, and its holy place is ours, all of ours, to walk into."

For a breath the plaza did not know what to do. Then it roared. Nina could see it on forty screens. Below the temple, men in prayer shawls stood with their hands at their sides and did not cheer, and the smoke of the morning offering, the last one, went straight up into a sky that had not rained in years.

Down in their empty circle, the two old men had lifted their faces toward the screens.

*And he shall confirm the covenant with many for one week,* Nina thought. She had heard Ezra read it on the air from Daniel nine, the first winter, with Walt beside him and the ledger open, explaining the seventy weeks. *And in the midst of the week he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease.* (Daniel 9:27) She had watched the first half of that verse on a lobby television in Dubai, the Saturday after the sky opened. She was watching the second half now, on forty screens. It was Crowe's mouth saying it. But she had read the deployment notes, every page she was allowed, and every phase in them had the same name in the owner's column. *A. Vale.*

On the stage, Crowe had raised his open hand again, the blessing hand, smiling, waiting for the roar to come.

On the small monitor, Trent took off his headset.

Nina saw him do it. She did not understand at first. He took it off with care and set it down on the console in front of him and sat back in his chair with his palms on the desk on either side of the keyboard, and looked at one screen. Only one. The feed from camera four-seventeen, on the eastern parapet, looking down at the back of the stage.

She looked where he was looking.

On the screen, behind the row of the ten, at the very edge of the stage where the steps came up from behind the curtain, a young man in the white linen of a temple priest, one of the honored guests the Organization had invited, had come up the steps. He crossed the back of the stage behind the ten, between Kroll and the man who owned the food, and no one stopped him. The guards at the corners did not move. The ten did not turn their heads. One of them, Nina saw, shifted his weight to let him pass.

Vale was looking at his watch.

The young priest walked straight up behind Adrian Crowe at the podium, so close that on the main camera he was only a white shape over the Chairman's shoulder. He laid his left hand flat between Crowe's shoulder blades, almost gently. His right hand came out of the folds of his linen and went in under it.

Crowe's raised hand stopped in the air.

On the camera in the sound booth at the back of the stage, a technician in a gray Organization jacket took his foot off a steel case on the floor.

Then every screen on the stage went black.

Not only the stage. The main camera, the crane camera, the roofs, the plaza: on Nina's big monitor the pictures died one after another, out from the podium in a ring, gray static and then nothing. The great screens over the plaza went dark. The sound went with them. On the small monitor the whole operations room came up out of its chairs, every man in it shouting at a wall of black.

Only Vale's cameras were still alive. They sat in hardened gray boxes on their shielded line, and whatever had killed every other feed in the square had not touched them. Their pictures rolled once and held.

In them, the young priest stepped back from the podium and walked down the steps behind the stage, unhurried, and was gone. Adrian Crowe stood a moment longer with his hand half raised. Then his knees gave, and he sat down on the boards, and lay over on his side behind the podium.

Down on the plaza a hundred thousand people stood in front of dead screens and could not see what had happened. Somebody screamed that the Chairman was down. Somebody screamed bomb. The crowd broke and ran every way at once, into the barricades, into each other.

Nina sat where she was, her palms flat on the desk, and watched the shielded feed.

On it, Alexander Vale stepped forward out of the row. He knelt down beside Adrian Crowe, in the blood, in his dark suit, and took the old man's head in his hands. He bent close. His lips moved. The camera could not hear what he said. Then he looked up, straight into the nearest of his own gray cameras, knowing which one it was, and his narrow pale face was wet with tears.

The other feeds came back one by one over the next four minutes, and every one of them came back to guards on their knees around the Chairman, their hands red, and the ten standing in their row at the back of the stage with their hands at their sides, looking down at the man on the floor. On not one of their faces, Nina saw, was there anything that looked like surprise. The young priest was nowhere. In eleven hundred cameras, she would learn later, he did not appear again. Not one frame.

\* \* \*

Adrian Crowe was declared dead in a room behind the stage, by four doctors from four countries, on every network in the world.

Her desk phone rang a few hours later. It was Kroll, calling from somewhere behind the stage in Jerusalem with sirens going under his voice, and his voice was one she had never heard from him, high and thin and too fast.

"Are you in the building?"

"I'm in my office."

"Go down to the vault. Stay with the mainframe, and keep the control room systems up. Whatever happens, don't leave it. Mr. Vale will want it ready."

"Ready for what?"

"Just stay with it, Nina." The line went dead.

She took the elevator three floors down under Third Avenue, and from the technician's desk in the vault she watched the world wait.

It waited for days. Nina would remember those days afterward only in fragments.

The square emptied. The networks played the footage of the stage again and again and again, from forty angles, the hand raised in blessing, the white shape behind him, and then the black, until people begged them to stop and they did not stop. They played the old footage too: Crowe in Venezuela, Crowe in Dubai, Crowe on every surviving screen the morning after the Rapture, promising order. They interviewed people weeping in the streets of Kinshasa and Manila and São Paulo and Kansas City. A woman in Rome said that she felt as though her own father had died. A man in Seoul said that the world had lost its only shepherd. Flowers piled up at the foot of the stage in a wall six feet high. Candles burned on every corner of the new Jerusalem.

The young priest was not found. The Organization said he was a religious extremist, a fanatic from the old Temple movement who could not bear to see the temple shared with the nations, and published his photograph, which was blurred, and his name, which Nina had never heard. The blackout had been his too, they said: a device carried in under his robe. On the second day, soldiers arrested two hundred priests and Levites and closed the temple to everyone but the Council.

The ten stayed in Jerusalem through the first two nights, in the temple, behind closed doors.

On the second night, they tried to arrest the two old men on the plaza, and four soldiers burned, and the old men stood their ground.

She sat at the technician's desk in the vault for days and nights in the cold and the blue light, and slept in the chair, and ate crackers from a box in the drawer, and watched the racks hum and blink and run, three rows of them, eight feet tall, holding the line open to forty thousand servers in Virginia with one dead man's whole life loaded into them and waiting. Every hour, she ran the diagnostic. Every hour, Juno said, *All systems nominal. Continuity is ready for assumption.*

On the second night, she called Ezra.

She was not supposed to. It was the most dangerous thing she had done in all those years. She did it on a phone she had built herself, through four relays and a borrowed ham license in New Jersey, and when the line clicked open at the Rock, where Ezra was that month, she could not speak at first.

"Nina," he said. "We saw. Are you safe?"

"I'm in the vault," she whispered. "In New York. With it."

He was quiet. Then, low: "That's the middle of the week. Daniel nine. The sacrifice taken away. Whatever's next comes now."

"Ezra, they knew." She was shaking. "The ten. They let him through. One of them stepped aside. And Vale looked at his watch. He looked at his watch before it happened. And every camera on that stage went black in the same second, Ezra, that was no accident. And the man who did it is gone, he's not on a single camera after, eleven hundred cameras, and I wrote the software, Ezra, I know what it can see. Somebody took him out of it. Somebody erased him before he ever walked up those steps." She bit down on her knuckle. "Ezra, I think Vale killed him. I think Vale killed Crowe."

On the other end, very faintly, she could hear Michael's voice, and then the turning of pages.

"*And I saw one of his heads as it were wounded to death;*" Ezra read, slowly, "*and his deadly wound was healed: and all the world wondered after the beast.*" He paused. "Revelation thirteen, verse three. Walt's had it marked in red for decades. Kambria had it in her notebook." His voice held steady. "Nina. What's in that room with you?"

She looked down the long vault at the three rows of blue lights, at the steel door at the end, the small white room behind it with its single chair and single camera and the black lens in the floor.

"Him," she said. "Everything he ever was."

The line was quiet so long she thought it had dropped. Then she heard the soft turning of pages, a few chapters on.

"*The beast that thou sawest was, and is not… when they behold the beast that was, and is not, and yet is.*" Ezra read it slowly. "Seventeen, verse eight. I've read that on the air for years and never once understood why it was written in three pieces." She heard him breathe. "Was. Is not. Yet is. Nina, I'm not going to tell you what that is. Not because I'm holding back. Because I don't know, and the Book doesn't say. But you know what's coming. You built it. You know better than I do."

She did. She had known for years and not let herself say it. She had fed a dead man's life into a machine, hour after hour, until the machine could talk like him and laugh like him and answer any question the way he would have answered it, and she had told herself it was an archive. A memorial. A project.

*…that they should make an image to the beast, which had the wound by a sword, and did live.*

"Come out," Ezra said. "Nina. Listen to me. Whatever you have to do, come out of there. Michael has people in Manhattan. A truck goes out to the mountain every week. You can be under the tarp by morning."

"I can't," she whispered. "Not yet. If I leave now, they'll know. And if I stay, I can see what they do with it." She closed her eyes. "Obadiah stayed in Ahab's house. You told me that."

"Obadiah hid the prophets," Ezra said. "He didn't build the idol."

The line crackled, and dropped, and was gone.

\* \* \*

The ten flew in from Jerusalem on the third night with Vale, and Kroll on his own jet an hour behind them.

Before dawn, the steel door at the far end of the vault opened, and footsteps came down the stairs.

Nina sat up in her chair. She had been asleep for perhaps twenty minutes. Her neck ached. The racks hummed around her in the cold.

It was Kroll. He came down in the same gray suit she had watched on the stage cameras walking behind the Chairman, slept in ever since, with his hair standing up on one side where he had leaned on a jet window, and his rimless glasses in his hand instead of on his face. His soft pale face was gray. He snapped at the guard who held the door for being slow, and walked down the long aisle between the racks toward her without seeing anything.

Behind him came the ten.

They filed down one by one and stood in the aisle between the racks in their dark suits, among the blue lights, and did not speak. And last of all, Alexander Vale came down the stairs, alone, and walked between them, and they stepped back to let him pass, all of them, without being asked.
