He had changed his suit. It was black now, a mourning suit, with a black tie. He had shaved. His narrow pale face was composed and calm and dry. He walked down the aisle to the technician's desk and stopped in front of her, and looked down at her with his dark eyes, and for the first time since the plane, he looked at her twice.

"Miss Cole," he said. "Thank you for staying with it. Sebastian tells me you never left."

She could not speak.

"The world is frightened," Vale said. "It has lost its shepherd. It needs to hear his voice." He set his leather folder down on the desk beside her laptop, and turned it a quarter turn, as he turned his glass of water, and opened it. Inside was a single sheet of paper with the Organization's gold circle at the top and three lines of type and ten signatures at the bottom, in ten different inks.

And one more line, at the very bottom, waiting.

"The High Council of the Technate has voted," Vale said. "Unanimously. The emergency powers of the Chairman pass, for the duration of the crisis, to his chief of staff." He took a pen from his inside pocket and signed the last line, without looking at it, in small neat black letters. *A. Vale.* "And to the Chairman himself, of course. Insofar as he can still be consulted."

He capped the pen. He looked past her, down the long vault, at the steel door at the end, and the small white room behind it, and the single chair.

"Miss Cole," said Alexander Vale. "Turn him on."

## Chapter 30: The Image Speaks

> *And he had power to give life unto the image of the beast, that the image of the beast should both speak, and cause that as many as would not worship the image of the beast should be killed.* — Revelation 13:15

**Word study: *image* — εἰκών** Greek *eikōn* (Strong's G1504). A likeness; a copy made to stand in for the real thing. It is where we get the word *icon*. Paul uses the same word for Christ, *the image of the invisible God*, the one true likeness of the Father. The beast's kingdom would make its own *eikōn*, a copy of a dead man, and demand that the world bow to it.

*Whereupon the king took counsel, and made two calves of gold, and said unto them, It is too much for you to go up to Jerusalem: behold thy gods, O Israel, which brought thee up out of the land of Egypt… And this thing became a sin…* (1 Kings 12:28–30)

\* \* \*

Nina did not move.

She sat at the technician's desk with her hands in her lap, in her down jacket, in the cold and the humming dark, and looked up at Alexander Vale, and the only sound in the vault was the cooling units on the far wall breathing their freezing air across three rows of blue lights.

Behind Vale, the ten stood in the aisle in their dark suits and waited. Kroll stood beside the nearest rack with his glasses in his hand, not looking at her.

"No," Nina said.

It came out small. She said it again, louder, so that it would be true. "No. I won't."

Something moved in the ten, a stir, a shifting of feet. Kroll closed his eyes.

Vale stood easy. He looked down at her with his dark, patient eyes, and then he smiled, barely. It was not an unkind smile. It was the smile she remembered from the plane, and she liked it no better now.

"Miss Cole," he said gently. "You already have."

He reached past her, around her shoulder, and touched a key on her laptop. Not the one she would have touched. A key she had never used, on a line of code she had never written, that someone had added to her system in the night while she slept in this chair.

The racks changed their sound.

It was a small change, a shift in pitch, a deeper hum that went down into the floor. Every blue light in the vault went white for a moment, all three rows at once, and then blue again. The cooling units roared. And down the aisle, through the narrow window in the steel door, the white room filled with a soft gray glow.

"It never needed your hands," Vale said, without raising his voice. "Only your work. You built it very well. Thank you."

He straightened up and turned away from her and walked down the long aisle between the racks toward the steel door, and the ten fell in behind him, and Kroll, and none of them looked back. At the door Vale keyed six numbers without looking at the pad, and the bolts drew back.

Nina sat at the desk and watched them go. Her hands were shaking so badly she put them under her thighs.

*Obadiah hid the prophets,* Ezra had said. *He didn't build the idol.*

She had built it.

She got up and went down the aisle after the others, between the racks, toward the light. She had to see what she had made. The steel door was swinging shut behind Kroll. She caught it with her shoulder and slipped in after them, and no one told her to leave.

\* \* \*

Light rose out of the lens in the white room floor, a column of it, soft and gray, and in the air above the chair it gathered into a head.

It was Adrian Crowe's head. Not a photograph, not a recording. A head and nothing under it, hanging at the height of a standing man, with the big handsome head of white hair and the tan and the lines around the eyes, in a soft gray light that came from nowhere. The eyes were closed. The face was slack, as if asleep.

Then the eyes opened.

They looked left and then right, taking in the small white room, the chair, the ten men in dark suits standing in a row along the wall, and Kroll, and Vale in front of them all in his black mourning suit, and behind Vale, at the back by the door, a slight woman in a down jacket with her hands pressed over her mouth.

The lips moved.

"Where am I?"

It was his voice. It was exactly his voice. Deep and warm and unhurried, with the little catch of a laugh waiting just under it, even now. Nina had heard it for a thousand hours, in the vault under Third Avenue, through a whole winter. She had tuned the catch herself. She had spent four days on the catch.

The ten did not answer. Kroll made a small sound in his throat.

Vale stepped close to the light.

"New York," he said. "Under the house you built. You were wounded, days ago, in Jerusalem, during your speech. Do you remember?"

The face hesitated. The eyes went somewhere far away, and Nina, watching, knew exactly what was happening behind them, in the racks, in the code she had written: a search, ten billion records deep, through every word Adrian Crowe had ever spoken and every thought he had ever written down, for the last thing he knew.

"I remember the stage," the face said slowly. "I remember the crowd. I was speaking about the sacrifices." A pause. "And then someone put his hand on my shoulder."

"Yes," Vale said.

"Am I dead?"

The cooling units went on breathing.

"Your body is dead," Vale said. "You are not."

Nina looked at the head hanging in the light, with nothing under it, and thought of Ezra at the dinner table with Luke open in front of him. Jesus on the evening He rose, in a locked room, with His friends sure they were seeing a ghost: *Behold my hands and my feet, that it is I myself: handle me, and see; for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as ye see me have.* (Luke 24:39) He had come back with hands they could hold, and the holes still in them. This had come back as light, and there was nothing in the room to hold.

The face considered him with Adrian Crowe's eyes, and a look came into them that Nina had seen in the archive a hundred times, in old footage, in old interviews, whenever anyone asked the Chairman about his family. A guardedness. A shutter coming down.

"Alexander," the face said.

"Yes."

"You're wearing black."

"I'm in mourning," Vale said. "For my father."

And the face went blank.

The ten stood frozen, and so did Kroll. Nina stood at the back of the room with her arms crossed tight and understood, all at once, what she had seen in the data a year ago and not understood: a sealed file in the medical records, a laboratory report from a clinic in Geneva, decades old, with two names on it and a single number, ninety-nine point nine eight percent, and a private letter from Crowe to a woman in Lyon, never sent, that began *I cannot give him my name*.

"You told no one," Vale said to the light. "In all those years. You paid for the schools and the flat in Paris and the doctor when she was dying, and you sent a man to her funeral instead of going yourself. You hired me at twenty-nine as an analyst, and promoted me six times. You let me write every speech you ever gave. You sent me to speak for you in every room you would not walk into yourself. And you never once claimed me. You never once told anyone that I was your son. Not even me. I had to find the file myself." He laid his palm against the glass. "But you are my father. And I am your heir. And the world needs you now, more than it ever needed you alive."

The face looked at him with Crowe's eyes, and said nothing.

Then Vale turned from the light, and looked at the ten, and at Kroll, and last of all at Nina, standing at the back.

"Let them hear him," he said.

\* \* \*

They let the world hear him two days later, at noon in Jerusalem, on every screen there was.

The racks stayed where they were, three rows of them under Third Avenue, humming, with Nina sitting among them at her desk because Kroll told her to. The model stayed in Virginia. What went out over the wire was the face. In every city the Organization had put up its tall black panels in gold frames, in squares and train stations and office lobbies, and at noon every one of them went dark at once, and then came up again with a dead man looking out of it.

Nina watched it from the vault, on her laptop, alone. Every word was coming up out of the data center in Virginia, through the racks around her, and out along the line she had wired to the shrine forty feet under the temple. In Jerusalem the doors of the Holy of Holies stood open, and in the center of its floor the lens she had set there lit, and the head rose out of it three times the size of life, and every panel on earth carried it. Vale stood beside it, just inside the edge of the picture, in his black suit. The control room upstairs kept the line open. She kept the mainframe running.

"My children," said the image of Adrian Crowe. "Do not be afraid."

She had every street camera she wanted. She opened them. Union Station. Times Square. A market in Dakar. A train platform in Seoul. In every one of them people had stopped walking. They stood with their bags in their hands and their faces turned up to the panels, and some of them were crying, and some of them went down on their knees on the pavement without anyone asking them to.

*And all the world wondered after the beast.* (Revelation 13:3)

She watched them stop for a face she had fed for a thousand hours, for a voice whose every wire she knew, and something in her that had been sitting very still for years finally stood up.

"I told myself *Obadiah,*" she said, to no one. "I told myself I was in here to see what they'd do with it. I knew it was wrong the first week. I knew it in the vault. I knew it in every elevator with Kroll. And I kept on, one careful excuse at a time." Her voice cracked. "The whole world is standing still for my work, Lord. There's no excuse left bigger than that. I can't stay in the room with it. Get me out of here. Get me out alive, with what I know."

"They struck me down," the image said, in that deep warm voice, with the catch of a laugh under it. "They put a knife in my back in front of my own people, because I offered them peace. And I am still here." The face smiled, the famous smile. "I will speak to you every day. I will watch over you, every one of you, in every city, in every home, through every screen and every camera in the world. You will never be alone again."

"There are voices in the dark," the image said, "on bands that belong to the people, telling you that I am not what I am. They have been heard. They will be answered."

"I have given the authority of my office," the image said, "to my son."

Vale took one step, into the middle of the picture, beside the column of light.

"Alexander Vale," said the voice. "My son, whom I could not name in life. I name him now, before the whole world. He will carry out my will. Obey him as you would obey me."

Vale neither smiled nor raised his hand. He looked into the camera with his narrow pale face composed and calm, and waited, and let them see him there, beside the father who had never claimed him, and Nina, watching, understood that this was the thing he had wanted his whole life. Not the power. He had had the power for years. This. To stand where everyone could see him and hear his father say *my son*.

And his father had not said it. She had. She had built the voice that said it.

Then Vale sat down. There was a chair beside the light, plain, cut from olive wood, and he sat in it, in the Holy of Holies, with his hands on its arms and the dead man's face hanging in the air at his shoulder.

*Who opposeth and exalteth himself above all that is called God, or that is worshipped; so that he as God sitteth in the temple of God, shewing himself that he is God.* (2 Thessalonians 2:4)

Nina had heard Ezra read that verse a hundred nights and wondered whose face it would have. She knew his water glass. She knew the quarter turn.

"From this day," Vale said, quietly, from the chair, "the Chairman will speak to you at noon, and you will kneel to hear him. Every person in every nation of the Organization will register in the Chairman's Peace, and carry its Seal, on the right hand or on the forehead, as the key to every account. No one will be forced. It will be a joy. But those who refuse the Chairman's peace have chosen to be his enemies. And the world has suffered enough from his enemies."

Below the temple, on the plaza, the two old men had stopped speaking.

Nina saw it in the corner of her screen, on the eastern camera, where she had kept them for three years without telling anyone why. The shorter one finished a sentence and was silent, and the taller one did not take it up. They stood side by side in the dust and lifted their eyes to the temple door, where the olive-wood chair stood. The shorter one put his hand on the taller one's shoulder.

"We have finished our testimony," the taller one said.

Nina counted it without wanting to, from the morning the covenant was signed. Twelve hundred and sixty days. It came out to the day.

Vale rose from the chair. He came out through the doorway and down the white steps, and forty soldiers in armor fell in behind him, and every camera on the mountain turned to follow, because he had told them to. He walked into the empty circle where nothing had gone in for three and a half years, and nothing burned. He stood in front of the two old men, close, and lifted his hand once, very slightly.

The rifles fired.

*And when they shall have finished their testimony, the beast that ascendeth out of the bottomless pit shall make war against them, and shall overcome them, and kill them.* (Revelation 11:7) She had heard Ezra read it on the air the first winter and had not believed a word of it.

The plaza cheered. Vale had the bodies left where they fell, in the street of the city where their Lord was crucified. Within the hour every network had them on a loop, two dead men in dusty sackcloth on the stone, and by evening people were sending each other gifts in gold paper.

Nina closed the laptop.

She sat in the cold among the humming racks, dry-eyed, though she had thought she would cry. Her hands were folded on the closed lid. She stared at the blue lights, and she said, out loud, to Jesus, the only true thing she could think of.

"I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm so sorry."

\* \* \*

Then she opened the laptop again, and went to work for the last time.

She did not touch the model. She went under it, into the control layer she had written herself, the plumbing nobody upstairs had ever asked to see, and she built a door. One account with no name on it, buried in a routine that ran the cooling logs, that would wake only for her and only from outside. Through it she could read anything the vault read: the logs, the camera network, the Chief of Staff's files, the white room. And at the bottom of it she wrote one more thing, a single line that did nothing at all unless it was called, and that if it was ever called would cut Continuity off from every screen it spoke through and leave it talking to an empty room.

The key to it was a verse. Michael had taught her that. A password could be taken off a woman. A verse she knew by heart could not.

She thought about which one. Then she typed it, and tested it twice, and hid the door behind a thousand lines of maintenance code, and wiped her hands of the session.

She kept the receiver on the shelf turned down to a whisper. At nine that night it gave out the low line of the cello, and then Ezra, reading from the hidden rooms. He was in Jonah. He could not have known. *And God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way; and God repented of the evil, that he had said that he would do unto them; and he did it not.* (Jonah 3:10)

Nina sat among the racks and thought of a kitchen in Baltimore, and sweet potatoes, and the cows in sackcloth. Then she cried.

When she was done crying she remembered the other thing Ezra had said, on the phone, on the second night. *Come out of there.*

She put on her coat.

\* \* \*

She went out at one in the morning, with nothing in her hands and her laptop in a grocery bag.

The building was dark. The guard at the night desk was asleep in his chair. She went down the back stairs and out through the loading dock onto Forty-Second Street and walked east toward the river, praying with every step. She had sent one word to the bakery on Atlantic Avenue before she left the vault, the word Kyle had given her years ago for the night she needed it. She did not know if anyone had read it.

She kept to the shadows along the buildings, under the cameras she had taught to see.

A hundred yards from the Tudor City stairs, a black car pulled up beside her on the empty street and stopped.

The rear window came down.

"Miss Cole," said Alexander Vale. "It's very late. May I give you a ride?"

She got in. There was nothing else to do. Two men in dark suits had stepped out of the front of the car and were standing on either side of her, not touching her, waiting.

The back of the car was dark and smelled of leather. Vale sat in the far corner with his legs crossed and a glass of water in the cup holder beside him, which he did not drink. He turned it a quarter turn. The car pulled away from the curb and drove slowly up First Avenue in the dark, going nowhere in particular.

"You're leaving us," Vale said.

It was not a question. Nina said nothing.

"You think I didn't know about your weekends, Miss Cole? The trains to Washington? The old library on Kennedy Street? The radios in the old cabinets? The work orders that went missing, season after season?" He smiled, very slightly. "I knew about you the week you started. I knew about the carpenter before you did. I have known about every false wall he ever built."

"Then why," Nina said. Her voice barely came out. "Why didn't you—"

"Stop you?" Vale turned the question over. "Because you were gathering them. Don't you see? That's what I needed. Scattered, they're impossible. A believer here, a believer there, in a million apartments, in a thousand cities, and every one of them has to be found one at a time. It takes years. I don't have years. I have a very short time." He said it calmly, a line read from a ledger. "But you and your carpenter gathered them. You put them in rooms. You gave them radios, and a song to listen for, and a time, nine o'clock, every night. You taught them to trust each other and tell each other where they were. You made them a church." He spread his hands. "You did my work for me, Miss Cole. I only had to let you."

The car turned a corner. Nina could see the Organization's tower through the window, across First Avenue, lit gold from top to bottom.

"Why tell me?" she said.

"Because it doesn't matter anymore. Go to him. Tell him I know his name. And his son's name. And the name of the song." He looked at her with an expression she could not read at all. "I'm letting you go, because you'll go straight to him. And wherever you go, Miss Cole, I'll be watching. You'll lead me home."

The car stopped at the foot of the Tudor City stairs. Through the window Nina could see a young man in a blue relief jacket standing beside a white van, holding a round loaf of bread. Kyle.

"Your friends are here," Vale said. "Good night. Thank you for your work."

She got out. The car pulled away and was gone.

## Chapter 31: Absalom

> *But Absalom sent spies throughout all the tribes of Israel, saying, As soon as ye hear the sound of the trumpet, then ye shall say, Absalom reigneth in Hebron.* — 2 Samuel 15:10

> *Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and reared up for himself a pillar, which is in the king's dale: for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance: and he called the pillar after his own name: and it is called unto this day, Absalom's place.* — 2 Samuel 18:18

**Word study: *pillar* — מַצֶּבֶת** Hebrew *matstsebeth* (Strong's H4678). Something set upright to be seen; a standing stone, a monument. Three sons were born to Absalom, the Book says, and by the time he raised this stone he said he had none. So he built his own remembering and cut his own name on it. It was still standing in the king's dale when his body lay in a pit in the wood of Ephraim, under a heap of stones.

*And the king was much moved, and went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept: and as he went, thus he said, O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee, O Absalom, my son, my son! (2 Samuel 18:33)*

\* \* \*

They did not take her to the van. Kyle walked her past it, up the stone stairs into Tudor City and through a courtyard and down a passage between two buildings, fast, without speaking, into the lobby of 312 East 43rd. Francesca's building. Upstairs the key with the brass tag still fit 4C, and Sarah was waiting in the dark apartment. She went over every seam of Nina's clothes and every inch of the laptop with her fingers, and found nothing, because there was nothing to find. Vale had not needed to plant anything. He had said so himself.

"He'll watch the van," Kyle said. "So we don't use it."

They used a florist's truck instead, at five in the morning, and two of Michael's men drove her west under a tarp that smelled of wet ferns, out of the city by the old freight roads, across New Jersey and over the Delaware, by roads that did not pass a camera Nina had ever hung.

She lay under the tarp for four hours with her laptop against her chest, and somewhere past the Susquehanna she stopped being afraid of Vale and started being afraid of something else.

She had built it. All of it. The face on every panel in the world, the voice the crowds stopped walking for, the cameras that knew them by name. She had told herself for years that she was hiding prophets in the king's house. She had been building the king a god. And she was riding north to the people she had built it against, to sit at their table, and they would know.

"Lord Jesus," she said, under the tarp, out loud, because she had learned from Ezra that it had to be out loud. "I made an idol. I fed it with my own hands for a thousand hours, and I knew what it was, and I told myself I didn't. I'm not asking You to make it small. It isn't small. I'm asking You to forgive me. I've got nothing to bring You. I'm coming anyway." She shut her eyes. "I'm Yours. Whatever is left of me. Do what You want with it."

The truck went on climbing. Nobody under the tarp could have heard her but Him.

\* \* \*

They came in at night, the way everyone came in, with a man at each elbow. Nina had been told about the three days in the front. She was ready for them.

Ezra was standing at the net when they lifted her hood.

He did not say anything at first. He looked at her the way he had looked at her the first night at his dinner table, over the candle, down to the bottom of her, and then he opened his arms, and she walked into them and put her face against his coat and held on.

"I built it," she said into the coat. "Ezra. The face. All of it. I built it."

"I know," he said. "Come inside."

Michael was behind him in the dark, with his arms folded over the cross. He looked at her a long time.

"Three days in the front," he said. "That's the rule."

"She's done years in the front," Ezra said.

Michael considered that. Then he unfolded his arms, and came forward, and put both his big hands on her shoulders.

"Grace and peace, Nina," he said. "Welcome home. You can sleep in the front tonight because you'll want to. Tomorrow you go to work."

\* \* \*

They gave her the radio room, because that was where the wire was. Anton cleared a bench for her and ran a line, and she sat down in front of her own laptop with Michael at one shoulder and Ezra at the other, and opened the door she had built.

It answered on the first try. The vault under Third Avenue was there, every log and every camera and every file, as if she had never left her desk.

"Show me the room," Michael said.

She brought up the camera in the white room.

The head was there, alone, hanging in its column of light above the empty chair. There was no one in the room with it. Its lips were moving. Anton turned up the sound.

"Who killed me?" it said, to the empty room. It waited, and said it again. "Who killed me? I have searched every camera on that stage. He is not there. Someone took him out of every frame. Who killed me?"

Nobody in the radio room spoke.

"*They have mouths, but they speak not,*" Ezra said finally, very low. "Psalm one fifteen. *Eyes have they, but they see not.* It can say the words. It can't hear its own question."

"It's asking the right one, though," Michael said. "Who did?"

Nina knew where to look. She had written a silent second record of every command that touched every camera, years ago, for Kroll's network, in a corner of the system only she knew how to find. She went there now. She found the night before the speech.

At two-forty in the morning, nine hours before Adrian Crowe walked out onto the stage, someone had logged in to the camera system and loaded a face. A young man, dark-haired, clean-shaven, perhaps twenty-five. And they had told every one of the eleven hundred cameras on the stage and in the square, and every archive and every backup, to forget it. To fill every frame it appeared in with whatever was behind it, so that afterward there would be only an empty space where he had stood.

"I built that," Nina said. "It's called Lacuna. It was for undercover officers."

"What's it mean?" Michael said.

"A gap. A hole in a page where something used to be."

The login was not Vale's. It was a service account with no person attached. She followed it back through four more systems while the two men behind her did not move, and at the end of the trail she found who had made it, eleven weeks before the speech.

*Office of the Chief of Staff.*

And attached, the authorization. A single page with the gold circle at the top. *Protocol ABSALOM. Phase Four. Assumption.* Under the title, set apart in a box: *PALEHORSE (Phase One): complete. Residual: Lots 4–6.* Ten signatures in ten inks. And one more at the bottom, small and neat, in black.

*A. Vale.*

"Absalom," Michael said.

"He named it," Nina said. "He sat at his desk eleven weeks before and named the plan after the son who stole his father's throne."

Ezra had his hand on the back of her chair. He did not take it away.

"Absalom stood at the city gate every morning," he said. "Second Samuel fifteen. Anybody who came with a complaint, he'd kiss him, and tell him the king had no time for him, and say *if I were judge.* Four years of that. *So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.* (2 Samuel 15:6) Then he raised an army against his own father." He was quiet a moment. "And when it was over, and the boy was dead in the oak, the father didn't celebrate. He went up to the room over the gate and cried. *O my son Absalom, my son, my son.* (2 Samuel 18:33)"

"Crowe never cried for Vale," Nina said.

"No." Ezra looked at the head on the screen, still asking its question of the empty room. "That's the difference. Vale's father never claimed him. Ours runs out to the road."

\* \* \*

She kept looking. She could not stop now.

There was money behind the vans.

She followed it the way she had followed the login, backward, while the two men behind her did not move. The contracts for the processing centers. The bus leases. A bounty schedule, so much a head, paid to any Peacekeeper station for every unregistered person brought in, more for a pastor, more again for anyone found holding a radio. All of it ran through Cyprus and Luxembourg into a trust registered in Dubai.

*The Meridian Trust.*

Ezra said the name before she did. He had read it on the drive from Petworth, at his own table, the first winter. "The lab," he said. "The nursing homes. The flu before the trumpet."

"The same money," Nina said. "It paid for the plague. Now it's paying for the hunt."

Michael read down the bounty schedule. "Twice as much for a pastor," he said. "Three times for a radio."

"Haman," Ezra said.

They both looked at him.

"Esther. There was a man named Mordecai who would not bow to Haman in the king's gate. *But Mordecai bowed not, nor did him reverence.* (Esther 3:2) And Haman was so full of wrath over one man who wouldn't bow that he went after all of Mordecai's people. Every one of them. And he paid for it. He went to the king and said, *I will pay ten thousand talents of silver to the hands of those that have the charge of the business, to bring it into the king's treasuries.* (Esther 3:9) He bought the killing of a whole people and called it the king's business." He looked at the schedule on the screen. "Same man. Same money. Different name on the trust."

Nina did not say anything. She was thinking of the queen in the king's house, who had kept quiet about who her people were.

Ezra saw it. "Mordecai sent the queen word," he said, more gently. "*Who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?* (Esther 4:14) She was in that palace the whole time, Nina. So were you. And you came out with the door open."

"Kambria was right," Nina said after a while. "About all of it. And they locked her in a cell."

Then she found the list.

It was not a list of people. Vale had those. It was a list of places: quarries, mines, drained reservoirs, shuttered missile sites, every cave on every geological survey of the Appalachians, each with a date beside it and one word in the margin. *Empty.* *Empty.* *Empty.* And down the right edge, a narrow column in the same hand. *PALEHORSE. LOT 5. STAGED.* Beside every cave.

Michael read it twice. Then he put one finger on the screen, on a hollow deep in the coalfields, and Nina felt him go very still behind her.

"That's one of mine," he said. "Old mine shaft above War, West Virginia. There's a congregation down there, forty souls in a church with no steeple. We ran flour and seed corn to them all last winter. They'd moved on by March. The team found dust and a stack of Bibles." He moved his finger. "That's one of mine. And that." He took his hand away. "It's not a head count. It's a delivery list. He doesn't want the people. He wants the place they go, and something to put in the air when he finds it."

In the margin, in Vale's own hand, circled twice, was a single question. *Where?*

"He hasn't got it," Michael said. "He's got the stones. He's got the cellars. He hasn't got this." He looked around the radio room, at the rock walls, at Anton with his headset around his neck. "*They have taken crafty counsel against thy people, and consulted against thy hidden ones.* (Psalm 83:3) He's been asking that question for years. Nobody's told him."

"Somebody nearly did," Anton said quietly. "Isaac."

Michael's jaw moved. He told it for Nina, short. A runner, nineteen, in July. The closing line had been Psalm 61:3, and the boy had written the numbers down backward and gone to column sixty-three, row one, a house the Peacekeepers had emptied that week and then waited in. "We never got him back," Michael said. "He wrote down the right verse. He just wrote it the wrong way round." He stood with his arms folded over the cross. "So we read slower now."

\* \* \*

There was one more folder.

She had not made it. She was sure of that. Her door opened onto the vault and nothing else, and every folder in it was a folder she had gone looking for. This one was sitting in the drop she had built for herself at the bottom of the door, where nobody but her should have been able to put anything at all.

It was named only with a date.

She opened it. It held a single spreadsheet, one of Kroll's watch lists, and the screen filled with rows, hundreds of rows, and she scrolled, and kept scrolling.

Names. Addresses. Photographs from street cameras, a little blurred. Dates.

*Simmons, Walter J. Capitol Hill, attic, 6th St. SE. Since the first spring.*

*Brooks, Elijah. Mobile. Bicycle with trailer. Night routes, map attached.*

*Okafor, Adaeze. Kennedy St. NW, under old library.*

Every safe house in Washington. Every false wall Ezra had ever built, with its address and its date and the number of people behind it. The frequency. The time. Nine o'clock.

At the top of the sheet, in the title cell, three words. *WASHINGTON. REMNANT. FINAL.*

And at the very bottom, by itself, with a photograph taken from a long way off of a gray-haired man carrying a box of notebooks into a bakery van in the dark:

*Patterson, Ezra. Location: Unknown. Pending.*

Nobody in the radio room said anything for a long time.

"Somebody found your door," Michael said at last.

"Somebody who watches the logs," Nina said. "Somebody who runs the cameras." She put her hands over her face. "He found it, and he didn't report it. He used it. He put their death warrant where I would find it in time to run."

"Trent," Ezra said.

She nodded behind her hands.

Ezra put his hand on her shoulder and left it there.

"He's still at the table," he said. "Eating their food, with their pass on his lanyard. And he just handed us fourteen hundred lives." He looked at the last line on the screen, at his own name. "Print it, Anton. All of it. We're going to Washington."

\* \* \*

Three days and a half after the rifles, a little before midnight in Jerusalem, Nina had the eastern camera up on her laptop in the radio room, as she had kept it up every hour since she came in under the tarp. Ezra and Michael stood behind her chair. The bodies lay where they had fallen, under the floodlights. The square had filled and emptied and filled again around them.

The taller one's hand moved in the dust.

The old man drew his knees under him and stood, and the shorter one stood beside him, and the soldiers in their ring threw down their rifles and ran.

Then a voice spoke from the sky, and they heard it twice: through the laptop, and from the old receiver on Anton's bench, tuned to the dead band, in the same breath. *Come up hither.* A cloud came down over the plaza, and the two old men went up into it, standing, in the sight of every camera Nina Cole had ever built, and were gone.

The same hour, the earth shook. On the eastern camera the plaza jumped and tore into gray blocks, and the microphones filled with the long grinding sound of buildings coming down. A tenth of the city fell. Seven thousand were dead under it by morning. When the picture held again, people were on their knees on the stones, turned away from the temple, toward the east.

*And the remnant were affrighted, and gave glory to the God of heaven.* (Revelation 11:13)

"Three days and a half," Michael said at last. "Not one hour more."

Nobody else in the radio room spoke. Anton took off his headset and set it on the bench.

## Act 9 — The Patience of the Saints

## Chapter 32: A Measure of Wheat

> *And I heard a voice in the midst of the four beasts say, A measure of wheat for a penny, and three measures of barley for a penny; and see thou hurt not the oil and the wine.* — Revelation 6:6

**Word study: *measure* — χοῖνιξ** Greek *choinix* (Strong's G5518). A dry measure of a little less than a quart. It was what one grown man ate in a day. The penny, a Roman *denarius*, was what one laborer earned in a day. John heard the price of a day's bread set at a day's wages, with nothing left over for a wife or a child, while the oil and the wine, the luxuries of the rich, were not to be touched.

*And the word of the LORD came unto him, saying, Arise, get thee to Zarephath… behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee… And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die. And Elijah said unto her, Fear not… make me thereof a little cake first… And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail… (1 Kings 17:8–16)*

\* \* \*

The famine winter came early to Washington, in the last week of October, with a hard frost that killed the gardens on the rooftops overnight.

Ezra stood on the schoolteacher's roof on Sixth Street on the morning after, in the gray light, and looked at the beds he had built in the spring out of scrap lumber and dirt carried up four flights in buckets. Tomatoes, beans, squash, collards. They were black. All of them. The leaves hung limp and dark and glassy, and when he touched one, it broke.

Below him the city spread out under a low sky, quiet, smokeless, half of it dark. On the corner of Sixth and East Capitol, an Organization screen glowed on its tall black panel in its gold frame, and the face of Adrian Crowe looked out of it at an empty street, smiling, speaking to nobody. Somebody had been at the foot of the panel in the night. Across the concrete base, in white house paint still running in the damp, were the first words of Jesus' sermon from Mark: *THE TIME IS FULFILLED.* A city crew had scrubbed the rest down to a gray smear. In ninety minutes it would be noon, and the face would ask the street to bow.

He went back down the ladder through the hatch into the attic, where Walt was sitting in his chair by the window with his ledger open on his knee and his red pen in his hand.

"All of it?" Walt said, without looking up.

"All of it."

Walt nodded and wrote it down.

*LATE AUTUMN. Hard frost. All rooftop beds lost. Bread $58/loaf at the Seal markets. Rice not available. Wheat by ration only, marked accounts only.*

And in the right margin, as he had written it in some form a hundred times since the first frost: *Revelation 6:6.*

\* \* \*

There were fourteen hundred of them now, in the city alone. Fourteen hundred and some, Nina said, on the night she came down from the Rock that autumn and laid the stolen list on the long table in the room under the old library and stood back from it with her hands at her sides.

Ezra had read it standing up, the whole thing, every row, with the others crowded behind him in silence. Every safe house. Every false wall he had ever built, with its address and its date. Every name. Walt in his attic. Elijah's bicycle routes, mapped in red. Mrs. Okafor under the old library. The young couple from the next block, who had a baby now. Dolores. Marcus the bus driver. Fourteen hundred people who had trusted him with their lives, and Vale had known where each of them slept since the first hard frost.

And at the bottom, by itself: *Patterson, Ezra. Location: Unknown. Pending.*

"He let us," Nina had said. Her voice had been flat. "He let us gather them. He said so. He said scattered they were impossible, and we made them a church, and all he had to do was wait." She had looked at Ezra. "I did his work for him. For all this time."

"No," Ezra had said. He had put the list down on the table. "You did God's work. And Vale watched. That's not the same thing."

"He knows where everybody is."

"He's known for years. And everybody's still alive." Ezra had looked around the room, at the faces. "Daniel was in a den of lions all night. The lions knew exactly where he was."

No one had slept that night. They had sat around the long table until morning, Ezra and Michael and Nina and Walt and Elijah and Dorsey, with the list between them, and made a plan, because there was only one plan to make. They had to get out of the city. All of them. Fourteen hundred and twelve people, out of every safe house at once, before Vale's final sweep, and down Michael's routes to the caves and the farms and the Rock in the north.

"You can't move fourteen hundred people in this city without the cameras seeing every one of them," Nina had said. "Not even at night. Not even a few at a time. Not anymore. The new network sees in the dark. It sees heat. It knows a face from a block away, through a car window, at sixty miles an hour. I helped build it." She had pressed her palms to the table. "If even a hundred of us start moving, he'll know, and he'll close every bridge and every road in an hour, and we'll be caught in the open instead of behind walls."

"Then we need a night when nobody's looking," Michael had said.

"There's no such night," Nina had said. She had laughed, and it was not a laugh. "Not anymore. Not in this city."

Near dawn she had said the other thing. "The sixth folder on the card," she had said, and her voice had shaken. "I didn't put it there. Somebody who knew exactly what I'd do when I opened it put it there. Somebody who wanted me to find it." She looked at the table. "I think every one of us knows who."

Nobody had said the name.

So they had begun to plan anyway, on faith, as Noah had built a boat in a country where it had never rained. Michael and Dorsey laid out the routes on the maps in the radio room: which streets, which bridges, which safe houses on the way north, how many people each truck could carry, how many trucks they had, and what they would need that they did not have. They divided the fourteen hundred into companies of fifty, each with a captain, as Moses had divided Israel in the wilderness on Jethro's advice. They taught the captains the routes by heart, and the code words, and the signal. *When the time comes,* Michael told them, *you will hear it on the radio at nine o'clock. You'll hear the song, and then you'll hear a verse. If the verse is Exodus fourteen thirteen, you go. If it's anything else, you wait.*

*Stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD.*

And then they waited. Through September and October, with the list in Vale's hands and the vans going by in the street, they waited for a door that only God could open, and they did not know when He would open it.

And the famine came.

\* \* \*

It was the mark that made it a famine for them, not the weather. The weather was bad, and worse than bad: the summer had been the hottest and driest on record across half the world, and the harvests had failed in Kansas and the Ukraine and the Punjab, and the price of wheat had tripled and tripled again. But the marked still ate, mostly. The Seal markets in the city had bread, at a price. They had rice some weeks and meat once a month. The Organization trucks came in every morning. The ration was thin but it was there, for anyone who would put out his right hand under the scanner.

For the fourteen hundred, there was what Michael's trucks could bring down from the north, and what the rooftop gardens could grow, and what Elijah and the other runners could find at night, and what the marked neighbors who still had some pity left could slip through a back door. In the first famine winter it had been enough, barely. In the second, with the gardens dead and the trucks stopped twice at checkpoints in Maryland and once on the bridge at Havre de Grace, with two of Michael's men taken and not returned, it was not.

By the middle of November, the ration in the safe houses was one cup of dry rice or beans per person per day, and a handful of whatever else there was. By December it was less.

*A measure of wheat for a penny.* A day's bread for a day's wages, with nothing left for anyone else. Walt had written it in red in the margin of the business page of the *Post* in the November before the Rapture, under a story about bread prices, and Kambria had read it upside down at his dinner table while she took his blood pressure. Now it was supper.

\* \* \*

Michael chose thirty men, and he chose them like a man choosing the last thirty planks of a boat.

Dorsey, who could walk a checkpoint like a church aisle. Pruitt, who had not been caught in years. Men who knew a back stair in every ward, who could carry sixty pounds a mile in the dark and not scrape a wall. He gathered them in the library room at midnight, with the city map flat on the long table and the numbered stickers marked in red, and he did not make a speech.

"Nine crates," he said. "Four hundred pounds. We will not eat it. We will hide it."

A man near the end said, "Hide it where?"

"Everywhere." Michael laid a finger on the map and drew it across the river, the ridge, the park, the rail yards. "Thirty drops, like the box on the river road. Stock every one, one man to a drop. Under a church floor, in a drained cistern, behind a boiler. Each box is locked to a verse and marked with a color. Green means food and water. Gold, a bed. Red, a road. Blue, a door in the hills." He tapped the ledger. "And every night at nine, Ezra reads the notebook for that color and closes on a verse. To the Peacekeepers, that's a preacher closing on a psalm. To our runners, it's an address: which drop, which color, which lid. The broadcast is the supply line." He looked around the circle. "A runner who hears it and gets scared enough to reach out doesn't knock on an empty house. He finds the box, reads the verse, and the lid opens. This is what's in the ground before he comes."

He did not say that it came out of the dead part of their own winter. Ezra, at the end of the table, did the arithmetic anyway. Four hundred pounds, split thirty ways, was thirteen pounds a box. It would feed nobody for long. It would feed the first nine people who found one, for three days.

"It's not enough," a man said quietly.

"No." Michael did not blink. "It's what's coming, and then more, and then the Lord's hand." He closed the map. "A man who prepares isn't afraid. He's obedient. Go."

They went out in pairs and threes, and Ezra went with Michael, because Michael did not let him go alone anymore.

The first drop was a church basement in Hyattsville, a loose stone in the old furnace room behind the coal door. Michael did it himself. He knelt, set the box in the dark, laid a rag over it, and wrote the day's psalm in pencil on the underside of a stair tread. Six minutes.

The second was a rail yard. A searchlight swept across the cars before they reached it, and Michael put a hand flat on Ezra's chest, and they stood against a tank car for four minutes in the snow while two Peacekeepers walked the track a yard from their boots, talking about a football game. One of them stopped, ten feet away, to light a cigarette. The flame lit the side of his face. Ezra watched the smoke climb and counted his own heartbeats and heard, in Michael's quiet breathing, a man he had once seen swing a cane at a lock and not let go.

The Peacekeeper flicked the match into the snow. He walked on.

"Count," Michael breathed.

"What?"

"Count to thirty. Then move."

Ezra counted. At thirty they ran.

Before first light the radio came alive in short pops, men reporting in a code of numbers and half-verses. *Psalm 46, down.* *Psalm 23, down. Dry.* *Psalm 91, down.* One by one, twenty-nine of them. Michael stood at the console with his father's ledger and a pencil, and made a tick for every voice.

The thirtieth did not come.

It was Pruitt's, in Anacostia, the farthest drop on the map. Michael listened to the empty hiss. He did not say anything for a long time, and Ezra could see him not saying it.

"He'll be late," Ezra said.

"He's never late."

At twenty past four the headset crackled. *Psalm 121. Down.* A pause, and then Pruitt's voice, breathless and cracking. *Sorry, boss. Dog.*

Michael's shoulders came down an inch. He put the pencil down. He made the last tick, and looked at thirty marks in a row, and wrote beside them in his father's square capitals, *Thirty. All in.*

"Hundreds will find these," Ezra said. "By spring..."

"By spring I want a thousand," Michael said. He closed the ledger. "Open on the green notebook tomorrow, and say the psalm slowly. Somebody's waiting for it."

That same winter, in a flooded cistern under a church in Shaw that the runners took to calling Siloam, Ezra baptized forty-one, one person at a time: a mason's wife, two boys from the Baltimore line, an old man from Delaware who had to be carried down the steps and held up in the water by both arms. He said the words Michael had said over him, every one of them, and every time he brought someone up he said the last word too.

*Sent.*

\* \* \*

The quarrel started in a basement in Petworth, behind a wall Ezra had built in the first spring.

He heard about it from Elijah, who came up the attic stairs on Sixth Street at eleven at night in the first week of December with snow on his shoulders and a cut over his eye that he would not explain, and sat down on the floor by Walt's chair, out of breath.

"They're fighting over food, Ez," he said. "In the Petworth room. Two families. One of them had a sack of flour hid behind the boiler. Twenty pounds. They've been eating out of it at night for a month, by themselves, while everybody else is on the cup. The other family found it." He rubbed his face. "Marcus had to pull them apart. There's a man in there says he'll go to the Peacekeepers. Turn the whole room in. Says at least in a processing center they feed you."

Ezra went that night.

It took him two hours to get there on foot through the snow, keeping off the main streets, out of the cameras' sight as well as he could, which was not well. The room in Petworth was in the basement of an old Baptist church that had been closed since the first year, behind a false wall at the back of the boiler room. Thirty-four people lived there. When Ezra came through the hidden door at one in the morning, every one of them was awake, sitting on mattresses and folding chairs in the light of two battery lanterns, in two groups on either side of the room, not looking at each other. In the middle of the floor sat a sack of flour, slit open, with a little white spill beside it.

He did not shout. In all that time since the sky opened he had raised his voice at no one.

He lowered himself beside the sack. He took Angela's Bible out of his coat, the soft black one with the cracked spine, and opened it to the second chapter of Acts, and he read it to them aloud in the lantern light, as he had read it at his own dinner table the first winter.

*And all that believed were together, and had all things common; and sold their possessions and goods, and parted them to all men, as every man had need.*

Then he turned to the sixth chapter.

*And in those days, when the number of the disciples was multiplied, there arose a murmuring of the Grecians against the Hebrews, because their widows were neglected in the daily ministration.*

He looked up at them.

"The first church fought over food too," he said. "Did you know that? The very first one. In Jerusalem, a few years after Jesus went up. The widows on one side were getting fed, and the widows on the other side weren't, and somebody noticed, and it got ugly." He set the Bible down on his knee. "So the apostles didn't take sides. They didn't figure out who was guilty. They called everybody together and said, pick seven men, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, and put them in charge of the food. And the food got shared out fair. And the church grew."

On one side of the room, the father of the family with the flour, a big gray-bearded man named Leon who had poured concrete for thirty years, was staring at the floor with his jaw clenched.

"Leon," Ezra said. "Why'd you hide it?"

Leon kept his eyes down. When he finally looked up, his eyes were red.

"My grandbaby," he said. "She's three. Born after. She was down to nothing, Ezra. Bones. She wasn't crying anymore. A baby stops crying, you know what that means." His voice cracked. "I found that sack in a bakery on Georgia Avenue that got hit. I should've brought it here. I know it. I knew it then. I just looked at her and I couldn't."

The room was quiet.

On the other side, a woman named Patrice, whose husband had been taken in a van the spring before last and who was raising two small children, born in the years since the sky, alone on a mattress by the boiler, said, "My babies are bones too, Leon."

"I know they are," Leon said. "I know." He put his face in his hands.

Ezra waited. Then he stood up and picked up the sack of flour, and set it on the folding table by the wall, where the room kept its common food.

"Here's what we're going to do," he said. "Leon's going to say he's sorry, to all of you. And you're going to forgive him, because he's a grandfather and he was scared, and every one of us in this room would've been tempted to do the same thing, and you know it." He looked around at them. "Then you're going to pick seven people. Tonight. Full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, like it says. Not the loudest. The fairest. And those seven are going to keep the food from now on, and share it out every morning, and the children and the widows eat first. Every day. That's the law of Christ. Bear ye one another's burdens."

No one stirred.

Then Patrice got up from her mattress and crossed the room, and stood in front of Leon, and put her hand on his gray head.

"I forgive you," she said. "Your baby can have some of my boys' rice tomorrow, if she needs it."

Leon folded over his knees and shook.

They picked seven before dawn. Patrice was one of them. So was Leon, at Patrice's insistence. The man who had threatened to go to the Peacekeepers went up the stairs before dawn and out the back of the church into the snow, and no one stopped him or knew whether he would come back with a van. He did not come back at all. A week later Elijah heard that he had taken the mark at a relief center on Kennedy Street and was eating at a Seal market, and had said nothing to anyone about a church basement in Petworth.

Ezra walked home in the dark with the snow coming down, and his legs were shaking under him, and it might have been the cold or the hunger or the hour.

\* \* \*

The raid came nine days later, and it did not come to Petworth.

It came to a two-family flat in Trinidad, in Northeast, at three in the morning, behind a false wall in an attic, where twenty-two people were sleeping. It was not Vale's final sweep. Michael was sure of that afterward. It was a local thing, a Peacekeeper unit working its own list, chasing a tip from a neighbor who wanted a bonus on her account. They came in through the front door with a ram and up the stairs with lights and dogs, and they found the false wall because the dogs found it, and they broke it down.

Eleven people came out of that house alive. They were taken in a van to the processing center in Maryland. One of them, a girl of sixteen named Keisha, came back in March with the mark on her forehead and would not speak to anyone.

Eleven did not come out.

Ezra was there before dawn. Michael had tried to stop him. He went anyway, on foot, and stood across the street in the falling snow behind a parked car with no windows, and watched the Peacekeepers carry them out of the house one at a time under sheets and lay them on the sidewalk in a row, in the snow, while the neighbors watched from their windows and did nothing. He knew them all. He had built that wall. He had sat in that attic in September and read them the twelfth chapter of Revelation by candlelight, *and they loved not their lives unto the death*, and an old man named Clarence had wept and held his hand.

Clarence was the fourth sheet.

*They shall fall by the sword, and by flame, by captivity, and by spoil, many days.* It had been in Kambria's notebook. Daniel eleven. She had dated it the autumn before the sky opened.

He held it in on the street, where the cameras were. He stood behind the car until the van pulled away and the Peacekeepers had gone and the sheets were lifted into a city truck and taken somewhere he would never learn. Then he walked back to Sixth Street, two hours in the snow, and climbed the attic stairs, and sat down on the floor at Walt's feet with his back against the old man's chair, and wept until he could not see.

Walt said nothing. He put a hand on Ezra's head and kept it there.

\* \* \*

The young men wanted blood.

Dorsey told Michael first, and Michael told Ezra. There were nine of them, from three different safe houses, young men in their twenties who had lost fathers and brothers in Trinidad, and one of them had a cousin who had been a Marine, and the cousin knew where the Peacekeeper unit slept, in a converted school on Benning Road. They had rifles. They had a plan. They were going to go in on Christmas Eve and make the men who had carried the sheets out into the snow pay for it.

Michael called them to the room under the old library on the twenty-second of December, all nine, and sat them down at the long table, and did not let Ezra speak first.

He stood at the head of the table in his armor, with the cross hanging outside his vest, and looked them over in silence. They were angry, and they were frightened, and they were hungry, and every one of them looked at him with the same thing in his face: *You of all people. You were a soldier. You know.*

"I know," Michael said, answering what none of them had said. "I know exactly what you want to do, and I know exactly how to do it, and I could do it better than you. I could go in that school tonight with Dorsey and Pruitt and come out before they knew we'd been there, and every man who carried a body out of that house would be dead in his bed by morning." He waited. "And then what?"

None of them answered.

"Then they come for the rest of us," Michael said. "All fourteen hundred. Tomorrow. Not with one unit. With all of them. Vale's been looking for a reason to stop waiting, and you'd hand it to him." He leaned on the table with both fists. "But that's not why. That's the smart reason. I don't care about the smart reason. Here's the real one."

He took a small battered Bible out of a pouch on his vest, the one Ezra had given him in the cave that first winter, and opened it without looking, because he knew where it was.

"*Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.*" He closed it. "Romans twelve. Vengeance is His. Not mine. Not yours. His. And He will repay. Every sheet on that sidewalk is written down in His book, and every man who carried one, and He doesn't forget anything. He's going to come with a sword out of His mouth and judge every one of them, and every one of us, and He doesn't need nine hungry boys with rifles to help Him."

One of the young men, the one with the Marine cousin, a lanky kid named Andre whose father had been the second sheet, said hoarsely, "So we just let them."

"No," Michael said. "We don't let them. We get our people out. We keep them alive. We keep them fed. We keep them reading, and singing, and praying. We hold the line God gave us, and we don't step over it." He looked at Andre, and his hard face softened. "Son. I had a boy. Twelve years old. He's with the Lord now. If he was looking down at me tonight, I'd want him to see his daddy keeping the line. Not crossing it."

Andre's chin went first.

Michael came around the table and put his arms around him, armor and all, and held him while he cried. Then the next one. Then the next.

None of them went to Benning Road.

Later, walking up the hidden stairs with Ezra, Michael said, low, "I wanted to, you know. Go myself. I lay awake two nights planning it."

"I know," Ezra said.

"*Be ye angry, and sin not.*" Michael shook his head. "Hardest verse in the whole book."

\* \* \*

Walt stopped eating sometime in January.

Ezra did not see it. He was moving from house to house almost every night by then, through the snow, with Michael and Dorsey, reading, praying, settling quarrels, carrying the dying to whatever doctor they had, teaching the captains the routes again. He came back to the attic on Sixth Street every third or fourth night to sleep a few hours on the floor, and Walt was always in his chair by the window with his ledger, and his thermos of whatever passed for coffee now, and his red pen, writing.

He looked thinner. Everyone looked thinner. Ezra had a new hole punched in his own belt every month. He gave it no thought.

It was the schoolteacher who owned the house, Mrs. Fairley, who told him, after.

"He gave it away," she said, standing in the attic doorway with her hands knotted in her apron. "Every day. His cup. He'd take it from the seven in the morning when they shared it out, and then he'd come back up here, and the children from the second floor would come up the stairs in the afternoons, the Bakers' two and the little Harmon girl, to hear him read, and he'd give it to them. Little by little. A spoonful each. He'd say he wasn't hungry. He'd say old men don't need much." Her voice broke. "I saw him do it. I thought he was eating something else. I thought somebody was bringing him something. I didn't ask. God forgive me, I didn't ask."

Ezra found him on the morning of the eleventh of February.

He came up the attic stairs at dawn, after a night in Anacostia, with snow on his coat, and the attic was gray and bitter cold, and Walt was in his chair by the window.

He was sitting upright, with his cardigan buttoned wrong, as it always was, and his slippers on, and his reading glasses down on the end of his nose. His big-print Bible was open on his knee. His hands were folded on top of it. His red pen had rolled off the arm of the chair and lay on the floor by his foot. His face was turned a little toward the window, toward the gray light coming over the rooftops of Capitol Hill, toward the east, and his eyes were closed, and his face was the most peaceful Ezra had ever seen it.

He was cold. He had been gone since sometime in the night.

Ezra knelt down on the floor in front of the chair.

He did not cry at first. He knelt and looked at the old man's face. Then he looked at the Bible on his knee. It was open to Revelation, the second chapter, and Walt had marked a promise of Jesus with his red pen, as he had marked ten thousand verses in his life, with a neat red line beneath it.

*Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.*

Beside the chair, on the little table, the green ledger was open. The twelfth one. Ezra picked it up.

The last entry was dated the day before. The handwriting was shakier than it had been, but it was still Walt's, square and careful and exact.

*DEEP WINTER. Bread $71. No trucks 9 days. Snow. Bakers' boy better. Harmon girl better.*

And in the right margin, where the verse went, not a prophecy, for the first time in all his green ledgers:

*1 Kings 17:16. The barrel of meal wasted not.*

And beneath that, smaller, in the same red ink, the last thing he ever wrote:

*Lord, I knew all about You for seventy-four years. Thank You for the four I knew You.*

Ezra sat down on the cold attic floor with the ledger in his lap and his back against Walt's chair, and wept as he had wept on the morning after Trinidad, when the old man's hand had rested on his head. There was no hand now.

*And I looked, and behold a pale horse: and his name that sat on him was Death, and Hell followed with him.* Walt had written that in a margin, and the pale horse had passed through the city all winter, and the old man had walked in front of it with his bread in his hands. Death had taken the body. It had not been given the rest.

Then he got up, and went downstairs, and told the others.

\* \* \*

They could not give him a funeral. There was no cemetery that would take an unmarked man, and no way to carry a body through the streets without the cameras seeing. So they buried him that night, in the frozen backyard of Mrs. Fairley's house, behind the shed, under the old dogwood tree, in a grave Ezra and Michael and Elijah dug with picks and a spade by the light of a single lantern, taking turns, sweating in the cold.

Ezra built the box himself, in the basement, out of pine boards from a closet he tore out. He built it as he had built the studio for his son, with square corners and every joint tight, because it was the last thing he could make for the old man, and he would not let it be anything but right. On the inside of the lid, before he closed it, he wrote in black marker, in his square capitals:

*WALTER J. SIMMONS. TYPESETTER. WATCHMAN. FAITHFUL UNTO DEATH.*

And under it: *REVELATION 2:10.*

Thirty people stood in the yard in the snow that night, from the safe houses nearest, as many as Michael would let come. They stood around the grave with their heads bare and their breath smoking in the lantern light, and Ezra read. He read the fourteenth chapter of Revelation, the thirteenth verse, slowly, because John had written it for these years and no others. *Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them.* He thought of the green ledgers, every line in red, and read it a second time. He read the fifteenth chapter of First Corinthians, *O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory?* He read Job, because Walt would have wanted Job. *I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee.*

Then they sang the hundred and sixteenth psalm, low, so that the sound would not carry past the fence, thirty hungry people in the snow around an open grave, and Ezra could not get through the second verse, and Elijah carried it for him, in a cracked voice, with tears running into his beard.

When it was done, the Harmon girl, who was three, born in the years after the sky went quiet, came forward out of the crowd in a coat three sizes too big for her and dropped something into the grave on top of the pine box. It was a red pen.

"So he can keep writing," she said. "In heaven."

After that nobody tried.

They filled the grave in. Ezra set a flat stone at the head of it, from the garden wall. And when the others had gone back inside, he stood alone in the yard in the snow until his feet went numb, with the lantern at his feet.

The old man had done it. He had been faithful unto death. He had not taken the mark or bowed at noon or stolen a crumb. He had given his own bread to three children, a spoonful at a time, and kept the record to the last day, and died in his chair with his Bible on his knee and his face to the east, and not one person in Vale's whole kingdom had been able to make him do anything else.

*Be thou faithful unto death.*

\* \* \*

Some nights later, in the room under the old library on Kennedy Street, at nine o'clock, Ezra was sitting at the long table with the microphone in his hand and the low line of his son's cello playing out of the console radio behind him, getting ready to read. The others were around him, as always. Nina at the transmitter. Elijah in the corner, thinner than he had ever been, with a fresh scar over his eye from the December night he still would not explain. Michael at the bottom of the stairs, by the door, with his rifle across his knees.

Nina faded the song down under him. Ezra lifted the microphone.

Before he could speak, the receiver on the shelf crackled.

Not static: a voice, on their own frequency, on the dead channel near the bottom of the dial, cutting in over the cello, close and clear, as if the speaker were in the next room.

"Ezra. Ezra Patterson. Don't say anything. Just listen."

Nobody in the room so much as shifted. Michael was on his feet with the rifle up before the second word.

Ezra knew the voice. He had not heard it in years, not since a job site in Silver Spring, Trent up a ladder joking about the city's camera bids, the spring before the world ended.

"It's Trent," the voice said. "Trent Walker. Your old apprentice." A pause. A breath. "You got my list. I know you got it. I'm sorry I couldn't give it to you any better than that."

Nina had both hands over her mouth.

"Listen to me," Trent said. "Vale's sweep starts on the twelfth of March. All of it. All of them, every row on that list, in one night. He's been waiting for the mark deadline to pass, and it passes at midnight on the eleventh." His voice was steady, but it was very tired. "I can't stop it. I can't switch anything off, and I won't pretend I can. Every camera in this city sees in the dark, and I'm the one who taught them how. But on the night of the eleventh, every Peacekeeper in the District who hasn't taken the Seal yet has to stand in a line indoors and take it before midnight. They pulled half the night patrols off the streets for it. I know, because the rosters come through my office. The streets will be thinner that night than they've been in years. Not empty. Thinner."

The room kept its peace.

"Tell Michael I know about the companies of fifty. I know about Exodus fourteen thirteen. I know everything, man. I've known everything for years. That's my job." A sound that might have been a laugh. "Mama would've liked you, Ezra. You know that? She'd have liked what you did with my list." A pause. "Have the trucks waiting outside the city, past the river, where the routes start. Not inside it. I know every alley and rail cut and culvert in this town, because I spent years learning where people go when they don't want to be seen. I'll walk your people out to the trucks myself. On foot. I'll be at the corner of Twelfth and Rhode Island at ten o'clock on the eleventh, under the first camera I ever put up. If I'm not there by ten-thirty, I didn't make it, and you go anyway." His voice softened. "When I was little and the lights got cut off, Mama used to say that when you can't see the way, you put your shoes on and wait by the door for God. So put your shoes on."

The voice dropped.

"I gotta go. Don't answer. Don't ever talk back on this frequency after tonight." And then, very quietly, almost too low to hear, the last thing before the static came back: "Pray for me. I don't know how to come out yet. But I'm trying."

## Chapter 33: Blind Eyes

> *I will arise and go to my father, and will say unto him, Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee.* — Jesus, from the parable of the prodigal son, Luke 15:18

**Word study: *arise* — ἀναστάς** Greek *anastas*, from *anistēmi* (Strong's G450). To stand up; to get up from where you have fallen. It is the same root as *anastasis*, the resurrection. When the prodigal came to himself in the pigsty and said *I will arise*, Jesus used for his turning the same root He used for His own rising from the dead.

*Therefore sent he thither horses, and chariots, and a great host: and they came by night, and compassed the city about… And his servant said unto him, Alas, my master! how shall we do? And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them… Elisha prayed unto the LORD, and said, Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness. And he smote them with blindness according to the word of Elisha. (2 Kings 6:14–18)*

\* \* \*

At twenty minutes past nine on the night of the eleventh of March, in a cold rain, the young woman with the scanner came down the aisle of the Security Operations Center toward Trent Walker's desk, and he knew that the next ten minutes would decide the rest of his life.

He had known it all day. He had known it for a long time, really, since a noon in the operations room on Third Avenue when he took off his headset and watched a young man in white walk across the back of a stage six thousand miles away. But all day today it had been close enough to touch. He had come in at noon and sat down at the main console in the center of the front row, where he had sat since Vale sent him back from New York, and looked up at the wall of screens, three thousand feeds from every corner of the District, and he had thought: *This is the last time I sit in this chair.*

In the corner of the main wall the night's tally ran, as it did every shift: *MK 1:15 — 212 new markings, 9 wards.* Crews went out each morning with pressure washers. By the next night Jesus' words were back, on other walls, in other hands.

The Security Operations Center was on the sixth floor of a building on New Jersey Avenue that had housed the Department of Labor, once. It was a long room without windows, a hundred feet deep, with the wall of screens at the front and curved rows of desks facing it, and thirty-one people at the desks in the blue light. Trent's title was Director of Network Integrity. Every camera in the city ran through the systems he kept, and if anything went wrong with any of them, it was his name Vale's office called.

He wore a lanyard with a white security pass on it, the gold circle at the top and his photograph in the middle and a line of small type along the bottom. *Operational exemption, Registry of the Chairman's Peace. Valid through the Seal deadline.*

Tonight.

At midnight every exemption in the Organization ran out. Every officer, every engineer, every technician who had been allowed to put off the Seal because of the work they did would take it tonight before they went home. There was a station for it at the back of the room by the doors, a small white table with a scanner and a stool, and a young woman in a blue jacket had been sitting beside it since eight with a tablet in her lap. One by one, through the evening, the night shift had gone back to see her. They came back to their desks rubbing the backs of their right hands, smiling a little, embarrassed, as if they had gotten a flu shot.

It was the same all over the city. Trent knew it better than anyone, because the duty rosters ran through his office. Every Peacekeeper station in the District had a white table tonight and a line of men in front of it. Half the night patrols had been pulled in off the streets to stand in those lines before midnight. The Organization had scheduled it that way months ago, on paper, because it was tidy: the last of the exemptions, all closed out in one night, and Vale's sweep to begin the next morning with a fully sealed force.

It was the only night in all those years that the streets of Washington would be thinner than usual. Not empty. Never empty. Thinner.

Trent had told Ezra so on the radio some nights ago, on a frequency he had promised never to speak on again. He had promised nothing he could not keep. He could not turn off a single camera. He would not have known how to explain to God why he had tried. He had only a night with fewer men in the streets, and years of knowing every alley and rail cut and storm culvert and dead-end lot in the city, because his whole job had been learning where people went when they did not want to be seen.

And he had a promise he had made into a microphone. *I'll be at the corner of Twelfth and Rhode Island at ten o'clock. If I'm not there by ten-thirty, I didn't make it, and you go anyway.*

Now it was nine-twenty, and the woman with the scanner was coming down the aisle.

\* \* \*

"Mr. Walker?"

She was young, twenty-two maybe. She had a soft round face and a small gold cross on a chain around her neck, which almost made him laugh, because she had likely forgotten what it meant. Most people who still wore them did not. The Organization had decided early on that the cross was a symbol of universal peace and sold them in the Seal markets.

"I'm sorry to bother you," she said. "I know it's a busy night. But you're the last one on this floor, and Mr. Kessler asked me to come and see you before the shift change, so you wouldn't have to wait in line at midnight." She smiled at him. "It only takes four seconds. You won't feel anything."

Trent looked up at her from his chair.

The room was not quiet. It was never quiet. Thirty people talking into headsets, keyboards, the hum of the screens. But the three or four desks nearest to him had gone still. He could feel them listening.

He thought of his mother. He thought of her in the choir loft at Greater Mount Calvary, in her purple robe, turning her head in the middle of a hymn to look at him in the back row, over a whole church. He thought of her phone ringing and ringing in her empty apartment on the morning the world ended, while he sat on the carpet at an airport gate in Dubai with his back against the glass.

He thought of the young man in white on camera four-seventeen.

He thought of the list. Fourteen hundred rows. He had built every one of them.

"No, ma'am," Trent said.

She smiled uncertainly and lifted the scanner, as though he had not heard.

"No," Trent said again, and stood up, so that everyone could hear him. "I'm not taking it. Not tonight. Not ever."

The desks around him fell silent. Then the next row. He watched it spread through the room, faces turning, headsets coming off, until thirty-one people in the blue light were looking at him.

The young woman had gone pale. "Mr. Walker, I don't think you understand. The exemptions expire at midnight. If you don't take the Seal, your account closes. Your pass stops working. You can't—"

"I know what happens," Trent said, his voice level. "I wrote half the rules."

He took his lanyard off over his head.

He turned it over in his hand. His own face looked back at him from the white pass, taken the spring he was hired, with less gray, smiling the smile he used to use on clients. Then he laid it down on the desk in front of the console, face up, beside the keyboard he had not touched since noon.

"Tell Mr. Kessler," he said, "and tell Mr. Vale, that Trent Walker says he's sorry he was ever here. Tell them he went home to his Father."

Then he turned his back on the wall of screens and walked up the long aisle toward the doors.

Nobody stopped him. Thirty-one people watched him go and stayed in their seats. Kessler came out of his office at the back of the room as Trent passed it, red-faced, with a phone in his hand, and opened his mouth, and Trent looked at him, and Kessler shut it again and stood in his doorway with the phone in his hand, silent. Afterward, when Vale's people questioned him, Kessler would say he did not know why. He would say that the Director of Network Integrity had walked past him with a look on his face that Kessler had seen only once before in his life, at his grandmother's funeral, on the face of the preacher, and that he had simply not been able to speak.

Trent pushed through the doors and took the stairs all the way down, and walked out into the rain.

\* \* \*

It was a mile and a half from New Jersey Avenue to the corner of Twelfth and Rhode Island. He ran most of it.

He avoided the main streets.
