He went by the ways he knew, behind the old government buildings, along the back lots and service alleys, under the railroad overpass on Florida Avenue, up the long dark cut beside the tracks where nobody ever walked, past the backs of warehouses with their loading docks chained, in the rain, with his hands in his pockets and his head down. He had no pass. He had no mark. If anyone stopped him and asked for either, there was nothing he could show them, and nothing he could say.

Nobody stopped him.

Twice he saw a patrol car. Once it came down the street toward him with its lights off, cruising as they did at night, and he did not run, because running was the thing they watched for. He kept walking on the sidewalk in the rain with his collar up, a tired man going home, and the car rolled past him six feet away, and the officer behind the wheel looked straight at him, and looked away, and drove on.

Trent stood on the corner afterward with his heart going so hard he could feel it in his teeth.

*Smite this people, I pray thee, with blindness.*

He had heard Ezra read it on the radio, years ago, in the first spring, sitting in his dark apartment with a beer in his hand and the radio tuned low so the neighbors would not hear. He had thought it a tale for children, and his mother's besides.

He walked on.

At five minutes before ten he came up Rhode Island Avenue toward Twelfth Street, past the dark church with the chains on its doors and the gold circle painted across them, and looked up, at the corner, at the old camera on its pole with the crack in its housing from a hailstorm three summers ago. He had put it up himself. Feed number one. On a ladder, in the rain, the September before the world ended, wearing the tool belt Ezra Patterson had handed him his first week, still stiff at the buckle.

Under it, in the rain, a gray-haired man in a work jacket was standing on the sidewalk with his hands at his sides, waiting.

\* \* \*

Trent stopped ten feet away.

They looked at each other. All those years. The last time they had stood this close, Trent had been up a ladder in Silver Spring joking about the city's camera bids, and Ezra had been grinning at his phone and not really listening, and neither of them had believed in anything.

Ezra was thinner. His hair was almost white at the temples, and his face had lines in it that had not been there. But his eyes were the same, and they looked at Trent as his mother had from the choir loft, to the bottom of him, and did not turn away.

"You came," Ezra said.

"I said I would."

"You walked out."

"I walked out." Trent's voice would not work. "Ezra. I built it. The list. All of it. Every name. I loaded the face of the man who killed Adrian Crowe into eleven hundred cameras and went back to bed. I don't know if there's anything for a man like me. I don't know if I'm even allowed to stand here." He could not go on.

Ezra crossed the ten feet between them in three steps and put his arms around him.

He held him, on the corner, in the rain, under the camera Trent had put up, with his big hands spread on Trent's back, and Trent stood stiff in his arms for a moment, and then he could not. He put his face down on his old boss's wet shoulder and wept as he had wept at the airport gate in Dubai, back against the glass, only this time someone was holding him.

It was the story Jesus told: *But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him.*

"I've sinned against heaven," Trent said, into Ezra's shoulder. "And before you. And everybody. I'm not worthy to—"

"Hush," Ezra said. "You're home. We'll talk about the rest later. We've got fourteen hundred people to walk out of this city tonight, and you're the only man alive who knows the way." He stepped back and held Trent by both shoulders and looked him in the face. "You pray?"

"My mama did."

"Start tonight," Ezra said. "Out loud's fine. God's not particular."

\* \* \*

At nine o'clock, in a room behind a false wall under an old library on Kennedy Street, Nina Cole pressed a key, and the low line of a cello went out over the dead frequency at the bottom of the dial, into every safe house in Washington.

She let it play for one minute, as she always did. Then she faded it down, and Elijah, who had the microphone because Ezra was standing on a street corner in the rain, read one verse in a voice that shook.

"*And Moses said unto the people, Fear ye not, stand still, and see the salvation of the LORD, which he will shew to you to day.*" A pause. "Exodus fourteen thirteen. Go now. God go with you."

He did not say *grace and peace*. That was Ezra's to say.

In basements and attics and the backs of closets all over the city, in stockrooms and church cellars and boiler rooms, fourteen hundred people stood up.

They had been ready for days. They had packed what they could carry, a blanket, a Bible, a little food, a photograph. They had sewn their notebooks into their coat linings. They had prayed every night since Trent's voice came over the radio, as Trent's mother used to say, with their shoes on, waiting by the door. And now the door opened, and the captains went first, and the companies of fifty came up out of the ground behind them into the rain.

\* \* \*

Trent walked them out.

There was no other way to say it, afterward, when people asked him. He did nothing clever; he had nothing clever left to do. He had a map of the city in his head that he had spent years learning in order to catch people, and on that one night he used it to lead them home.

He knew where the patrols would be thin tonight, because he had seen the rosters. He knew which streets ran past stations where the men were indoors standing in line before a white table. He knew the long rail cut along the tracks north of Union Station where the fences were down and nobody went after dark. He knew the storm culvert under New York Avenue that a grown man could walk through bent double, and the vacant lots behind the old warehouses on Bladensburg Road, and the path along the bank of the Anacostia River under the trees where the homeless used to camp. He knew where the light was bad and the shadows were deep.

He had no way to keep a camera from seeing them. No one did. Every one of them saw. Somewhere on New Jersey Avenue, on a wall of screens fed by three thousand cameras, thirty-one people were watching fourteen hundred believers walk out of their city in the rain, company after company, and Trent knew it, and every one of the fourteen hundred knew it.

No order went out. In the morning, not one of the thirty-one could say why.

They walked anyway.

Ezra walked at the front of the first company with Kambria's lamp wrapped in a towel under his coat, beside Trent, with his hand on Trent's shoulder. Behind them came old women and children and young men and a blind man with his hand on his grandson's arm, and a mother carrying a baby in a sling, and Leon from the Petworth basement with his granddaughter on his back, and Patrice with her two boys. They walked in silence, two by two, close together, through the dark streets and the alleys and the rail cut, and every hundred yards, low, so that only the people beside him could hear, someone said the watchword.

*Strengthen ye the weak hands, and confirm the feeble knees. Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not.*

At a quarter to eleven, at the bottom of the rail cut, the first company came around a bend in the tracks and walked straight into a checkpoint.

Two Peacekeepers in blue, under a light on a pole, with a barrier across the path and a scanner on a folding table. It had not been on the roster. Trent stopped dead. Fifty people stopped behind him. There was nowhere to go. The cut was too narrow to turn fifty people around, and the walls were too steep to climb, and the Peacekeepers had already looked up and seen them.

Ezra's hand tightened on his shoulder.

And then Ezra did the strangest thing Trent had ever seen. He stepped forward, past Trent, into the light, with his empty hands at his sides and his gray head bare in the rain, and he walked up to the barrier and stood there, and faced the two young men in blue, and said, in the voice he used on the radio:

"Evening. We're just passing through."

The older of the two Peacekeepers studied him. Then his eyes went past him, to the fifty people standing on the tracks in the rain, and stayed there, and Trent watched his face and saw a look he could not explain then or afterward. It was neither fear nor pity but the look of a sentry shaken from sleep who has lost his orders.

The Peacekeeper rubbed his eyes with his knuckles. He looked down at the scanner on the table, and then back up, and blinked the rain from his lashes.

"Go on, then," he said vaguely. "Mind the rail. It's slick."

The younger one lifted the barrier.

Fifty people walked through the checkpoint two by two in the rain, past the scanner on its table, past the two men in blue, and not one of them was asked for a mark or a name. The older Peacekeeper stood with his hand on the barrier and watched them go by and did not seem to see them at all. When the last of them had passed, he let the barrier down again and sat down on his stool under the light and stared at the empty tracks, rubbing his eyes.

Trent walked on with his knees shaking.

"Ezra," he whispered. "What was that?"

"Second Kings six," Ezra said. "You know it. Your mama made you learn it." He did not look back. "*They that be with us are more than they that be with them.*"

Trent looked up, then, without meaning to, at the dark sky over the rail cut and the black walls of the warehouses on either side and the rain coming down through the light. He saw nothing; he had not expected to. But for one moment, walking up the tracks in the rain with fifty frightened people behind him, he would have sworn that the dark around them was full. Crowded, like the air in the choir loft at Greater Mount Calvary on a Sunday morning, when his mother sang, before he ever understood what it was.

He started to pray then. Out loud, under his breath, in the rain. He did not know how. He said what was true.

\* \* \*

It went on like that all night.

Company after company, by different roads, through alleys and lots and culverts and along the river under the trees, in the rain. Trent walked the first three companies out himself, and then went back, and walked three more, and by the small hours he had taught the routes to Dorsey and Pruitt and four of Michael's captains, and they walked the rest. Michael's trucks were waiting outside the city, past the river, past the last streets, in the parking lots of shuttered stores and the yards of dead farms along the Maryland roads, where the routes north began. Bakery vans and produce trucks and a school bus with its lights off. They filled, and pulled away, and others took their places.

Twice more that night, a company walked into a patrol it could not avoid. Once on the riverbank, once on a bridge. Both times the same thing happened. The men in blue looked at them, and could not seem to fix their eyes on them, and let them by. No one could explain it afterward, and no one tried very hard. Nina, who had built the cameras and believed in nothing she could not measure for most of her life, said only that the Bible had a word for it, and the word was *holden*, as in the two disciples on the road to Emmaus, whose *eyes were holden that they should not know him*.

At midnight, the Seal deadline passed. Trent was standing on the bank of the Anacostia under the dripping trees, counting heads as a company went by, when the church bell of some marked congregation across the river began to ring the hour, and he thought of the white table on the sixth floor of New Jersey Avenue, and his lanyard lying face up on the desk beside the keyboard, and he felt nothing but relief.

*That no man might buy or sell, save he that had the mark.* He would never buy or sell anything again. He had nothing. He had the clothes he stood in and a map in his head and a lamp burning under the coat of the man beside him.

\* \* \*

The last company came out a little before five in the morning, as the rain was stopping and the sky over the river was beginning to turn from black to gray.

Ezra was at the last truck, a produce van in the lot of a dead garden center on Route 50 in Maryland, with Michael beside him and a clipboard in his hand, counting. He had counted every company that came in all night, by name, from the list that had been Vale's and was theirs now. When the last one came stumbling across the wet asphalt out of the trees, two teenage girls at the front of it holding up an old woman between them, Ezra counted them, and checked the last names, and lowered the clipboard, and could not speak.

Michael took it out of his hand and looked at it. Then he looked again.

"Every one who came out," Michael said. His voice was rough. "Not one lost tonight."

Nobody cheered; they were too tired and too wet. They stood in the gray light in the parking lot among the trucks, fifty and a hundred of them at a time, and some of them were crying, and some of them were praying, and a little girl in a borrowed coat was holding a pencil stub in her fist, asleep on her mother's shoulder.

Trent dropped onto the wet curb at the edge of the lot.

He had not sat in eight hours. His legs were spent. His shoes were soaked through and his hands were raw and he could not feel his feet. He sat on the curb with his head low and looked at the asphalt between his shoes, and he thought: *Now what?* He had no mark. He had no pass. Every camera in the city had seen his face all night long, at the front of every company. By noon his photograph would be on every screen in the Organization, beside Adrian Crowe's smiling face. He had no home, and no money, and no name anymore that he could say out loud to anyone who had the Seal.

Words from that story of Jesus' came back to him: *Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before thee, and am no more worthy to be called thy son.*

Someone sat down on the curb beside him.

It was Ezra. He said nothing at first. He reached into his coat and took out Kambria's lamp, unwrapped the towel from around it, and set it on the wet asphalt between them. It was still burning. It had burned all night under his coat, through the rain and the rail cut and the culverts and the river path, small and gold and steady behind its glass chimney, and it had not gone out.

"That's Kambria's," Ezra said. "My wife's best friend. She kept it burning in her window every night, until the night they came for her. I filled it the morning after I came to the Lord, and I've lit it every night since, wherever I was." He looked at it. "All these years."

Trent looked at the small flame.

"The prodigal," Ezra said. "Jesus' story. You know how it goes. Your mama made you learn that one too, I bet. He came to himself in the pigsty, and he said, I will arise and go to my father. And he got up, and he walked all the way home rehearsing his speech. *I am no more worthy to be called thy son. Make me as one of thy hired servants.*" He smiled a little, tiredly, at the lamp. "And his father saw him a great way off and ran to him, and the boy never got to finish the speech. Did you ever notice that? He got halfway through it, and his father was already shouting for the robe and the ring and the shoes."

Trent could only shake his head.

"You got up, Trent," Ezra said. "In front of thirty-one people, with a scanner in your face. So you don't have to finish the speech." He put his hand on the back of Trent's neck and held it there. "Nobody's asking you for it. You're home."

And Trent Walker, who had built Vale's list of the saints and walked all of them out of his city on foot in the rain, sat on the curb of a dead garden center on Route 50 in the gray light with his old boss's hand on his neck, and wept.

Nina had pressed a card the size of a thumbnail into his palm before the first truck left, three words on it in her small hand: *Jesus, forgive me.* "You loaded the face into the cameras," she had said. "Now say it out loud."

"Jesus," Trent said. His voice cracked on the name. "It's Trent. Mama's boy. I don't know how you're supposed to do this." He wiped his face with the heel of his hand. "I built the list. I loaded the face. I sat on the floor in Dubai and You were right there and I didn't look up. I'm sorry. I'm sorry. I'm not worthy of any of it." Ezra's hand tightened on his neck. "You died for the ones on my list. Die for me too. Lord Jesus, take me anyway. Please. Take me anyway."

The lamp burned on the asphalt between them and the trucks started their engines one by one and pulled away north.

When he lifted his head, the sun was coming up over the Maryland fields, and Ezra had not moved.

## Chapter 34: Ichabod

> *And she named the child Ichabod, saying, The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God was taken.* — 1 Samuel 4:21

**Word study: *Ichabod* — אִיכָבוֹד** Hebrew *i-kavod* (Strong's H350). Two words joined: *i*, meaning *where is*, or *no*, and *kavod*, glory, weight, the heavy, shining presence of God. *Where is the glory?* Or: *no glory.* The wife of Phinehas gave her son that name with her dying breath, in the hour she heard that the ark was taken, and named a whole generation with it.

*Now Eli was very old, and heard all that his sons did unto all Israel… And he said unto them, Why do ye such things?… Nay, my sons; for it is no good report that I hear… For I have told him that I will judge his house for ever for the iniquity which he knoweth; because his sons made themselves vile, and he restrained them not. (1 Samuel 2:22–24; 3:13)*

\* \* \*

Elijah Brooks had always been the one who made everybody laugh.

It was the first thing anyone said about him and the last. At Rooney's, for thirty years, he had been the man at the end of the bar with the joke, the one who kept the whole room going on a cold night, the one nobody wanted to leave out of anything. He had married once, young, an older girl named Marsha who saw straight through the jokes, and when she left him over the drinking he had not begged her to stay, because begging meant being looked at as one in need. He never married again, because marrying meant choosing, and choosing meant that some other door, some other table, might close to him forever. He had stood at the back of his sister's church for forty years and never once walked the aisle, because walking the aisle meant everybody looking at him, and being looked at that way, as one in need, was the one attention Elijah Brooks could not bear.

He had come to Christ on the sticky floor of the back room at Rooney's, with Ezra's hand on his back, and he had meant it. Nobody who knew him doubted that he meant it. For all those years he had been the laughter of the hidden church, the one who kept the children laughing in the dark rooms, who ran food at night on a bicycle with a trailer and sang the low line of Jalen's song under his breath so the people behind him would know who was in front. He had been good. He had been brave, as the frightened are brave among their friends, with everyone watching, where courage is the price of a place in the circle.

His weakness never went all the way away. Ezra knew it. Ezra had watched it, and prayed over it, and loved him, and hoped.

The crack opened that winter, in a cabin in the Berkshires, among strangers.

\* \* \*

They were not all in one place anymore, by then.

The fourteen hundred who had walked out of Washington on foot in the rain on the night of the deadline had scattered north along Michael's routes, into the farms and the cabins and the caves and the bunker, in groups of fifty and twenty and ten, because fourteen hundred people in one place was a thing that could be found and taken all at once, and scattered they could not be. It was the opposite of what Vale had wanted in the city, and it cost them dearly. It meant that the warmth of the big dinner table was gone. It meant that a man could end up in a cold cabin in the Berkshires with nine strangers and a bad radio, a hundred miles from anyone who had ever heard him make a joke.

That was where Elijah ended up, that winter, after the raid.

The raid had been on the farm in Dutchess County where he had been living, where he had been happy, as happy as a man could be in those years, cooking for forty people in a big stone farmhouse kitchen and making the children laugh. The Peacekeepers had come at dawn, with dogs, following a drone that had followed a heat trail in the snow. Most of the forty had gotten out through the woods, the way Michael's people drilled, scattering in ten directions. Elijah had gotten out too. But he had taken a rifle butt across the jaw going over a stone wall, and he had run three miles through the snow in the dark with his jaw broken and blood freezing on his face, alone, because the man he was supposed to run with had gone down behind him and not gotten up, and Elijah had not stopped. He had told himself there was nothing he could do. He was probably right. It did not matter whether he was right. He had left a brother in the snow, and run, and he could not forgive himself for it, and Elijah Brooks had never in his life known how to carry a thing he could not forgive himself for, except by making a joke, and there was no one left to laugh.

He fetched up, after two weeks of moving at night, at the cabin in the Berkshires, with nine strangers. They were kind. They were frightened. The radio was bad; they could get Ezra's broadcast only one night in three, through the mountains, in bursts. The food was almost gone. By February they were down to boiling the same bones over and over and drinking the gray water, and a child in the cabin, a boy of six, had the same look Leon's granddaughter had worn in the Petworth basement, the look of a child who has stopped crying.

And Elijah's jaw ached where the rifle butt had cracked a tooth, all the time, a deep grinding ache that would not stop, and there was no one to fix it, and no laughter in him to cover it, and at night he lay in the cold and heard the man he had left going over the wall behind him, again and again, and in the dark the old fear came back, the fear he had carried his whole life, that he was alone, and that he had been left out, and that this time it was forever.

There was a town at the bottom of the mountain. There was a Seal market in the town. He had seen it from the ridge, the lights of it, warm, at night.

\* \* \*

He told himself he was going for the others.

That was the thing he said to himself, walking down the mountain in the gray morning in the second week of February, with his collar up and his broken face down. He would go to the market, and he would see what there was, and he would find a way to bring something back for the child who had stopped crying. He did not let himself think past the door of the market. He had spent his whole life not letting himself think past the door of whatever room he was afraid to be left out of.

The market was warm. That was the first thing, when the door closed behind him. It was warm, and it was bright, and it smelled of bread. There were shelves with food on them. Not much, by the old days, but after the bones and the gray water it was a vision: bread, and rice, and cans with pictures of soup on them, and oranges, actual oranges, in a wooden crate by the counter. There were people in the market, in coats that were not frozen, talking quietly, and above the entrance there was a screen, and on the screen was the face, the warm kind face, smiling down at the bright room, and nobody in the room was afraid. Outside, on the brick beside the door, under a coat of fresh gray paint, the ridges of the letters still showed through: *REPENT YE.* Jesus' words. He had walked past them to come in.

A woman near the oranges caught Elijah's eye and smiled at him. Just a smile. A stranger's smile, such as had come to him a hundred times a day his whole life, in the before, at the bar, on the street, the small warm current of being seen by other people and liked. He had not felt it in a year. He had been a hunted man in a cold cabin with strangers who were too frightened to laugh. And this woman by the oranges smiled at him, and it went through him like heat through a frozen hand, painful and wonderful at once, and his eyes filled, and he had to look away.

At the counter there was a scanner, and a stool, and a young man in a blue jacket, and a small card that said in friendly type: *New to the Chairman's Peace? Register here. It only takes four seconds. Welcome home.*

Welcome home.

Elijah stood in the warm bright market with the smell of bread in his broken mouth and read those two words, and the old fear and the old need rose up in him together and became one thing, and the one thing said, in his own voice: *You don't have to be left out anymore. You don't have to be alone. You don't have to be cold, or hungry, or hunted, or ashamed. All of this can be yours. All these warm people can be your people. You just have to put out your hand. Four seconds. Welcome home.*

He thought about the man he had left in the snow.

He thought, *I already couldn't save him. I already failed. The glory already left me, back there at that wall. What difference does it make now?*

He thought about Ezra, and Walt in his chair with his Bible, and the law of Christ, and the twelfth chapter of Revelation that he had heard read in a dozen dark rooms. *And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.*

He thought, *I'm not like them. I was never like them. I was only ever the one who made them laugh. Take the joke away and what was I? I was a scared man at the back of the church who never walked the aisle. They walked the aisle. I just stood where they could see me.*

He walked to the counter.

He would tell himself later, on the long nights after, that he did not decide to. That his feet took him. But that was the last joke, and he knew it even as he thought it, the last time he would make something lighter than it was so that he would not have to look straight at it. He decided. A man always decides. He walked to the counter, and the young man in the blue jacket smiled at him. "New to the Chairman's Peace?"

"Is the soup real," Elijah said, "or just the picture?" It came out cracked. It was the last one he had.

"Real as you like. It only takes four seconds, sir. Welcome home."

Elijah Brooks put out his right hand under the scanner. It took four seconds. It did not even hurt.

The young man gave him an account, and a card, and an orange from the crate, free, for new members. And Elijah stood in the warm bright market and held the orange in his right hand, and the face on the screen over the door turned and looked at him, and smiled, and said, in that deep warm voice, so that everyone in the market heard it and turned to see who it was:

"Welcome home, Elijah."

It knew his name.

\* \* \*

He came back up the mountain once.

He did not bring the food. He had bought food with his new account, a whole bag of it, bread and rice and the cans with the soup, and he had carried it halfway up the mountain in the snow, toward the cabin and the child who had stopped crying, and then he had stopped on the ridge, and set the bag down in the snow, and he could not take it another step.

Because it was marked food now. It had been bought with the mark. And he knew, he knew as he knew his own name, that if he carried that bag into the cabin and the nine strangers and the child ate out of it, he would have made them eat from his hand, and his hand had Vale's Seal on it, and he could not do that to them. That was the one thing left in him that the market had not bought. He could damn himself. He found, standing on the ridge with the bag in the snow, that he could not quite damn the child.

So he left the bag on the ridge, where they would find it, and he turned around, and he went back down the mountain to the warm town, to be alone with what he had done, among people who would never know to be ashamed of him.

But first he went to Ezra.

It took him days to find him. Michael's people did not want to let him near; word had gone ahead, the way such word does, and a man fresh from the scanner was a danger to every hidden room he came near. But Elijah stood in the snow outside a barn in the Pennsylvania hills for a day and a night and would not leave, and would not come in, and only said, over and over, to the armed man at the door, "Tell Ezra it's Eli. Tell him I just want to see him once. I won't come in. I won't touch anybody. I just want to see him once."

Ezra was not at the barn when Elijah came; he was on the road with Michael. Michael had asked for the new wing that winter, when the hill had filled past counting: a bunk room for the hunted, dug into the north wall of the barn cellar, fourteen beds, a stove, a vent that would not smoke. Ezra drew it on the back of a ration sheet. Michael read the sheet, nodded once, and went to find the lumber.

They went together, in the box truck, to a shuttered mill nine miles off, and they loaded it by hand: two-by-fours, a half sheet of plywood, a box of nails Ezra had paid for in a coat. On the way back, a mile from the barn, a checkpoint rose out of the dusk where there had been none the day before.

A Peacekeeper in a gray coat walked up with a rifle across his chest, scanned the truck's bed with a flashlight, and did not bother to look at their hands. "Out," he said.

They got out.

"Generator's dead at the post." He jerked his chin at a squat black machine on a handcart, forty yards up the road, beside a sandbagged shack. "Cart's got a bad axle. You two. Haul it to the depot."

Ezra felt Michael go rigid beside him.

"Where's the depot?" Michael said.

"Mile down the road." The Peacekeeper smiled a little. "Move."

For a moment Ezra thought the soldier in Michael would come up out of his boots. The jaw. The hand. A whole career of knowing what to do with a man like this, and nobody to do it to. A cold lumber truck, four hundred pounds of timber, the whole hill waiting up the road on a bunk room, and a rifle three feet away.

*Compelled.* Ezra had read the word on a kitchen table, in a margin, in Angela's round hand, and had skimmed it.

"We'll haul it," Ezra said.

Michael looked at him as though he had spoken in Greek.

They took the handles. The cart was heavy, the axle shrieked, and the generator slid with every rut. Michael pulled with his shoulders and his teeth. For the first half mile he said nothing. For the second quarter mile, under his breath, he said something that was not a prayer.

"Jesus said it," Ezra told the road. "*And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain.*"

"I know the verse."

"Then you know it doesn't say go a mile *happily*."

A bark, a short ugly laugh. They pulled. The depot lay at the mile mark, a lit tent, six more soldiers, a sergeant with a clipboard. They set the generator down. The sergeant signed a slip without looking up.

"The second mile," Ezra said quietly.

"No," Michael whispered.

"Yes."

They turned back to the cart. The axle had split coming into the depot, and the Peacekeeper who had stopped them was at the tent now, cursing at the broken wheel. Ezra walked up and, without being asked, held the lantern. Michael, shaking with a rage he was holding in both hands, knelt and put his shoulder under the axle and lifted. For ten minutes, in front of six rifles, a hunted man and a hunted man knelt in the mud and fixed a Peacekeeper's wheel.

The soldier stood watching them. At the end of it, he stared at the mended axle and then at the men, and for one second the face under the cap was just a face, young, tired, very far from home.

"Why'd you do that?" he said.

"Somebody asked," Ezra said.

They drove back in the dark with the lumber. Michael did not speak until the barn lights showed on the hill.

"I'd have killed him," he said. "In the road."

"I know."

"I'd have been right, too."

"I know," Ezra said. "And you'd have lost the wing, the fourteen beds, and the hill."

Michael looked at the barn. At the cellar door, where a man stood in the snow with his right hand in his pocket, waiting for a word. He kept looking at it.

"Go," he said at last. "I'll hang the door myself."

And he went in ahead of Ezra, to the wall they had not yet raised, and left the gate unbarred.

Ezra came out to him at dusk.

"Grace and peace, Eli," he said. It came out of him on its own. He had said it to every soul who walked up out of the dark to that barn, and he heard it land on the snow between them. Elijah did not give him the answer.

They stood ten feet apart, in the blue dark, the man from the radio and the man who had made everybody laugh, and for a long time neither of them said anything more. Elijah had his right hand jammed in his coat pocket. His face was still crooked from the broken jaw. He had lost more weight. He looked, Ezra thought, dead already and only waiting to be told.

"I can't hear it anymore," Elijah said finally. His voice was wrecked. "The call. Ez. Every night of my life, even at the bar, even when I was laughing, there was something, way down, calling. I used to drink to not hear it. Then you gave it to me, and all this time it was the best thing I ever had. It was so loud. It was everything." He pressed his marked hand harder into his pocket. "I put my hand under that scanner and it stopped. It just stopped. Like a radio shut off. There's nothing there now, Ez. There's nothing there. I keep listening and there's nothing there."

Ezra's eyes were streaming. He let them run.

"Eli," he said.

"Don't tell me it's not too late." Elijah's voice broke all the way. "I read it too. I was in those rooms. I know what it says. I'm not here for that. I know what I did." He was crying now, openly and ugly, with nothing left to protect. "I just wanted to see you once. You were the best friend I ever had. You and Angela. She prayed for me for six years and I made jokes about her doomsday club. And you got down on that floor with me." He wiped his face with his unmarked hand. "I just wanted to say I'm sorry. And thank you. For all of it. It was the best thing that ever happened to me, and I threw it away for an orange and a warm room, and that's the whole of me, Ez, that's the whole sad joke of me, right there."

Ezra did not say it was not too late. He did not know whether it was. He was not the Judge of all the earth; he had learned that at his father's grave, years ago, kneeling in the cold. What God would do with a man like Elijah, he could not say, who had worshipped nothing, really, only feared being alone, and had reached out one frozen hand for a warm room, and could not now hear the call. He had decided, long ago, that he would leave the things he did not know with the One who did.

So he did not preach.

He crossed the ten feet of snow, and he put his arms around his oldest friend, and he held him, and he wept with him, in the dark, outside the barn, while the armed man at the door looked away. He held on until Elijah's shaking stopped, and then a while longer, so that the last thing Elijah Brooks would remember of the hidden church, whatever came, would be that it did not let go of him first.

"You listen to me," Ezra said into his ear, rough and low. "I don't know what He's going to do. That's His. But I know you're not alone tonight. Right now, this minute, you are not alone, and I am not ashamed of you, and I love you. And I'm going to pray for you every day I've got left, by name, the way Angela prayed for you. Every day. You hear me?"

Elijah could not answer.

Then he stepped back, out of Ezra's arms, into the dark, and he took his right hand out of his pocket and looked at it, and he laughed, one last time, the old crooked laugh, with no joy in it at all and a whole life of fear behind it.

"Tell the kids I said something funny," he said. "Make one up. They liked it when I—" He couldn't finish.

Then he turned and walked back down into the dark, toward the warm town, and Ezra stood in the snow outside the barn and watched him go, and did not follow, because there was nowhere left to follow him to, and when he could no longer see him he went inside and found the children.

"Uncle Eli says I'm to tell you the one about the two fish in a tank," he said. His voice shook. "Two fish in a tank. One turns to the other and says, 'Do you know how to drive this thing?'" He had to stop. Tears ran down into his beard.

The children laughed, because they were children, and because somebody who loved them had told them to.

\* \* \*

That night Ezra wrote in the back of Angela's notebook, under the page with his own name on it, in his square capitals, and it was the hardest thing he ever wrote.

*Elijah Brooks. Registered, February. Dutchess raid before. Broken man, not a wicked one. Afraid his whole life of being left out and alone, and that is what took him at the end. Lord, he is Yours to judge, not mine. I only know You see him. I leave him in Your hands. I cannot do anything else. — E.*

And in the right margin, where Walt would have put the verse, Ezra wrote two.

*1 Samuel 4:21. The glory is departed.*

And under it, smaller, because he could not help it, because he had been given the second chance his friend had thrown away, and could not stop hoping even against the plain words of the Book, a line from the story Jesus told:

*Luke 15:20. When he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran.*

He had no assurance it was true for Elijah. He wrote it anyway, and left it with God, and closed the notebook, and went to bed, and for the first time in all those years, there was no one in the next room making anybody laugh.

## Chapter 35: One Hour

> *For in one hour so great riches is come to nought. And every shipmaster, and all the company in ships, and sailors, and as many as trade by sea, stood afar off, and cried when they saw the smoke of her burning.* — Revelation 18:17–18

**Word study: *hour* — ὥρα** Greek *hōra* (Strong's G5610). An hour; a fixed, appointed time; the moment a thing has been waiting for. It is the word Jesus used all through John's gospel: *mine hour is not yet come*, and then, at the end, *the hour is come.* Babylon spent her whole reign sure her hour would never come. It came, and it took an hour.

*In the same hour came forth fingers of a man's hand, and wrote over against the candlestick upon the plaister of the wall of the king's palace… And this is the writing that was written, MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN… MENE; God hath numbered thy kingdom, and finished it… In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom… (Daniel 5:5, 25–31)*

\* \* \*

Every day at noon the face came up in the hayloft too, on Nina's laptop, through the back door, asking the world to kneel.

Most of them knelt. It cost nothing. It was a gesture.

The ones who did not kneel were noticed. Nina knew exactly how, because she had written the code. A face that did not lower at noon was flagged. A flag became a visit. A visit became a van.

"Turn it off," Michael said one noon. "You've got the door."

"Not yet," Nina said. "If I kill it now, they rebuild it in a week and they know the door was there. I get one shot." She looked at the face on the screen, asking the world to kneel. "I'll know when."

Ezra had read her to the barns for years, the one John saw riding the beast, arrayed in purple and scarlet, with a golden cup in her hand full of abominations. She was every blessing the Council had ever spoken over the peace, from its first session on the Mount of Olives to its last: the robes, the prayers to everyone and no one, the hand-holding in the kingdom's name by people who stood for nothing in particular and called it unity. She was the red strings knotted at ten thousand wrists, and every pulpit and parliament that had come together and not stood in the truth. And in the week after the image went up, the ten, who had needed her to bless them, found that they no longer did. *And the ten horns which thou sawest upon the beast, these shall hate the whore, and shall make her desolate and naked, and shall eat her flesh, and burn her with fire.* (Revelation 17:16) The Council for Universal Moral Law was dissolved by a single vote. The Olivet Crown burned that night. By Saturday the red-string circles were being turned out of their offices, their accounts closed, and the lists the kingdom had kept on them so carefully, for so long, were read down in the other direction. Rabbi Arcangeli was not seen again. *For God hath put in their hearts to fulfil his will, and to agree, and give their kingdom unto the beast, until the words of God shall be fulfilled.* (Revelation 17:17)

Nobody wept for her but the ones who had never stopped telling her the truth.

\* \* \*

The dragon's time was short, and he knew it, and in the months after the image went up his rage at the saints ran hotter than it ever had.

That was the part the Book had warned them of, and it came exactly as it was written. *Woe to the inhabiters of the earth and of the sea! for the devil is come down unto you, having great wrath, because he knoweth that he hath but a short time.* Vale had the whole world on its knees at noon, and it was not enough for him. It never would be. There was only one people in all the earth who had refused him from the beginning, who had never bowed to the image, never taken the mark, never wept when his prophets died, never cheered when his enemies fell. The hidden ones. The ones who had walked out of his cities between his feet. The ones whose voice came up out of the ground every night at nine o'clock and would not stop.

He came for them with everything he had left.

Not only with rifles. In a cold room beneath Fort Detrick, in a column Nina had once read through her back door, sat the remainder of what had been staged for the caves marked *Empty*: PALEHORSE, Lots 4 through 6, sealed and waiting for a window that would not open. Vale meant to loose it on the hidden the day he found them. He had not found them yet.

The raids in those last weeks were not like the raids before. Before, the Peacekeepers had come for food and bonuses, following tips, working lists. Now they came for blood, in numbers, in the fury of a world going under. Camps that had been hidden for years were found and burned. The front of the hill, the cave where strangers waited until they were known, the great hub of the supply lines, was betrayed at last, by a man who took the mark to save his family and told them where the door in the rock was. Not everyone made the deep door in time, and the ones who did not, Ezra did not let himself think about, except to pray for them by name, every day, on the list.

Michael told what happened under the hill once, in a truck with the engine off, and never again.

"They came at dawn," Michael said. "Sixty men, dogs, lamps. Through the door the traitor showed them. I'd known a month someone would. I gave that man his white stone myself. I wasn't angry. He had a girl of nine. I'd have thought about it too." He watched the windshield. "Three of mine had been bomb techs in the old service. Whole careers spent learning how things fail. For a month they taught the hill how to fail on purpose. In the dark, in the front passages the patrol would walk. Nothing a man would look twice at."

"We close the road, I told them. Not the men. Wait until they're standing in the dome with the sky over their heads, and the way they came is open behind them."

"I counted my people through the deep door and stood in it with the last of them. The first lamps came into the dome. A dog sat down in the middle of the floor and wouldn't go on. The captain walked to the left-hand wall and put his palm flat on the slab, the one that swings, and looked straight at it." He shook his head slowly. "And saw rock."

"I prayed what Elisha prayed," Michael said. "I'm not proud of it. I asked Him to smite them with blindness." *And he smote them with blindness according to the word of Elisha.* (2 Kings 6:18) "He did it gentle. They stood in my house and couldn't see it."

A voice behind him said, very quietly, "Now."

The hill came down behind his people. The sound went through the mountain like a door being shut in the house of God, and Michael, with a stone-white face, said the only verse that came to him. *And the LORD shut him in.* (Genesis 7:16)

The patrol stood in the dome among their lamps and cursed the dust. The way they had come stood open behind them, and they took it, shaken, with a dog that would not stop howling, and the captain wrote one word in his report. *Empty.*

Beyond the fall, the deep halls went on, and most of the people lived there still, in the warm dark, drinking water that did not fail. Michael had come out with the transmitter and with Ezra and a few more, because the voice needed a guard, and because somebody had to walk the long way round and tell the others the road behind them was gone. The deep halls had a second door, on the far side of the ring, that no patrol had ever found.

News of the others reached him in pieces, by runner and by radio, the way it always had. Leon had carried his granddaughter, born in a hidden room the winter after the sky opened, to a farm in Vermont, and she had learned to walk there. Patrice's little ones were thin but whole. Andre and Pruitt ran the northern routes between them now, and Andre had not touched a rifle since Christmas Eve. Mrs. Fairley had kept the dogwood and the stone behind it, and the Harmon girl still asked every week whether Walt had enough paper. Michael said the names of the two men lost at Havre de Grace at every supper, and no one asked him to stop. On New Jersey Avenue the wall of screens had gone dark in the hour Babylon fell, and Kessler, they said, sat in his doorway until the lights went out; of the thirty-one who had watched Trent walk out of that room, a few had come north since with their passes in their pockets, asking for the radio. And a runner from Brookland brought the oldest news last: Lionel Hart's door had been found unlocked and his house empty on the first morning, the viola in its case on the piano and the ram's horn gone from its wall.

Trent Walker was not with them. He had gone north the season before, on foot, with a copy of Nina's card sewn into his coat, from room to room, reading the Absalom papers and Kambria's Meridian filings aloud to anyone who would hear what the Chairman's son had done. Most of the rooms did not need it, he said, but it was true and it was written down, and one who had loaded a face into eleven hundred cameras could carry it. The last word Ezra had, he was in the Adirondacks, walking a company out of a town one day ahead of the vans, with a map in his head and a prayer he was still learning to say.

And through all of it, Ezra kept broadcasting.

Every broadcast was a beacon now, in a kingdom that had nothing left to do but hunt, and everyone in the room knew it. Michael moved the transmitter every night and posted Dorsey on the roof, and never once asked Ezra to stop. He only asked where they would set up next. Michael read the same Book Ezra did, and he knew the road a watchman walks, and he would not be the one to turn him around. Ezra would not stop, because the people in the dark needed it more in the last weeks than they ever had, and because he had been made a watchman, and a watchman does not come down off the wall because the enemy has finally noticed him. Every night at nine, wherever he was, he found a transmitter, and the low line of his son's song went out over the falling kingdom, and then his voice, reading the plans, all the way to the end of the plans now, to the bowls of wrath and the fall of Babylon and the marriage supper of the Lamb and the King on the white horse. He read them the end of the Book, in the end of the world, and he closed every night the way he always had.

*Grace be unto you, and peace.*

He would not have stopped if he could.

On one of the last nights he broadcast, Michael stood at his shoulder in the dark with the ledger open and chose the closing line himself. Ezra read the chapter as he always did, and when he came to the boxed line he slowed and read it twice, the psalm and then the verse with a breath between, as he had read every address since the night Isaac went down the wrong street. *From the end of the earth will I cry unto thee, when my heart is overwhelmed: lead me to the rock that is higher than I.* (Psalm 61:2) To anyone listening in the cities it was a psalm about weariness. To the ones who kept the blue notebook it was a column and a row, and a door in the mountains, and they were to go on foot, by night, to the people who would be waiting there. Michael wrote the hour in the ledger, and nothing else, and Ezra said the benediction.

\* \* \*

Michael sat on an upturned crate in the barn with his father's ledger open on his knee, and he did not write in it.

"Nineteen houses," he said. He kept his eyes on the ledger. "Eleven hundred names. Forty trucks. Every door numbered, every key by the Book." He turned a page and the page was blank. "I counted it all. Everything I counted is worth nothing, Ezra. He'll have it by morning."

"Counting kept them alive."

"Counting kept me from feeling it." He closed the ledger. "My father never lost a drum of water. And he never got to see a thing he built be needed." He shook his head. "I built a city under a city. And in one hour..."

"*In one hour,*" Ezra said.

Michael laughed, a low, wrecked sound. Then he stood up, crossed to the corner where Anton's old cassette deck sat on a feed bin, and thumbed it on, and put the mic in his hand like a man picking up a tool he had put down long ago.

He did not rap. He spoke over the hiss, low and even, so that the loft above the barn could hear.

*They counted bread. They counted breath.*
*I counted names on a wall.*
*A thousand doors, a hundred miles,*
*and Lord, I'd count them all.*
*But the Count is in Your hand,*
*and I was only the pen.*
*You numbered every hair of them,*
*and You numbered my men.*

Up in the loft, Anton's hands had gone still on the board. Months ago he had looped four bars of Jalen's cello off the broadcast under a drum pattern, and played it for no one but himself, late, with the volume low. On the floor beside the cassette deck sat a milk crate of Michael's old discs, the ones he had cut in his father's basement, and the boy was looking down at the crate and then at the man, and his face was the face of someone who has just seen a door in a wall.

"That's a good verse," Ezra said quietly.

"It's the only one I've got left."

\* \* \*

Then a runner came: the barn was known. In that last week they crossed the state line to a burned farmhouse above the Hudson. One night near the end, Ezra broke bread with the brethren.

There were forty of them, in the cellar of a burned farmhouse near the Hudson, the ones who had been with him longest and the ones who had come to him last: Michael, scarred and gray now, with the cross still outside his vest. Nina, who had come up from the coast and not gone back, because she had said she was done running from the thing she helped build and meant to stand with the people who had forgiven her for it. Dorsey. David Levin, the old Jewish neighbor from Kambria's street in Washington, who had stood at his grill the week before the sky opened and told Kambria that a law about faith gave him the creeps, and had found his Messiah at last in the back of a bakery van, reading Isaiah fifty-three by a flashlight propped on a flour sack. Kyle and Sarah, who had answered Ezra from a church basement in Brooklyn on the first night, and had a little girl now, born in a hidden room, who had never once in her life been outside in the daytime.

They had bread, that night. Real bread. Nina had traded the last of what she had for a sack of flour from a farmer who still had some and would not take the mark, and Ezra had baked it himself in the farmhouse oven, and the whole cellar smelled of it, warm, in the dark.

He broke it as the Lord broke it. He had done it a hundred times in a hundred dark rooms, but that night his hands were not quite steady.

"The Lord Jesus the same night in which he was betrayed took bread," Ezra said. "And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me."

He broke the loaf, and it went around the cellar, hand to hand, forty hands in the candlelight, and every one of them tore a piece and passed it on, and the little girl who had never been outside in the daytime tore her piece with small careful fingers and ate it, watching her mother to see how.

They were afraid, all of them. Ezra could see it on every face and did not pretend otherwise.

"I'm afraid too," he said, when the bread had gone all the way around. "I want to say that out loud, so nobody in this room thinks they're the only one, or that being afraid means something's wrong with their faith. I'm afraid. I've been afraid a long time. The morning they were taken, I slept through the trumpet." A few of them almost smiled. "The brave ones in the Book were afraid. David was afraid. Elijah ran into the wilderness and asked God to let him die. The Lord Himself, in the garden, sweat like it was blood and asked if the cup could pass. Being afraid isn't the sin. Bowing is the sin. You can be afraid and not bow. That's the whole of it. That's all He's ever asked of us."

He looked around at them, at the forty faces, at the cross on Michael's vest and the little girl in Sarah's lap.

"We missed the morning," he said. "Every one of us. We had the chance to go up with the ones we loved, without ever tasting any of this, and we missed it, because we didn't believe, or we didn't want to, or we were too busy, or too angry, or too afraid. I slept through it. I know what that is to carry." He waited until the room was his. "But listen to me. He died for us in the dark, before we ever loved Him back. While we were yet sinners, the Book says. He went first. He went to the cross first, before we deserved any of it, and He did it looking at us, as my boy looked at an empty seat and played anyway." His voice caught, and he waited, and went on. "So now we get to show Him. That's what this is. The ones who went up in the morning were spared this. We weren't. So we get to show Him here. At the appointed time, we get to look at Him and say: I love You too. I love You enough to go last. I love You enough to die, as You loved me enough to die first."

The candle burned. Far above them rolled the sound that was always in the sky now, a deep thunder that was not quite thunder.

"*Strengthen ye the weak hands,*" Ezra said quietly, "*and confirm the feeble knees.*" He had said it in the first dark room, the winter after the trumpet, and in a thousand since. "*Say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not: behold, your God will come.*"

"*Behold, your God will come,*" the room said back to him, forty voices, as they had learned to, and the little girl said it too, in her high small voice, the words she had known her whole short hidden life.

It was Dorsey who started it, of all of them. Dorsey, who had not smiled since the hill came down, sat on an overturned bucket with his big hands hanging between his knees, and said into the quiet, to nobody, "He's still good, though."

Nobody answered. Then Ezra said, "Yes, He is," and Dorsey looked up, startled, as if he had not known he'd spoken aloud.

"Say it again," Ezra said.

"He's still good."

"Again."

"He's still good." Dorsey's voice broke in the middle, and something let go in his face. "He's still good. Lord, You are still good."

Ezra found he was on his feet. He did not remember standing. "*Bless the LORD, O my soul: and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits.* (Psalm 103:1–2) Forget not. Not one. Let's count them, right now, out loud. I'll go first." His voice cracked, and he laughed at it. "Thank You for the bread."

"Thank You for the bread," the cellar said.

"The roof," Kyle called from the corner, looking up at the black rafters and the stars between them. "Such as it is."

"For the roof, such as it is!" And the cellar laughed, all forty of them, the first real laughter that room had held, low and helpless, hands over mouths so the sound would not carry, and failing.

They could not stop then. It went around the cellar as the bread had, hand to hand, and nobody could have said where one person's gladness left off and the next began. Sarah drew her daughter close. "Thank You for her heartbeat," she said. "I can feel it against my ribs right now."

Nina stood, wet-faced. "Thank You for forgiving me," she said. "I built the thing. I didn't earn this. You gave it to me anyway." Dorsey said *amen* so hard the candle leaned.

David Levin thanked Him for the Messiah he had waited for all his life and found at last in the back of a bakery van, and the cellar howled. "Of all the places," David said, spreading his hands, delighted. "The God of Abraham, and He sends me to a bakery van. He has a sense of humor, this God, I tell you."

Michael let a mile go by, and then said quietly, "For every man who got off that mountain alive. And for the ones who didn't, that You have them."

Nobody laughed at that. Everybody said amen.

And then the little girl, who had never been outside in the daytime, who knew the world only as a hidden room and her mother's lap, stood up on her mother's knees and said in her high small voice, "Thank You for everybody."

The whole cellar broke.

David Levin began to sing. He sang it in Hebrew, softly at first, the old tune to the old words, *Bar'chi nafshi et Adonai*, bless the LORD, O my soul, as his fathers had sung it for three thousand years. The Gentiles caught the tune before they knew the words, and then the words. Dorsey was clapping softly on his knees, a muffled heartbeat. Kyle swayed. Nina had Michael by the arm, and Michael, scarred and gray Michael, was laughing out loud with his head thrown back like a young man.

Ezra stood in the middle of it and had not known he could feel this. Not here. Not at the end. He told them about Paul and Silas, because he could not help it: the inner prison at Philippi, their backs laid open with rods, their feet fast in the stocks. "*And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them.* (Acts 16:25) Nobody told the prisoners to listen. They listened because it was the last thing in that prison anyone expected to hear. So let them hear us. *The joy of the LORD is your strength.* (Nehemiah 8:10) Not our joy. His. And He has plenty to spare tonight."

They sang it through three times. In the morning every one of them knew the boots would come down the stairs. It was the brightest room Ezra had ever stood in.

When the song finally burned down, he asked them to sit, and they sat, flushed and breathing hard, some of them still laughing under their breath. The candle was low. Ezra stood with his hands hanging empty at his sides, and looked at them, and found for a moment that he could not begin.

"I want to tell you something," he said. "And then I want to sing the rest of my life."

They waited.

"I came into all of this carrying a pack. You couldn't see it. Most days I couldn't see it myself. *Let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us.* (Hebrews 12:1) Every weight. I read that verse for years the way a man reads a speed limit." He took a breath. "I was carrying stones. A little boy holding out his hand at a bus station, and a father who patted his head and turned around. A wife who reached for me every night for twelve years, and a hand I did not always take. A trumpet I slept through. A boy who played to an empty chair, and a little girl's bed with the covers thrown back. I carried every one of them so long I thought they were part of my body. I thought they were what held me up."

The candle moved in some draft none of them could feel.

"They were pulling me under. And tonight, standing here laughing like a fool in a cellar with all of you, I put my hand in my pocket to check, the way you do, and they were gone." His voice finally broke, all the way. "Every one. I went looking for that bus station, and I could not find it. He took it. He took all of it at the cross, before I was ever born, and I have been walking around for years carrying it for Him as if I'd been paid to." He was laughing and crying at once. "Jesus said it. *If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.* (John 8:36) Free indeed. Not brave. You know I'm not brave. Free."

He did not wipe his face. He lifted both his hands, open, palms up, the way a woman he loved had held hers out across a table for twelve years, and held them there in the candlelight where all forty of them could see that they were empty.

"I am going to walk out of here in the morning with nothing in my hands," Ezra said. "Wherever they take me. I have nothing left to carry. And I have never in my life been this light."

Nobody spoke. Then Michael stood, and then Nina, and then all of them, until the whole cellar was on its feet with their hands lifted and open in the light of one low candle, and the little girl on her mother's shoulder lifted both of hers too, not knowing why, with her fingers spread, laughing.

Then, when they could, they sang the last song of the night, low, as they always sang, so the sound would not carry: the forty-sixth psalm, all eleven verses, the one Ezra's mother used to hum over the dishes. They sang it in the cellar of a burned farmhouse, forty hungry people around a candle and a torn loaf, while Vale's kingdom fell to pieces over their heads, and when they came to the last verse, Ezra led it, and his voice did not shake at all.

*The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our refuge. Selah.*

Nina was the one who found it.

She had not slept. When the singing ended and the others lay down along the cellar walls in their coats, she sat on an upturned crate at the foot of the stairs with the old laptop on her knees, wired to the last good battery, and read the logs the way she had read them every night since the sky opened. Near four she stopped scrolling. She read the same lines again. Then she closed the lid very gently, went and knelt beside Michael, and said it into his ear.

"It was never the notebooks."

Michael was awake. He was always awake. "Say it plain."

"They never broke the books. They never needed to." Her voice was flat and low. "Every night the carrier goes up from a new place for eight minutes, and every night the nearest receiver logs a signal and a clock. They stopped trying to read us. They drew a circle around each night and waited. Years of circles, Michael. Every night since we came here, every one of them crosses here."

Ezra heard it from where he sat against the wall, with the cold of the stone coming through his coat. He did not ask her to say it again.

"I knew the radio would be how they found us," he said.

Nina turned. "You never told me."

"I told Him."

Then he got up off the floor and crossed the cellar to her, and sat down on the crate beside hers, and said, very low, "Come with me a minute."

He took her to the back of the cellar, past the people lying along the walls in their coats, to the shelves where the farmhouse jars had stood. He put his hand flat on the boards beside the shelves and pushed, and a section of the wall swung in on a hinge she had never seen, onto a space the size of a closet. There was a crate in it, and a blanket, and a jug of water.

"I built it Tuesday," he said. "Nobody knows but Michael."

She understood before he said anything else, and she shook her head.

"No," she said. "Ezra. I told them I was done running. I'm standing with you."

"Standing with us is staying." He kept his voice down. "They'll count heads in the morning, and they won't count you. Stay. Do what you can, with what you've got, for whoever's left. You'll know what that is better than I will."

She stood with her hand on the hinge and did not say anything for a long time.

He went back to the shelf and took Kambria's lamp down in its towel and put it in her hands.

"Keep it lit," he said.

The cellar door overhead gave one soft knock, then two. Kyle came down the stairs with his hand flat on the wall and his boots in his other hand, and he did not whisper, because there was no longer anyone to hide the sound from. "Grace and peace," he said, and did not wait for the answer. "Lights on the river road. Both ends. No headlamps, just the running lamps, and a helicopter somewhere high up with its own lights out. I counted nineteen trucks before I quit counting."

Around the cellar people were sitting up. A child coughed and was hushed. Somebody found a shoe in the dark.

Michael stood. "The tunnel comes out in the orchard," he said. "We have six minutes before the trees are lit. Anyone who can run, runs now, in twos, and no one in this room will think less of you for it. I mean that." He said it to the room, not to Ezra.

Nobody moved.

Sarah drew her daughter back against her chest and put her chin on the top of the child's head. "I have run for years," she said. "I'd like to see the end of it with my eyes open."

David Levin laid his hand on the nearest wall as if it were a door post. Dorsey did not stand, and did not speak, and did not take his eyes off Ezra.

Ezra thought of a man standing before a governor and saying nothing at all. *He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth.* (Isaiah 53:7) He had read that verse into a microphone a hundred times, to the barns, as a promise about Someone else.

"If I go out the back," he said, "the carrier goes with me, and they follow it to whoever is next. Let it stop in this cellar. Let it stop here."

Michael had not moved either. He stood at the mouth of the tunnel with the rifle on its sling and his eyes on Ezra, and Ezra could see that he meant to stand there until the boots came down.

Ezra crossed the cellar to him. "Not you."

"Don't."

"There's a hill full of people behind that fall. Andre and Pruitt are running the north with nobody over them. Seven stations on that map, and one man alive who knows what all the numbers mean." He kept his voice under the sound of the room waking. "Tomorrow night they'll be sitting in the dark with the radio off, waiting to hear who's coming. It has to be you."

"I'm not leaving you in a hole."

"You're not leaving me. You're going to them." Ezra laid his palm flat on the cross outside Michael's vest. "When David wanted to march out with his men against Absalom, the people wouldn't let him go. *…but now thou art worth ten thousand of us: therefore now it is better that thou succour us out of the city.*" (2 Samuel 18:3)

Michael's jaw worked under the beard. He looked past Ezra at the room, at Sarah with her chin on her daughter's head, at Dorsey on the floor, at the shelves where a wall swung in that only the two of them knew about. Then he unslung the rifle and stood it against the stone by the tunnel mouth, and took his hand off it.

"*He that leadeth into captivity shall go into captivity,*" he said, low, to the Book he had lived by. "*He that killeth with the sword must be killed with the sword. Here is the patience and the faith of the saints.*" (Revelation 13:10)

From the pocket where he had carried it all this time, he took out a smooth white stone and closed his fist around it.

"Grace and peace, brother."

"And unto you," Ezra said.

Michael bent into the tunnel and was gone. Ezra stood at its mouth a moment longer and listened, and heard nothing, which was what Michael had taught him to listen for.

Outside, a truck door shut, very carefully.

"*As it is written,*" Ezra said, quietly enough that the people at the back leaned forward to hear it, "*For thy sake we are killed all the day long; we are accounted as sheep for the slaughter.*" (Romans 8:36)

It was Dorsey who answered, in a voice that came up from the floor of him. "*Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.*" (Romans 8:37)

Someone took Ezra's hand, and he did not see whose. The candle had burned down to a thumb of wax. Behind the shelves, behind a wall nobody else in the room knew was there, Kambria's lamp was still burning low. Thirty-eight people stood up in the dark of a burned farmhouse cellar in their coats and their stocking feet, and nobody reached for the tunnel, and nobody wept aloud. They stood with their hands joined and listened to the gravel above them take the weight of boots.

They came for them at dawn.

\* \* \*

They did not fight.

Dorsey could have. He was Michael's man to the bone, and the rifle stood against the wall by the tunnel mouth where Michael had left it, and for a moment, in the gray light, with the boots coming down the farmhouse stairs, Ezra saw him look at it.

Then Dorsey looked at Ezra, and Ezra shook his head, once.

Dorsey stepped away from the wall and put his hands where the Peacekeepers could see them, and stood beside Ezra, and Ezra gripped his shoulder. They waited together as the soldiers came down into the room with their lights and their rifles and found thirty-eight people standing around a guttered candle and a loaf of bread, singing, with their hands open and empty and raised, and not one of them afraid enough to bow. Nobody looked at the tunnel. The soldiers never found it.

They took them all. Ezra, and Dorsey, and David Levin, and Kyle and Sarah and their little girl who had never been outside in the daytime, every one of the thirty-eight, up out of the cellar into the gray dawn of the last days, into the trucks.

And when the lead officer, a young man with a tired hard face, demanded to know which one of them was the one called Ezra, the voice from the ground, the one Vale himself had put at the very top of the list, Ezra did not make them guess.

"I am," he said. "It's just Ezra. I come in peace."

Before they put him in the first truck, he asked the young officer for one minute on the cellar stairs, and the officer, who could not have said why, gave it to him. Ezra took Kambria's lamp down from the shelf, carried it up into the gray light, and set it in the kitchen window of the farmhouse where anyone coming after could see it. Then he held out his wrists. As the truck pulled away, through the slats, he could see the farmhouse behind them, and the small gold light in its window, and the sky over it, and in the sky, high in the east, where the sun was coming up, the clouds had begun to move as he had never seen clouds move, and he did not yet know what it meant, and he was not afraid.

## Chapter 36: The Witness of Jesus

> *…and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.* — Revelation 20:4

**Word study: *witness* — μάρτυς** Greek *martys* (Strong's G3144). One who testifies to what he has seen; a witness in a court. It is the word that became *martyr*, because in the days of the early church so many who witnessed to Christ were killed for it that the word for testifying and the word for dying became the same word. To bear witness and to lay down your life came to mean one thing.

*If it be so, our God whom we serve is able to deliver us from the burning fiery furnace, and he will deliver us out of thine hand, O king. But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up. Then was Nebuchadnezzar full of fury… therefore he spake, and commanded that they should heat the furnace one seven times more than it was wont to be heated… Did not we cast three men bound into the midst of the fire?… Lo, I see four men loose, walking in the midst of the fire, and they have no hurt; and the form of the fourth is like the Son of God. (Daniel 3:17–19, 24–25)*

\* \* \*

They took them south by train, down the river to New York, chained to the seats of an old commuter car with its windows painted over except for a strip along the top.

Through the strip Ezra watched the world go by. At noon the train stood still at a station on the river, and on the platform, under a gold-framed shrine with a dead man's face in its light, a hundred people went down on their knees all at once, briefcases and strollers and all, while a soldier walked the length of the platform and looked at every bowed head. One man did not kneel. The soldier stopped in front of him. The train moved on before Ezra could see the rest.

Ezra prayed, the whole way, for all of them. For the ones in the car with him, by name. For the man on the platform. For the soldiers. For Trent, on whatever road he was walking. For Elijah, somewhere, if he was still alive. He only loved him still, and went on asking. For the little girl in Sarah's lap, who had never been outside in the daytime and was outside now, with her face turned up to the strip of gray sky at the top of the painted window, because it was the first sky she had ever seen.

He was not afraid. He kept waiting to be afraid, and it did not come. He had been afraid for years, and for most of his life before that, and now, at the end, chained in a train car on the way to his own death, the fear had simply lifted off him and gone, and in its place was a calm he had no word for except Paul's, the peace that passeth all understanding, and he held onto it with both hands and did not ask where it had come from, because he knew.

Somewhere past the Bronx he thought about how Jesus had never once let them be surprised. *Behold, I have foretold you all things,* He had said on the Mount of Olives (Mark 13:23), and at the very end of the Book, *I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.* (Revelation 22:13) He had told them the end from the beginning. The seals in their order. The witnesses and their days. The image and its hour. The accuser had come down in great wrath, *because he knoweth that he hath but a short time* (Revelation 12:12), and the kings had their one hour with the beast, and Ezra knew how the hour ended, because John had already been shown it end.

They brought them up out of the station at dawn and marched them east along Forty-Second Street to First Avenue, in the shadow of the Organization's tower.

On the plaza at its foot, where the flags used to stand, was a ring of black stone set in the pavement, and a lens in the middle of it the width of a truck, and above it, in a column of gray light three stories high, the head of a dead man, looking out over First Avenue at what was about to happen, and smiling. Across the avenue, the stone stairs of Tudor City went up into the morning.

There was a block at the foot of the light. A low block of gray stone, and a soldier beside it with a sword.

And there was a crowd, held back along rope lines, because Vale had wanted a crowd, and cameras, because Vale had wanted the world to see: the voice from the ground, the man whose radio had told the truth every night, and all his people with him, killed under the face the world had just begun to bow to.

He lifted his eyes to the dead man's smiling face in the light, and the old verse stood up in his mind whole. *Was, and is not, and yet is.* The whole world had wondered at it. Ezra did not.

He knew how it ended. He had read it to the barns a hundred times and never once read it like this, with a sword at the foot of the light and his hands chained in front of him. The whole proud, bright city around him, and every city like it, every market and tower and screen that had ever asked the world to bow, would come down in a single hour. An angel would cry it with a strong voice, and John had written it down so that a man in chains on First Avenue would know it before he knelt.

*Babylon the great is fallen, is fallen.* (Revelation 18:2) *Alas, alas, that great city Babylon, that mighty city! for in one hour is thy judgment come.* (Revelation 18:10)

Not yet. But it would. The One who had told him the end from the beginning had never been wrong once.

\* \* \*

Alexander Vale was waiting for him at the foot of the image.

He had come down from the tower himself, in person, to watch the carpenter die. Ezra had never seen him in the flesh. He was smaller than Ezra had imagined, narrow and pale, in a flawless black suit, with flat dark eyes, and he stood beneath the floating face of his dead father's image, small and composed, while across the city people knelt at noon to the same face, and he looked at Ezra with something that was almost curiosity.

"You're the carpenter," Vale said.

"I'm the carpenter."

"All this time." Vale studied him. "Do you know, I could have taken you at any time? Any night. I let you run, because you were gathering them for me, and then, when you had gathered them, I let you keep talking, because a voice in the dark is useful to a man building a kingdom. It gives people something to be against." He tilted his head. "You built my walls for me, Ezra, the same as she did. Every frightened family that heard you and did not come over to us, you kept them in their holes, where I could find them when I was ready. You were the most useful enemy I ever had. The carrier gave me the night, and the nights since you came gave me the cellar. A man from your hill, who took the Seal to keep his daughter, gave me the door."

"Maybe," Ezra said. "Or maybe you kept me alive all this time because God wasn't done with me. You don't know which it was. Neither do I. That's His to know, not ours."

"There is one thing in all this time I never learned," Vale said. The warmth had gone out of his voice and left only the hunger. "I have your cellars. I have your attics, your false walls, your radio rooms. I have a box of white stones I cannot read, and a mountain in Pennsylvania that fell on nothing, and a hundred caves that held cans and Bibles. Most of your people go somewhere, Ezra, and I have never once found where." He leaned a little closer. "Tell me, and every one of the others walks home tonight."

"You would not keep that," Ezra said.

"Perhaps not."

"And I wouldn't tell you if you would." Ezra did not raise his voice. "I couldn't draw it for you if I tried, Alexander. You'd walk past the door in daylight." *Thou shalt hide them in the secret of thy presence from the pride of man.* (Psalm 31:20)

"A verse," Vale said.

"A promise."

"I told Miss Cole I knew your name," Vale said, "and your son's name, and the name of the song. Ezra Patterson. Jalen. 'Tears of a Father.' I had the file open the first week, and I let you play it over my kingdom every night, all those years. It was the one part of you I never learned to use." He looked up at the image. "A boy who plays for a father who will not come. I understood that song better than you think."

"It was my son's song for me," Ezra said. "But it was never mine. The tears in it are His."
