A flicker crossed the dark eyes.

"There is something else I kept," Vale said. He said it softly, and the softness was wrong, like a man opening a drawer he had promised never to open. "A recording. The morning of the twenty-sixth. A cell in a federal building. A woman in chains." His eyes did not leave Ezra's face. "The chains locked around nothing. Seven of eleven cells did the same. I have never been able to explain it. I have men who cannot sleep over it, and one woman who tried to take it to the grave." He looked at the block. "Tell me what happened to her."

"She was caught up," Ezra said.

"Where?"

"To meet the Lord in the air." Ezra spoke gently. "*For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout…*" (1 Thessalonians 4:16)

For one second Vale's face did what Ezra had never seen it do. It did nothing at all. Then the old smile came back and closed over it, and he said, "I do not believe in your God."

"I know," Ezra said. "He believes in you."

"Your Jesus," Vale said. The word came out of him stiffly. He had never had a use for it. "Tell me about your Jesus. You spent all those years on the radio telling the world about Him. Here He is, then. Here is the hour He warned you about, and where is He? Your kingdom is in holes in the ground. Your people are in chains. Your old men starved and your friends broke and your scribe died in a chair. And mine—" He lifted one hand, slightly, toward the image above him, toward the crowd, toward the cameras. "Mine has all the authority on the earth."

"My Jesus has authority over all things," Ezra said.

"Your Jesus has all the authority. Is that right." Vale smiled, and the smile was not kind. "Then tell me, carpenter, before you kneel. What can your Jesus do with all His authority, against the authority that I have been given, for this hour?"

Ezra looked at him. Behind him, across the plaza, the believers were being brought forward two by two between the soldiers, and someone among them had begun to sing the ninety-first psalm, and the sound of it came across the plaza thin and steady under the shouting of the crowd.

"You said it yourself," Ezra said. "For this hour. You were given it. You didn't take it, Alexander. It was handed to you, for one hour, and the hour has an end. You know it does. That's why you came down here yourself today, instead of watching it on a screen. Because you know it ends, and you wanted to stand in front of one man who isn't afraid of you, and find out why." He held the dark eyes. "My Lord Jesus said it to a man a lot like you, a long time ago, a man who thought he had the power of life and death. He said, *Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above.* The authority you're so proud of was handed to you by the One you're mocking. For an hour. To do exactly this. And He will take it back before the sun goes down. He will remove you from your place, and the power will go with it."

Vale did not answer. For just a moment, standing beneath his dead father's smiling face, the composure flickered, and his eyes went up, once, to the face in the glass.

Then Vale stepped back, and gestured to the soldiers, and his face was smooth again.

From the line behind them, chained at the wrist, Dorsey spoke for the first time since the cellar, clear and level. "Protocol Absalom, Alexander. It is sewn into the coats of men in every room north of here, and it has your name on it." The nearest soldier glanced at his officer, and the officer looked at the ground.

"Kneel him down," Vale said, a little too loud.

\* \* \*

Ezra walked first.

He had told them he would, two nights before, over the last of the bread. Behind him the others came two by two across the plaza, between the soldiers, toward the light. Halfway there, Kyle stumbled beside Ezra. Sarah had his other hand, with their little girl walking between them, her fist in her mother's skirt and her eyes on the sky, but his legs had started to shake so badly he could not keep them under him.

Ezra took his arm and held him up. "Strengthen ye the weak hands," he said quietly, "and confirm the feeble knees." It was what they said to each other in the hidden rooms, every night, before the lamps went out.

Kyle said the rest of it with him, through his teeth. "Be strong, fear not." He kept walking.

Not one of them bowed. When the soldiers ordered them down in front of the image, they stood. They knelt only at the block, and only to the King.

They made him kneel on the stone.

It was cold through the knees of his jeans. Behind him, someone among the believers was still singing the ninety-first psalm, thin and steady. The crowd along the rope line was shouting, and the cameras were turned on him, but all of it was far off now. Past the crowd the city was coming apart. Black smoke rolled up from beyond the museums, and from somewhere to the north came the flat crack of gunfire, steady, with no one answering it. A building on the far side of the Mall was burning with no one fighting the fire. The rope line had been staked in a hurry and was holding only because the soldiers were holding it, and even they glanced over their shoulders, sentries who knew no relief was coming. Babylon no longer fell in the distance. It was coming down around the very platform Vale had built to show the world his strength.

He looked up once, past the guards, into the crowd.

There was a little girl near the rope. She could not have been more than three. She held a bunch of daisies against her chest, the cheap kind from a grocery store bucket, and she was smiling. Not at the soldiers. At him. She had Mia's face: the round cheeks, the gap where a front tooth had come out, the smile that used her whole face.

It was not Mia. He knew it was not Mia. His Mia, his own daughter, taken up that first morning while he slept, was with her mother, and with the Lord. But he could not look away from her, and he was not afraid.

Farther back, a man stood alone at the rope with his jaw set crooked and his right hand shut deep in his coat pocket. He was not watching the block. He was watching Ezra.

He saw Mia in Row C, standing on her chair with daisies in her fist, shouting her brother's name.

He saw his father. Not the deacons' table, and not the bottle. His father at the bus station, turning around, the father Ezra had wanted when he was eight years old. Ezra lifted his hand to him as he had at eight, and the word came out of him as it had then. "Daddy."

He saw Angela at the dinner table with the evening light on her, laughing at something he had said, holding her hand out to him across the table. He reached for her.

"But if not," he said. He said it out loud, so they would all hear it. It was what Kambria had written in the notebook, from the three men before the furnace, the words she had underlined twice: *…our God whom we serve is able to deliver us… But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods…* He had read it a hundred times by candlelight, and now it was his own.

Then he lifted his hand one last time, open. He had lifted it like that once before, at the dinner table, the night he was forgiven.

"Jesus," he said.

And Jesus heard him.

He did not feel the sword.

A hand took his. It was warm and strong, and there was a scar in the palm of it, and it held on.

The cold was gone. The shouting was gone. There was light all around him, and it was gold, the same gold that had flared over the city the morning they were taken.

He was standing. There was grass under his bare feet, wet and cool, and there was no fear left in him anywhere.

To be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord. Kambria had written that in the notebook, with a star in the margin. He had read it by candlelight and never known it would be this fast. One moment on his knees on the stone. The next, here.

He looked down at his hands. They were clean.

On the air, faint and warm, came a smell he had not known since his mother's kitchen: flour and butter, and a pan coming out of the oven on a Sunday morning.

Then Ezra wept. He had not cried like this since the night on the studio floor with his son. There was no shame in it at all, because the hand that was holding his reached up and wiped his tears away.

\* \* \*

*And I beheld when he had opened the sixth seal, and, lo, there was a great earthquake; and the sun became black as sackcloth of hair, and the moon became as blood; And the stars of heaven fell unto the earth, even as a fig tree casteth her untimely figs, when she is shaken of a mighty wind.* (Revelation 6:12–13)

## Scripture in the Story

### Read Alongside the Bible

This novel is written and intended to be read alongside its study guide and the Holy Bible. The goal is to use the narrative and help lead many to the true and living Word of God, which He has shared with us through the testimony and faith of His servants and prophets of old.

Take a journey from Genesis to Revelation in a deeply personal and exciting way. The Lord is at the door knocking. He seeks a personal, genuine, honest, and truly everlasting relationship with you. Will you let Him in to dine?

A companion for readers who want to go back and study. The story itself never stops for a citation; every verse spoken, read, sung, remembered or echoed in a scene is listed here instead, chapter by chapter, in the order it appears.
